title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Reuse the workflow
text:
Reuse the workflow



The analysis workflow moves from finding and checking data to analysing, explaining, and reproducing.


Today adds no new statistical method.

Keep the final day as protected practice and catch-up. Students need reliable file handling and report rendering more than another model. Use their saved projects and reference sheets, not an assumption of memorised commands.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Begin where you need practice
text:
Begin where you need practice



Practice stations branch into files, R recovery, interpretation, and report reproduction.


Use references and explain the action you chose.

Students may start at different stations. Everyone should practise file recovery, R recovery, and interpretation. Remote access is another skill when the actual service is available, not a reason to delay local practice indefinitely.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Repair meaning as well as spelling
text:
Repair meaning as well as spelling
This is intentionally broken code:
seedling <- read_csv("seedlings.csv")
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm + initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$Growth_mm)
Find the path, name, case, and calculation problems.

Correct path is data/seedlings.csv from the project root. Use a consistent seedlings object and growth_mm column, load readr/dplyr, and subtract initial from final length. P01 grew 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: A mean does not describe every observation
text:
A mean does not describe every observation



Two toy groups have equal means but different SDs and individual spreads.


Keep centre, individual spread, and uncertainty in an estimate distinct.

The groups have means 14 mm, SDs 1 and 6 mm. A larger SD need not mean worse technique; biological differences also cause spread. Neither SD is automatically a confidence interval or a range containing every observation.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Count the independent units
text:
Count the independent units



Flasks and synthesis runs supply independent treatment units; fronds or repeated weighings do not.


A large number of readings cannot repair a lack of independent replication.

Transfer to future practicals: ask what was independently sampled or assigned to treatment. Cells, time points, or repeat balance readings may be related. Determine sample size from independent units and available measurements.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Interpret an uncertain result carefully
text:
Interpret an uncertain result carefully
A treatment-minus-control estimate is 3 mm, with a 95% interval from −2 to 8 mm.
Does this establish no effect?
No: it includes zero and effects in both directions. State the uncertainty.

Pause before showing the answer. This is a supplied interpretation exercise, not a calculation from the course dataset. Avoid equating absence of a small p-value with proof of equality. No additional test is needed.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Your next-lab questions
text:
Your next-lab questions

What does one row represent, and what was independently assigned?
What are the units and the meaning of blank cells?
Which figure answers the question without hiding observations?
Where are the source, raw data, output, and backup?


Invite students to write a question they would ask a later practical teacher. The workflow replaces manual spreadsheet calculations, but still needs subject context and a valid experimental design. Asking these questions is competence.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Evidence of a skill is an action you can repeat
text:
Evidence of a skill is an action you can repeat
Locate the raw input, source, derived table, figure, HTML, and backup.
Explain the role of each without relying on recent files or session memory.

The portfolio is not judged by its number of files. Ask students to demonstrate one reproducible path from question to result. Keep the day as consolidation: no new package, model, or examination format is introduced. The references are part of competent practice rather than forbidden assistance.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: A high recorded value is a question to investigate
text:
A high recorded value is a question to investigate



Reference culture A11 is the largest algae observation and is highlighted without removing it.


No source evidence confirms that A11 is erroneous.

The value is 41.7 mg. A high point can affect a small-sample summary, but that observation alone does not justify exclusion. The source notes identify A19 as spilled; they do not identify A11 as a transcription error. Distinguish evidence for a repair from a preference for a simpler-looking plot.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Name the primary and diagnostic datasets separately
text:
Name the primary and diagnostic datasets separately
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
algae <- read_csv("data/algae.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
algae_without_a11 <- filter(algae, culture_id != "A11")
The primary result uses all available measurements.

The new object is a sensitivity demonstration, not a replacement raw file. Recompute counts for each version and preserve A19 as missing. The task examines how one record changes a descriptive summary; evidence for exclusion must come from the study records.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: The diagnostic changes the answer, not the evidence for exclusion
text:
The diagnostic changes the answer, not the evidence for exclusion



Omitting A11 increases the observed mean difference, but the result is explicitly diagnostic.


Primary difference ≈ 5.72 mg; diagnostic difference ≈ 6.95 mg.

The supplement mean stays 33.91818 mg. The reference mean falls from 28.20 mg to 26.97273 mg, so the observed difference increases to 6.94545 mg. There is no confirmation that the omitted value is wrong. The primary analysis remains the main report; a sensitivity result must carry its changed count and rationale.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Different problems require different explanations
text:
Different problems require different explanations



A19 has an unavailable measurement after a spill; A11 has a high recorded value.


Missing is not zero. Unusual is not automatically erroneous.

Ask students to explain each issue without giving both the same label of bad data. A19 reduces available n. A11 remains a recorded observation unless independent source evidence supports a correction. Model assumptions are a third issue: they do not disappear merely because the file is tidy.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: An uncertain estimate does not establish equality
text:
An uncertain estimate does not establish equality



A supplied difference estimate of 3 mm has a 95 percent interval from minus 2 to 8 mm spanning zero.


State the uncertainty rather than turn it into “no effect”.

This is the same interpretation case already in the practical. The picture supports a discussion of compatible differences in both directions. It is not a new computation from algae. It does not mean that 95 percent of plants lie inside the interval or that the null hypothesis has 95 percent probability.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Match the output to the question
text:
Match the output to the question

What values were recorded? Inspect and describe.
How variable are observations? Show points and SD.
How uncertain is a guided mean comparison? Use the taught interval/test.
What concentration matches a signal? Use the supported calibration.


Students are not learning a menu of tests. These are familiar workflow questions that should lead to an interpretable output. A calculated dilution formula is not empirical evidence needing regression; an observational line is not proof of an intervention’s effect.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: A handover should survive a change of reader
text:
A handover should survive a change of reader



A recipient follows the source and inputs into a tested project rather than relying on the author’s memory.


Give directions another person can follow, then test them.

Test the handover instructions in a freshly extracted folder: locate input, render source, and identify a limitation. Clearly label revisions, including separate Windows and Ubuntu copies.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Choose the next rehearsal from evidence
text:
Choose the next rehearsal from evidence
Write three reliable actions, two weak steps, and a concrete next practice task.
Keep unfinished remote skills explicitly pending.

Ask for checkable actions such as “I can render after restarting”, rather than a broad claim such as “I understand R”. Use the identified weak step for further practice.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Exercises: leave with work you can find again
text:
Exercises: leave with work you can find again
Open exercises · Quiz.

Locate your project without a recent-files menu.
Render your chosen report from a fresh session.
Save reports/next-lab.txt as your reusable workflow.
Identify the supported backup and any pending remote-access skill.
Keep a labelled sensitivity check, handover, and readiness review.


Use the consolidation tasks for further practice. The organic alternative stays descriptive; higher yield alone does not demonstrate higher purity.

title: From a question to a report
section: One question, one report
text:
One question, one report



Choose either duckweed biomass or the supplied organic-product-yield study.


Complete one selected study; both use the workflow already practised.

The default duckweed exercise includes a guided Welch comparison. The organic alternative is descriptive and does not require a new test or chemistry knowledge. Week 4’s statistical work remains part of the course in either pathway.

title: From a question to a report
section: Decide what is independent
text:
Decide what is independent



Separate flasks or synthesis runs supply independent units; internal readings do not.


The number of rows must be interpreted through the experimental design.

Twenty duckweed flasks were independently allocated nutrients or control. The organic table has twelve independent runs allocated a collection protocol. Many fronds in a flask or repeated weighings of one run do not add independently treated units. Students should state this before calculation.

title: From a question to a report
section: A missing measurement is not zero
text:
A missing measurement is not zero



Twenty flasks were started, but F17 spilled before weighing, leaving 19 available measurements.


Retain the raw record. State 10 control + 9 nutrient available measurements.

The supplied source record explains F17. We do not know its biomass. A zero would invent a very small biomass and change the comparison. Keep counts of started units and available outcomes distinct.

title: From a question to a report
section: Import and check before analysing
text:
Import and check before analysing
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
duckweed <- read_csv("data/duckweed.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(duckweed)
available <- duckweed |> filter(!is.na(biomass_mg))
Check IDs, labels, types, units, missing values, and plausible ranges.

Run from the extracted course project root. All report prerequisites must be in its code. The available object makes the exclusion explicit without overwriting the raw table. No other value is confirmed as an error.

title: From a question to a report
section: Show observations before a test
text:
Show observations before a test



Individual available duckweed biomass measurements and group means.


Each dot is one flask; diamonds are means. Explain overlap and variation.

This plot uses the actual teaching CSV. It excludes only the unavailable F17 y-value and the caption in the report should say so. A lower control value does not automatically justify exclusion. Group means are not new observations.

title: From a question to a report
section: State the comparison direction
text:
State the comparison direction
nutrient <- available |> filter(treatment == "nutrient")
control <- available |> filter(treatment == "control")
comparison <- t.test(nutrient$biomass_mg, control$biomass_mg)
Nutrient minus control: about 7.35 mg, 95% CI 2.27 to 12.44 mg.
Report sample sizes and assumptions, not only the p-value.

The supplied data give Welch p about 0.00723. The interval concerns the mean difference, not 95% of flasks. The inference remains conditional on independence, the distributional assumptions, and the missing-outcome limitation. Students need not derive the test or choose an alternative method catalogue.

title: From a question to a report
section: Organic alternative: the maximum is given
text:
Organic alternative: the maximum is given



Y01 yielded 0.62 grams from a supplied maximum of 1.00 gram, giving 62 percent.


Yield (%) = 100 × collected mass (g) / supplied maximum mass (g).

Define theoretical mass as the supplied maximum and isolated mass as collected dry product. Purity is assumed solely for this simplified calculation, not measured. Other runs start at different scales, making raw masses incomparable as yield without normalisation.

title: From a question to a report
section: Compare percentages across independent runs
text:
Compare percentages across independent runs



Individual product yields in standard and modified protocols with group means.


Describe means, SD, and overlap. No new test is required for this alternative.

Six runs per group, no missing outcomes. Means 68.67% and 77%; SDs 4.32 and 3.74 percentage points. The observed mean difference is 8.33 percentage points, not an 8.33% relative increase. Higher yield alone does not establish purity or general superiority, safety, or sustainability.

title: From a question to a report
section: Match the output to the selected question
text:
Match the output to the selected question







Duckweed
Organic alternative




Outcome: dry biomass in mg
Outcome: isolated yield in %


Independent unit: flask
Independent unit: synthesis run


Guided Welch comparison and interval
Descriptive mean/SD comparison


One missing biomass
All outcomes available



Adapt the interpretation to the selected design and outcome.

Students may reuse code patterns, but must change the roles, units, and study interpretation. They should not invent a confidence interval to fill a heading in the descriptive alternative. Neither study needs a new statistical method.

title: From a question to a report
section: Write a result someone can assess
text:
Write a result someone can assess
Include:

Direction and size, in the outcome’s units.
Numbers of available independent units.
Individual variation and the required uncertainty, if estimated.
One limitation tied to the design, missing data, or simplified assumptions.


Prompt students to distinguish an observed numerical difference from a universal claim. Simulated teaching data do not establish real biological or chemical effects. Ask which code or table supplies each number in their paragraph.

title: From a question to a report
section: Keep the whole recipe in the report
text:
Keep the whole recipe in the report

Import data and load packages.
Perform checks and calculations.
Produce figures and summaries.
Explain the results and limits.
Save, restart, and render.


The report must not depend on console-only objects. Source files stay in the project root so data/relative paths keep the same meaning. Preserve the input CSV and keep derived output separate.

title: From a question to a report
section: Start with the claim you intend to support
text:
Start with the claim you intend to support



An analysis moves from question to independent unit and data to a descriptive result; inference needs additional model assumptions.


Write the plan before changing the code.

The analysis plan covers question, unit, outcome, units, missingness, plot and direction. The descriptive organic route stops at a directed observed comparison; the duckweed route adds the taught independent inference. One chosen main study is enough.

title: From a question to a report
section: Make checks inspectable
text:
Make checks inspectable
For each check, retain operation and finding:

Identifiers and allocation labels.
Measurement types, units, and unavailable values.
Derived outcome and available counts.
Comparison direction and interpretation.


“All checks passed” is not enough for another reader. Ask students to show a count or a named record. They can use existing commands rather than a new validation package. One hand calculation helps test the operation’s meaning, but does not by itself validate experimental independence.

title: From a question to a report
section: Transfer the workflow to a fresh culture study
text:
Transfer the workflow to a fresh culture study



Twenty-four algae cultures include twelve reference and twelve supplement records, with A19 unavailable.


New file: data/algae.csv; outcome: dry biomass in mg.

Algae are photosynthetic organisms, but the task requires no microbiology: independent cultures were randomly assigned, and one seven-day harvest produced a biomass reading. A19 spilled before weighing. This is a short transfer memo, not a requirement to do both duckweed and organic main reports.

title: From a question to a report
section: Check before summarising
text:
Check before summarising
library(readr)
algae <- read_csv("data/algae.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(algae)
anyDuplicated(algae$culture_id)
sum(is.na(algae$biomass_mg))
Expect 24 rows, 0 duplicated IDs, 1 missing measurement.

The available counts are twelve reference and eleven supplement. Keep A19’s raw row and missing value. State that the culture, not its number of cells, is the independent unit. The transfer table has different column and allocation names from the plant table: adapt the roles, not only the title.

title: From a question to a report
section: Look at the observations before the summary
text:
Look at the observations before the summary



Individual biomass measurements overlap between the two culture allocations.


Which group contains the largest individual observation?

Reference culture A11 has 41.7 mg, larger than every supplement observation. This does not contradict a greater supplement mean. Let students answer the individual-observation question before showing means, so the plot is read as data rather than treated as decoration behind a chosen conclusion.

title: From a question to a report
section: A group mean is not a rule for every culture
text:
A group mean is not a rule for every culture



Red diamonds mark the group means while individual reference and supplement observations remain visible.


Reference mean ≈ 28.20 mg; supplement mean ≈ 33.92 mg.

The supplement group has the higher mean but its values do not all exceed the reference values. Both individual observations and the summary are informative. The plot alone does not isolate every possible source of biological variation; the supplied design and assumptions still matter.

title: From a question to a report
section: Zero would invent a different result
text:
Zero would invent a different result



Incorrectly inserting zero for the unavailable culture lowers the supplement mean relative to using available measurements.


The unavailable value has not become observed information.

The correct available supplement mean is 33.91818 mg. Adding a false zero as a twelfth measurement changes it to 31.09167 mg. This is a demonstration of why the rule matters, not an alternative recommended analysis. Keep the raw missing value and explain the loss rather than choosing a convenient invented number.

title: From a question to a report
section: Repair claims as carefully as code
text:
Repair claims as carefully as code
Faulty statements to challenge:

“All enrolled flasks have measured biomass.”
“The group SD is the error in the treatment effect.”
“A higher product yield proves greater purity.”

Use the specific data and assumptions in the correction.

Duckweed has nineteen available outcomes out of twenty enrolled flasks. SD is individual spread. Organic purity was assumed for a simplified calculation, not measured by yield. A useful rewrite changes the claim’s meaning, not only its strength from proves to suggests. Students record their corrections.

title: From a question to a report
section: Give the difference a direction
text:
Give the difference a direction



Supplement-minus-reference and reference-minus-supplement have equal sizes and opposite signs.


The observed supplement-minus-reference difference is about 5.72 mg.

Reversing the order changes the sign without altering the underlying observations. In the duckweed test, the order also determines the interval’s direction. For the algae transfer memo no new hypothesis test is required. If a taught test is run, it does not replace the requested descriptive reasoning.

title: From a question to a report
section: Write a bounded result paragraph
text:
Write a bounded result paragraph
Include unit, available n, direction, spread or overlap, and a limitation.
A larger mean does not imply every treated observation is larger.

The algae memo includes a saved summary and figure. Calculate with unrounded means and report A19’s loss. Interpret this simulated study within its design and assumptions.

title: From a question to a report
section: Retain a decision trail with the result
text:
Retain a decision trail with the result
Save the analysis plan, checks, chosen direction, and interpretation revision.
Then restart and recreate the outputs from the saved source.

The analysis plan records decisions for the chosen main study. The algae memo applies the workflow to new data and becomes the next reproduction task.

title: From a question to a report
section: Exercises: a first complete version today
text:
Exercises: a first complete version today
Open exercises · Quiz.

Default: duckweed-report.Rmd plus HTML.
Alternative: organic-study.Rmd plus HTML.
Keep the chosen source and HTML in the project, with raw data intact.
Retain the analysis plan and short algae transfer memo/script.

If extending day 15’s organic-report.Rmd, use Save As to preserve it.

The immediate goal is a complete first version, not decorative perfection. The next fresh-folder reproduction will expose hidden dependencies. Students should save a note of any failed step rather than conceal it.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Where is the report?
text:
Where is the report?



A laptop and remote computer hold separate course-project folders.


A filename needs a computer and location, not just a familiar name.

Ask where a browser download normally arrives. Then ask whether logging into a remote desktop changes that location. It does not. Both projects may contain report.Rmd while holding different contents. Start with this distinction before demonstrating a login.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Two interfaces to a remote environment
text:
Two interfaces to a remote environment



SSH and remote desktop lead to a remote environment through different interfaces.


The service guide will tell us whether these views share a home directory.

SSH provides the shell. Remote desktop provides the graphical workspace. The actual service, authentication, permitted execution host, R application, and transfer route are still to be supplied. Confirm shared storage using that guide.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Identify the computer, then the folder
text:
Identify the computer, then the folder
After connecting through the supplied route, run in the remote shell:
hostname
pwd
ls

hostname: which machine answered?
pwd: where am I on that computer?
ls: what is in that folder?


Demonstrate only on the approved environment. Explain that an HPC service may assign different machine names. No invented hostname or account is needed for this teaching slide. Record the service and path, never passwords or codes.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: A path is interpreted in its environment
text:
A path is interpreted in its environment
Laptop R:    data/seedlings.csv
Remote R:    data/seedlings.csv
The text is identical. The accessible files may be different.
In the R console of the application you are using:
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")

Ask what FALSE means: R did not find that relative path in its current working directory. It does not establish that the dataset is missing everywhere. Check computer, project, and folder before inserting an absolute laptop path.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Closing the session does not erase saved files
text:
Closing the session does not erase saved files



Ending an SSH session closes a connection while the saved project remains in storage.


exit returns from SSH to the local shell. Reconnect and find the file again.

Saved storage is different from an interactive session. Whether a running program continues after disconnecting depends on the service.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Transfer creates a copy in a named place
text:
Transfer creates a copy in a named place



A deliberate transfer copies a report between laptop and remote storage.


Name the source, destination, and direction before transferring.

Use the service’s supported upload/download method. If scp is eventually used, its syntax belongs in the actual service guide. SSH and remote desktop by themselves are not file synchronisation. Editing one copy need not update another.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Render where the inputs are accessible
text:
Render where the inputs are accessible
Open the remote project and use its supported R application.
If the remote shell has R, packages, and Pandoc configured:
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd")'
Run from the project root on the permitted execution host.

This is an alternative way to start the same rendering function. Local Ubuntu on Windows need not contain R; students can keep using native RStudio there. Demonstrate the command only when the remote service setup supports it.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Complete the round trip
text:
Complete the round trip



The source and data are transferred in, rendered remotely, and the output transferred back.


Open the returned HTML on the laptop. Retain source and data for reproduction.

An HTML output is useful to read but is not the recipe. Ask students to point to both the remote output and local downloaded copy, then to the source and input. The location log should record this without any authentication details.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Predict the recovery step
text:
Predict the recovery step
The report rendered remotely. Local Downloads is empty.
What should you check before rendering again?

Locate the output on the remote computer.
Check whether it has actually been transferred.
Find the destination used by that transfer.


Invite an answer before revealing the list. The absent local copy does not prove the remote render failed. Avoid creating multiple reports with names such as final2 while the real problem is location.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Plan the copy before performing it
text:
Plan the copy before performing it



Source and destination projects identify the intended algae file and the content checks to repeat.


Record computer, project path, filename, and intended output.

Use the actual service only when supplied. A local rehearsal needs two different parent folders, both explicitly labelled local. These locations are not account credentials. Ask students what a receiver would need to distinguish two files with the same name. A plan written afterwards can conceal an incorrect assumption.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Count what the receiving copy should contain
text:
Count what the receiving copy should contain



Twenty-four separate culture records contain one unavailable supplement measurement, A19.


24 records; 23 available measurements; one documented spill.

The fresh transfer table is data/algae.csv. Define algae simply as the organisms in separate cultures; harvested dry biomass is measured in mg. Twelve cultures were independently assigned each allocation. There are twelve reference and eleven available supplement measurements. These are content checks, not a new model.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Verify the intended input in R
text:
Verify the intended input in R
library(readr)
algae <- read_csv("data/algae.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(algae)
sum(!is.na(algae$biomass_mg))
algae$biomass_mg[algae$culture_id == "A19"]
Repeat after transfer: 24, 23, and NA.

Run in the receiving R project’s Console. A path printed by a shell elsewhere is not R’s current folder. The brackets select the entry matching the ID, not the nineteenth row by assumption. Correct counts are useful evidence, but they do not establish that every individual value matches the source.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: A matching filename is not a version check
text:
A matching filename is not a version check



Two files named receipt.txt contain different first and second revisions.


Inspect the saved contents before choosing which copy to send.

Demonstrate with receipts, not raw data. Edit a disposable destination note, save it, and reopen both copies. The remote desktop is a view of a computer; it is not a guarantee that a laptop’s copy updates. Preserve both versions until their roles are understood instead of deleting an unfamiliar folder.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Write a receipt another reader can use
text:
Write a receipt another reader can use
A short receipt names:

The input and receiving project location.
Checks performed and their actual results.
The returned artifact and its destination.
Any real remote steps still pending.


Ask students to avoid vague claims such as “uploaded successfully”. A useful receipt can distinguish a file selected, a file sent, and the received file opened and checked. No passwords, authentication codes, or private account details belong in it. A local rehearsal should say exactly that.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: An unsaved edit has not travelled
text:
An unsaved edit has not travelled



A changed editor buffer and the saved receipt can contain different revisions until saving occurs.


Save, close, reopen, then inspect the copy you intend to transfer.

This returns to the file-system baseline deliberately. Some editors autosave or restore buffers, so the practical test is the actual saved file. Source-code edits likewise do not change an old rendered HTML document until rendering runs. The transfer audit needs a named source artifact, not only what is on screen.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Why not check only the file size?
text:
Why not check only the file size?



Different version text occupies the same number of character positions.


Equal size is a limited check, not proof of equal contents.

The strings version 1 and version 2 have equal lengths but different final characters. Students need no hashing theory. For these small notes, read both saved files and compare their contents. Row counts also have limits: two tables can have identical dimensions yet contain different values.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: “File not found” needs a location investigation
text:
“File not found” needs a location investigation
In the receiving R Console:
getwd()
file.exists("data/algae.csv")
Check computer → project root → relative path → actual file.

A FALSE result tells us that R did not find this path from this starting location. It does not mean the input is absent from every machine. Open the right project and inspect extraction nesting before inserting a personal absolute path. Keep the search sequence reproducible in the log.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Diagnose before rendering another copy
text:
Diagnose before rendering another copy
The expected local result is absent.

Did rendering succeed, and where did it write?
Was that specific output transferred?
Which destination received it?
Which copy did the browser open?


Let students trace a deliberately misplaced HTML file without immediately rerunning the analysis. A second render may only create another identical artifact in the same unexpected folder. Distinguish failure to calculate, failure to transfer, and failure to locate the result.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: A bounded handover is more useful than a promise
text:
A bounded handover is more useful than a promise
Save transfer-plan.txt, the receipt, and the audit in reports/.
State what was checked, which copies were compared, and what remains unknown.

These files support the transfer audit and result-recovery tasks. A local copy check is valuable but cannot complete SSH authentication or remote desktop access. Likewise a successful transfer does not establish a backup policy or guarantee that a disconnected process continues running.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Exercises: locate, render, return
text:
Exercises: locate, render, return
Open exercises · Quiz.

Save reports/remote-log.txt with computer names and project locations.
Connect, disconnect, reconnect, and find saved work.
Transfer and identify one output copy.
Retain the transfer plan, receipt, version checks, and audit.

Until access is provided, complete the local rehearsal and mark remote steps pending.

Local rehearsal checks portable paths and project structure; remote connection skills remain pending until practised on the actual service.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: A reading is not yet a concentration
text:
A reading is not yet a concentration



Six known standard concentrations establish a measurement scale before an unknown is interpreted.


Use known standards before estimating unknown samples.

These are simulated values for a fictional colour assay; no reagent or prior chemistry course is assumed. A standard is a solution whose concentration is supplied. Absorbance describes light attenuation and is dimensionless. The standards span 0–10 mg/L.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Know which quantity was prepared and which was measured
text:
Know which quantity was prepared and which was measured
We prepared concentration and measured absorbance.
Fit:
absorbance = intercept + slope × concentration
One standard is a calibration point, not a biological treatment replicate.

This direction is deliberate. Later we rearrange the forward calibration to estimate an unknown concentration. Regressing concentration directly on absorbance would be a different fit. The zero-concentration standard includes background signal; no blank subtraction has been performed.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Fit the straight line
text:
Fit the straight line
library(readr)
standards <- read_csv("data/calibration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
calibration_fit <- lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l,
                      data = standards)
coef(calibration_fit)
Intercept ≈ 0.03957; slope ≈ 0.06489 per mg/L.

Load readr, dplyr, ggplot2 as usual. Explain the tilde as response on the left and explanatory variable on the right. The practical supplies full precision. A nonzero intercept may represent background, so “zero concentration” does not justify forcing the fit through zero.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Does a line describe the tested range?
text:
Does a line describe the tested range?



Prepared standards are shown with their fitted linear calibration.


A fitted line need not pass through every measured standard.

Point to each measured value and the line’s fitted value. The fitted slope is the rise in absorbance for one mg/L increase in concentration. This is a working approximation within the tested range, not a chemical law established for every concentration.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: A residual is observed minus fitted
text:
A residual is observed minus fitted



Calibration residuals show measured readings minus their fitted readings.


Look for curvature or an unusual point, not zero residuals everywhere.

Positive means the observed absorbance is above the line. The six small residuals show no obvious curved pattern, but six standards remain limited evidence. A plot is a check on the approximation, not a guarantee of validity outside the data.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Read backward from the measured signal
text:
Read backward from the measured signal



A measured absorbance 0.520 intersects the fitted line near 7.40 mg/L.


The unknown concentration is obtained by rearranging the line.

Trace horizontally from the observed reading to the calibration line, then down to concentration. This visual separates the measured input from the estimated output. Keep the unrounded coefficients for the calculation even though slide labels are rounded.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Calculate a supported point estimate
text:
Calculate a supported point estimate
intercept <- coef(calibration_fit)[1]
slope <- coef(calibration_fit)[2]
concentration_mg_l <- (0.520 - intercept) / slope
Result ≈ 7.40 mg/L.
This simple estimate omits full calibration and measurement uncertainty.

The[1] and[2] select coefficients. The denominator is the fitted slope, with absorbance per mg/L units. The practical uses range checks to avoid pretending every numeric inversion is supported. The inverse result is an uncertain point estimate.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: A number can be calculable but unsupported
text:
A number can be calculable but unsupported



The U3 absorbance 0.900 is greater than every measured standard reading.


U3 is beyond range: flag for a new suitable measurement.

The practical assigns NA to the unsupported concentration rather than presenting an extrapolated number. A dilution correction requires a new measurement and recorded volumes. The instrument’s calibrated range is evidence, not an inconvenience to bypass.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: A new diluted measurement can bring the signal in range
text:
A new diluted measurement can bring the signal in range



One millilitre of original sample is brought to ten millilitres total by adding solvent.


1.00 mL original → 10.00 mL total gives a dilution factor of 10.

This is a stated new numerical example, not a wet-lab protocol or a new reading for U3. Define dilution without assuming chemical preparation knowledge. Total 10 mL does not mean adding 10 mL of solvent to the 1 mL sample. Assume no measured material is lost or reacts.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Distinguish the measured and original concentrations
text:
Distinguish the measured and original concentrations
New diluted reading: 0.520 → 7.40 mg/L diluted.
Original estimate = diluted estimate × total volume / original volume.
7.404227 × 10 ≈ 74.04 mg/L original.
The new measured reading, not the original concentration, is within calibration range.

An original concentration above 10 mg/L can be estimated through a new in-range diluted measurement and a justified factor. That is different from extrapolating the old calibration directly to a high absorbance. Full dilution and calibration uncertainty remain outside this exercise.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Show the complete quantity map
text:
Show the complete quantity map
Known standards: concentration → measured absorbance. Fit: absorbance as a function of known concentration. Unknown: measured absorbance → inverse point estimate.
Keep the fitted direction and requested output distinct.

The standard concentration is prepared and the response is measured. A new direct regression of concentration on absorbance is a different fit. Students should label predictor,response,intercept,slope units,range,and unknown estimate.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Rounding a display can change a later calculation
text:
Rounding a display can change a later calculation



Inverse estimates differ when full coefficients are replaced by coefficients rounded to two decimals.


Retain fitted coefficients; round results when communicating.

For reading.310, rounding intercept and slope to.04 and.06 gives4.50 rather than4.17 mg/L. It is a deliberate diagnostic, not a recommended new calibration. Extra display precision does not remove measurement uncertainty either.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: A residual has a direction and a scale
text:
A residual has a direction and a scale
standards$observed_minus_fitted <-
  standards$absorbance - fitted(calibration_fit)
residuals(calibration_fit)
Positive means the observed signal is above the line.

Compare one value by hand. Both expressions should match. A residual is not the concentration error of an unknown and not a p-value. Use the first standard while its measured concentration and signal remain visible.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Trace a corrected estimate through its evidence
text:
Trace a corrected estimate through its evidence



A new diluted reading feeds its inverseestimate and suppliedfactor to recover an original estimate.


The corrected original estimate is not a direct instrument reading.

A numerical table should retain the new reading,original aliquot volume,total final volume,factor,diluted estimate,and original estimate. Nothing in this chain validates U3 without its own new measurement.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: A second calibration needs a second fit
text:
A second calibration needs a second fit



The new six-standard instrument calibration has its own intercept and slope.


Create separate coefficient objects for the second instrument.

Transfer standards span0–5 mg/L. Fit absorbance on known concentration. Their fitted intercept is.02161905 and slope.10008571 per mg/L. This is another empirical calibration,not a universal optical law.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Rebuild the transfer fit explicitly
text:
Rebuild the transfer fit explicitly
transfer_standards <- read_csv(
  'data/calibration-transfer.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)
transfer_fit <- lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l,
                   data = transfer_standards)
coef(transfer_fit)

Load readr before this block. Keep separate names so the primary instrument report is not silently altered. The independent transfer report must contain its own import,checks,fit,and inverse calculations.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Inspect the new residuals, not the old picture
text:
Inspect the new residuals, not the old picture



Residuals fromthe new six-standard fit remain small onthe absorbance scale.


A tidy residual plot is limited evidence with only six standards.

Look for obvious curvature or an unusual point. Absence of an obvious pattern does not establish chemical specificity,measurement accuracy in every condition,or performance beyond the tested range.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Preserve the unsupported unknown as a record
text:
Preserve the unsupported unknown as a record



X1at0.270 is within the new standard range;X2at0.700 is above it.


Keep the ID and reading; flag the unsupported concentration.

X1 estimates about 2.48168 mg/L. X2 is not supported by the supplied standard readings. Missing estimate due to out-of-range input differs from a missing measured signal; retain the reason rather than dropping the row.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: An algebra check is useful but not independent validation
text:
An algebra check is useful but not independent validation
transfer_a <- coef(transfer_fit)[1]
transfer_b <- coef(transfer_fit)[2]
x1_mg_l <- (0.270 - transfer_a) / transfer_b
transfer_a + transfer_b * x1_mg_l
The forward calculation returns 0.270, apart from rounding.

The check can catch reversal or arithmetic mistakes. Because it reuses the same fitted relationship, it does not independently establish calibration validity or eliminate uncertainty.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: A next action needs new information, not an invented result
text:
A next action needs new information, not an invented result
For an unsupported sample, state what must be supplied next:

A new suitable measurement.
Any recorded sample and total volumes.
The supported range and applicable calibration.

No fabricated corrected concentration.

The transfer report should recommend a sensible information-gathering step for X2. It is not a wet-lab protocol and does not require prior chemistry. Full uncertainty propagation remains beyond this simple exercise.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Exercises: report the line and its limits
text:
Exercises: report the line and its limits
Save calibration-report.Rmd, supported concentration estimates, and both figures.
Explain U3’s missing estimate and the new dilution example.
Open exercises.

Students should explain the standard, slope units, residual sign, supported range, and uncertainty limitation. They need no memorised optical law. Keep the dataset and formula visible so the chemistry setting does not become a prerequisite.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Observed difference is a starting point
text:
Observed difference is a starting point



The two seedling groups overlap despite a higher treated mean.


How uncertain is the estimated treated-minus-control mean difference?

Use the comparison.Rmd prepared on day 16. The difference in this sample is 6.21667 mm. The inferential question concerns a population mean difference under assumptions, not whether every individual plant must follow the group ordering.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Check the design and observations first
text:
Check the design and observations first

Independent plants, allocated to separate groups.
One growth value per plant.
Inspect severe skew and influential observations in small samples.
Keep genuine unusual values; seek advice when the simple model is unsuitable.


Welch’s method does not require equal population variances, but does not repair dependence, biased allocation or data quality. Describe the assumptions in biological terms.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Run the comparison in the direction we named
text:
Run the comparison in the direction we named
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
treated <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "treated")$growth_mm
control <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")$growth_mm

comparison <- t.test(treated, control,
                     var.equal = FALSE,          # Welch: spreads may differ
                     alternative = "two.sided",  # a difference in either direction counts
                     conf.level = 0.95)
comparison

The first vector minus the second: here treated − control. The order of arguments sets the sign.
var.equal = FALSE is already the default; writing it makes the method visible to a reader.
Save the result as an object so you can extract numbers: comparison$conf.int, comparison$p.value.


This builds on Day 16’s comparison.Rmd, which already creates the treated and control vectors. Students should run it, not copy numbers from the slide. Emphasise naming the direction in words before running the code, so that the sign of the output is a check rather than a surprise.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: An interval around the estimated difference
text:
An interval around the estimated difference



The estimate 6.22 mm and 95 percent confidence interval 2.70–9.73 mm are shown against zero difference.


Estimate 6.22 mm; 95% CI 2.70 to 9.73 mm.

Units and sign matter. Zero denotes equal population means under this comparison. The interval quantifies uncertainty in the mean difference under the model; it is not an interval containing 95% of individual plants, nor a guarantee that the true difference lies inside this particular interval.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: The 95% refers to a repeated-sampling procedure
text:
The 95% refers to a repeated-sampling procedure



Illustrative repeated studies produce intervals around separate estimates; the true difference is fixed.


A valid 95% procedure covers the fixed truth in about 95% of repeated samples.

This is a conceptual repeated-study illustration, not additional seedling experiments or the actual Welch intervals. Some intervals can miss the fixed truth. We do not know whether this particular experiment’s interval covers it. The frequency statement concerns the procedure under its assumptions.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: What does the p-value condition on?
text:
What does the p-value condition on?



The Welch equal-means reference distribution shades both tails beyond the observed statistic magnitude.


If the equal-means model held, how often would a statistic be at least this extreme?

For these data p is about 0.001517. The reference curve uses the actual Welch statistic and approximate degrees of freedom. It is not a distribution of possible treatment effects. State the conditioning model and assumptions. The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true or that the treatment works.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Spread among plants is not the difference interval
text:
Spread among plants is not the difference interval

Individual measurements and the estimated mean-difference interval answer different questions.
Left: individual growth values. Spread here is natural variation between plants (SD).
Right: uncertainty in the treated − control mean difference (CI).
Before reading any error bar, ask: which quantity, and on which axis? A figure caption must say.


Students frequently read any bar as individual spread or any bar as a confidence interval. Ask them to identify the axis and the summarised object in each panel before interpreting. Link back to Day 13: if you draw whiskers, define them.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Write a result, not just a threshold label
text:
Write a result, not just a threshold label
“Treated mean growth exceeded control mean growth by 6.22 mm (95% CI 2.70–9.73 mm; Welch two-sided p ≈ 0.0015).”
Then explain the biological size, assumptions, and limits.
A small p-value does not establish a large or causal effect.

The study’s random allocation supports a causal comparison within its conditions, but a p-value alone never establishes causality or universal generalisation. If an interval included zero, it would not prove equality. Encourage a sentence on biological relevance rather than “significant” alone.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Read units as well as numbers
text:
Read units as well as numbers
Mean growth and the confidence interval use mm. The p-value has no measurement unit.
Neither a group SD nor a p-value is the interval for a difference.

Ask students to annotate a real output table with quantity,value, units,interpretation. The sample counts come from actual input vectors, not the number of lines printed in the test output.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Reversing order reverses the interval
text:
Reversing order reverses the interval



The same comparison in opposite directions produces reflected confidence intervals.


For a two-sided test, the p-value remains the same.

A treated-minus-control interval[2.70,9.73] becomes a control-minus-treated interval[−9.73,−2.70]. Both describe the same estimated contrast in opposite units of direction. This is not a new experiment.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Check the reversal directly
text:
Check the reversal directly
reverse_comparison <- t.test(control, treated)
comparison$conf.int
reverse_comparison$conf.int
comparison$p.value
reverse_comparison$p.value
Use separate objects so the stated primary result is preserved.

This follows the independent-group setup from day 16: treated/control are numeric growth vectors. The function order determines the sign, not an object name such as treatment_effect.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Coverage level and interval width are a trade-off
text:
Coverage level and interval width are a trade-off



The90%,95%,and 99%intervals use identical observations but different widths.


Keep the 95% interval as the stated main analysis.

Higher long-run coverage requires a wider procedure under the same model. Keep the confidence level chosen for the main analysis. Changing conf.level does not change the observed means.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: A small experiment can remain inconclusive about direction
text:
A small experiment can remain inconclusive about direction



An illustrative2 mm difference has a95%interval from−1 to 5 mm,covering zero and both directions.


Including zero is not proof of equality or equivalence.

Ask what positive and negative differences remain inside the supplied range. These are illustrative numbers, not output from the course plant file. No new test or sample-size calculation is needed.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Repair the interpretation, not the desired result
text:
Repair the interpretation, not the desired result
Incorrect: “The null hypothesis has probability 0.0015.”
Better: under the equal-means model and assumptions, a statistic at least this extreme is rare.
Then report effect size, units, interval, and design limits.

A frequentist p-value conditions on the model; it does not assign the hypothesis a probability. Biological importance and causality require context. Precision in wording is part of analysis, not an optional editorial add-on.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Two studies: n alone does not explain interval width
text:
Two studies: n alone does not explain interval width



Main and transfer study intervals differ in estimate and width while also having different spreads and sample sizes.


Both sample size and observed variability contribute.

Here the smaller transfer study happens to have a narrower interval because its observed spread is smaller. Do not teach a universal ordering from n alone when other quantities change.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Recreate the guided comparison for the new source
text:
Recreate the guided comparison for the new source
transfer <- read_csv('data/seedlings-transfer.csv',
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
new_treated <- transfer |>
  filter(treatment == 'treated') |> pull(growth_mm)
new_control <- transfer |>
  filter(treatment == 'control') |> pull(growth_mm)
transfer_test <- t.test(new_treated, new_control)
transfer_test

Use transfer from its own saved import/growth calculation, not hidden console state. There are9 available values per group. Difference4.2111 mm;95% interval 1.9484 to6.4738 mm; p about.00124. Include actual observations and assumptions in the interpretation.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: A complete result can be read without R
text:
A complete result can be read without R
A reader should identify:

What was independently assigned and measured.
The estimated difference and its direction/units.
Uncertainty under the model and a design/context limitation.

A printout alone does not answer all three.

Students extend transfer-comparison.Rmd with a concise results paragraph, then check direction and units in the rendered HTML. Earlier descriptive work remains useful and should not disappear after adding a test.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Exercises: add interpretation to the report
text:
Exercises: add interpretation to the report
Keep the individual-point plot. Add the method, directed estimate, interval, sample sizes and p-value.
Restart R and render comparison.Rmd.
Open exercises.

Have students find comparisonconf.int and comparisonp.value and relate them to the printed output. They should report the two group means and available sample sizes as well. The written interpretation should be understandable without seeing R’s long printout.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: One question, one short evidence trail
text:
One question, one short evidence trail



A biological question connects measured data to a readable report.


How does seedling growth vary among plants and groups?

This briefing consolidates descriptive analysis. The reader should learn the question, how the measurements arose, and what the observations show. An organic-yield report may replace this context, but is not an extra required report.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Give each part of the report a job
text:
Give each part of the report a job



A short report has a question,data and methods,results with a figure,and an interpretation.


The plot shows the result; your words explain its meaning.

Walk through the drawing as a structure, not as a required page count or formatting template. Distinguish methods from results. A caption identifies the unit and visual encodings. Interpretation describes direction, variation and limits rather than repeating all printed output.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Choose and name the actual input
text:
Choose and name the actual input
Use data/seedlings.csv for the complete core example.

24 independently potted plants; 12 per group.
Initial and final lengths are measured in mm.
Growth is final minus initial length.
State explicitly if you choose the repaired incomplete file instead.


The complete and repaired datasets have different available counts. Keep those distinctions visible. The existing practical uses the complete file for the main report. The alternative organic-report.Rmd must identify independent synthesis runs and yield percentage units throughout.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Keep the source where its relative paths make sense
text:
Keep the source where its relative paths make sense



The report sits at the project root beside its data and output subfolders.


Save the .Rmd at the project root, not inside reports/.

Knit normally resolves relative data paths from the source report’s folder. Moving the source into reports/ would change where data/ points. An output_dir argument can place the generated HTML in reports/ while leaving the source at root.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Render from files, not from your memory of the session
text:
Render from files, not from your memory of the session



A fresh session rebuilds results from the saved data and saved report source.


Restart, then Knit without running console calculations first.

The report needs its own library calls, import and derived columns. An object existing only in the Environment pane is not a reproducible report dependency. Installation commands belong in setup, not inside an analysis that should run repeatedly.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Check the interpretation against the figure
text:
Check the interpretation against the figure
“Mean treated growth was about 21.5 mm; control growth about 15.3 mm. Individual observations overlap.”
What would be wrong with “every treated plant grew more”?
We have described the sample; we have not estimated uncertainty in the difference.

The individual-point plot shows overlap. Keep SD as spread, not uncertainty in a group mean. In the optional organic context, standard mean yield 68.67% and modified 77% describe independent runs; higher yield does not verify purity or general protocol superiority.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: A result should have a visible lineage
text:
A result should have a visible lineage



Saved data feed reportcode that produces the numerical table and results prose.


Trace each reported number back to a saved input and calculation.

Ask a reader to identify where the mean came from, which rows contributed, and which units apply. A report with an impressive table but an unidentified input is not complete.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: The project file does not contain every dependency
text:
The project file does not contain every dependency



A missing input file breaks the path fromreport source to a newly rendered output.


Include the ordinary input CSV, not just a shortcut to its old location.

An Rproj provides context; it does not package data. Reproduction in a newly named folder tests personal paths and omitted files. Record any failure before fixing it, then rerun.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Keep claims at the level supported by the work
text:
Keep claims at the level supported by the work



Measurements support a sample description; an unsupported jump to universal causation is blocked.


Descriptive work is useful even before a hypothesis test.

Repair sentences such as results were good or computer removed bad values. Identify a measurement pattern, a defined summary, or a documented correction. Current day15 reports do not quantify uncertainty in a treatment difference.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Adapt a structure, not an old conclusion
text:
Adapt a structure, not an old conclusion



The transfer study has different individual values,means and spread from the firststudy.


A changed title alone does not create a report about new observations.

The new source is seedlings-transfer.csv with 18 plants,9 per group. Replace old imports, descriptions, counts, and labels together. If using a previously saved analysis, recreate its objects inside the new report.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Inline results keep prose connected to code
text:
Inline results keep prose connected to code
A count or mean can be calculated inline after its object is created.
Literal source example: `r nrow(transfer)`
The sentence still needs a quantity, units, and interpretation.

Use escaped entities to display literal R Markdown code in these slides. During a student report render the inline expression executes. Installing packages or rendering the report from inside itself is not a solution to missing objects.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Do a reader review and an analyst review
text:
Do a reader review and an analyst review
Reader review: question, unit, outcome, figure meaning, conclusion.
Analyst review: input, checks, transformations, available n, regeneration.
A change log records the issue, correction, and rerun result.

The exercises include a revision of the selected report and a report on the second seedling study.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: A short report can contain strong evidence
text:
A short report can contain strong evidence
Keep one relevant table, one useful figure, and a specific interpretation.
Remove a redundant printout before removing a limitation or a unit label.
Can another person regenerate and explain the result?

Review the saved checks, interpretation, and fresh-session render.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Exercises: one report that reopens and renders
text:
Exercises: one report that reopens and renders
Save descriptive-report.Rmd or the chosen organic-report.Rmd, plus HTML.
Put explicit rendering commands in the R Console, not inside the report.
Check that the HTML states the question, independent unit, measurement units, and limitation.
Open exercises.

Have students locate both source and rendered output. No hypothesis test is required today. If rendering fails, use the first meaningful error and chunk name to recover. Avoid spending the entire session on cosmetic formatting while inputs or interpretation remain unclear.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: A summary row is not a new observation
text:
A summary row is not a new observation



Twenty-four plant measurements become two group summary values, with information necessarily compressed.


Keep the measurement table as well as its summary.

A table with two group means is not a dataset with two newly measured plants. Show the original and summary objects in R. Summarisation deliberately compresses information, which is why an individual-point plot remains useful.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Tell R which groups to summarise
text:
Tell R which groups to summarise
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_plants = n(),
    n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
    mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
The result has one row per treatment.

Recreate the clean import and growth calculation in the practical before this code. Read the pipe aloud. n counts plant records; !is.na selects available measurements. .groups=“drop” leaves an ordinary ungrouped summary table. No missing growths occur in today’s clean data.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: How many plants contributed?
text:
How many plants contributed?
In the complete teaching file:

Control: 12 plants, 12 available growth values.
Treated: 12 plants, 12 available growth values.

The repaired file from day 11 has only 11 available control growths.

Explicitly distinguish the two supplied files. Missingness changes the contributing count without inventing a zero measurement. The counts belong beside the summaries, not hidden in an undocumented filter.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Show observations and identify the mean
text:
Show observations and identify the mean



Individual growth measurements are shown with red diamonds marking group means.


Small dots = plants. Red diamonds = group means.

Control mean 15.275 mm; treated mean 21.49167 mm. Overlap means the larger group mean is not a claim that every treated plant outgrew every control. Horizontal jitter only separates overlapping dots; measured vertical values remain unchanged.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: If you draw whiskers, define them
text:
If you draw whiskers, define them



Mean plus or minus sample SD is drawn alongside individual plant measurements.


These whiskers show mean ± SD, not confidence intervals.

Ask what a reader could infer if the caption simply said “error bars”. The answer is too little. SD describes spread among plants. A confidence interval for an estimate has another interpretation, introduced later. It is acceptable to omit whiskers today and show observations and means.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: A histogram describes the distribution
text:
A histogram describes the distribution



Separate histograms show the counts of control and treated growth values in four-millimetre bins.


The vertical axis counts observations, not a biological response.

The horizontal axis contains growth intervals; the height counts plants in each bin. The panels use comparable scales. With 12 plants per group, apparent shape is unstable. A histogram does not show measurement order or the identities of plants.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: A bin boundary can change the picture
text:
A bin boundary can change the picture



The same twelve control values produce different histogram detail under bin widths two,four,six millimetres.


Describe stable features; be cautious with tiny samples.

Nothing about the plants changed between panels. Changing a display choice changes what detail looks prominent. Invite students to compare the raw dot plot with all three histograms before interpreting an apparent peak or gap.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Save the right object for the intended use
text:
Save the right object for the intended use
write_csv(group_summary, "output/growth-summary.csv")
A CSV stores numbers; a PNG stores a figure. Keep both traceable to raw data.

The practical defines group_plot and output/ already exists in the supplied project. Assigning an R object does not export it. After saving, ask students to find the two ordinary files in a file manager and explain which application could open each.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: A summary can hide the very observations it describes
text:
A summary can hide the very observations it describes



Means alone conceal the individual measurements and overlap shown by a point plot.


Both panels use the same group means.

Ask which panel permits inspecting overlap and unusual values. The point plot need not become cluttered: horizontal jitter can separate overlapping dots without changing their measured vertical positions.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Summary rows are not new plants
text:
Summary rows are not new plants
The original table has 24 plant rows. The grouped table has two summary rows.
These are different objects answering different questions.
Which table should supply individual points? Which supplies mean markers?

Individual-point layer uses the raw/derived plant table. Mean-marker layer uses group_summary with explicit mappings. A two-row summary cannot substitute for the individual observations in a treatment test.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Histogram details depend on display choices
text:
Histogram details depend on display choices



Three histograms of the same transfer growth values use different bin widths.


Record the bin width and distinguish stable patterns from unstable detail.

The underlying18 measurements are unchanged. Small samples can look multimodal or gapped depending on bins. Compare broad stable patterns across bin widths.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: An axis range changes the visual emphasis
text:
An axis range changes the visual emphasis



The same individual growth observations appear under broader and narrower vertical ranges.


Read values and axis labels when comparing effects.

Both displays can be useful with clear axes, but a reader should not mistake a changed scale for changed observations. This is particularly important when comparing figures from different groups or experiments.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Repair the caption precisely
text:
Repair the caption precisely
Weak caption: “Treatment makes everything larger; error is shown.”
Repair it by naming:

Independent unit and outcome/units.
Individual points and any mean symbol.
Available n and the actual meaning of any error bars.


Identify only the symbols actually plotted. Mean±SD describes individual spread. A confidence interval describes uncertainty in an estimate. Neither phrase can be replaced by a generic word error.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: A new class needs a complete figure package
text:
A new class needs a complete figure package



A point plot of the transfer data identifies points asplants and diamonds asgroup means.


Keep the input, summary CSV, figure, and analysis script distinct.

Transfer data have9 plants per group. Students export the summary and plot, verify one mean using a filtered vector, and write a handover request listing actual file dependencies.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: A script should name the files it creates
text:
A script should name the files it creates
library(ggplot2)
group_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(treatment, growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(
    width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 13)) +
  labs(x = 'Treatment', y = 'Seven-day growth (mm)') +
  theme_minimal()
ggsave('output/growth-summary.png', plot = group_plot,
       width = 6, height = 4)
Use distinct output filenames for the two studies.

In the independent task students create transfer_summary and transfer_plot with analogous exports. Explain why a plot object in memory, a PNG, and a summary CSV are not interchangeable outputs.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: A reader test is more specific than “does this look good?”
text:
A reader test is more specific than “does this look good?”
Check the exported figure for:

One observation and the mean marker.
Units, available sample size, and independent unit.
A pattern supported by both the table and figure.

Record the ambiguity and the correction.

The exercises include a caption-repair log and reproducible outputs. Reread the figure with the code closed. Biological claims need numerical meaning, not just attractive layout.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Exercises: describe the sample before testing it
text:
Exercises: describe the sample before testing it
Write a caption that identifies the unit, units, and symbols.
Choose a transfer summary: repaired seedlings or supplied organic yields.
Save the script, summary CSV, and figure.
Open exercises.

The organic option reuses the same computations, not a second required practical. Each row is an independently prepared run; yield uses supplied theoretical and isolated masses. SD is expressed in percentage points. No t-test is introduced here.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Did we measure 25 plants?
text:
Did we measure 25 plants?



One independently measured plant can produce two duplicated file records.


The study has 24 plants. The export has 25 rows.

Ask whether the extra row proves another plant existed. It does not. The supplied source notes confirm that P01 was imported twice. A repeated ID can be legitimate in other designs, such as measurements over time; this study specifies one row per plant.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Keep the original and explain every repair
text:
Keep the original and explain every repair



Original CSV, repair script and derived CSV remain distinct files.


A script makes the changes inspectable and repeatable.

Locate the raw file in the project before showing code. Preserve it unchanged. A script is not just a way to save typing: it records which evidence justified each transformation. A copy with unexplained edits is harder to audit.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Inspect the original entries as text
text:
Inspect the original entries as text
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
raw <- read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv",
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
  trim_ws = FALSE, show_col_types = FALSE)
unique(raw$treatment)
Control, control, and treated are different stored strings.

The import deliberately preserves whitespace and mixed entries. Demonstrate the trailing space by pointing at the printed quoted value. We are not asking beginners to memorise the importer options; explain why these options help inspect this particular file.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: A suspicious number is a question, not a verdict
text:
A suspicious number is a question, not a verdict



Rulers show the same length expressed as 43.8 millimetres and 4.38 centimetres.


The source notebook confirms P21: 43.8 mm.

The entered 4.38 is not automatically an error because it is small. The supplied source note confirms that a centimetre value was transcribed into a millimetre column. A confirmed conversion is different from changing an inconvenient biological observation.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Unknown is different from zero
text:
Unknown is different from zero



An unavailable final reading for P06 is different from an observed zero change.


Keep P06’s final length as NA.

A missing final measurement prevents us calculating its growth. A measured growth of zero would mean that initial and final readings were equal. The complete teaching file is a separate dataset, not a source for filling this missing observation.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Repair only what the evidence supports
text:
Repair only what the evidence supports
cleaned <- raw |>
  mutate(treatment = tolower(trimws(treatment)),
    initial_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P18", "18.7", initial_mm),
    final_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P21", "43.8", final_mm)) |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(initial_mm = parse_double(initial_mm),
    final_mm = parse_double(final_mm),
    growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
The original file stays unchanged; missing measurements remain missing.

This is a supplied worked repair. Explain trimws as removing edge spaces and tolower as standardising the confirmed labels. distinct removes identical rows here because the duplicate import is documented. It would be unsafe to keep one arbitrary row for every repeated ID when records disagreed.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Count records and available measurements separately
text:
Count records and available measurements separately



Both groups retain twelve plant records; one control plant lacks a usable growth value.


24 unique plants; 23 available growth measurements.

After numeric conversion and subtraction, the corrected table has 24 rows, zero duplicated IDs, and one missing growth. Control has 12 records but 11 available growths; treated has 12 and 12. Removing a missing value inside a mean does not make the missingness disappear from reporting.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Prediction: what should these two means return?
text:
Prediction: what should these two means return?
mean(cleaned$growth_mm)
mean(cleaned$growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
Explain the missing observation before choosing the second calculation.

The first returns NA. The second is about 18.48696 mm across the 23 available growth values. It is not a grouped treatment comparison. Ask students to say how many observations were used and what is unknown about the missing plant.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: A repair needs an audit trail
text:
A repair needs an audit trail



Source evidence connects a specific correction to a checked output.


For every changed value: observation → evidence → action → check.

Demonstrate a five-column correction log for P21. The log explains a supported unit correction, not a rule to multiply all small lengths by ten. Keep original, script, and derived output.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Two matching IDs do not automatically mean a duplicate
text:
Two matching IDs do not automatically mean a duplicate
Compare all fields, then consult the design and source note.

One row per plant: a repeated identifier prompts investigation.
One row per time point: repeated identifiers may be expected.
Disagreeing records need investigation, not arbitrary deletion.
