Show both P01 records in the actual raw file. Here they are identical and the recorder confirms an import duplication. Do not teach distinct(plant_id) as a universal repair.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Number text and a measurement are different objects
text:
Number text and a measurement are different objects



A text entry with a unit suffix is converted only after its meaning is confirmed.


Check meaning before converting text to numbers.

R cannot infer that every suffix or magnitude reflects the same unit. P18 is confirmed as 18.7 mm. Compare character versus numeric columns using str before and after parse_double.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: What an invented zero would claim
text:
What an invented zero would claim



The defensible available-case mean differs from the mean after inventing a zero final length.


P06 initial length is 24.7 mm: a final zero invents −24.7 mm growth.

The defensible overall available mean is about 18.49 mm from 23 observations. Replacing the missing final reading by zero gives about 16.69 mm from 24 invented/observed values. This changes meaning, not only sample size. Keep wrong_zero_example separate.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Check the saved output, not only the Environment pane
text:
Check the saved output, not only the Environment pane
write_csv(cleaned, 'output/seedlings-cleaned.csv')
check_copy <- read_csv('output/seedlings-cleaned.csv',
                       show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(check_copy)
anyDuplicated(check_copy$plant_id)
sum(is.na(check_copy$growth_mm))
Expect 24 unique plants and one unavailable growth value.

A successful in-memory calculation does not establish that the exported file is correct. Save the corrected CSV in the practical, read it back, and compare identifiers and availability. Restart and rerun to test the full script.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: A new class is a new source
text:
A new class is a new source



The transfer file contains eighteen new measured plants with initial and final lengths.


The column pattern is familiar; the values, identifiers, and checks are new.

The transfer study has 18 independent potted plants,9 per allocation, measured7 days apart. No source note authorises corrections. Check the new file and calculate its own counts and summaries.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: A schema is an expectation you can check
text:
A schema is an expectation you can check
Before importing, state:

What one row represents and which ID should be unique.
Column names, types, labels, and units.
What missingness and derived growth would mean.

Then record what you actually observed.

This is a checklist, not a new validation package. Use familiar names, str, missing-value checks and group counts. Units come from the dictionary, not solely from numerical size.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Decide whether a change is justified
text:
Decide whether a change is justified
An unfamiliar value appears in the transfer file.
What can you do immediately, and what requires more evidence?
Inspect the record and unit; preserve the input; ask the recorder. Keep valid unusual observations.

Ask students to distinguish a diagnostic flag from an authorised correction. Their independent transfer output must explicitly state that no correction is supported in the supplied complete transfer file.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Exercises: leave a repair trail
text:
Exercises: leave a repair trail
Save day11-cleaning.R, a derived CSV, and short cleaning notes.

Which source fact justified each change?
Which measurement stayed unknown?
Can the script recreate the corrected file after restarting R?

Open exercises.

Students should run inspection first, then the repairs, then verify counts. Have students locate the original, script, field notes, and output in their saved project. Corrections need source evidence.

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Keep explanation connected to calculation
text:
Keep explanation connected to calculation



An R Markdown source combining prose and code is rendered into an HTML report containing a plot.


Your report source is .Rmd. Its readable output is .html.

Open the supplied report.Rmd beside its HTML. These lecture webpages are made with Quarto, but students do not need to author Quarto. The course’s report format is R Markdown. Rendering runs the calculations and combines their output with prose instead of requiring manual copy-and-paste of results.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Code chunks have opening and closing fences
text:
Code chunks have opening and closing fences
```{r import}
library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
```

Ordinary sentences go outside chunks. Give each chunk a unique label.

The displayed fences are literal R Markdown syntax. Show the opening three backticks, braces with r and an optional label, then the closing fence. The report header between — lines sets title and html_document output. Demonstrate in the supplied template rather than asking students to reconstruct everything from memory.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: A report runs in order
text:
A report runs in order



Import and package loading must precede derived calculations, which precede the plot and interpretation.


Ask what each chunk needs before it can run.

Use seedlings then growth_mm then a figure as the concrete dependency. A correct expression can still fail when its input object does not yet exist. Package installation is separate setup; library calls belong in the report. Repeated unnecessary imports can obscure the sequence.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Read the first useful error
text:
Read the first useful error
Suppose a plot refers to growth_mm, but the report only imports the raw table.

Which earlier calculation is missing?
Is the name spelled exactly as created?
In which chunk should the repair go?


The raw CSV does not contain growth_mm. Add final minus initial in a preparation chunk before plotting. Include the dependency in the saved report. Deliberately introduce one misspelling in a demonstration, read the reported chunk, fix it, and render again.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Your Console is not the report’s saved method
text:
Your Console is not the report’s saved method



An object in an interactive R session does not automatically exist in a fresh report render.


Put all required imports and calculations in the source document.

Run an import only in the Console, then explain why a recipient cannot reproduce that unstated step. The Knit route uses a separate rendering process; the direct render function can use a calling environment, so the practical’s restart-and-render check is important. Explain why the fresh-session check matters.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: HTML is useful, but keep its inputs and source
text:
HTML is useful, but keep its inputs and source



The report source, original data, and HTML output have distinct roles and should be kept together.


The report belongs at the project root so data/ paths stay consistent.

A .Rmd file does not contain the original CSV simply because it mentions its name. An HTML file can be read without RStudio, but it is not the editable analysis source. Moving the report into reports/ would change ordinary relative paths; output HTML may go there while the source remains in the project root.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Render from the Console, not from inside itself
text:
Render from the Console, not from inside itself
Save the document, then use Knit, or run in the R Console:
rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")
Run this command in the Console, outside the report.

The double colon calls a function from a package. output_dir changes where the HTML is written, not where the source belongs. The Knit button may put the output beside the source; locate the actual file. Restart R before a reproducibility check. A self-rendering chunk would create a recursive workflow and is not required.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Chunk labels locate code in a report
text:
Chunk labels locate code in a report



Two chunks named import collide; unique labels allow the report to identify code locations.


Unique descriptive labels help diagnose an error.

Duplicate a label only in the disposable workshop copy. Read the first meaningful error, restore unique labels, and render successfully. Chunk labels locate code sections; they are not the headings in the final prose.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Break one thing, record it, then repair
text:
Break one thing, record it, then repair
In a workshop copy, test:

A duplicated chunk label.
A misspelt input filename.
A plot placed before its required calculation.

Restore a successful render after each test.

Change one cause at a time. Log the changed line, exact error, diagnosis, repair and successful rerun. Keep the original template available. Adding repeated imports randomly is not a diagnostic strategy.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Inline results are calculated dependencies
text:
Inline results are calculated dependencies



A number in report prose derives from the imported table and its row count.


When the input changes, the data description must change too.

The transfer report must describe 18 plants, nine per group, from the correct input. Inline calculations reduce copied stale numbers, but they do not automatically repair a written description of the wrong experimental design.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Input replacement needs a narrative audit
text:
Input replacement needs a narrative audit
Change the import to seedlings-transfer.csv.
Then check the question, methods, caption, inline count, and interpretation.
A new plot beneath an old 24-plant description is inconsistent.

The source and narrative must describe one deliberate study. Search for the old filename and the number 24 as prompts to investigate; not every occurrence is necessarily wrong. Retain separate workshop and transfer reports.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Source alone cannot supply a missing dataset
text:
Source alone cannot supply a missing dataset



Both source and ordinary input files are needed to regenerate the HTML.


A shortcut or screenshot does not replace the measurement file.

The local portability test uses a separate extracted project and its own root. Preserve relative input paths. This rehearsal does not verify authentication, remote software, or actual network transfer.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Run the renderer outside the report
text:
Run the renderer outside the report
Use Knit, or run in the R Console:
rmarkdown::render("report-workshop.Rmd")
Run this command in the Console, outside the report.

A render call inside the document would cause the report to try to render itself. Packages and calculations belong in its appropriate chunks; installing software belongs to the separate setup step.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Change the recipe, then rebuild its output
text:
Change the recipe, then rebuild its output



Editing an HTML output does not update the saved RMarkdown source.


Make revisions in .Rmd, then render and inspect the new HTML.

Source prose and code are editable instructions; HTML is the reading copy. A browser can show an older file if a student opens the wrong output location. Locate the actual rendered filename and folder.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: A recovery log preserves the lesson from an error
text:
A recovery log preserves the lesson from an error
Save the exact failure and successful repair.
Then restart R and render the corrected source without manual Console preparation.

Keep report-workshop.Rmd, transfer-report.Rmd, their HTML outputs and render-recovery.txt. Ask students to explain why code order and input location matter rather than memorising one particular error message.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Make one change and check it
text:
Make one change and check it
Open the exercises.
Render the unchanged template first. Then add your question, methods, labelled figure, and interpretation. Restart and render the saved source again.

Begin with a known-working baseline. Ask the student to name the source, output, and input locations before editing. The practical supplies a complete minimal report and error-recovery hints. A short caption plus clear prose is more useful than formatting additions that obscure the calculation.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Importing creates an object in this session
text:
Importing creates an object in this session



read_csv reads the saved seedling file into a 24-row, four-column object in R memory.


The saved input is separate from the imported object.

Open the course project before importing. A CSV is text; importing interprets it as a table. Editing the object leaves the CSV unchanged. Conversely, changing the CSV does not update an already imported object until reread. These are the same disk/memory distinctions from week 1.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Columns have roles and types
text:
Columns have roles and types



Plant IDs and treatments are labels, while initial and final length columns contain numeric measurements in millimetres.


One row is one plant. The column header is not another observation.

Read P01’s entire row aloud. The two length readings refer to the same plant seven days apart, not two independent plants. Numeric-looking IDs remain labels. The file’s contents cannot establish units or randomisation; use the data dictionary’s study description.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Load the importer, then inspect the result
text:
Load the importer, then inspect the result
library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
dim(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
str(seedlings)
Expect 24 rows × 4 columns in this complete teaching dataset.

A package is installed on storage but loaded in each session. read_csv returns a tibble, a table format; head prints only its first rows. Suppressing the importer message does not replace checking types. Point students at names rather than expecting exact column names from memory.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Start paths from the project root
text:
Start paths from the project root



The course folder contains data with seedlings.csv, alongside output and reports.


getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")

The second command should give TRUE. If not, identify the current folder, the actual extracted tree, and the computer holding the file. Common causes are an extra extraction folder or opening a ZIP preview. Reopen the intended project before retrying the relative path.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: An unavailable value is not a measured zero
text:
An unavailable value is not a measured zero



Two measured lengths surround an unavailable value; the available-value mean is based on two readings.


NA means not available. Explain missingness when reporting a result.

This is a separate toy vector, not a missing entry in seedlings.csv, which is complete. Replacing the unknown value by zero would invent a length measurement. A denominator should count what was actually observed for that summary. The practical later explains missing values more fully.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Ask R how the calculation handles missingness
text:
Ask R how the calculation handles missingness
example_mm <- c(12, NA, 18)
mean(example_mm)
mean(example_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
is.na(example_mm)
The first mean is NA; the second is 15 mm from two available values.

na.rm is an argument to the calculation, not deletion of the original row or an explanation of why data are missing. Ask students to read the is.na result. Later exercises will count missing observations explicitly and retain evidence for data corrections.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: A computation needs a biological description
text:
A computation needs a biological description
seedlings$initial_mm
length(seedlings$initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$initial_mm)

$ selects one column as a vector.
Count plants, not the header.
Describe an average length in mm, not only a number.


Have students distinguish the count from the mean. The mean initial length combines both allocations; it does not estimate a treatment difference. No hypothesis testing is needed today. The code only answers a meaningful question when the variable and observational unit are understood.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Type and meaning are different checks
text:
Type and meaning are different checks



Imported fields include identifier labels and measurements with stated units.


Numeric storage alone does not authorise averaging or dividing columns.

The solutions table has IDs and names as labels, with numeric mass, molar mass and volume. A supplied chemical name is context, not a request to identify a structure. The dictionary establishes units and row meaning.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Inspect more than the first displayed rows
text:
Inspect more than the first displayed rows
transfer <- read_csv("data/seedlings-transfer.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(transfer)
head(transfer)
tail(transfer)
head() is a preview, not the sample-size definition.

The imported table is 18 by 4; initial and final measurements belong to the same plant in each row. Inspect both ends and object structure rather than inferring 24 plants from the preceding lesson.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Check the supplied study’s expected structure
text:
Check the supplied study’s expected structure



The independent transfer study has 18 plants split nine per group.


Row counts, unique IDs, and group counts answer related but distinct questions.

Use length(plant_id), length(unique(plant_id)), and table(treatment). Repeated IDs can be legitimate in another design; here one row per plant sets the expectation. Random allocation is stated in the design, not demonstrated by sorted rows.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: A filename that opens is not the whole audit
text:
A filename that opens is not the whole audit
Record the source path, dimensions, types, identifiers, groups, and missing counts.
Name two facts that only the dictionary provides.

Units, random allocation, experimental unit, elapsed time and simulation status are not established by a successful import. Suppressing the type message does not replace inspection.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Zero and unavailable give different calculations
text:
Zero and unavailable give different calculations



Ignoring one unavailable reading gives mean 15, while recording a genuine zero gives mean 10.


The number of available measurements changes too.

For c(10, NA, 20), ordinary mean returns NA; na.rm = TRUE gives 15 from two available values. The vector c(10, 0, 20) has mean 10 from three measurements. Replacing missing by zero invents a value.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Read the next table before choosing operations
text:
Read the next table before choosing operations
Import solutions.csv, then inspect:

Six rows and five columns.
Unique solution IDs and two solute labels.
Numeric mass, molar mass, and final volume.
Units and row meaning from the supplied dictionary.


Define a mole as a chemical amount unit and molar mass as grams per mole. Today the learner audits inputs; the next lesson derives concentrations. These are numerical preparation cases, not independently allocated experimental groups.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: The same kind of project may hold different inputs
text:
The same kind of project may hold different inputs



Separate study folders may contain 24 or 18 records with similar column names.


Check which input produced the result before changing the written sample size.

A wrong project with a plausible-looking filename can produce plausible output. Restart R, rerun the script, and identify the input behind each audit. Source provenance matters even when file.exists returns TRUE.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Keep the import audit useful to another person
text:
Keep the import audit useful to another person
A strong audit gives evidence:
“18 rows, 18 distinct IDs, nine per group, no missing lengths.”
It also states what was supplied by the study design.

A useful audit records specific evidence rather than simply saying checked. Save the two audit notes and script. Unusual range values prompt questions and source inspection, not automatic deletion.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Import a second table deliberately
text:
Import a second table deliberately
Open the exercises.
Save day07.R, then inspect data/leaf-mass.csv too.
Which columns and units differ? What does one row represent there?

The leaf table has eighteen independent plants, one leaf each, area in square centimetres and dry mass in milligrams. A scatter plot can describe association without establishing causation. Reuse the import/inspect workflow while reading that dataset’s dictionary rather than assuming the seedling schema applies.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Share files, then meet R
section: A package should contain the useful files
text:
A package should contain the useful files



A report folder containing findings and selected records is packaged into a separate ZIP.


First make the ordinary folder understandable; then archive it.

Today consolidates the previous days rather than introducing a new shell language. The working folder contains findings explaining the question and selected sample records. A ZIP should be outside the folder being archived. It is a transport package, not proof that its contents are correct.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: A copy and a rename do different things
text:
A copy and a rename do different things



A copy retains the source and creates another file; a move changes a name or location.


Check source and destination names before running either command.

Ask which entries exist after cp, then after mv. The drawing isolates each operation; the practical uses course files. Changes to the ordinary report folder do not automatically change a previously created archive. Repackage after revisions.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Test the ZIP by making the return trip
text:
Test the ZIP by making the return trip
From the folder containing report/:
zip -r report-bundle.zip report/
unzip -l report-bundle.zip
unzip report-bundle.zip -d check-report
Open the extracted files and check that the findings make sense.

Explain -r as including folder contents, including nested folders. The extraction destination should be fresh. Inspect the resulting tree rather than assuming extraction put findings directly in check-report; the report folder itself is included. A same-disk archive is not a backup against losing the laptop.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Remote access and file transfer are separate
text:
Remote access and file transfer are separate



A laptop displays a remote session, while explicit transfer moves a file between separate storage locations.


Always name the computer that holds the file or runs the command.

This is a conceptual preview; actual service settings remain pending. SSH gives a terminal and remote desktop a graphical workspace. Neither automatically synchronises Downloads. Explain that process behaviour after disconnection depends on how it was started. Use the supported course route when available.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Transfer the same skill to another lab record
text:
Transfer the same skill to another lab record
Optional choice: inspect organic-lab.zip and its supplied inventory.
grep -F ester inventory.tsv
grep -F ester inventory.tsv | wc -l
Two records match: O02 and O03.

Students choose this or the seedling file-route check. The sample classes are already assigned labels. Searching ester is a text operation, not identification from a molecular structure. The archive also contains a later numerical practice table; no need to analyse it today.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Shell commands and R expressions differ
text:
Shell commands and R expressions differ



A shell searches text files, while an R console evaluates a numerical expression.


Ask “which interface is waiting?” before typing.

Open RStudio only after students can explain the shell task. Its Console accepts R, while its editor holds a saved script or report. Windows students will use native RStudio in the extracted project, not assume that R is installed inside Ubuntu. Keep the two working locations explicit.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: One biological calculation in R
text:
One biological calculation in R
In the R Console:
44.3 - 25.7
P01 grew 18.6 mm between the two measurements.
Saving the instructions will let us repeat that calculation tomorrow.

The numbers come from the complete 24-plant R dataset, not the four-record shell archive. Type the expression after the Console prompt. [1] in printed output labels the first element; it is not part of the measurement. Demonstrate a supplied report briefly to show where these skills lead without teaching its syntax yet.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: A ZIP is a snapshot
text:
A ZIP is a snapshot



An older ZIP retains version1 while the ordinary source and a newly made ZIP contain version2.


Editing a source folder does not update an existing archive.

Create v1, extract and inspect it; revise the ordinary note; inspect v1 again before packaging v2. The change must be recognisable in contents, not only a renamed archive. This is file version discipline, not a Git topic.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: What must the receiver know?
text:
What must the receiver know?
A README should identify:

The source and what each included file does.
What one record represents and its units.
Which selection was performed.
Any input the receiver still needs.


Students should close the source windows and identify a selected sample using only the extracted README and files. A shortcut is not the target dataset. If the raw source is not included, the receipt must give its actual available source rather than pretending the package is complete.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Extraction can add another folder level
text:
Extraction can add another folder level



The received note is inside receiver-v1/report/findings.txt, not directly inside receiver-v1.


Inspect the extracted tree before constructing a path.

The folder name inside the archive is preserved. A new extraction destination is outside it, so an additional level is expected. This connects the archive exercise to the extra wrapper folder sometimes created when the course project is downloaded.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Keep the archive outside what it packages
text:
Keep the archive outside what it packages
zip -r report-v2.zip report/
unzip -l report-v2.zip
unzip report-v2.zip -d receiver-v2
Run from the folder containing report/.

The package should not contain itself. When source changes, create a fresh named snapshot rather than assuming an old ZIP is live. The receiver test checks ordinary extracted files, not merely an archive listing.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Test the handover from a new location
text:
Test the handover from a new location



A sharing archive is extracted in a separate receiver location and checked from its README.


The receiver’s successful check is stronger evidence than your own familiar view.

A single laptop copy tests portability but not all cross-machine software differences. If remote transfer is available, identify the supported direction and destination. Distinguish testing another local folder from transferring between computers.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Find the stale copy before recalculating
text:
Find the stale copy before recalculating
The extracted copy lacks your correction.
What would you ask first?
Check the archive version, extraction folder, and actual note contents.

A missing revision can be a location/version problem rather than an editing failure. Have students compare v1 and v2 contents and record the correction sentence in handover-check.txt. Use distinct version names and a change note to identify the current package.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: The interpreter matters too
text:
The interpreter matters too



Shell and R Console accept different instruction languages.


The wrong window needs a changed context, not system repair.

Classify pwd, grep, unzip as shell commands, and arithmetic/mean as R. Run 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 and mean(c(12, 14, 16)) = 14 in R if setup works. Keep Windows native RStudio and local Ubuntu workspace separate.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Explain what was actually reproduced
text:
Explain what was actually reproduced
A receiver can identify the selection and inspect the saved records.
What would they still need to recompute a future report?
Keep a source/input/output distinction in the receipt.

The current week5 R work has not happened yet; students are meeting R, not required to construct a report from scratch today. The ordinary source files, data dictionary and later R code will make calculations repeatable. A screenshot or HTML alone is not the complete recipe.

title: Share files, then meet R
section: Finish with a clear handover
text:
Finish with a clear handover
Open the exercises.

Retain the ordinary report folder and a tested report-bundle.zip.
Explain which files were inputs and which were derived.
Follow the R/RStudio setup guide if installation support is needed.


Ask students to find all the relevant files after closing their windows. Save the optional ester extract if that route was chosen. Resolve file-location problems before starting next week’s R work.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Same folder, another interface
text:
Same folder, another interface



A file-manager window and terminal listing show the same practice folder.


A shell reads commands; the terminal is the window we use to interact with it.

Explain why this is worth learning: repeatable file work and remote Linux access. Windows uses Ubuntu; Mac uses Terminal. Show the workspace in both interfaces. Changing the folder in one window does not automatically move the other; each has its own current location.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Read the prompt before typing
text:
Read the prompt before typing



The terminal prompt, cd command, and practice destination have distinct roles.


Type only the command after the prompt. Press Enter to run it.

A prompt indicates readiness, not a command to copy. A Mac prompt may end in percent. Our example username is illustrative. Distinguish command from argument now; an option such as -p is an instruction modifying a command’s behaviour.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Build a small workspace
text:
Build a small workspace
Run one line at a time:
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing-shell/practice
cd introcomputing-shell
pwd
ls
pwd reports the location. ls should include practice.

cd without a destination takes the user home. mkdir -p creates needed parent folders and accepts an existing folder. This workspace is deliberately separate from the native R project on Windows. Pause to confirm pwd and the practice name; browser Downloads may be elsewhere.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Navigation changes the starting point
text:
Navigation changes the starting point



Forward cd commands move into child folders; cd dot-dot returns to a parent.


. means here; .. means the parent; ~ means your home directory.

Walk into practice and then make seedlings and observations as in the practical. Ask students to predict the end of pwd before each command. The schematic workspace is introcomputing-shell. A path uses names already present; cd does not create a new destination.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Silence can be a successful result
text:
Silence can be a successful result



An empty observations folder produces no names between the ls command and the next prompt.


An empty directory exists even when ls prints no visible entries.

Run ls in a newly created directory. Contrast it with cd no-such-folder, which reports an error. The terminal is not a chat interface: commands often finish quietly. This example concerns visible entries; hidden entries are not needed for today’s practical.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Recover by checking, not guessing
text:
Recover by checking, not guessing
cd no-such-folder
pwd
ls

Read the error: the destination does not exist.
Match spelling and case to actual names.
Return with cd ~/introcomputing-shell if lost.


The failed cd leaves the current directory unchanged. Ubuntu is case-sensitive; a default Mac disk may accept case differences. Always match names so work transfers. Don’t teach deletion or broad system repair to handle a navigation typo.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Make typing easier without changing the task
text:
Make typing easier without changing the task

Tab: complete an unambiguous filename or folder name.
Up arrow: recall a command; read it before rerunning.
Ctrl+C: interrupt a command or cancel partly typed input.
Quote a space-containing name: mkdir "field notes".


Demonstrate each on disposable course folders. Ctrl+C is not the terminal copy shortcut; local Ubuntu commonly uses Ctrl+Shift+C/V while Mac uses Command+C/V. The practical gives platform detail. Ask why two unquoted words may become two arguments.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Spaces change argument boundaries
text:
Spaces change argument boundaries



Unquoted mkdir field notes creates separate names while quoted field notes is one name.


Quote a space-containing name, or use a simple name while learning.

Demonstrate only inside a disposable practice tree. The shell divides unquoted words into arguments; it does not read a natural-language folder description. Tab completion helps use names actually present.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Read a command as an action with inputs
text:
Read a command as an action with inputs
mkdir "field notes"
cd "field notes"
pwd
Name the command, destination argument, and resulting location.

Options modify behaviour; arguments supply values. Here quotes group the two-word destination, not a new kind of folder. Type only the command after the prompt. Explain the distinction before students copy the examples.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: A failed cd leaves you where you were
text:
A failed cd leaves you where you were



A failed change-directory command leaves the original current directory unchanged.


An error message is information about the attempted action.

Record the failed destination and pwd result. Return to a known workspace and inspect names to recover.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Prediction: which commands create something?
text:
Prediction: which commands create something?
pwd
ls
mkdir readings
cd readings
Which line changes storage? Which changes the shell’s starting location?

mkdir creates a directory; cd changes that shell’s working directory; pwd and ls inspect. Their output or silence should be connected to an action rather than judged as successful solely because text appeared.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Two shells can look at different folders
text:
Two shells can look at different folders



Two terminal windows have independently maintained current working directories.


Moving Shell A does not automatically move Shell B.

Open two actual windows and record each pwd. It is possible to inspect the same files from both while standing in different folders. File-manager location is another independent view. These are local shells unless an SSH connection has been made.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Recover with a named return point
text:
Recover with a named return point
cd ~/introcomputing-shell
pwd
ls
Check the actual tree before taking the next route.

The tilde refers to the current account’s home on this computer. It is not the root of the entire filesystem. This return point is useful because the course deliberately created it; a path to a missing workspace cannot conjure it into existence.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Follow the route from the stated start
text:
Follow the route from the stated start



A route from nested notes to neighbouring inputs must go up twice.


From results/notes, reach inputs through the common parent.

Have students draw the tree and predict before commands. The independent route challenge asks for root to notes, notes to inputs, and inputs to the workspace. A correct path needs the correct starting place and existing destination names.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: A command log records reasoning
text:
A command log records reasoning
For each test, save:

Starting folder and command.
Predicted ending location.
Actual pwd or listing.
Recovery if the prediction was wrong.


The log can be a plain-text note edited graphically; no logging software or shell scripting is needed. Include the computer, especially if the exercise is later repeated remotely. A recorded error and successful recovery are useful evidence of understanding.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Connect words to the graphical view
text:
Connect words to the graphical view
Open the exercises.

Ubuntu on Windows: explorer.exe .
Mac: open .
Save navigation-notes.txt in the shell workspace.

Be able to state what cd changes and what it leaves unchanged.

These graphical-opening commands are local conveniences, not remote transfer. Have students independently reproduce the workspace tree, recover from one ordinary mistake, and identify the same folder in the file manager. Their note should give a route back from home and three command meanings.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: A file is not the window showing it
text:
A file is not the window showing it



One saved CSV can be read as text or as a table in different applications.



The same seedlings.csv can be opened in a text editor or a spreadsheet.
Closing the window does not delete the file.


Show it both ways. Ask what happens to the measurements when both windows close: nothing, they are still saved. Avoid a discussion of which program is best; the point is one file, several programs.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Downloading is only the first step
text:
Downloading is only the first step

Download the course ZIP using the browser.
Show the download in File Explorer or Finder.
Extract the whole folder into a place you can find again.
Open a file from the extracted folder, not from a ZIP preview.


Demonstrate on the supported operating system. Pause after locating Downloads and check that everyone can find the file. Windows Extract All and Mac double-click may produce an extra parent directory. Choose one working copy.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Locate the measurement inside its folder
text:
Locate the measurement inside its folder



The project contains data, output, and reports folders; seedlings.csv is inside data.


Find data/seedlings.csv by opening folders, without using “recent files”.

Use this as a map before introducing the formal path vocabulary tomorrow. The diagram is deliberately incomplete: the real project has other datasets too. Identify data as the input location and output as a place for derived work. Ask students to point at the correct file in their own graphical window.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: The filename gives clues, not a calculation
text:
The filename gives clues, not a calculation



Name
Intended content




seedlings.csv
A text table of measurements


day01-notes.txt
Your plain-text note


report.Rmd
Source for a future report



The extension is part of the name. Renaming a file does not convert its contents.

Show file extensions in the file manager. Define CSV as comma-separated values; students do not need to know parsing yet. Read P01’s first row as a plant ID, treatment label, initial length 25.7 mm, final length 44.3 mm. Units and meaning come from the dictionary, not from an application guessing them.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Preserve the original measurements
text:
Preserve the original measurements



Copying the raw CSV into output creates a separate practice file while retaining the original.


Our supplied data are simulated. Keep the raw file unchanged.

Demonstrate copying data/seedlings.csv to output/seedlings-practice.csv. Point out the two locations and the two names. Edit only the practice copy. A duplicate is useful here because it separates input from practice; unexplained duplicate projects are different and should be resolved before continuing.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Save, close, and reopen
text:
Save, close, and reopen



An edited note is saved to disk and then reopened from its folder.


Save day01-notes.txt in reports/. Close the editor. Find the note through its folder and open it again.

Use a plain-text editor. Some editors restore unsaved text when reopened, so the test is: can you find the saved file in its folder? Have students say where their note is: which folder, which full name.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Predict before clicking
text:
Predict before clicking
Answer each one, then check on your own computer:

You close the editor. Did the saved note disappear?
You edit seedlings-practice.csv. Did data/seedlings.csv change?
You know a file’s name. Do you know which folder it is in?
You rename a .csv to .txt. Did the measurements change?
A colleague sends a screenshot of the table. What can you check from it, and what must you still ask for?


Expected answers: 1 no, a saved file survives closing; 2 no, the practice copy is a separate file; 3 not necessarily, several folders can contain the same name; 4 no, renaming does not convert; 5 a screenshot shows visible headings and values and can help discuss a problem, but may omit rows, cannot be read by R, and cannot be updated; ask for the CSV and its dictionary. Have students demonstrate 1, 2 and 4 on their own files rather than just answering.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Read the whole filename
text:
Read the whole filename



The base name and .csv extension play different roles in seedlings-practice.csv.



The ending (.csv, .txt) is part of the name. Turn on “show file extensions”.
Renaming a file does not change what is inside it.


Show the file-manager setting for extensions. With extensions hidden, a note can end up as notes.txt.rtf without anyone noticing. Renaming .csv to .txt leaves the same commas and numbers inside; the exercises let students try this on a copy.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: A format is not an application
text:
A format is not an application
A CSV can open in a spreadsheet or a text editor.

The saved information is still comma-separated text.
The application presents that information differently.
A filename extension is a clue; it does not prove the contents.


Ask students to close one view and reopen the same ordinary file in the other. Keep the input unchanged. The key observation is identity of the file and path, not that a particular application is always best.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Connect a row to a plant
text:
Connect a row to a plant



The header labels fields while a record describes one plant.


P01 ended at 44.3 mm; it did not increase by 44.3 mm.

Read all four P01 fields in order and give the mm units from the dictionary. Work 44.3 minus 25.7 equals 18.6. The computer cannot infer that study design or those units from the comma characters.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Prediction: what would a screenshot preserve?
text:
Prediction: what would a screenshot preserve?
You receive a picture of the measurement table.
What can you inspect? What would you still request before calculating?

A screenshot can help discuss an error, show column headings, or locate a visible value. It is not the ordinary machine-readable table, may omit rows, and is awkward to update. Ask for the CSV and its dictionary.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Several copies need an explicit choice
text:
Several copies need an explicit choice



Downloading twice gives course-files (1).zip; extracting twice gives two similar folders.
Similar names do not mean identical contents — one may have your edits.
Choose one working project by its contents and path: data, output, and the .Rproj file directly inside.
Do not delete a similar folder until you know what is in it.





One original can lead to several extracted project folders with similar names.




This is the row “a report was rebuilt from an older copy” in the motivation table. Show a second extraction and a “(1)” download. Open folders until the chosen root is clear. No deletion is required today; students should ask before removing anything that might contain their own work.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Check saving with a closed window
text:
Check saving with a closed window

Write a sentence in a plain-text note.
Save to a named folder.
Close the editor and file manager.
Navigate back and reopen the ordinary file.


An application may autosave or restore drafts. The reliable check is the actual saved ordinary file. Have students state its computer, folder and full name, and compare it with the source measurements rather than storing observations only in a screenshot.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Renaming does not convert the contents
text:
Renaming does not convert the contents



Renaming seedlings-practice.csv to name-test.txt changes only the label.
The commas and measurements inside are identical.
To change a format you must export or convert with a program that rewrites the content.
An extension is a clue, not proof of what is inside. A wrong extension makes a file misleading.

Experiment only on a copy, then restore the informative name.




A CSV and the same text renamed .txt contain identical records.




This connects to the motivation table: renaming report.docx to report.pdf does not make a PDF. Demonstrate on output/name-test.txt made from a practice copy and open it in a text editor: the same records are there. Then restore the .csv name. Students should leave able to say: the name is a promise about the content; only a converting program changes the content.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: A receipt makes another input understandable
text:
A receipt makes another input understandable
For the transfer study, save a note identifying:

The source and your inspection copy.
What one row records and its units.
T01’s initial, final, and change values.
Where to find the ordinary file again.


Use the new eighteen-plant table only after defining its study. T01 is 25.3 to 40.3 mm, an increase of 15.0 mm. T18 is treated, 21.6 to 43.0 mm. The independent task assesses file handling and interpretation, not importing into R yet.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Now practise the complete route
text:
Now practise the complete route
Open the exercises.
Leave with:

reports/day01-notes.txt.
output/seedlings-practice.csv.
The ability to locate both after closing their applications.


The practical supplies the detailed click sequence and hints. Give time for independent reopening. A student unable to locate their files needs support before tomorrow’s path lesson; finishing a screenshot alone does not establish this skill.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Today’s purpose
text:
Today’s purpose
Practise the workflow for later biology laboratories: locate measurements, check them, make a figure, explain variation, and produce a reproducible report.
Choose the station where you need practice first. Everyone should eventually complete the file recovery, R recovery, and interpretation checks. Use the reference pages when needed.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Station 1 — find and inspect the laboratory files
text:
Station 1 — find and inspect the laboratory files
Download a fresh copy of lab-data.zip and locate it. In your shell workspace, inspect the archive, extract it into a new folder, read the README, locate the sample manifest, and find the treated records. Before running a pipe, predict how many matching records it should count.
Save an extract named treated-samples.txt, then locate it in a file manager. Explain what > changed and whether the source manifest was modified. Package the extracted folder into a new archive placed outside it; list the archive and confirm the text extract was included.






Hint: the small vocabulary is enough





Use pwd, ls, cd, unzip -l, unzip … -d …, less, grep -F, wc -l, and zip -r. Check the terminal reference. The manifest has two treated records; its header is not one of them.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Station 2 — repair a small R analysis
text:
Station 2 — repair a small R analysis
The following code contains errors. Identify them and write a corrected version in recovery.R in your project root:
seedling <- read_csv("seedlings.csv")
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm + initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$Growth_mm)
Consider package loading, file location, object names, case, and the meaning of growth. Confirm the repaired calculation using P01: initial length 25.7 mm, final length 44.3 mm. Save a labelled plot without changing raw data.






A working repair





library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- seedlings |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$growth_mm)
P01 grew 18.6 mm. The original used a wrong relative path, inconsistent object names, addition rather than subtraction, and inconsistent column case. It also did not establish that readr and dplyr were loaded in this session.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Station 3 — explain before calculating
text:
Station 3 — explain before calculating
Explain each situation:

One treated plant has 100 cells measured; one control plant also has 100. A student says there are 100 independent replicates per group. What is wrong?
Two groups have the same mean but one has twice the SD. What can you say about their observations?
A missing biomass value is replaced with zero. Why can that change the biological meaning of the analysis?
A treatment-minus-control estimate is 3 mm with a 95% interval of −2 to 8 mm. Does this establish no effect?
An unknown sample gives absorbance greater than the largest calibration standard. What should happen before reporting its concentration?
A fitted leaf-area/mass slope is positive. Does it prove that changing area experimentally will produce the same change in mass?







Compare your reasoning






There is only one independent treated and one independent control plant; cells within them do not supply independent treatment allocation.
Spread differs even though the means match. Equal means do not imply identical observations or distributions.
Unknown biomass and genuinely absent biomass are different observations. Zero invents a value and can shift the mean, SD, and comparison.
No: the interval includes zero and effects in both directions. Explain the range of compatible values rather than declaring equality.
Flag it as beyond range; dilute and remeasure using the assay protocol.
No: this is an observational association. Other plant properties may vary too.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Station 4 — your complete report
text:
Station 4 — your complete report
Return to the report from day 23 or one that still needs work. Starting from a fresh session, render it without running console code first. Check that it has:

A biological or laboratory question and the correct independent experimental unit: a flask for duckweed or a synthesis run for the organic alternative.
The input filename, measurement units, and missing-data account.
A readable plot of observations and a small relevant summary.
An appropriately directed comparison or a line fit, if the question needs it.
An interpretation with size, variation or uncertainty, and a limitation.
Relative input paths, all required code, and an HTML output you can locate beside the source or in the documented reports/ output folder.

Repeat the workflow on an earlier dataset. Record which steps would change for a new biology practical and which would stay the same.
If you chose the organic alternative on day 23, use organic-study.Rmd and data/organic-recovery.csv here. Its descriptive group means and SD are enough; a new test is not needed. Higher yield alone cannot demonstrate higher purity.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Station 5 — local and remote, when available
text:
Station 5 — local and remote, when available
Identify the computer and folder behind an SSH session, locate a supplied file, disconnect, reconnect, and find it again. Locate the designated shared folder through remote desktop and transfer one output to your laptop. If access is still pending, record this as an outstanding practical skill; completing local stations does not complete the remote-access task.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Your handover to the next biology course
text:
Your handover to the next biology course
Save reports/next-lab.txt with a short workflow you can reuse: where to store raw data, how to open a project, which checks to make, how to choose a figure, and how to render and back up your report. Include one question you would ask a lab teacher before analysing a dataset, such as “what was independently assigned to treatment?” or “what do blank cells mean?”

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Investigate a high measurement
text:
Investigate a high measurement
Use your algae script and brief report from days 23–24, so the final day consolidates familiar methods. Work in copies for diagnostic changes, keep the primary result from all available measurements, and record what you changed in reports/final-investigation.txt.

From the file manager, locate the project, algae-transfer.R, algae-brief.Rmd, input CSV, and generated HTML without using recent files. Write their project-relative paths. If one is missing, repair that part of the portfolio before changing the analysis.
Open the supplied algae CSV without editing it. Identify the largest reference-group measurement and its culture ID. Check the dictionary for evidence that it is erroneous. There is none: a large value is a question to investigate, not permission to remove an observation.
Recreate the primary group summaries from all available measurements. State the observed supplement-minus-reference mean difference in mg. Label this result “primary, all available measurements”. A19 remains unavailable.
Create a separately named diagnostic object that omits A11, and repeat the group means and observed difference. The aim is to see how one high reference value influences a small-sample summary. Label the diagnostic result “sensitivity check, A11 omitted without evidence of error”. This label distinguishes it from the primary result.
Compare the two differences and reference means. Explain why the supplement mean is unchanged, why the reference mean changes, and why the diagnostic sample count is different.
In a copied report, add a short limitations paragraph distinguishing unavailable A19, unusually high but recorded A11, and the simplifying assumptions of the study. These are three different issues. Restore or retain the primary analysis as the main result, with the diagnostic clearly marked if included at all.
Render, close, and reopen the report. Confirm the prose, counts, and plotted observations all refer to the primary dataset. A diagnostic object left in memory must not accidentally change the main figure or inline results.







Hint: separate objects make the decision visible





Start from the imported algae object and use a name such as algae_without_a11 <- filter(algae, culture_id != "A11") for the diagnostic. Use na.rm = TRUE in a summary while still reporting available counts. Save derived output separately from data/algae.csv. The primary reference mean is about 28.20 mg and the available supplement mean about 33.92 mg; use your unrounded values for the difference. Omitting a high reference value will lower that reference mean and increase the observed difference, without establishing that the altered estimate is more scientifically justified.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Test a laboratory handover
text:
Test a laboratory handover
Write a workflow from the question and saved files, then test it. Use references when needed.

Write handover instructions for a future reader: the scientific question, where the original data are, what one row means, and which report should be rendered. Include the missing-value meaning and expected output. If using your organic main report, restate the supplied theoretical maximum, collected mass, and percentage formula.
Close RStudio and reopen the project from its saved location. Starting in a fresh session, run your chosen source from the top or Knit the report. Record the first point at which you needed a reference and how it helped.
Independently verify one input record and one group summary using a small separate calculation. For the algae memo, count the available values in each group; for an organic report, check one yield’s numerator, denominator, and units. Explain how an arithmetic check differs from validating the experimental design.
Extract the tested package into a new parent folder. Follow the handover instructions to locate the input, render the source, and identify the main result and a limitation.
If you find an ambiguity, revise the source or README and make a new clearly named package. Extract and check that replacement too. An edit in the original Windows copy does not update an Ubuntu copy already packaged; use the transfer/version checks from day 21.
Open the returned HTML as a reader. Find the axes’ units, figure’s observational unit, available counts, and limitation. Explain why a successful render alone cannot supply those meanings.
Save reports/readiness-review.txt: three actions you can now perform reliably, two actions needing another rehearsal, and the concrete next practice task for each. List remote login/desktop/transfer as pending if you have not used the actual service. Store your final source, data, results, and retrievable backup according to the supported course route.

Keep: the primary report, labelled diagnostic calculation, investigation log, verified handover package, and readiness review.
Before you finish: locate the final report, source, input, and backup without using a recent-files menu. Keep the reference pages and your working project template for later practicals.

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
A result on screen may depend on console objects or files outside your project. Find those dependencies and test a complete project in a new location.
You need: yesterday’s .Rmd, its data, and your project folder. Save the revised report, its HTML, and reports/reproduction-log.txt.
Use the study you selected on day 23. The folder example below uses duckweed; for the organic alternative, substitute organic-study.Rmd, its HTML, and data/organic-recovery.csv. Keep the data dictionary in either case. You only need to reproduce one report.

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
section: 1. Close the gaps in the report
text:
1. Close the gaps in the report
Read the report as if you had not conducted the exercise. Does it identify the biological or laboratory question, simulated study design, independent units, data source, missing measurement, methods, and conclusion? Are figure axes and the comparison direction labelled? Can you distinguish SD among flasks from uncertainty in the estimated difference?
For the descriptive organic alternative, check SD among independent synthesis runs and the observed difference in percentage points.
Replace notes such as “insert result here” with your interpretation. Keep enough code to reproduce the result, alongside an explanation of its meaning.

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
section: 2. Render after restarting
text:
2. Render after restarting
Save the .Rmd, restart R in RStudio, then use Knit without manually running analysis lines in the console first. Restarting removes session objects, while saved input files remain. If the render fails, locate the named chunk and read the first meaningful error before changing several things at once.








Failure
Likely dependency
Repair




object 'duckweed' not found
Import happened only in the console
Put import code before analysis chunks


A function is unavailable
Package was loaded only interactively
Add its library() call to setup


Input path cannot be opened
Personal absolute path or missing project files
Use data/duckweed.csv and include that file


Export fails
Destination directory was not included
Include the empty output folder or create it explicitly


Old text contradicts new numbers
Result was manually typed and not updated
Check interpretation and use inline results where useful



List required packages in the README. Install them during setup and load them in the report’s setup chunk.

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
section: 3. Package the necessary inputs and source
text:
3. Package the necessary inputs and source
Create a folder named report-share outside your working project using the file manager. Copy the following into it:
report-share/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── duckweed-report.Rmd
├── duckweed-report.html
├── README.txt
├── data/
│   ├── duckweed.csv
│   └── README.md
└── output/
    └── README.txt
Keep the data dictionary so the recipient knows the study design. The output folder is needed if the report explicitly saves a figure there. Exclude session files, credentials, and unrelated personal work. Write a short README stating that the data are simulated, required packages, the file to render, and the expected HTML output. The HTML alone is readable but is not the source analysis.
In a shell, from the folder containing report-share, make a ZIP:
zip -r report-share.zip report-share/
unzip -l report-share.zip
On Windows you may first use File Explorer to copy report-share into the Ubuntu shell workspace. Check its location before running the command. Native RStudio still uses the Windows copy. If you revise that Windows copy, copy the revised files into Ubuntu again before creating a replacement ZIP; the copies do not synchronise. Copy the finished ZIP back to a normal Windows folder before extracting it for the native RStudio check below. Keep the archive outside the folder being archived.

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
section: 4. Reproduce from a different location
text:
4. Reproduce from a different location
Extract the ZIP into a new parent folder with a different path. Open its .Rproj and render the .Rmd in a fresh R session. Record the outcome before changing any source. This tests relative paths and included files on your laptop; it does not test every software environment.
Compare the numerical results, group counts, and interpretation. Plot layout may vary slightly across software versions; a jitter seed helps point placement stay consistent. Record the software information if results differ:
sessionInfo()
Save this output in your log when needed. R and loaded package versions help investigate differences.






Hint: the project opens, but input is still missing





Look at the actual extracted folder tree. A .Rproj file does not contain the data; it sets the project context. A shortcut to your original data folder is also not a transferred dataset. Include the ordinary CSV itself.

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
section: What to record
text:
What to record
In reports/reproduction-log.txt, write the source archive name, destination folder, whether rendering succeeded before fixes, any exact error, the correction, and whether the rerun reproduced the key values.

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

Why can a report work after “Run All” but fail for a recipient?
Does a ZIP stored on the same disk protect against losing that disk?
What does a successful fresh-folder render establish?







Short answers






It may rely on session state, personal paths, or files not included in the ZIP.
No. A separate supported backup is needed for that failure.
That the supplied source and inputs can regenerate the report in the tested environment. It does not prove that the biological design or interpretation is correct, or that every future software version will behave identically.

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
section: Investigate controlled failures
text:
Investigate controlled failures
Use a disposable copy of the share project, named report-investigation, outside your original working project. Keep the original report and raw data intact. Use the same main study as yesterday.

Render the unmodified copied report first. Record the input filename, available group counts, one key numerical result, and the output location in reports/reproduction-cases.txt in your original project. This is the successful reference run against which later cases will be compared.
In the disposable copy only, rename the required input CSV by adding -temporarily-missing to its name, leaving the report’s path unchanged. Restart R, render, and record the first meaningful error and chunk. Predict whether any valid new result can be produced from the now unavailable input.
Restore the input’s exact name, render again, and confirm that the key result matches the reference. A repair is not complete just because the error message disappeared; check the result and record the restored relationship.
Make another fresh disposable copy. In its .Rmd, replace one calculated result sentence with the deliberately wrong sentence “All enrolled samples had an available outcome.” Render without altering the code. Compare the sentence with the counts and raw data for duckweed. For the organic route, use “The percentage yield independently demonstrates product purity.” Rendering can succeed while this interpretation is false or unsupported.
Record whether each case is an execution failure, an interpretation failure, or neither. Rewrite the incorrect sentence using the evidence. Keep the final source correct and label each diagnostic copy.
After completing the algae exercise below, revisit one diagnostic copy. Follow your written procedure to locate the input, render from a fresh session, and compare prose with results. Revise ambiguous instructions.

A useful case record has columns for changed item, predicted effect, observed error or inconsistency, repair, and confirming rerun.






Hint: three questions before making a repair





Which computer and project are running? Is the named input actually present at that relative path? Does the saved source create the objects and make claims supported by the data? Renaming a copied CSV should cause an input error; replacing a sentence with a false claim may cause no software error at all. A successful rerun therefore checks computational reproduction, not scientific validity by itself.

title: Day 24 — reproduce your report from saved files
section: Package the algae analysis
text:
Package the algae analysis
Use yesterday’s algae script and results. If the input is missing, copy data/algae.csv and its dictionary from a separately extracted course ZIP.

Create algae-brief.Rmd at the project root. Include a short question, the supplied culture design, the missing A19 account, your import/check/summary code, one individual-point figure, and the interpretation. All required objects and packages must be created or loaded in its chunks.
Turn the stated available sample sizes into inline calculated results rather than typing them independently of the data. Check the rendered counts against the summary. Use HTML as before; no new document format is required.
Render after restarting. Open the HTML in a browser and ask whether a reader can identify biomass units, culture as the unit, what the points represent, and the missingness limitation without seeing the source code.
Create a new folder algae-share outside the working project. Include the .Rproj, algae-brief.Rmd, its HTML, data/algae.csv, the dictionary, and the output folder if your source exports there. Add a README specifying the required packages and the file to render. Do not include console session files, account information, or links to an untransferred local data folder.
Package the folder, extract it into a different parent location, open that copy’s project, and render without first running console lines. On Windows, preserve the explicit Windows/Ubuntu copy steps used above; a ZIP created in Ubuntu must be returned to normal Windows storage for a native-RStudio check. Check source, data, and rendered output in the extracted copy.
Compare the available counts, two means, and observed difference with your earlier memo. If they differ, inspect the inputs and code before blaming rounding. Record sessionInfo() only if needed to explain environment differences; it is a record for diagnosis, not a replacement for the data.
Save reports/algae-reproduction.txt with what you tested, the outcome, any correction, and a limitation of the test. A second folder on one laptop does not establish that every other software environment will work.

Keep: the tested main-study package, controlled-case record, algae source/HTML, and tested algae-share package.
Before you finish: retain the corrected report, tested ZIP, and a copy on the supported backup storage. Next: consolidation and error recovery.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: The question
text:
The question
Duckweed is a small aquatic plant that grows as floating fronds. In our simulated study, twenty separate flasks started with equal amounts of duckweed. Ten flasks were randomly allocated additional nutrients; ten were controls. Final dry biomass was measured after seven days. How does biomass differ between the two allocations, and how uncertain is that estimated difference?
Save duckweed-report.Rmd in the project root and render its HTML. Keep the original CSV intact.
Complete one study: duckweed below, or the organic-laboratory alternative if your teacher selects it. Duckweed includes a Welch comparison; the organic study uses a descriptive comparison.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 1. Read the design before the numbers
text:
1. Read the design before the numbers
Open the data dictionary, then locate data/duckweed.csv. The columns are flask_id, treatment, and biomass_mg. The two allocation labels are control and nutrient. One nutrient flask, F17, was spilled before weighing, so its final biomass is unavailable.
State the question, independent experimental unit, outcome and units, and what happened to F17. Fronds in one flask share their environment; counting them as separate independent replicates would misrepresent the design.
Before analysis, predict the kind of output needed: a plot showing flasks, a summary by group, and an estimate of nutrient minus control mean biomass with its confidence interval.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 2. Make a report that runs from its own code
text:
2. Make a report that runs from its own code
Copy the starter report.Rmd using Save As, naming the copy duckweed-report.Rmd in the same project root. Replace the title and biological description. Remove seedling-specific chunks and interpretations before adding duckweed code. Load the same three packages in the setup chunk.
Begin with an import and inspection:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
duckweed <- read_csv("data/duckweed.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(duckweed)
Check row count, distinct identifiers, group labels, missing measurements, and the plausible range of biomass. Record checks as evidence, not simply “the data were checked”. Retain F17’s missing value in the original input.






Hint: count missing and available measurements





Within group_by(treatment), use summarise() with n(), sum(!is.na(biomass_mg)), and sum(is.na(biomass_mg)). The number of rows and the number of usable measurements are different here. Use na.rm = TRUE for the mean and SD, while still reporting the missing count.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 3. Make the descriptive result first
text:
3. Make the descriptive result first
Create a group summary with available n, mean, and SD, all clearly labelled. Make a plot of individual biomass measurements by allocation, using only the available measurements for plotted y values. State how many are unavailable in the caption. A separate available object makes the exclusion explicit:
available <- duckweed |>
  filter(!is.na(biomass_mg))
Use the plot to ask whether the groups differ in location, how much overlap there is, and whether an observation needs checking against source records. No source evidence identifies another value as erroneous.






Hint: adapt a familiar plot





Start with the week 3 individual-point plot. Change the data to available, x to treatment, y to biomass_mg, and the y-axis label to “Dry biomass after seven days (mg)”. Use horizontal jitter only, so vertical positions stay accurate.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 4. Estimate the difference
text:
4. Estimate the difference
Explain why an independent comparison is appropriate and why this is not a paired before/after analysis. Inspect the individual measurements for severe skew or an influential point; seek advice if the simple model appears unsuitable. Use the guided Welch approach from week 4. Extract nutrient and control vectors and give them in that order to t.test() so that the difference is nutrient minus control. The missing F17 measurement is absent from available, not replaced with an invented value.






Hint: preserve the stated comparison direction





nutrient <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "nutrient")
control <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "control")
comparison <- t.test(nutrient$biomass_mg, control$biomass_mg)
comparison
Read the two means and compute their difference explicitly. comparison$conf.int is the confidence interval for the difference in the order used above.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 5. Write the interpretation before polishing
text:
5. Write the interpretation before polishing
Use a short paragraph containing the observed direction and size of the difference in mg, the available sample sizes, the confidence interval, and the p-value with an explanation tied to the question. Add a limitation concerning the missing measurement and the conditions of this small simulated experiment.
Distinguish “these observations support a difference under this model” from “nutrients always produce this change in all plants”. If an interval includes zero, report the uncertainty rather than claiming no effect.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: Completion check
text:
Completion check

Could a reader identify the flask as the independent unit without opening code?
Are measurements missing for 1 flask, with 19 available in total?
Does the plot show observations and units, and explain the missing value?
Does the direction of the reported difference agree with the code and means?
Does every object used in the report originate in its chunks?







Check the counts and direction





There are 20 rows and unique flask IDs. Ten control and nine nutrient flasks have biomass measurements. F17 remains a documented missing value. A positive nutrient-minus-control estimate means greater mean biomass in nutrient flasks. The conclusion still depends on design, assumptions, uncertainty, and context.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: Alternative study: product yield in an organic laboratory
text:
Alternative study: product yield in an organic laboratory
Question: how does the percentage of product collected vary among the supplied runs and between two labelled protocols? Use this study instead of the duckweed report. Save organic-study.Rmd and its HTML at the project root. If you made organic-report.Rmd on day 15, keep that earlier work and use Save As to create organic-study.Rmd for this study.
An organic synthesis is a procedure intended to make a chemical product. For this exercise, the maximum possible product mass, called the theoretical mass, is supplied. Isolated mass is the dry product collected. Assume it is pure solely for this calculation. Define percentage yield by the supplied relationship:
