yield (%) = 100 × isolated mass (g) / theoretical mass (g)
The file data/organic-recovery.csv contains 12 simulated independent synthesis runs, six randomly allocated standard and six modified protocol labels. The starting scales differ, so theoretical masses differ. Compare yields in percent, rather than comparing grams without accounting for those scales. All measurements are present. Repeated weighings of one collected product would not create new synthesis runs.
Start from a root-level copy of the template and remove the seedling-specific code and prose. Import and derive the outcome:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- organic |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)

Check the 12 unique run_id values, six rows per protocol, numeric mass columns, no missing values, and positive theoretical masses. Check Y01 by hand: 0.62 g collected from a supplied 1.00 g maximum gives 62%.
Summarise n, mean, and SD of yield_percent by protocol. Label SD in percentage points, since it describes spread on a percent scale.
Plot individual yields by protocol with horizontal jitter only. Each point is an independent synthesis run. Save one summary CSV and one labelled PNG in output/, using names beginning organic-.
Describe the observed group difference and overlap. Report it in percentage points, defined as the modified mean minus the standard mean. No hypothesis test or confidence interval is required for this descriptive alternative.
Explain why higher yield alone does not establish greater purity, safety, sustainability, or general superiority. The simplified purity assumption is not an experimental verification of purity.
Render in a fresh R session. The report should identify its question, supplied theoretical masses, formula, independent units, units, checks, and limits.







Hint and completion checks for the alternative





Reuse group_by(protocol) and summarise(n = n(), mean_yield_percent = mean(yield_percent), sd_percentage_points = sd(yield_percent), .groups = "drop"). There are six available runs per protocol. The standard mean is about 68.67% and the modified mean about 77.00%, a descriptive difference of 8.33 percentage points. Percentage-point difference and relative percentage change are different quantities. These summaries describe the supplied runs.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: Plan and review the chosen study
text:
Plan and review the chosen study
Continue your selected report. Save the plan and decisions in reports/study-decisions.txt.

Before changing code, write an analysis plan. State the question, observational unit, input file, outcome calculation, units, missing-value rule, plot, and comparison direction. State which uncertainty statement your chosen route supports. For the organic descriptive route, explicitly say that no confidence interval or hypothesis test is being added.
Create a small check table in your notes with one row each for identifiers, group labels, numeric measurements, missing values, and derived values. Put the command or inspection used in one column and the actual finding in another.
Select one record and verify its arithmetic by hand. For duckweed there is no change score: final biomass itself is the outcome. For organic Y01, 100 times 0.62 g divided by the supplied 1.00 g maximum gives 62%. Explain why subtracting the two organic masses would answer a different question.
Compare the two group means in both directions. Confirm that reversing their order changes the sign, not the size of the observed difference. In the duckweed route, check that the confidence interval’s direction agrees with the order passed to the taught test. The descriptive route needs only the directed observed difference in percentage points.
Write one draft interpretation before looking at the next paragraph. Then audit the supplied faulty interpretation below for your chosen route. Name at least three problems, and rewrite it using the actual evidence.

Duckweed draft to repair: “There were 20 biomass results. The nutrient plants all grew more, and the group SD is the error in the treatment effect. The p-value tells us the probability that nutrients work.”
Organic draft to repair: “The protocol collecting more grams must have higher percentage yield. Each balance reading is another independent run. A larger yield proves that the product is purer.”

Insert the corrected interpretation into your report, with a caption that identifies observations, units, and any missing measurement. Include the source of the missingness/assumption information rather than pretending the numbers alone explained it. Add at least one inline calculated result using the pattern from week 2, so a rerun updates that result automatically.
Restart, render, and compare the rendered statements with the current summary table. Save the plan and key decisions.







Hint: repair the meaning, not only the wording





Duckweed has 20 enrolled flasks but 19 available biomass measurements, and the observations overlap. SD describes flask variation, not uncertainty in an effect. The p-value is conditional on a null model and assumptions. In the organic case, starting scales differ, yield has a supplied denominator, the run is independent, and purity was assumed. Use these distinctions to rewrite the draft rather than merely replacing “proves” with “suggests”.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: Analyse a fresh culture dataset
text:
Analyse a fresh culture dataset
Use data/algae.csv to make a short memo and script. Algae are photosynthetic organisms; the outcome here is harvested dry biomass in mg. Twenty-four cultures were grown separately and randomly allocated reference or supplement, twelve each. They were harvested once after seven days. A19 spilled before weighing. One culture is the independent experimental unit; its many cells do not add independent replicates.

Save algae-transfer.R at the project root. Import the file and inspect the columns culture_id, treatment, and biomass_mg. Record rows, unique IDs, labels, and missing measurements before calculating a summary.
Summarise enrolled, available, and missing counts by group, then mean and SD of available biomass. Keep A19 as a missing raw value. Explain the difference between the two counts rather than replacing the blank with zero.
Make an individual-point plot with treatment on x and biomass in mg on y. Use the same display pattern already taught. Include the unavailable measurement in its caption, although it has no plotted y value.
Calculate the observed supplement-minus-reference mean difference. Report its units and direction.
In reports/algae-transfer.txt, write a result paragraph containing the independent unit, counts, direction, group spread/overlap, and a missingness limitation. State one question the plot cannot settle.
Save a summary CSV and plot in output/ with the prefix algae-transfer. Restart and run the script from the top. Tomorrow’s reproduction work will use these saved inputs and code, not your current Environment pane.

Checks: there are 24 unique cultures; 12 reference and 11 supplement biomass measurements are available. A19 remains missing. The group with the larger mean need not contain the largest individual observation. Use your table and plot to check that distinction rather than assuming every treated unit must be larger.
Before you finish: save a first rendered report and a note of anything that failed. Next, test a freshly extracted copy: Day 24.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Is a computer handling something fundamentally different when it stores a DNA sequence or a picture? The information has different meanings, but we can reuse familiar ideas: characters, numbers, vectors, tables, and saved files.
Save your code as representations.R in the project root, and your interpretations in reports/representations.txt.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: 1. A DNA sequence as character data
text:
1. A DNA sequence as character data
At the storage level, files are sequences of bytes. A bit has two possible values, 0 or 1; a byte contains eight bits, giving 256 possible patterns. Software interprets those patterns using a format: they might encode text, brightness, or something else. The file extension helps applications choose how to read a file, but renaming photo.jpg to photo.csv does not convert its contents.
DNA can be represented with letters A, C, G, and T. Our file is a tiny invented string, not a real gene. It is one line of plain text; the final newline separates lines in the file and is not an extra DNA base.
Run in R, with the course project open:
dna <- readLines("data/dna.txt")
dna
nchar(dna)
readLines() reads text lines; here it produces one character string. nchar() counts its characters. Compare with length(dna), which is 1: one stored string is different from forty separate character elements.
To count individual letters, split that string:
bases <- strsplit(dna, split = "")[[1]]
length(bases)
table(bases)
strsplit() returns a collection of results, one for each input string. [[1]] selects the first result. An empty split separates every character. table() then counts the occurrences of each different letter.
Try it: copy the printed sequence into a quoted R string, change one A to a G, and repeat the counts. Predict which counts change before running the code. Keep the supplied file unchanged. A total count of letters does not reveal what a sequence does in an organism; meaning needs biological context.






Hint: one string versus many letters





length(c("ACG", "TT")) is 2 because the vector has two strings. nchar(c("ACG", "TT")) gives 3 and 2. Ask which of these questions you want before interpreting a count.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: 2. A small image as a table
text:
2. A small image as a table
A grayscale image can be stored as rows and columns of brightness values. Our deliberately tiny teaching image has eight rows and eight columns. On its 0–255 scale, 0 means black and 255 means white; it is not a measurement in mm. One byte can represent one intensity on that scale. The 64 intensities would need 64 bytes if stored directly as one byte each. Our CSV is larger because it stores the digits as text, plus commas, a header, and line endings. The same information can have different file sizes in different representations.
pixels <- as.matrix(read.csv("data/pixels.csv"))
dim(pixels)
pixels
pixels[1, 1]
pixels[4, 4]
read.csv() is used here to obtain a simple numeric table for the supplied matrix demonstration; ordinary course tables still use read_csv(). as.matrix() represents this all-numeric table as a rectangular matrix. pixels[4, 4] selects row 4, column 4. A pixel is a location in the image, not an independent organism.
To display the values, the following supplied code converts brightness to a 0–1 grayscale representation and draws it:
plot.new()
rasterImage(as.raster(pixels / 255), 0, 0, 1, 1)
The bright central object should be visible. The 0 and 1 coordinates specify the plotting region, not a calibrated physical scale. You cannot turn its pixel area into square millimetres without knowing the image calibration.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: 3. Count a visibly defined region
text:
3. Count a visibly defined region
bright <- pixels > 100
bright
sum(bright)
mean(bright)
The comparison produces a matrix of TRUE/FALSE values. In a sum, R counts TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0. mean(bright) is therefore the fraction of pixels above 100. We are reusing logical comparisons from table filtering. For this supplied image, 24 of 64 pixels are above 100: the fraction is 0.375.
Try it: compare thresholds 50, 100, and 220. Which pixels count as bright? Explain why this constructed two-level image is unusually easy to separate. Real microscope images may have noise, uneven lighting, and overlapping objects; a bright region is not automatically one cell.






Hint: a quick check without new syntax





Use sum(pixels > 50), then replace 50 with 100 and 220. The image contains only 25 and 210. Predict the outcome from these values before running each line.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: Interpretation and limits
text:
Interpretation and limits
Answer each question:

What is represented by a DNA character, a matrix cell, and a plant-table row?
What extra information would you need to call a bright area a cell?
Why is the number of pixels not an appropriate sample size for a test of a treatment applied to one plant?







Short answers





A DNA character represents a base label; a pixel cell represents brightness at a location; our plant-table row records measurements of one plant. Image interpretation needs acquisition context, scale, and biological validation. Pixels from one image are spatially related measurements, and one treated plant remains one experimental unit regardless of its number of pixels.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: Change an object and predict what changes
text:
Change an object and predict what changes
Keep the supplied DNA and pixel files unchanged. Extend representations.R with a prediction before each change, then record the observed result.

Recreate dna, bases, and pixels from their files in a fresh session. Record the three different sizes: one text string, 40 separate base labels, and an 8-by-8 matrix. Explain which function answers each size question.
Make bases_changed <- bases, then use bases_changed[1] <- "G" to replace only its first element. Square brackets select positions; position 1 is the first letter. Predict the total length and the A and G counts. Check both the changed object and the original bases to see which was modified.
Define a GC fraction for this invented example as the number of letters labelled G or C divided by the total number of letters. This is only a count-based description. Compute it before and after the replacement using sum(bases == "G" | bases == "C") / length(bases) and the corresponding changed object. Here | means “or” between logical comparisons in R; it is different from the shell pipe. Explain why neither fraction identifies a gene.
Save the changed sequence as a new file, then read it back. This supplied line joins the letters into one string before writing ordinary text:

bases_changed <- bases
bases_changed[1] <- "G"
writeLines(paste(bases_changed, collapse = ""), "output/changed-dna.txt")
changed_from_disk <- readLines("output/changed-dna.txt")
paste(..., collapse = "") joins without separators. Check that the saved string has 40 characters. Saving a changed object should not overwrite the raw file. Record both names in your notes. 5. Make pixels_shifted <- pixels + 30. Predict the two new intensity levels, the number above 100, and the number above 220. Check your predictions and display the shifted image using the existing supplied plotting pattern. Values stay within the image’s 0–255 intensity scale. 6. Compare the original and shifted objects at row 1, column 1 and row 4, column 4. The positions did not move; brightness changed. Explain how a brightness change differs from an increase in physical size.






Answer checks for the controlled changes





The original counts are A11, C9, G9, T11; GC fraction is 18/40 = 0.45. Replacing the first A by G gives A10 and G10, still 40 letters, and GC fraction 19/40 = 0.475. The original object should retain its original counts. Shifted intensities are 55 and 240. There are still 24 pixels above 100, but now 24 rather than zero above 220. A fixed threshold can therefore change its answer after brightness changes even when the represented object’s positions are unchanged. Real image interpretation needs more than this toy arithmetic.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: Explain a threshold and a file format
text:
Explain a threshold and a file format
Produce representation-report.Rmd at the project root, using the familiar report structure. Include two small figures and a compact table rather than pasting a long console transcript.

Construct a results table for thresholds 0, 25, 100, 209, 210, and 255. For each, count original pixels strictly greater than the threshold and divide by 64 for the fraction. Use repeated sum(pixels > value) expressions. Name the threshold, count, and fraction columns.
State why a pixel equal to 210 is excluded by > 210. Contrast the meaning with >= 210, which includes equality. Predict and check the count for the latter. This is the same logical distinction used when filtering a table.
Show the original and shifted grayscale objects in separate report chunks, with captions identifying the operation and intensity scale. Use the same plot.new() and rasterImage(as.raster(... / 255), 0, 0, 1, 1) pattern, so the display method stays fixed while its input changes.
Explain which thresholds give the same result, where a count changes, and what the example establishes about cells or physical area. Identify the independent unit if the image came from one treated organism.
In a plain-text editor, make output/four-bases.csv containing the header position,base and four rows 1,A, 2,C, 3,G, 4,T. Import it with read_csv(). Explain why it gives four table observations whereas reading ACGT from a text line gives one string. The information is related, but the file organisation and the question asked of it differ.
Restart R and render your report without running its chunks interactively first. Locate its HTML and source. Check that the captions and table explain the threshold comparison without requiring the reader to inspect code.

Keep: the script, changed text file, four-row CSV, report source and HTML. Your results table should show counts 64, 24, 24, 24, 0, 0 for the stated strict thresholds. If your counts differ, check the loaded object, comparison symbol, and whether you used the shifted copy.
Before you finish: rerun representations.R from a fresh R session and save your explanatory notes. Next: a small integrated study.

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
You saved a report on a remote computer. Where is it, and how can you bring it back? Track the computer, folder, and copy of each file.
You need: the course project, a working local R setup, and the course’s remote-access instructions when issued. Save a short reports/remote-log.txt with the locations and checks below. Never record passwords or login codes.






Remote connection details are pending



HPC2N or another Linux environment will be used. The hostname, account route, authentication, remote desktop, transfer method, permitted execution location, and supported R application will be provided separately. Use those instructions for remote work. Until access is available, complete the local rehearsal below and mark the connection tasks pending.

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
section: 1. Draw the locations before connecting
text:
1. Draw the locations before connecting
A path identifies a place on a particular computer. /home/anna/course and C:\Users\Anna\Documents\course need not contain the same files. Two identical-looking folder names on different computers do not synchronise.
Laptop                         Remote Linux environment
course project                 course project (a separate copy)
  data/seedlings.csv              data/seedlings.csv
  report.Rmd                     report.Rmd
  report.html                    report.html
          -- supported transfer -->
          <-- supported transfer --
SSH provides a shell on the remote system. A remote desktop provides a graphical workspace. These are interfaces, not automatic transfer services. The course instructions will confirm whether both sessions share the same home directory.
In your log, draw two boxes labelled laptop and remote service, with their actual project paths.

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
section: 2. Connect, find your work, and return
text:
2. Connect, find your work, and return
Use the supplied SSH command from Ubuntu on Windows or Terminal on Mac. Its general form is:
ssh your-course-username@the-provided-host
Replace these placeholders using the service guide when issued.
Follow the supplied host-key verification and authentication instructions. After connecting, run these commands in the remote shell:
hostname
pwd
ls
hostname identifies the machine answering you; a service may use more than one machine. pwd identifies your current directory there. Record the service and folder. Make a practice folder using mkdir -p introcomputing-practice, then enter it with cd introcomputing-practice. Run pwd again.
Run exit to disconnect. You should return to the local shell, where pwd refers to your laptop. Reconnect using the supported route and find the practice folder again. Persisting files belong to saved storage, not to the terminal window.

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
section: 3. Find the same designated folder from remote desktop
text:
3. Find the same designated folder from remote desktop
Open the remote desktop using the course guide. Locate the designated course folder in its file manager. Compare the full location with the SSH session. Do they share it? Record your observation rather than assuming they must.
Transfer the course ZIP using the supported upload or file-transfer method, extract it, and open its .Rproj in the provided R environment. If the service uses a browser-based R application, follow its course-specific project route.
In the remote R console, run:
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
The second result should be TRUE. If it is FALSE, locate the project and its data before attempting analysis. A path from the laptop will not repair a missing remote input.

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
section: 4. Produce one result and transfer it back
text:
4. Produce one result and transfer it back
Open report.Rmd and render its HTML output using the provided R application. If R, packages, and Pandoc have been configured in the remote shell, the teaching team may instead ask you to run:
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd")'
Run this only from the project root in the supported execution environment. It renders the saved document in a new R process. On Windows, continue using native RStudio locally; this command is for a configured remote shell.
Transfer the resulting HTML back to your laptop into a folder you can name. Open the downloaded copy in your browser. Record both paths and the transfer direction. An HTML result is convenient to read, but the source .Rmd and input data are still needed to reproduce it.

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
section: Local rehearsal while remote access is pending
text:
Local rehearsal while remote access is pending
In the file manager, copy the complete extracted course folder to a separately named introcomputing-rehearsal folder. Open that copy’s .Rproj, verify getwd(), render the report, and locate the HTML. This rehearses a portable project, not a remote computer. In your log write “local rehearsal only” and list the remote tasks still to complete.






Hint: the file exists, but R cannot find it





Check which computer R is running on, getwd(), and the actual path beneath that folder. Look for an extra folder created during extraction. Keep report paths relative to the project root.

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

Does exit delete the files you saved remotely?
You rendered remotely, but local Downloads is empty. Is that evidence the render failed?
Can a remote shell use a laptop’s data/ folder without any transfer or configured sharing?







Short answers






No: it ends the shell/session; saved files remain subject to the service’s storage policy.
No: the output may still be on the remote computer. Check its location and transfer it.
Not automatically. File access must be explicitly provided or files transferred.

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
section: Audit a transferred project
text:
Audit a transferred project
Use the real service when available, or two clearly named local rehearsal folders. Record which route you used.

Before copying anything, create reports/transfer-plan.txt. Name the source computer, source project path, destination computer, and destination project path. For a local rehearsal, label both as local and give different parent folders. List the intended input data/algae.csv, its dictionary, and the report source you will use.
Open data/algae.csv in the original project without editing it. Read its dictionary: 24 separately grown cultures were assigned to reference or supplement, twelve each, and harvested once after seven days. A19 spilled before weighing, so its biomass is unavailable. The culture is the independent unit; the many cells within it are not independent cultures.
Record three checks in your plan: number of culture records, number of available biomass measurements, and A19’s state. Use nrow(), sum(!is.na(...)), and filtering by identifier.
Transfer or copy the complete project into the designated destination. Open the destination .Rproj, run getwd(), and repeat the checks there. Record both paths, the method, and the results in reports/remote-log.txt.
Write a new plain-text note, reports/transfer-receipt.txt, in the destination copy. Include the date, the destination project path, the input filename, and the three checked results. Locate it through the supported graphical workspace as well as through the file listing.
Bring that note back to the source using the supported route and open the returned copy. State whether you now have two independently stored copies. Close both applications and follow your written directions to locate the returned receipt.

Now investigate a deliberately stale copy. In a disposable copy of the project, change only the returned receipt’s text to say “second revision”. Save it, close the editor, and reopen both receipt copies. Does the other copy change? Keep both receipt copies and explain the observation. Identify which version you would transfer next.






Hint: compare contents as well as names





The algae table should have 24 records and 23 available biomass measurements. A19’s biomass remains missing. For small text receipts, open both in a text editor and compare the actual sentences. If you use R, the supplied expression identical(readLines("path-to-first-note"), readLines("path-to-second-note")) asks whether the text lines match; replace the two descriptions with your real paths. readLines() reads saved text, not an unsaved editor buffer.

title: Day 21 — the same workflow on another computer
section: Recover a misplaced result
text:
Recover a misplaced result
Use a report you already know renders. Save directions that identify its output, source, and input.

In the destination project, render the report once and locate its real HTML output. It may be beside its .Rmd or in a documented output folder. Write its full location and the time of your check in the transfer log.
In the file manager, copy that HTML into a new folder named returned-results. Open that copy and check its location in the file manager or browser file address.
Write the project location and a description of the desired result. Close applications, then follow those directions to find the HTML, source, and input without using recent files.
Record one failed assumption or ambiguous direction, and repair the instructions. Include a concrete recovery sequence such as “identify the computer; open the project; find its output folder; inspect the file”.
Check that an unchanged raw input has not been confused with the derived HTML. Explain which files must travel if the recipient needs to recalculate, rather than only read, the result. Add this distinction to your receipt.
Save a final reports/transfer-audit.txt containing source, destination, checks, version decision, and one remaining limitation. If remote access is pending, include a separate list of the authentication, desktop, and transfer steps that still need real service practice. Local success cannot tick them off.

Keep: your plan, receipt, location log, and audit.
Before you finish: save your location log, mark any pending access-dependent steps, and identify the report copy you opened. End the desktop session using the service’s instructions. Next: DNA and images as data.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
text:
Review questions from the week. Use the stated design, units, and comparison direction. See the statistics reference for definitions.
Topic quizzes:

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 1. Interpret the direction and interval
text:
1. Interpret the direction and interval
For independent seedlings, the estimated treated-minus-control mean growth difference is 6.22 mm, with a 95% confidence interval from 2.70 to 9.73 mm. What quantity is this interval describing? Is it a range for 95% of the plants?






Answer





It describes uncertainty in the population mean difference, under the model assumptions and in the stated treated-minus-control direction. It is not a range containing 95% of individual plants. A 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed true quantity in about 95% of repeated samples when its assumptions hold.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 2. What does the p-value condition on?
text:
2. What does the p-value condition on?
Does a p-value of 0.0015 mean a 0.15% probability that the null hypothesis is true, or prove that a 6 mm difference matters biologically?






Answer





Neither. It describes the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not the probability of the hypothesis. Biological importance needs the effect’s size, units, uncertainty, organism, and purpose. The test cannot repair dependent units.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 3. Pair by identity
text:
3. Pair by identity
The same ten plants were measured before and after increasing light. Why should the analysis use within-plant differences? Could independently sorting the two measurement columns improve their pairing?






Answer





The two readings belong to each same plant, so calculate after minus before within matching IDs. There are ten independent pairs, not twenty independent plants. Sorting columns independently destroys that identity and does not improve pairing. The fixed before/after order also leaves a time/order limitation.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 4. Invert the calibration in the stated direction
text:
4. Invert the calibration in the stated direction
The fitted line is approximately absorbance = 0.03957 + 0.06489 × concentration_mg_l. For an in-range absorbance of 0.310, what formula estimates concentration?






Worked answer





Rearrange to concentration = (0.310 - 0.03957) / 0.06489, giving about 4.17 mg/L. Use full fitted coefficients in code. We fitted absorbance as the measured response to known concentration; reversing the regression is a different fit. The inverse calculation is a point estimate, not full calibration uncertainty.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 5. A diluted reading is new evidence
text:
5. A diluted reading is new evidence
An unknown’s original reading is above the measured standards. Can you simply report the line’s extrapolated concentration? If a new in-range reading gives 7.40 mg/L after 1.00 mL was diluted to 10.00 mL total, what is the original estimate?






Answer and check





Flag the original as outside range rather than treat extrapolation as a supported result. A new in-range diluted measurement permits a stated correction: 7.40 × (10.00 / 1.00) ≈ 74.0 mg/L, using rounded numbers. The dilution assumes no measured material was lost or reacted. It does not validate another old out-of-range reading without its own new measurement.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 6. Slope units and causal limits
text:
6. Slope units and causal limits
A fitted dry-mass-versus-leaf-area slope is about 4.11. Dry mass is in mg and area in cm². What are the slope’s units, and what claim is not established by this observational fit?






Answer





The units are mg per cm²: fitted change in dry mass for a one-cm² increase in area. The sample association does not establish that experimentally changing area would cause this mass change. Inspect residuals and the measured range, and avoid extrapolating far beyond observed leaf areas.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 7. Reversing the contrast
text:
7. Reversing the contrast
A treated-minus-control95% interval is2.70 to9.73 mm. What is the control-minus-treated interval? What happens to the two-sided p-value?






Answer and reasoning





The reversed interval is−9.73 to−2.70 mm. Reverse the endpoint order as well as their signs. The two-sided p-value is unchanged because the equal-means question and observations are the same. Clearly label the reported direction.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 8. Different confidence levels, same observations
text:
8. Different confidence levels, same observations
With identical data and model, would a99% interval normally be narrower or wider than a90% interval? Does changing the interval level alter the observed means?






Answer and reasoning





The99% procedure gives the wider interval to target greater long-run coverage. The sample means do not change. Retain the confidence level chosen for the main analysis.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 9. What if the smaller study has a narrower interval?
text:
9. What if the smaller study has a narrower interval?
The transfer study has 9 plants per group instead of 12, yet its interval is narrower. Must R have failed?






Answer and reasoning





No. Interval width also depends on observed variability and model assumptions. The transfer study has lower observed group spread. When several features differ, sample size alone does not determine the ordering of interval widths.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 10. Pairing checked only by means
text:
10. Pairing checked only by means
Independently sorting before and after columns preserves their separate means. Does that validate the paired analysis?






Answer and reasoning





No. It destroys subject identity and can alter the spread of within-subject changes while preserving their average. In the actual ten-plant file the correct and artificial pairings have the same mean change but very different SDs and intervals. Sort complete rows together or match by recorded identity.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 11. A new instrument gives two unknown readings
text:
11. A new instrument gives two unknown readings
Transfer standards cover measured signals0.024–0.525. X1 reads0.270 and X2 reads0.700. Which gets an inverse estimate, and what should happen to the other record?






Answer and reasoning





X1 is within the measured range and estimates about 2.48 mg/L using the new fitted coefficients. X2 remains in the output with its reading, an out-of-range flag, and no supported concentration estimate. A suitable new measurement is required.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 12. A unit conversion changes a slope
text:
12. A unit conversion changes a slope
A mass-on-area slope is4.11 mg/cm². Area is converted to mm² by multiplying by 100. What happens to slope and fitted masses?






Answer and reasoning





The slope becomes about 0.0411 mg/mm², a factor of 100 smaller numerically. The intercept and fitted masses remain the same apart from rounding. The biological association did not become weaker merely because the predictor unit changed. A line through formula-calculated values is also not independent empirical evidence.



Return to association practice, or continue to remote workflow.

title: Quiz: A biological association
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A dry-mass-on-leaf-area line has slope 4.11, with mass in mg and area in cm². Give the slope units and interpretation.






Hint





A slope is change in response divided by change in predictor.









Answer





4.11 mg/cm². Within the observed range, an additional 1 cm² of area is associated with about 4.11 mg greater fitted mean dry mass.




Q2. For mass_mg = 9.48 + 4.11 * area_cm2, calculate fitted mass at 8 cm². Must an individual leaf at that area have exactly this mass?






Hint





Insert 8 into the fitted equation; distinguish a mean relationship from an individual measurement.









Answer





\(9.48+4.11\times8 = 42.36\) mg. No: individual masses vary around the fitted relationship, and the fitted line also has uncertainty.




Q3. Areas were observed from 2.96 to 14.68 cm². Is the intercept 9.48 mg a measured mass of a zero-area leaf? Is prediction at 80 cm² supported by this range?






Hint





Both zero and 80 are outside the observed predictor range.









Answer





No to both. The intercept positions the fitted line over the observed range; zero-area mass is not measured. A prediction at 80 cm² extrapolates far beyond the evidence.




Q4. A18 changes the slope when omitted, but has no documented error. What belongs in the main analysis, and what does the omitted-point fit show?






Hint





Influence and invalidity are different questions.









Answer





Retain A18 in the main fit. The separate fit is a sensitivity check showing how much this observation influences the line; influence alone does not justify removal.




Q5. If area is converted from cm² to mm² by multiplying by 100, what happens to the 4.11 mg/cm² slope and fitted masses?






Hint





The same physical area has a numeric value 100 times larger in mm².









Answer





The slope becomes 0.0411 mg/mm². The intercept and fitted masses stay the same apart from numerical rounding.




Q6. Leaf area was measured rather than randomly assigned. Which statement is supported by the fitted line?

Larger leaves tended to have greater dry mass in this sample.
Adding 1 cm² causes every leaf to gain 4.11 mg.
Area is the only influence on mass.







Hint





Association is a pattern among observed variables; causation needs design and subject knowledge.









Answer





(i). Age, species, environment, and other factors may influence both measurements. The observational line alone establishes neither causation nor a complete explanation of mass.

title: Quiz: Calibration and unknown samples
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Known concentration is in mg/L; the measured response is absorbance. Which formula fits the calibration used here?

lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l, data = standards)
lm(concentration_mg_l ~ absorbance, data = standards)







Hint





The response is left of ~; the predictor is right of it.









Answer





(i). Prepared concentration is the predictor and absorbance the response. The unknown concentration is later estimated by rearranging that fitted line.




Q2. For absorbance = 0.04 + 0.065 * concentration_mg_l, estimate concentration from an in-range reading of 0.30. What does the slope mean?






Hint





Rearrange to (reading - intercept) / slope.









Answer





\((0.30-0.04)/0.065 = 4\) mg/L. The slope is an increase of 0.065 absorbance per mg/L increase in concentration.




Q3. A standard has observed absorbance 0.30 and fitted absorbance 0.28. What is its residual, and where is its point relative to the line?






Hint





Residual = observed − fitted.









Answer





The residual is +0.02 absorbance, so the point lies above the fitted line. It is a signal-scale difference, not a concentration.




Q4. Measured standard signals span 0.024–0.525. Unknown X1 reads 0.270 and X2 reads 0.700. Which gets a supported inverse estimate, and how should the other appear in the saved table?






Hint





Check the measured signal range before inverting.









Answer





X1 is in range. Retain X2’s ID and reading with an out-of-range flag and a missing concentration estimate. A suitable new measurement is needed.




Q5. A new sample is diluted from 1.00 mL to 10.00 mL total volume. Its new in-range reading corresponds to 7.40 mg/L. Estimate the original concentration assuming no measured substance is lost or reacts.






Hint





Multiply the diluted estimate by final total volume / original-sample volume.









Answer





\(7.40\times(10.00/1.00) = 74.0\) mg/L using the rounded estimate. This uses a measured dilution and stated volumes; it does not validate a different sample’s out-of-range reading.

title: Quiz: Paired measurements
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Plants D1, D2, D3 have before readings 5, 8, 6 and after readings 7, 9, 9 in the same order, in µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Calculate their changes and mean change.






Hint





Subtract before from after for each matching identifier.









Answer





Changes are 2, 1, 3; mean change is 2 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. These are three independent pairs, not six independent plants.




Q2. Which function call estimates after minus before for matched plants?

t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)
t.test(after, before, paired = FALSE)







Hint





Both the pairing argument and vector order matter.









Answer





(i). (ii) estimates the reverse direction; (iii) treats the two vectors as independent groups.




Q3. Independently sorting the before and after columns preserves their means. Does that make the resulting paired test valid?






Hint





Pairing carries subject identity, which is more information than two means.









Answer





No. Sorting columns separately destroys the original plant matching. The mean difference can remain unchanged while the SD of within-plant changes and the confidence interval change. Move complete rows together.




Q4. A 95% interval for mean change is [−0.48, 4.48] in the stated rate units. Does it prove no change, or contain 95% of individual changes?






Hint





The interval describes uncertainty in a mean change under the assumptions.









Answer





Neither. It spans zero and both positive and negative mean changes; the small dataset does not resolve direction at this interval level. It is not an individual-change range or proof of equivalence.




Q5. All plants are measured before, then after changing light. A paired test gives a small p-value. Why is light alone still not established as the cause?






Hint





What else changes between the first and second reading?









Answer





Elapsed time, acclimation, measurement order, or equipment drift may contribute. The test addresses mean change; a suitable comparison and design addressing order effects are needed to isolate causes.

title: Quiz: Welch t-test
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Which study matches the independent groups used in this lesson?

The same plants measured before and after treatment.
Separate plants randomly allocated to treated and control groups.
Several leaves taken from one plant in each group.







Hint





Identify the unit that received treatment independently.









Answer





(ii). The independent unit is a plant. Measurements on the same plant are related; many leaves from one plant do not supply many independently treated plants.




Q2. Mean growth is 21.49 mm in treated plants and 15.28 mm in controls. What difference does t.test(treated, control) estimate, and in what units?






Hint





Subtract the second group’s mean from the first group’s mean.









Answer





Treated minus control: \(21.49 - 15.28 = 6.21\) mm using the rounded means. The difference from the full data is about 6.22 mm.




Q3. A treated-minus-control 95% confidence interval is [2.70, 9.73] mm. What interval and two-sided p-value would result from reversing the vector order?






Hint





Negate both endpoints, then put the lower endpoint first. The equal-means question is the same in either direction.









Answer





The interval is [−9.73, −2.70] mm. The two-sided p-value is unchanged.




Q4. Which statement correctly interprets a 95% confidence interval for a mean difference?

It contains 95% of individual plants’ growth values.
Its procedure covers the true mean difference in about 95% of repeated experiments under the assumptions.
Every value inside it has the same probability of being the true difference.







Hint





The interval describes uncertainty in a population mean difference.









Answer





(ii). The coverage statement concerns repeated use of the procedure. The interval is not an individual-growth range, and it does not give equally probable values of the fixed population difference.




Q5. The p-value is 0.0015. Does this mean there is a 0.15% probability that the treatment has no effect? What does the p-value describe?






Hint





Begin with “If the equal-means model and its assumptions held …”.









Answer





No. If the equal-means model and assumptions held, a two-sided t statistic at least this extreme would occur with probability about 0.0015. The p-value does not assign a probability to the hypothesis or measure biological importance.




Q6. For the same observations, will a 99% confidence interval be wider or narrower than the 95% interval? Will the group means change?






Hint





A higher coverage target requires more room around the same estimate.









Answer





Wider. The observed group means stay the same; only the interval level changes.

title: Quiz: A difference between groups
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Control mean growth is 15.28 mm and treated mean growth is 21.49 mm. Calculate treated minus control from these rounded means. What does a positive sign mean?






Hint





State the subtraction order before calculating.









Answer





\(21.49-15.28=6.21\) mm (about 6.22 mm from unrounded data). A positive sign means greater mean growth in the treated sample.




Q2. Twelve plants per treatment are measured initially and finally. How many independent growth values are there per treatment: 12 or 24?






Hint





The two measurements belong to the same plant and yield one growth value.









Answer





12. Initial and final measurements are combined into one final-minus-initial growth value per plant.




Q3. Some control plants grew more than some treated plants. Does that force the two sample means to be equal?






Hint





Individual overlap and equality of group means are different properties.









Answer





No. Groups can overlap and still have different means. Use the observations to describe overlap and calculate the group means separately.




Q4. Which is the null hypothesis for the planned two-sided comparison?

Every plant has identical growth.
The two population mean growths are equal.
The treatment must increase growth.







Hint





The hypothesis concerns population means, and a two-sided question allows both directions of difference.









Answer





(ii). The alternative allows either population mean to be larger. Individual plants may vary under either hypothesis.




Q5. The new class has a smaller sample mean difference than the first class. Does the difference alone establish that the treatment stopped working? What else do you need?






Hint





An estimate varies across samples and conditions.









Answer





No. Consider sampling uncertainty, observed variability, sample size, and study conditions. A sample difference alone does not determine its uncertainty or establish a universal treatment effect.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Can a reader understand the seedling measurements, their variation, and the limits of our description? A useful biological report does not need a significance test on every page. Today you will make the data handling, figure, summary, and interpretation fit together.
Save a new source document, descriptive-report.Rmd, at the project root. You may copy your first report’s structure, but deliberately revise its methods and interpretation. Keep data/ paths relative to this root. The supplied measurements are simulated. Plants received a control or nutrient treatment and were measured seven days apart; the nutrient formulation is unspecified.
Produce one descriptive report today. The teacher may choose the organic laboratory alternative below instead of the seedling report. In that case save organic-report.Rmd at the same project root and use its stated variables and units throughout.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Choose and state which input you use
text:
Choose and state which input you use
Use data/seedlings.csv for the core report. It contains 24 complete plant records. Include a data-quality note explaining the checks you performed: unique plant IDs, allowed treatment labels, numeric length columns, and missing-value counts.
If the teacher asks you to report the repaired day 11 data instead, include the repair code or source it from a saved script within the project. State the source and retain the unavailable P06 observation. Keep all results consistent with that input.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Build the report in a clear order
text:
Build the report in a clear order
Use this order inside the report:

Load packages and import the input file.
Inspect its structure and document relevant data checks.
Derive growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm.
Calculate the grouped summary with sample counts, mean, median, and SD.
Draw the individual-plant figure with group means.
Explain the centre, spread, overlap, and limitations in ordinary language.

Here is a compact data-check block that can appear after import:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anyDuplicated(seedlings$plant_id)
seedlings |> count(treatment)
sum(is.na(seedlings$initial_mm))
sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

anyDuplicated() returns zero when it finds no duplicate; a positive result identifies the position of the first duplicate, not a count of duplicates. Include only checking output that helps the reader, but keep the code available in the source. Reuse your day 13 summary and figure rather than replacing them with a screenshot of the RStudio Environment pane.
A table in an R Markdown chunk can be displayed neatly with:

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(group_summary, digits = 2,
             caption = "Observed growth and variation by treatment; lengths in mm.")

The table is generated from code. If the data change, the rendered table can change too. A caption must distinguish SD among plants from uncertainty in the mean. This report has SD, not confidence intervals.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Write with the question in view
text:
Write with the question in view
A useful description distinguishes three ideas: group averages differ in this sample; plants vary within each group; and sample descriptions do not quantify all uncertainty about a treatment effect. You can report observed values with units and identify the independent unit without declaring a universal result.
For the complete data, the group means are about 15.3 mm for controls and 21.5 mm for treated plants. Check your table rather than copying these numbers into prose without verification. The treated group also has more spread in these data. The individual observations overlap even though group means differ.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Alternative context: report collected-product yield
text:
Alternative context: report collected-product yield
Use this in place of the seedling report if selected. The question is: what percentage of the supplied maximum product mass was collected in each run, and how does it vary between protocols? All data are simulated. A synthesis run is one independently carried-out product-making experiment. Twelve independent runs were randomly assigned to two protocols, six to each. A protocol is a specified method.
theoretical_mass_g is the supplied maximum possible product mass for that run’s starting amounts. isolated_mass_g is the dry collected product mass, assumed pure for this simplified calculation. Both are in grams. Calculate percentage yield with 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g, so Y01 is 100 * 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%. Theoretical masses differ with starting scale; compare percentage yields to account for the different starting amounts.

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
organic_summary <- organic |>
  group_by(protocol) |>
  summarise(n_runs = n(), mean_yield_percent = mean(yield_percent),
            sd_percentage_points = sd(yield_percent), .groups = "drop")
organic_summary

Follow the same report order: import and check IDs, labels, numeric masses, missing values, and positive theoretical masses; calculate yield; show a table and individual-run plot; then interpret centre, spread, and overlap. Both groups have six available runs. Mean yields are about 68.67% and 77.00%; SDs are about 4.32 and 3.74 percentage points for standard and modified protocols. Label the y-axis “Isolated product yield (%)” and identify one point as one run. Repeated weighings of one product batch are technical repeats, not new runs.
This is descriptive work: no t-test is needed. A higher mean yield does not establish greater purity, safety, environmental benefit, or superiority in other reactions. Write a limitation tied to the small simulated set and the assumed purity. Keep the source and data together so the report can render from scratch.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Build and check the report
text:
Build and check the report

Complete the report with a question, data/design paragraph, methods, table, figure, and interpretation. Keep it short enough that each part earns its place.
Include the number of independent plants, or independent synthesis runs for the alternative, and state what the figure’s symbols represent. Name any exclusions or missing measurements.
Restart R and run this command in the R Console, not in a code chunk inside the report (a report must not try to render itself):


rmarkdown::render("descriptive-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")

For the organic alternative, replace the quoted filename with "organic-report.Rmd"; render only the report you chose.

Read the HTML with RStudio closed. Check that it identifies the units, input file, observational unit, main pattern, and main limitation.
If remote R access is available, locate the project on that computer and repeat the render there using the supplied connection instructions. First identify whether the R session and data are local or remote. Otherwise, repeat from a newly opened local project.







Hint: reproducibility is a file relationship





An HTML file beside an .Rmd is not enough if the source expects data in your personal Downloads folder. Keep the documented project structure, original data, and source together. The fresh-session render reveals missing dependencies.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






A good limitation is specific





“The sample is small” is less informative than naming the independent unit, noting overlap or variation, and explaining that today’s report describes the sample without yet estimating uncertainty in a treatment difference. Missing observations, when present, should also be counted and discussed.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Revise the report
text:
Revise the report
Revise your selected descriptive report. Save a revision log in reports/day15-revision.txt; keep the report source at project root.

Read only the rendered HTML, with the code initially closed. Write down the question, independent unit, input filename, measurement or derived outcome, and units. If any cannot be found, add a specific sentence or label rather than relying on the reader to infer it from an object name.
Inspect every numerical statement. Match it to the code and table that produced it. Check n against available observations, not all lines in a CSV. Record whether you used complete seedling data, the repaired exercise, or the independent organic-run context, and carry that choice through all counts, captions, and limitations.
Replace three weak sentences. Use these starting examples: “The results were good”; “the treatment had more error”; “the computer removed the bad values.” Your replacements must identify a measured pattern, a defined quantity such as SD, or an evidence-supported action. Avoid claiming an effect has been tested in this descriptive report.
Check that the figure shows observations with units. Identify what each summary symbol means. Put the figure beside a small table that answers a complementary question; remove redundant raw printouts if they do not help a reader.
Add two inline values in the results prose using the R Markdown pattern already introduced: one count and one mean or SD. Test them by rendering. The object must be created earlier inside the document. Keep interpretation in ordinary prose rather than assuming inline code writes a conclusion.
Extract a fresh course folder in a new location, add your source and required inputs, and render there. Record and fix any failure, then rerun.
Save the revised HTML and its .Rmd source. Write a compact change log: issue, evidence, correction, and rerun result. Keep the previous source as a clearly named backup.







Hint: separate numerical checks from wording checks





The complete seedling table has 24 plants; the repaired exercise has 24 plant records but 23 observed growths. The organic alternative has 12 independent runs, six per protocol, with no missing masses. A report may use any selected route, but cannot switch silently between these denominators. Use the Console for a rmarkdown::render() call; never put a self-render command into the report.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Describe a second study
text:
Describe a second study
The second study supplies data/seedlings-transfer.csv: 18 independent potted plants, nine randomly assigned to each allocation, initial and final lengths in mm seven days apart. The task is to describe growth and its variation; use descriptive summaries and figures.

Create transfer-description.Rmd in the project root. Start from your chosen source’s structure, but remove old imports, variable names, numbers, and biological descriptions that no longer apply. A template is a structure to adapt to the new data.
State the new question, independent unit, input, units, and growth formula. Include checks for identifiers, group counts, and missingness in the saved source. If you used the transfer dataset in earlier scripts, recreate its objects inside this report rather than depending on the Environment pane.
Produce one labelled individual-point figure and a group table with n, mean, median, and SD. Choose sensible rounding in the displayed table. Explain the distinction between the 18 input rows and the two summary rows.
Write results and interpretation using calculated numbers and one limitation. Address direction, overlap, and spread among plants.
Render after restarting and locate the actual output HTML. If you render into reports/, document that destination. Confirm that changing only the report title does not change its calculations, and that changing an input filename requires appropriate new checks and prose.
Make a handover note listing the files needed to reproduce the new report. Open the report on another computer if supported; otherwise use a separately located project copy. Record which kind of portability check you actually performed, without claiming an untested environment.

Additional outputs: revised chosen report, revision log, the self-contained transfer report and HTML, and the handover note.
Keep: your chosen descriptive-report.Rmd or organic-report.Rmd and its HTML, with the code and data needed to render it. Next: from description to a comparison.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Would measuring the same plant ten times tell us as much about other plants as measuring ten different plants? The answer changes how we count evidence and interpret an average. Today is about experimental reasoning, supported by a supplied sampling simulation.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Identify what was independently sampled or treated
text:
Identify what was independently sampled or treated
In the seedling experiment, plants are grown in separate pots and treatment is randomly assigned to plants. The plant is our independent experimental unit. An independent biological replicate provides another unit relevant to the question. A technical replicate repeats measurement of the same material, helping reveal measurement variation.
Three ruler readings of P01 can help assess how consistently it was measured. They do not turn it into three independently treated plants. Similarly, 100 cells from one organism are not automatically 100 independent organisms, and ten time points from one culture are not ten independent cultures. The unit follows the design and biological question, not the number of rows in a spreadsheet.
Imagine a nutrient treatment assigned to two trays, each holding twelve plants. If each tray receives a single shared treatment, the tray is a treatment unit. Treating all 24 plants as independently randomised units would overstate the independent treatment information. More data rows cannot repair that design.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Spread among plants versus uncertainty in a mean
text:
Spread among plants versus uncertainty in a mean
SD describes how much measured plants vary. Sampling uncertainty concerns how our estimated mean would change if we repeated the sampling process. Even when a population’s spread stays the same, a mean based on more independent plants typically varies less from sample to sample.
Here is a teacher-provided demonstration. The clean seedling growth measurements serve as a fixed toy population for repeated sampling. This is not a new experiment and is not evidence about all plants in nature. Sampling with replacement is used to illustrate repeated draws from a fixed distribution.
Save the block in day14-sampling.R, then run it unchanged first:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
population_mm <- seedlings$growth_mm
set.seed(14)
means_4 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 4, replace = TRUE)))
means_16 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 16, replace = TRUE)))
sampling <- data.frame(mean_mm = c(means_4, means_16),
                       sample_size = rep(c("4 plants", "16 plants"), each = 400))
ggplot(sampling, aes(x = mean_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ sample_size, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean growth in one simulated sample (mm)",
       y = "Number of simulated samples") +
  theme_minimal()
sd(population_mm)
sd(means_4)
sd(means_16)

sample() draws a sample; replicate() repeats the calculation 400 times. replace = TRUE allows a source value to be drawn more than once. set.seed() sets the starting state of the random-number generator so the demonstration can be repeated exactly. The resulting 400 means are summaries of simulated samples, not 400 newly measured plants.
Notice the horizontal axis: each value is a sample mean. Compare its spread between sample sizes. Do not confuse sd(means_16) with SD among the 16 plants inside one particular sample. The former describes variation among repeated estimates and approximates a standard error in this toy sampling process.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Compare sampling and study designs
text:
Compare sampling and study designs



Repeated sample means from samples of sixteen plants cluster more tightly than means from samples of four. The source distribution is fixed in this toy demonstration.



Before running the demonstration, predict which sample means will spread out more. Compare the plot and printed SDs with your prediction.
Change the random seed to 25 and rerun. Exact bins change; does the main relationship between sample size and spread remain?
Draw a small diagram for each design: twelve independent pots; one pot with twelve ruler readings; two trays with twelve plants each and tray-level treatment. Label the unit assigned to treatment. As an alternative to the one-pot diagram, draw one synthesis run whose collected product is weighed twelve times: there is one independently prepared run, not twelve. In the simulated organic dataset, six separately prepared runs were randomly assigned to each protocol; those runs provide independent protocol units.
Complete this explanation for each design: “We have many measurements, but our number of independently treated units is …”.
Explain the difference between SD among plants and uncertainty in a group mean for your report.







Hint: keep the sampling target fixed





Both means_4 and means_16 draw from the same population_mm. A larger sample does not alter those source values or their SD. It changes how much the repeated sample means vary. These combined-treatment values are only a teaching population; this simulation is not a treatment comparison.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Is a precise mean enough?





No. Repeated measurements may be biased, dependent, or drawn from an unrepresentative source. A narrow sampling distribution does not establish that the sampling process answers the intended biological question. Independent units and an appropriate design still matter.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Count independent units in four designs
text:
Count independent units in four designs
Save drawings or descriptions in output/day14-design-notes.txt and keep the sampling code in today’s script.

Draw twelve separate pots, each with one plant, with nutrient allocation independently assigned to pots. Label the unit assigned to treatment, the measurement, and the number of independent units. Give the conditions under which it is reasonable to regard the pots as independent.
Now draw one pot per treatment, with twelve ruler readings of its plant. Identify what variation those readings could help assess. Explain why the number of recorded lengths does not provide twelve independent treatment assignments.
Draw two trays, each containing twelve plants, where treatment was applied to the whole tray. Identify which plants share a treatment unit and possible environment. State what independent replication is missing.
Transfer the reasoning to either one culture measured at ten times, or one organic synthesis product weighed ten times. Name the biological or laboratory unit and the repeated measurements. Specify which question the repeats can inform and which comparison needs separately prepared units.
Run the supplied sampling demonstration unchanged and save its histogram. Read the horizontal axis aloud: each value is a sample mean, not an individual plant. Make a small table containing SD among source values, SD among means from samples of four, and SD among means from samples of sixteen. Label what each row describes.
Change only the random seed and rerun. Compare exact numerical results and the broad relationship. Then return to the stated seed. Explain why a reproducible simulation can use randomness, and why selecting a convenient seed is not evidence that one sampling method is generally better.
Write a short response to: “The histogram is narrow, so the design must be good.” Identify assumptions about independence, sampling, and measurement that a narrow distribution of means cannot establish. Precision in a biased or irrelevant measurement is not a substitute for answering the question.







Hint: label the level at every stage





In this demonstration, population_mm is the fixed source vector. A single sample() call gives a group of draws. One mean() gives one estimate from that sample. replicate() collects many such estimates. Neither a hundred simulation runs nor ten technical readings creates additional measured plants. Keep the source SD and the SD of repeated means under different names.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Change sample size with a new source
text:
Change sample size with a new source
Use the growth measurements from data/seedlings-transfer.csv as a new toy source distribution, not as proof about every plant. It combines allocations for this teaching demonstration; this is not a treatment comparison or a confidence interval for a treatment effect.

Import and calculate growth from all 18 records. Document that one row is one measured independent plant in its source study, but repeated draws from this stored vector are simulated samples rather than new measurements.
Adapt the supplied code to collect 400 means from samples of size three, then size twelve, with replacement, keeping the same source values. The changed setting is sample size. Predict which set of means will be more spread out before running it.
Save both numerical vectors as columns of a derived table, or in a long table using the supplied data.frame() pattern. State that the 400 rows represent simulated estimates, not enrolled plants or independent protocols.
Make comparable histograms or plots of the two distributions. Use shared axis limits and a stated bin width. Compare SD among means with SD among source observations. A larger sample size changes the estimate’s variation, not the original recorded plant values.
Repeat with a second seed, retaining the first result as a separate object. Write a paragraph identifying a broad stable feature and an unstable exact value. Explain why the number of simulation repeats and number of plants per simulated sample are different settings with different meanings.
End with a real design decision: if you could either measure each of two plants twenty more times or obtain ten additional independent plants, which option better informs a population mean, assuming comparable measurements? State the assumptions and also name a situation where checking measurement repeatability first would still be useful.

Additional outputs: four labelled design diagrams, a table distinguishing source spread from estimate spread, transfer simulation CSV/figure, and a interpretation of sample size, simulation repeats, and independent units.
Keep: day14-sampling.R, your replicate diagrams, and your explanation. Next: write a descriptive report.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
How can a figure and a small table show both the typical growth and differences among individual plants? A pair of bars showing only means would conceal sample size, spread, unusual observations, and overlap. We will show the observations and use summary numbers as an additional description.
Start day13-groups.R at the project root:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: One row per group in a summary
text:
One row per group in a summary

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_plants = n(),
            n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")
group_summary

group_by(treatment) tells the next operation to work separately within each treatment. summarise() returns one row of results per group. The names on the left of = become output column names. n() counts rows; sum(!is.na(...)) counts observed measurements. Here ! means “not”, so the expression identifies values that are not missing. .groups = "drop" makes the resulting summary an ordinary ungrouped table.
This clean dataset has twelve observed growth values per group. The means are about 15.3 and 21.5 mm, and SDs about 3.19 and 4.87 mm for control and treated plants, respectively. The table is a different object from seedlings: group_summary contains two rows describing groups, not two newly measured plants.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Add a clearly identified mean
text:
Add a clearly identified mean

group_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 13),
             alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = group_summary, aes(x = treatment, y = mean_mm),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "darkred") +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)",
       caption = "Small dots: individual plants. Red diamonds: group means.") +
  theme_minimal()
group_plot

The second point layer uses the summary table. Its inherit.aes = FALSE means we supply its mappings explicitly instead of inheriting a column absent from that table. Reuse this pattern for other grouped plots.
If adding error bars, name exactly what they represent. Mean ± SD describes spread among observations. A confidence interval describes uncertainty in an estimated mean; the two are not interchangeable. It is fine to keep today’s figure as observations and means only.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: A histogram answers a different question
text:
A histogram answers a different question

ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = growth_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 4, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Change in seedling length (mm)", y = "Number of plants") +
  theme_minimal()

A histogram groups nearby numeric measurements into intervals, or bins. It shows a rough distribution, not the order in which plants were measured. With only twelve observations per group, its shape changes noticeably with the bin width. facet_wrap() gives a separate panel per treatment. Shared scales help compare the panels; small samples warrant cautious descriptions.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Create the table and figures
text:
Create the table and figures

Reproduce the summary table and dot plot. Check one group mean using filter() and mean() as on day 12.
Save the table as output/growth-summary.csv and the plot as output/growth-summary.png, using write_csv() and ggsave().
Change the histogram’s bin width from 4 to 2, then 6. Describe which features are stable and which apparent details depend on the bins.
If you completed day 11, summarise output/seedlings-cleaned.csv. Check the distinction between n_plants and n_observed. Explain why its control mean need not exactly match the complete clean teaching dataset’s mean. If the teacher selects the organic transfer below instead, substitute it for this step rather than adding a second analysis.
Draft a caption that identifies the observational unit, units, and symbols.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Transfer choice: summarise product yield
text:
Transfer choice: summarise product yield
In data/organic-recovery.csv, one row is one independently carried-out product-making experiment, or synthesis run. The supplied theoretical_mass_g is its maximum possible product mass; isolated_mass_g is dry collected product, assumed pure for this simplified exercise. Both are in grams. Derive yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g; the first run is 100 * 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%.
Import the file, derive yield, then adapt today’s grouped-summary pattern to group by protocol. Report the number of runs, mean percentage yield, and SD in percentage points. Adapt the individual-point plot to show yield by protocol, using the run-level table for individual points. Save output/organic-yield-summary.csv, output/organic-yield-summary.png, and its caption instead of the extra cleaned-seedling summary.






Hint: keep the denominator and the experimental unit





Use mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g), then group_by(protocol) and summarise(). Both groups have six independent runs. The standard mean is about 68.67% and the modified mean is 77.00%; show the individual values before interpreting the difference. Different starting scales mean that comparing raw grams would answer a different question.









Hint: keep object roles clear





write_csv(group_summary, "output/growth-summary.csv") saves the summary, while ggsave("output/growth-summary.png", plot = group_plot, width = 6, height = 4) saves the plot. These outputs have different purposes. Check names() if a layer mentions a column absent from the table used by that layer.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Why show individual dots?
