Dots reveal how many observations overlap, where unusual values lie, and how measurements vary around each mean. A higher mean does not mean every treated plant grew more than every control plant. The repaired dataset retains twelve control plants but only eleven observed control growth values.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Make the figure and caption agree
text:
Make the figure and caption agree
Use your selected plant or product-yield dataset and its existing group summary.

Write down the number of input rows, the number of groups, and the number of summary rows. Locate one actual observation in each group. Explain why the two summary rows are not two additional experimental units.
Save a first figure showing individual observations only. Save another with group means added. Use identical axis limits, units, and point positions so the difference between figures is the added information, not rescaling. Describe one feature that the observations reveal and a mean alone hides.
Draft a deliberately inadequate caption, such as “Treatment makes everything larger; bars show error.” Then replace it with a caption identifying the independent unit, plotted quantity and units, mean symbol if used, available n, and whether any error bars exist. Keep both versions in a caption log and explain at least three specific repairs.
Create histograms using two defensible bin widths. Compare apparent modes, gaps, and group overlap. Record which broad statement remains supported in both displays and which detail depends on the bin choice.
Produce a compact table containing available n, mean, median, and SD per group. Round for readable display only after calculation. Preserve the full-precision summary object for further arithmetic and any CSV export. Explain why printing six decimal places does not add measurement precision.
Inspect how plot labels change between contexts. Plant growth uses mm; organic yield uses percent, and an SD of yield is expressed in percentage points. Revise both the axis and the caption if switching contexts. Merely changing a figure title can leave a convincing but false unit label.
Close the code and inspect the exported figure and table. Locate n, an individual observation, the mean marker, units, and group overlap. Revise labels or captions where these are unclear.







Hint: two tables have different roles





The raw table supplies individual points; the grouped summary supplies means. In a second geom_point() layer, use data = group_summary and explicit x/y mappings. If you omit error bars, your caption should not mention them. If a teacher demonstrates mean ± SD, label it as SD among observations, not a 95% interval or a measurement instrument’s error bound.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Create figures for a second study
text:
Create figures for a second study
Use data/seedlings-transfer.csv to produce a report figure and a summary table. The file contains 18 independently potted plants, with nine observations per allocation and no missing lengths. All lengths are mm, measured seven days apart.

Create day13-transfer.R from a blank script. Import, inspect, and derive growth_mm; check the meaning and units from the dictionary. Retain all rows and original columns.
Create one group summary and export it as output/day13-transfer-summary.csv. Include available n, mean, median, and SD, using distinct informative column names. Describe the difference between nrow(transfer) and nrow(transfer_summary) in a code comment.
Create a point plot with a group mean marker using the summary as a separate layer. Save a PNG. Check that every individual point’s vertical position is its measured growth; jitter is horizontal only. Explain why moving points vertically would misrepresent the recorded values.
Make a faceted histogram using a common horizontal range and one stated bin width. Compare it with the point plot for this small sample. Which better permits identifying individual observations? Which highlights the grouping of nearby numeric values? Keep both, with different filenames and captions.
Save a handover note listing the data files and script needed to recreate the figures. Identify supplied inputs and derived outputs.
Run the script in a fresh R session. Open the PNGs and CSV in the file manager, not only through RStudio’s recent tabs. Verify one summary against a filtered vector and mean(). Save a short reproducibility note identifying the check.

Additional outputs: a caption-repair log, the chosen-context figure pair, transfer summary/figures, and a saved handover note.
Keep: day13-groups.R, the summary CSV, figure, and caption. Next: replicates and uncertainty.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Two groups can have the same average growth yet look very different. How can we say where measurements are centred and how much individual plants vary? Today we use small numbers first, then connect them to the seedling experiment.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Mean and median answer slightly different questions
text:
Mean and median answer slightly different questions
The mean adds all observed values and divides by their number. The median is the middle of the ordered values, or the mean of the middle two for an even number of values. Both describe a centre; neither replaces the observations.

growth_mm <- c(12, 14, 16)
mean(growth_mm)
median(growth_mm)

Both results are 14 mm. Now inspect a more uneven set:

uneven_mm <- c(10, 10, 10, 100)
mean(uneven_mm)
median(uneven_mm)

The mean is 32.5 mm and median 10 mm. Neither is an arithmetic error. The large observation affects the mean strongly. Investigate whether a large value is supported by the source record. Keep valid large observations. The appropriate description depends on the question and shape of the measurements.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Variance measures spread around the mean
text:
Variance measures spread around the mean
For the three measurements 12, 14, and 16 mm, the deviations from their mean are −2, 0, and 2 mm. Their sum is zero, so an ordinary mean deviation would hide the spread. Squaring deviations prevents positive and negative values cancelling.
The sample variance adds squared deviations and divides by one less than the number of observations. The choice of this denominator helps estimate population variance from a sample.

growth_mm <- c(12, 14, 16)
deviations_mm <- growth_mm - mean(growth_mm)
squared_deviations <- deviations_mm^2
sum(squared_deviations) / (length(growth_mm) - 1)
var(growth_mm)
sd(growth_mm)

The squared deviations are 4, 0, and 4. Their sum divided by 2 is 4 mm², the sample variance. The standard deviation, or SD, is its square root: 2 mm. SD is expressed in the original measurement’s units, which makes it easier to interpret alongside the mean. Variance uses squared units. Neither is the error in the mean or a claim that every plant lies within one SD.

close_mm <- c(13, 14, 15)
spread_mm <- c(8, 14, 20)
mean(close_mm)
mean(spread_mm)
sd(close_mm)
sd(spread_mm)

Both means are 14 mm. The SDs are 1 and 6 mm. The second set varies more among observations. A group with larger spread is not automatically measured less carefully: organisms can really differ. Measurement noise and biological variation can both contribute to observed spread.



Two toy groups share a mean of 14 mm but differ in spread. Dots are measurements; the dashed line is their common mean.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Apply the descriptions to plants
text:
Apply the descriptions to plants
Use the clean supplied table today so that variation is not confused with the repair exercise. Recreate all prerequisites in day12-variation.R.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
control <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")
mean(control$growth_mm)
median(control$growth_mm)
var(control$growth_mm)
sd(control$growth_mm)

The control mean is about 15.3 mm and its SD about 3.19 mm. Report them with units and a sensible number of decimals; extra decimal places do not create more precise measurements.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Calculate centre and spread
text:
Calculate centre and spread

Work through the three-measurement variance by hand, then compare with R.
Predict the mean and SD if every value in close_mm increases by 10 mm. Check using mean(close_mm + 10) and sd(close_mm + 10).
Predict what happens if lengths are converted from mm to cm by dividing by ten. Check the mean, variance, and SD in the new units.
Calculate the treated group’s mean, median, variance, and SD. Compare centre and spread with the control group. The product-yield task below is an alternative to this step.
Add a note explaining why “the average plant grew 15.3 mm” does not mean every control plant grew exactly that amount.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Transfer choice: variation in collected product
text:
Transfer choice: variation in collected product
An organic synthesis is an experiment intended to make a product. In our simulated data/organic-recovery.csv, each row is one independent run. The supplied theoretical mass is the maximum product mass possible from that run’s starting materials. Isolated mass is the dry product actually collected, assumed pure for this simplified calculation. Both are in grams. Calculate percentage yield as 100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass.

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
standard_runs <- filter(organic, protocol == "standard")
mean(standard_runs$yield_percent)
var(standard_runs$yield_percent)
sd(standard_runs$yield_percent)

Y01 gives 100 × 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%. For the six standard-protocol runs, the mean is about 68.67%, variance 18.67 squared percentage points, and SD 4.32 percentage points. A difference from 62% to 70% is eight percentage points, not an eight-percent relative increase. Repeat the summaries for the modified protocol and describe centre and spread.
The runs used different starting amounts, so raw collected grams do not make the same comparison as percentage yield. A higher yield alone does not establish greater purity or a generally better method. Save this calculation in today’s script.






Hint: use the units to check yourself





Adding a constant shifts the centre but leaves deviations unchanged. Dividing lengths by ten divides the mean and SD by ten, but divides variance by one hundred. Check ?var and ?sd for the functions’ definitions and missing-value arguments.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Which spread is larger?





The treated SD is about 4.87 mm, larger than the control SD. This describes variation among these plants; it does not by itself quantify uncertainty in the difference between group means. We will separate those questions next.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Shift and rescale the measurements
text:
Shift and rescale the measurements
Continue day12-variation.R. Use your selected plant or product-yield dataset for the final write-up.

Make a three-row hand table for values 12, 14, and 16 mm. Include the mean, each signed deviation, squared deviation, their sum, and the denominator used for sample variance. Check the hand table against R. Save the table as a short text note or CSV, retaining the units in its explanation.
Replace the last value with 26 mm. Predict the direction of the mean, median, variance, and SD changes before calculation. Then calculate them. Identify which statement about “a typical observation” is affected most by this one high value.
Add 10 to every value in the original three-value vector. Explain why the signed deviations, variance, and SD stay the same while the mean changes. Draw both sets along the same horizontal scale, on paper or with a supplied point-plot pattern. An axis with inconsistent limits would obscure the shift.
Convert the original vector from mm to cm by dividing by ten. Write the new mean, variance, and SD with units. Check that changing unit does not make the biological sample less variable. The numeric variance changes by a factor of 100 because its unit changes from mm² to cm².
For your selected supplied context, compute centre and spread separately within both groups. For plants use growth_mm; for organic runs first use the supplied 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g relationship to obtain yield_percent. Explain why raw grams would answer a different question when starting amounts differ.
Make an individual-observation plot and add one mean marker per group using the familiar separate-summary-table pattern. Find at least one observation above and one below its group’s mean. Explain why a mean need not itself be an observed value and why showing only a mean conceals these differences.
Write a short response to this claim: “The group with the larger SD must have the less reliable mean and the worse experimental technique.” Separate variation among measured units from uncertainty in an estimate and from possible biological or measurement sources of spread. The SD alone cannot identify the source or evaluate the entire design.







Hint: check the transformation, not a memorised rule





For the original vector, the sample variance is 4 mm² and SD 2 mm. In cm, variance is 0.04 cm² and SD 0.2 cm. Adding 10 mm changes only the centre. For the changed vector c(12, 14, 26), ask R for mean(), median(), var(), and sd() after writing predictions. Keep the two vectors under distinct names.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Describe variation in a second study
text:
Describe variation in a second study
Import data/seedlings-transfer.csv into an object called transfer and calculate final minus initial length. These are 18 new independent plants, nine per randomised group, with lengths in mm and complete measurements. The seven-day study uses the same column structure as the first experiment.

Start a separate script, day12-transfer.R, containing its own package loading, import, checks, and derived growth. Identify T01 and verify its subtraction by hand. A plausible overall mean would not reveal a sign error.
Compute mean, median, sample variance, and SD for each treatment. Save a labelled table to output/day12-transfer-summaries.csv. State n alongside the summaries, even though neither group has missing values here.
Draw both groups’ individual measurements on a common scale. Use your summaries to describe which group has the larger mean and which has the larger SD. Use the calculated values to distinguish centre from spread.
Convert the derived growth to cm in another column. Verify one group mean, SD, and variance in the new units. Preserve the mm column so the conversion is transparent. Give a sentence explaining which numeric changes reflect unit choice and which comparisons between groups remain the same.
Write an explanation to accompany your table and figure. Define what SD describes, include units and independent sample sizes, and state one thing the descriptive summaries cannot establish. Explain how overlap between the groups affects your description.
Reopen the output table in another application and verify that it contains summaries, not the original plant-level rows. Restart R and regenerate the outputs. Keep the code, plot, and explanatory note together in your project.

Additional outputs: output/day12-transformations.txt, the transfer script, summary CSV, output/day12-transfer.png, and your interpretation. Checkable anchors: T01 grew 15.0 mm; both groups have nine observations. Save your own calculated group values.
Keep: day12-variation.R and the interpretation in comments or report notes. Next: summarise groups while still showing individuals.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
What if a length was entered in the wrong unit, a plant appears twice, or a measurement is missing? R can calculate a precise-looking answer from a poor table. Our job is to check what the values mean and leave a record of justified repairs. Keep the raw file unchanged and save derived outputs separately.
data/seedlings-messy.csv contains deliberately planted errors. Read data/field-notes.txt for the source records needed to resolve them.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Inspect before converting
text:
Inspect before converting
Create day11-cleaning.R in the project root. Read every column as text so that mixed entries remain visible. Keep leading/trailing spaces for this inspection.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
raw <- read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), trim_ws = FALSE)
dim(raw)
unique(raw$treatment)
filter(raw, plant_id %in% c("P01", "P06", "P18", "P21"))

cols(.default = col_character()) requests text columns instead of guessing. unique() shows distinct values, so "control" and "Control" can be noticed. %in% asks whether a value belongs to the listed set of IDs. A CSV importer may normally trim surrounding spaces; we temporarily keep them so we can see the problem rather than mistake automatic tidying for a clean source.
The file has 25 rows although the study has 24 plants. Confirm the duplicated ID:

raw |> count(plant_id) |> filter(n > 1)

count() counts rows by the named column. Repeated IDs can be legitimate if a table has one row per time point. Here the protocol says one row per plant, so we inspect both P01 rows and the source record before deciding what to do.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Make evidence-based repairs
text:
Make evidence-based repairs
The supplied field notes establish the following:

The two P01 rows are an accidental duplicate of the same record.
Control means control, and a trailing space on a treatment is accidental.
P18’s initial length is 18.7 mm; its cell includes the unit as text.
P21’s source record gives final length 43.8 mm, not the entered 4.38.
P06’s final measurement is unavailable. There is no supported replacement.

The number 4.38 alone would not justify multiplying by ten. The source record authorises that correction. Similarly, missing P06 is not a length of zero.

cleaned <- raw |>
  mutate(treatment = tolower(trimws(treatment)),
         initial_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P18", "18.7", initial_mm),
         final_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P21", "43.8", final_mm)) |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(initial_mm = parse_double(initial_mm),
         final_mm = parse_double(final_mm),
         growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

trimws() removes surrounding whitespace, and tolower() standardises letters in these documented labels. if_else(condition, yes, no) makes the stated replacement only for the identified record. distinct() removes exact repeated rows; we use it only after confirming the import duplication. parse_double() turns verified number text into numeric values, preserving missing values.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Check the repaired table
text:
Check the repaired table

nrow(cleaned)
anyDuplicated(cleaned$plant_id)
sum(is.na(cleaned$growth_mm))
cleaned |> count(treatment)
write_csv(cleaned, "output/seedlings-cleaned.csv")

Expect 24 rows, zero duplicated IDs, and one missing growth value. Both groups still contain 12 plants, but the control group has only 11 observed growth values. Counting enrolled plants and counting usable measurements answer different questions. Keep the raw file, repair script, and field notes so another person can trace these decisions.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Inspect, repair, and check
text:
Inspect, repair, and check

Run the inspection steps before the repair block. Write comments recording what prompted each check.
Run the repairs and verify the expected counts. Inspect P06, P18, and P21.
Calculate the mean of cleaned$growth_mm with and without na.rm = TRUE. Explain what each result means.
Save a short output/cleaning-notes.txt explaining the evidence for each change and the observation left unavailable.
Restart R, rerun your script, and confirm the original CSV has 25 rows while the derived CSV has 24. Different row counts are expected and documented.







Hint: avoid silently losing records





Inspect raw |> filter(plant_id == "P01") before using distinct(). Do not use distinct(plant_id, .keep_all = TRUE) to discard different records merely because they share an ID. Real disagreements need investigation.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






What makes a repair justified?





A check identifies a question; the source record supports the repair. A very small or large value may be real. Omitting missing values from a calculation does not make their absence disappear from the report.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Trace each repair to its evidence
text:
Trace each repair to its evidence
Continue day11-cleaning.R using the raw CSV and source notes. Save new outputs with names beginning day11- in output/.

Before running the cleaning block, write a compact audit table in output/day11-audit.txt. Give a row for each problem: observed entry, affected identifier, source evidence, action, and a check of the result. Distinguish an unavailable measurement from an incorrectly transcribed one.
Inspect the two P01 records together. Compare every field, not just their identifiers. Explain why identical duplication plus the source note permits removal here. Write what additional investigation would be needed if their final lengths disagreed.
Import a second raw object with the usual whitespace-trimming default and compare its treatment labels with raw. Find the difference concealed by that convenience. An importer can standardise representation without proving the source is free of errors. Record which option made the original visible.
Create an intermediate object after label repairs but before numeric parsing. Inspect str() and the P18 record. Then inspect the corresponding columns after parsing. Describe why the same printed digits can have different R types, and why the unit suffix needs documented interpretation before removal.
In a separate derived copy, deliberately replace P06’s unknown final length with zero. Calculate that row’s growth and the overall available mean. Label this object wrong_zero_example, separate from the corrected table. Compare its result with the defensible missing-value calculation. Explain what the invented zero claims about the plant and why that is different from choosing na.rm = TRUE for an explicitly reported available-case mean.
Compare the available group counts before and after your repairs. Include total plant records and usable growth values separately. State why removing the duplicate should change a record count, while leaving P06 unknown should change availability without changing the number of enrolled plants.
Save the corrected CSV, close R, reopen the project, and regenerate it from the unedited source. Read the derived file back into a new object and check its identifier count, missing growth count, and P21 final length.







Hint: compare stages with a specific question





Use filter(raw, plant_id == 'P01'), str(), unique(), nrow(), sum(is.na(...)), and the same group_by()/summarise() pattern used elsewhere. The defensible table has 24 unique IDs and one unknown growth. P06’s initial length is 24.7 mm: an invented final zero would imply −24.7 mm growth.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Check a second study
text:
Check a second study
A second simulated class has supplied data/seedlings-transfer.csv: 18 independently potted seedlings, nine randomly assigned to each allocation, measured seven days apart. The columns and units match the clean seedling table, but the values and identifiers differ. No source note identifies an error in this new file.

In day11-transfer.R, state your expected schema in comments before importing: column names, types, meaning of one row, valid group labels, measurement units, and which identifier should be unique. Obtain those meanings from the data dictionary.
Import, inspect, and save the results of your checks in output/day11-transfer-audit.txt. Check row count, unique IDs, actual labels, missing values, numeric types, and whether final-minus-initial is calculable. A check should record what you observed, not just say “passed”.
Find T01 and calculate its growth by hand. Then calculate growth for every row in code. Keep the original four columns as well as the derived one.
Make a disposable copy with an extra copy of its first row. Detect the duplicate and explain why the original transfer file remains unaffected. Keep the source CSV unchanged. Record the difference between a classroom-created error and source evidence about an actual observation.
Review your audit for missing checks and conclusions stronger than the evidence. Reproduce one check from the saved script in a fresh session.
Write a handover paragraph: what was checked, whether any correction was justified, and what information you would ask the recorder for if an unusual value appeared. Save output/day11-transfer-growth.csv and rerun from a fresh session. Your handover must make clear that no correction was supported in this supplied transfer file.

Additional outputs: both scripts, the audit and handover notes, and a derived transfer CSV.
Keep: day11-cleaning.R, the derived CSV, and your cleaning notes. Next: describe variation.

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
text:
Predict the result, explain it, then use R to check. The R reference is available.
Topic quizzes: 6 · 7 · 8 · 9 · 10
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 1. Assignment is an action when the line runs
text:
1. Assignment is an action when the line runs
You saved growth_mm <- 37 - 20 in a script but did not run it. Must growth_mm now exist in R’s memory? What are its value and units after running?






Answer and check





Saving the script does not run it. After execution, the object contains 17 mm. Restarting removes that session object, while the saved script remains. Run the source from the top to recreate the calculation.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 2. Matched values in vectors
text:
2. Matched values in vectors
For three plants, initial lengths are 20, 22, 19 mm and final lengths are 37, 40, 34 mm. What does position-by-position subtraction assume, and what are the resulting growth values?






Answer and check





Both vectors must refer to the same plants in the same order, with compatible lengths. The growth vector is 17, 18, 15 mm. Its mean is about 16.67 mm. Correct arithmetic on unmatched plants would still answer the wrong question.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 3. A table is more than its numbers
text:
3. A table is more than its numbers
The imported seedling table has 24 rows and four columns. What identifies a plant, what units do the length columns use, and why is averaging the plant ID not a meaningful biological summary?






Answer and check





plant_id identifies the plant; the two length columns use millimetres, as specified in the dictionary. IDs label observations rather than measure a quantity, so an average ID has no interpretation. The header names columns and is not another plant. Initial and final lengths in one row belong to one plant.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 4. Plot the quantity asked for
text:
4. Plot the quantity asked for
For P01, initial length is 25.7 mm and final length is 44.3 mm. Calculate growth. Does a plot with initial length on x and final length on y directly display that growth on its vertical axis?






Answer and check





Growth is 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm. The first plot’s vertical axis is final size, not change. Create growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm and plot that derived column when growth is the outcome. Label axes with the actual variables and units, and keep the original CSV unchanged.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 5. A report works in the Console but fails when knitted
text:
5. A report works in the Console but fails when knitted
The error says an object is not found. You created that object interactively before opening the report. What needs repairing, and which files should remain after a successful render?






Answer and check





Put the needed import/calculation into the report before it uses the object, and load its packages there. Keep the .Rmd source, input data, and generated HTML. Render from a fresh session. A Console call to rmarkdown::render() must not be placed inside a report that would then try to render itself.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 6. Transfer choice: a fully supplied product calculation
text:
6. Transfer choice: a fully supplied product calculation
The supplied maximum product mass is 1.00 g; collected dry product is 0.62 g, assumed pure for this simplified task. Percentage yield is 100 × collected mass / maximum mass. What is the yield, and does that number independently establish the product’s purity?






Answer and check





The yield is 62%. The gram units cancel. Purity was an assumption, not a finding from this ratio. Keep the maximum and collected masses as distinct inputs; a larger raw mass is not necessarily a greater percentage when starting scales differ.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 7. A stored result becomes stale
text:
7. A stored result becomes stale
After assigning initial_mm <- 20, final_mm <- 37, and growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm, you set final_mm <- 39. What is growth_mm before and after rerunning the subtraction?






Worked answer





It remains 17 until the subtraction runs again, then becomes 19 mm. An assigned object holds its stored result; it is not a live spreadsheet formula that automatically recomputes every dependency. Save the correct order in the script and rerun from its inputs.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 8. Equal lengths but wrong plants
text:
8. Equal lengths but wrong plants
Initial lengths are c(20,22,19). The correct final vector is c(37,40,34), but a copy has been reordered to c(34,37,40). Both vectors have length three. Is subtraction biologically justified?






Worked answer





Not by equal length alone. R subtracts positions, so the reordered copy gives 14,15,21 mm for incorrect pairs. The correct correspondence gives 17,18,15 mm. Verify identities and order as well as compatible vector lengths.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 9. Audit the new input
text:
9. Audit the new input
The transfer study is supplied as 18 independent plants, nine per group. Your report still says 24 plants. Which evidence and source lines should you inspect?






Worked answer





Check the imported filename, project and object; inspect dim(), distinct plant IDs, group labels/counts and missingness. Then check inline and manually written prose against that input. The expected transfer table is 18 by 4 with 18 unique IDs, nine records per group and no missing lengths.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 10. A supplied concentration calculation
text:
10. A supplied concentration calculation
Amount in mol = mass_g / supplied molar_mass_g_mol; concentration in mmol/L = 1000 × amount / final_volume_l. For 0.2922 g, 58.44 g/mol and 100 mL final volume, what is the result?






Worked answer





100 mL = 0.100 L. The amount is 0.005 mol, giving 0.050 mol/L or 50 mmol/L. Doubling only mass gives 100 mmol/L; doubling only volume gives 25 mmol/L. The quantity refers to final total solution volume, not a solvent volume before addition.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 11. An impossible dilution request
text:
11. An impossible dilution request
The supplied rule is stock volume = target × final volume / stock concentration. A request has stock 100 mmol/L, target 200 mmol/L and final volume 50 mL. What numerical result appears, and why is it not a valid preparation recipe?






Worked answer





The formula gives 100 mL of stock, exceeding the requested 50 mL total. The target is more concentrated than the stock, so dilution by adding solvent alone cannot achieve it. Preserve the row and flag it rather than deleting it or inventing stronger stock.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 12. Source, HTML and a revision
text:
12. Source, HTML and a revision
You corrected an HTML caption directly, then rendered the R Markdown source again and the correction vanished. Where should the revision live, and what should be tested?






Worked answer





Edit the .Rmd source and render it. The HTML is a generated reading copy and can be replaced. Check the new output location, caption, units, input description and inline counts, then rerender from a fresh session with the required ordinary data files included.



Return to your first report, or continue to data quality.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Quiz: A complete first report
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A report includes an attractive figure but gives no input filename, sample size, or definition of a point. What information should be added?






Hint





A reader needs to connect the question to the data and result.









Answer





Identify the input and study design, number of plants, what one point represents, measured quantity, and units. Include methods explaining how the plotted outcome was calculated.




Q2. A plant-growth plot shows overlapping groups, with treated observations tending higher. Which statement is supported by that description?

Every treated plant grew more than every control.
The treated observations tended to show greater growth in this sample, with overlap.
The treatment always increases growth.







Hint





A description of this sample has a narrower scope than a universal claim.









Answer





(ii). Overlap contradicts (i), and this plot alone does not establish the universal claim in (iii).




Q3. One figure has initial length on x and final length on y. Another has treatment on x and change in length on y. Which more directly addresses whether growth differs between the groups?






Hint





Identify where change in length is actually plotted.









Answer





The treatment-versus-change figure directly compares growth by group. Initial versus final length addresses a different relationship.




Q4. A concentration is calculated as 1000 × (mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol) / (final_volume_ml / 1000), in mmol/L. For glucose mass 0.9008 g, molar mass 180.16 g/mol, and final volume 100 mL, what is the result? Is a graph of these calculated cases independent evidence of a biological treatment effect?






Hint





Trace the supplied formula, then ask where its plotted values came from.









Answer





50 mmol/L. The cases illustrate a supplied calculation; they are not independent evidence of a biological treatment effect.




Q5. What check tests whether a saved report can be reproduced: (i) seeing an old figure in RStudio, or (ii) restarting R and rendering the source with its input files?






Hint





A visible old result may depend on earlier session state.









Answer





(ii). Check that the fresh render succeeds and that its figures, numbers, units, and input description agree. Rendering success alone does not prove the interpretation is correct.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Quiz: R Markdown reports
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Which file is the editable recipe for a report: (i) report.Rmd, (ii) report.html, or (iii) the plot shown in RStudio?






Hint





One file combines prose and code chunks.









Answer





(i). The .Rmd is the source. Rendering it produces HTML for reading; the input data remain separate files.




Q2. A report plots growth_mm before the chunk that imports measurements and calculates growth. What should be changed?






Hint





Rendering follows the document’s chunk order.









Answer





Put package loading, import, and calculation before the plot. The saved report should create every object it uses.




Q3. You created a table only in the Console. A chunk runs interactively, but the report fails in a fresh session because that table is missing. What belongs in the report?






Hint





A fresh session cannot rely on earlier manual commands.









Answer





Include the required package calls, import, and transformations in the report before their results are used. Restart R and render again.




Q4. After changing the input from 24 seedlings to an 18-seedling study, the figure updates but the methods still say 24 plants. Has the report transferred correctly?






Hint





Code output and written descriptions must refer to the same study.









Answer





No. Update the methods, question, captions, and manually written counts. Inline R can connect reported counts to the imported table, but it cannot automatically fix an incorrect study description.




Q5. You correct a caption directly in report.html. What happens when you render report.Rmd again, and where should the correction be saved?






Hint





HTML is generated from the source.









Answer





The generated HTML can overwrite the direct edit. Correct the caption in report.Rmd, render again, and inspect the resulting HTML.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Quiz: Derived tables and figures
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A plant begins at 25.7 mm and ends at 44.3 mm. What should growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm produce? Does adding this column change the source CSV?






Hint





Distinguish the derived R table from the file it was imported from.









Answer





18.6 mm. mutate() creates or changes a column in its returned table. The source CSV stays unchanged unless a separate write operation replaces it.




Q2. Which chooses rows and which chooses columns?
filter(seedlings, treatment == "treated")
select(seedlings, plant_id, growth_mm)






Hint





Ask whether the operation selects observations or variables.









Answer





filter() chooses rows meeting the treatment condition. select() chooses the two named columns.




Q3. 
What does one point represent, and why does horizontal jitter not create additional observations?






Hint





Read the vertical axis and distinguish display position from a measurement.









Answer





One point is one plant’s change in length, in mm. Horizontal jitter separates overlapping points; height = 0 keeps every growth value unchanged. The number of plants is unchanged.




Q4. Collected product is 0.62 g from a supplied maximum of 1.00 g. Another run collects 0.90 g from a maximum of 2.00 g. Using 100 × collected / maximum, which has the higher percentage yield?






Hint





Compare ratios rather than collected masses alone.









Answer





The first yields 62% and the second 45%. The larger collected mass has the smaller percentage because the starting scales differ.




Q5. Required stock volume is target concentration × final volume / stock concentration. For stock 500 mmol/L, target 50 mmol/L, and final volume 50 mL, how much stock is required? What if stock is instead 100 mmol/L and target is 200 mmol/L?






Hint





The concentrations use the same units. Compare the calculated volume with the requested total.









Answer





The first case needs 5 mL. The second formula gives 100 mL for a requested 50 mL total, so that request cannot be met by adding solvent alone. Keep and flag the impossible request.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Quiz: Importing and inspecting tables
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. An imported table has 24 rows and four columns. head() displays six rows. How many plants are in the full table if each row represents one plant?






Hint





A preview and the full table dimensions answer different questions.









Answer





24 plants. head() displays a preview; dim() reports the full row and column counts.




Q2. What does file.exists("data/seedlings.csv") returning TRUE establish? Does it establish that the file contains the intended study and units?






Hint





Separate finding a path from interpreting its contents.









Answer





The file exists at that path relative to R’s working directory. Inspect the table and data dictionary to establish the study, column meanings, and units.




Q3. Predict mean(c(10, NA, 20)), mean(c(10, NA, 20), na.rm = TRUE), and mean(c(10, 0, 20)).






Hint





NA represents an unavailable value; zero is an observed number.









Answer





The results are NA, 15, and 10, respectively. The available-value mean uses two observations, while the last mean uses three.




Q4. An 18-row table is described as one row per plant. It has 17 distinct plant IDs. Should you immediately delete a row?






Hint





A discrepancy is a reason to inspect the data and study description.









Answer





Investigate which ID repeats and why. A recording error, mistaken import, or different row structure could explain it. Repeated IDs can be legitimate in a repeated-measurement table, so deletion needs evidence.




Q5. A solution table contains solution_id, solute, mass_g, molar_mass_g_mol, and final_volume_ml. Which are labels, and what does the numeric type tell you about units?






Hint





Distinguish an identifier from a measured or supplied quantity.









Answer





solution_id and solute are labels. The other columns are quantities. Numeric storage alone does not supply units or justify combining different quantities; use the dictionary and formula.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Quiz: R calculations
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. What does the last line print?
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
final_mm <- 39
growth_mm

17 (ii) 19 (iii) 39







Hint





Which assignment last changed growth_mm?









Answer





(i), 17. R stored that result when the subtraction ran. Running growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm again would update it to 19.




Q2. Three plants have initial lengths c(20, 22, 19) mm and final lengths c(37, 40, 34) mm, in the same plant order. What are their growth values and mean growth?






Hint





Subtract position by position, then divide the total growth by three.









Answer





Growth is c(17, 18, 15) mm. The mean is 50 / 3, about 16.67 mm. The matching plant order makes the position-by-position subtraction meaningful.




Q3. Which survives closing a fresh R session: an object created only in the Console, or instructions saved in day06.R? How can you recreate the object?






Hint





One is in session memory; the other is a file on storage.









Answer





The saved script survives. Open it and run the instructions from the top to recreate its objects. This assumes the session workspace was not separately saved and restored.




Q4. A collected product mass is 0.62 g and the supplied maximum is 1.00 g. Using yield_percent = 100 × collected mass / maximum mass, what is the yield? What would change if the collected mass were 0.70 g?






Hint





Both masses use grams, so their units cancel in the ratio.









Answer





The yields are 62% and 70%, respectively.




Q5. Amount in mol is mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol. Concentration in mol/L is amount divided by final solution volume in litres. For 0.2922 g, 58.44 g/mol, and 100 mL final solution, what is the concentration in mmol/L?






Hint





Convert 100 mL to 0.100 L. Multiply mol/L by 1000 to obtain mmol/L.









Answer





Amount is 0.2922 / 58.44 = 0.005 mol. Concentration is 0.005 / 0.100 = 0.050 mol/L, or 50 mmol/L.




Q6. In the previous question, what happens to concentration if you double only the mass? What if you instead double only the final volume?






Hint





Mass is in the numerator; final volume is in the denominator.









Answer





Doubling mass gives 100 mmol/L. Restoring the original mass and doubling final volume gives 25 mmol/L.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Repeat a useful workflow
text:
Repeat a useful workflow
Today you will repeat yesterday’s investigation with fewer prompts. Repetition helps make file handling a tool you can rely on. The biological task remains: identify the treated samples and prepare a small package that another person can understand.
We then meet R, which will calculate and plot the measurements. The terminal and R console are different places to enter instructions; recognising the difference will prevent a common beginner problem.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: A fresh investigation folder
text:
A fresh investigation folder
Return to your shell workspace:
cd ~/introcomputing-shell
pwd
Use commands from the previous lessons to do the following. Read the whole list once before starting.

Create a fresh folder called day5.
Copy lab-data.zip into it and move into day5.
List the archive’s contents without extracting it.
Extract it into a folder called lab-data inside day5.
Enter the extracted folder and read the README.
Print the treated sample records and save them as treated-samples.txt.
Count the matching records using a pipe. Explain why the result is two.







Help me get started without doing everything





From the workspace use mkdir day5, cp lab-data.zip day5/, then cd day5. The slash after day5/ makes it clear that this destination is a directory. Use unzip -l lab-data.zip before unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data. If a name already exists, inspect it before choosing whether to reuse it.









I cannot remember the search commands





Inside the extracted folder use grep -F treated samples.tsv. Add > treated-samples.txt to save the output, or | wc -l to count it. Do not redirect output into samples.tsv: that is the original input.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Make a package another person can inspect
text:
Make a package another person can inspect
Inside the extracted lab-data folder, make a folder called report. Copy treated-samples.txt into it. Copy README.txt into it with the destination name context.txt. These copies keep the original files available.
Through the file manager, add report/findings.txt describing the sample count, which samples received treatment, what the measurements mean, and the limits of this file-selection exercise. For example, identifying a treated sample does not establish that its treatment changed growth.






Copy and rename commands





mkdir report
cp treated-samples.txt report/
cp README.txt report/context.txt
Create your own findings text in a plain-text editor. Check its saved location with ls report before packaging the folder.



Create and inspect a ZIP package:
zip -r report-bundle.zip report/
unzip -l report-bundle.zip
unzip report-bundle.zip -d review
ls review/report
zip creates an archive. -r includes the folder’s contents recursively, including any nested folders. unzip -l lets you inspect the package, then extraction into review tests what a recipient would receive. You should find context.txt, findings.txt, and treated-samples.txt inside review/report. Open findings.txt from there and check it is readable.
An archive is a snapshot of the files included when it was created or updated. Editing the ordinary report/findings.txt does not automatically update the ZIP. Make a new clearly named package after making changes. An archive stored only next to its originals is still vulnerable if the whole computer is lost.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Choose one transfer check
text:
Choose one transfer check
Choose the seedling file check or the organic-laboratory inventory task.

Check the seedling file routes
Make a note identifying the original archive, extracted files, selected records, findings, and final report archive. Explain each file’s role. Close any open measurement file, then locate S04’s measurement using the manifest.
If the supported remote environment is ready, repeat just the navigation and inspection part there. Use the provided transfer route to move a small file, then identify the local and remote copies. If it is not ready, this step waits; the local practical still stands on its own.


Or: find records in a small organic-laboratory inventory
An inventory is a list of samples. Our simulated organic-chemistry inventory already labels each sample with a class, such as alcohol or ester. Find the records labelled ester using text search.

Download organic-lab.zip and locate it in your file manager. As on day 4, open ~/introcomputing-shell graphically and copy the download there. A browser download is not automatically in Ubuntu.
Return to that workspace in the shell, list the archive before extracting, then extract to a fresh organic-lab folder and enter it. Read README.txt and DICTIONARY.txt with less before inspecting inventory.tsv.
Use grep -F ester inventory.tsv to print matching records. Save them in ester-samples.txt and use a pipe to count them. Locate the saved extract in the file manager, then explain which file remained unchanged.







Hint: the same commands, different filenames





cd ~/introcomputing-shell
unzip -l organic-lab.zip
unzip organic-lab.zip -d organic-lab
cd organic-lab
less README.txt
less DICTIONARY.txt
head inventory.tsv
grep -F ester inventory.tsv > ester-samples.txt
grep -F ester inventory.tsv | wc -l
There are four sample records plus a header. Two records match: O02 and O03. The header does not contain ester. This command matches literal text, not chemical structures or a particular table column. The extracted organic-recovery.csv is for later calculations. If the extraction folder already exists, inspect it and use a fresh name.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Meet R and RStudio
text:
Meet R and RStudio
R is a language and computing environment for working with data. RStudio is an application that provides an editor, an R console, and other tools around R. The editor holds saved instructions; the console runs them. A terminal is a shell prompt, not an R console.
Open RStudio using the R/RStudio setup instructions. If it is not installed yet, watch the demonstration and use setup support before week 2. In the R console, enter:
44.3 - 25.7
R should return 18.6: the increase in length of plant P01, in millimetres. The console might print [1] before the answer. That marks the position of the first displayed element; it is not part of the measurement.
Enter this small supplied example in the R console:
initial_mm <- c(25.7, 24.3, 18.0)
final_mm <- c(44.3, 32.3, 32.9)
plot(initial_mm, final_mm,
     xlab = "Initial length (mm)",
     ylab = "Final length (mm)")
The c(...) pieces collect three values. <- gives each collection a name. plot(...) makes a scatter plot: each point is one plant with an initial and a final length. We will learn these ideas carefully next week; today identify the axes and check that there are three points. This example includes only three plants, not the full experiment.
Use the shell for cd, grep, and unzip, and the R Console for calculations. When a command fails, first identify which program is reading it.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: From a plot to a report
text:
From a plot to a report
The teacher will show a complete HTML report generated from saved measurements and an R Markdown file. Notice the biological question, code, figure with units, and a written interpretation. The goal is to make these together so that the report can be produced again when new measurements arrive. You will build your first version next week.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Test a handover as the receiver
text:
Test a handover as the receiver
Make two versions of your practice report package and test what each contains after extraction.
Use previously unused ZIP names for each snapshot; if a suggested name already exists, choose the next unused version name before running zip. Updating an old archive can retain entries that are no longer in the source folder.

Open the ordinary report folder from today’s earlier exercise. Inspect its findings note and selected records. Add a README that identifies the simulated seedling source archive, what one record represents, length units, which samples were selected, and the purpose of each included file. Avoid a note that merely says “these are the results”.
From its parent directory, create report-v1.zip with zip -r. List the archive with unzip -l, then extract it to a new destination named receiver-v1. Navigate through that destination to find the report folder. Notice that the archived folder name can add another level after extraction.
Open the extracted findings note in the file manager. Check a stated sample ID against the extract and source manifest. If a source file is not included, state in the README where it can be obtained.
In the original ordinary report folder, add a dated correction sentence or clearer unit label. Reopen the unchanged received copy inside receiver-v1 and explain why it still contains the older text. A ZIP is a package made at a particular time, not a live connection to its source folder.
Make a new report-v2.zip, list it, and extract it to receiver-v2. Check the revised sentence in that second received copy. Retain a brief change note so the recipient can tell which version to use without guessing from file modification times alone. Keep the ZIP outside the folder it packages.
Save handover-check.txt in the shell workspace, recording the source folder, both archive names, receiver locations, checked sentence, and one problem that your first README did not explain well. State which computer holds these copies and whether you actually transferred a copy to another computer.







Hint: follow a concrete file, not the word “report”





For example, an extraction into receiver-v1 may place the note at receiver-v1/report/findings.txt. Inspect the actual tree. Editing report/findings.txt does not update that separate ordinary copy or the older ZIP. Repackage after correcting, then verify the newly extracted result; naming it v2 alone is not evidence that it contains the new text.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Prepare a new laboratory receipt
text:
Prepare a new laboratory receipt
Choose the seedling archive or the organic-laboratory archive from your earlier file check. Complete the following workflow for that archive.

Begin with a fresh extraction and read its README/dictionary. Write your own receipt listing the input filenames, their roles, and the known number of sample records. For seedlings this is four records in samples.tsv; for the organic inventory it is four records in inventory.tsv. Distinguish a line naming columns from an actual sample record.
Define one selection question: treated seedlings, or inventory records with the supplied ester label. Predict the count, run the literal search, save its output with an informative filename, and inspect the IDs.
Create a sharing folder containing your receipt, selected records, and a source note. Explain what a recipient could reproduce from that package and which original inputs they would still need. Include the files needed for this exercise.
Package the sharing folder and extract it into a new test location. Close the source windows. Use only the extracted README and files to answer the selection question, and record the route you followed.
Make a short two-column note titled “shell or R?”. Classify pwd, grep -F, unzip, 44.3 - 25.7, and mean(c(12, 14, 16)). In RStudio, run the two R expressions if setup works. They should give 18.6 and 14 respectively; run shell commands in the shell instead. An error from the wrong interpreter does not mean the computer is broken.
Finish with a recovery plan: how will you find your working folder tomorrow, which file will you open to continue, and where is the separately stored backup? If the university’s supported backup or remote access is pending, say so rather than pretending another local copy fulfils that requirement.

Check and retain: your tested sharing ZIP, receipt, handover check, and shell/R note. Both selection routes have two matching sample records in the supplied files. Next week’s R work will use the ordinary extracted course project, not an .Rproj opened from inside either shell-practice archive.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Why inspect an archive after making it?





The name of the ZIP does not guarantee what it contains. Listing and extracting it checks the folder structure and the actual saved files a recipient gets.









Where should grep run, and where should 44.3 - 25.7 run?





Use grep in the terminal’s shell. Enter the calculation in the R console. The prompt tells you which program is waiting for instructions; learn to check it before entering a command.



Save today: a tested report-bundle.zip and the ordinary report folder. Add one sentence to findings.txt explaining how the package differs from its extracted contents. Repackage it if you want that change included in the ZIP. If you chose the inventory transfer check, also keep organic-lab/ester-samples.txt in the shell workspace.
Next: R objects, calculations, and vectors.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Which seedlings received the treatment?
text:
Which seedlings received the treatment?
A laboratory has supplied a small archive containing measurements and sample information. Before doing statistics, we need to establish what is in the archive and which files belong to the treated samples. We will do this with ordinary command-line utilities. The data are simulated for teaching.
The archive in this exercise is a small separate practice dataset with four samples. It is not the 24-plant dataset we will analyse in R. A manifest is a table describing which samples and files are present. Sample identifiers connect the manifest to the measurements.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Put the download in a known place
text:
Put the download in a known place

Download lab-data.zip with your browser.
Locate the downloaded file in File Explorer or Finder.
In your terminal, run cd ~/introcomputing-shell, then pwd.
Open that folder graphically using explorer.exe . in local Ubuntu on Windows or open . on Mac.
Copy the downloaded ZIP into this workspace using the file manager.
Back in the terminal, run ls. Confirm that lab-data.zip appears.

On a remote computer, use the course’s supported transfer route when available. The browser’s local download is not automatically a remote file.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Look before extracting
text:
Look before extracting
From ~/introcomputing-shell, run:
unzip -l lab-data.zip
The -l option lists archive contents without extracting them. Identify README.txt, samples.tsv, and the measurements and field-notes folders. There should be four measurement files, S01 through S04. The displayed sizes and dates describe the archive entries.
Now extract:
unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data
cd lab-data
ls
less README.txt
The -d lab-data option chooses the destination folder. Extraction creates ordinary files you can open; it does not remove the ZIP. In less, use Space to move down, arrow keys to move by lines, and q to quit and return to the prompt. A short file may already fit on one screen.






Extraction asks whether to replace a file





You have probably extracted into the same destination before. Stop and inspect the destination in the file manager. For this first run, choose a fresh destination name if necessary and use that name in cd.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Read a table without changing it
text:
Read a table without changing it
Run:
head -n 3 samples.tsv
wc -l samples.tsv
head -n 3 prints the first three lines. wc -l counts newline-terminated lines. The supplied manifest has a header and four sample records, so the count is 5, not four biological samples. Tabs separate the columns in this TSV (tab-separated values) file. A CSV uses commas instead.
The columns are sample_id, treatment, and file. Follow the file path for sample S03:
head measurements/S03.csv
Before interpreting a number, use the README to find out what it measures and which units were used. The filename locates measurements; it does not explain their biological meaning by itself.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Search the manifest with grep
text:
Search the manifest with grep
Run:
grep -F treated samples.tsv
grep prints lines matching a search. -F asks for a literal text match, so we do not need to learn pattern syntax. The supplied manifest should return two lines, S03 and S04, labelled treated.
This is text search, not an understanding of table columns or experiments. Searching for treated would also match untreated if that word were present. Our prepared labels are control and treated; the header does not contain the search word. Always inspect what a search actually selected.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Save a search, then count its records
text:
Save a search, then count its records
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
less treated-samples.txt
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
> redirects the output to a file instead of displaying it. It replaces the contents if that output file already exists. Never use the input filename on the right side here. treated-samples.txt is a new text extract; the original samples.tsv remains unchanged. It has no header, because the header did not match our search.
The vertical bar | is a pipe. It passes the matching lines from grep to wc -l, which counts them. The result should be 2. The pipe does not need an intermediate saved file. Count lines only when lines really represent the records you intend to count.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Preserve and organise a working copy
text:
Preserve and organise a working copy
Still inside lab-data, run:
mkdir working
cp samples.tsv working/samples-copy.tsv
mv working/samples-copy.tsv working/manifest-practice.tsv
ls working
cp creates a copy; mv moves or renames an entry. Here only the practice copy was renamed. Confirm that the original samples.tsv still exists. Both commands can replace existing destinations, so check names before running them.
Use the file manager to create observations.txt inside working. Record: how many sample records there are, which two received treatment, and which measurement file you would open for S04. Add the distinction between the five manifest lines and the four samples.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: A first look at the remote computer
text:
A first look at the remote computer
The teacher will demonstrate SSH and remote desktop. SSH gives a terminal on another computer. A remote desktop gives a graphical workspace there. In either case, saved files can be on that other computer, even while your laptop displays the session.
When account details are available, follow the supplied instructions and try pwd and ls remotely. Record which computer runs the command and holds the files. If accounts are not ready, continue with the local exercises.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Audit the archive and the search
text:
Audit the archive and the search
Extract a fresh copy as lab-audit. Use its four known sample records to test searches and redirection. Save the commands and results in an audit note.

From the folder containing lab-data.zip, list its entries with unzip -l. Predict the extraction tree, then extract with unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-audit. Identify README, manifest, measurement files, and field notes. Listing an archive did not extract its entries; extraction did not remove the ZIP.
Enter lab-audit and inspect samples.tsv with head or less. Follow each manifest path to its measurement file. Record which sample and units appear in that file. Confirm that S03 and S04 are the treated records and that their saved lengths differ; two matching labels are not identical samples.
Run wc -l samples.tsv, then grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l. Explain both answers in words, including the header. Inspect the actual matched lines rather than assuming a count proves that the right records were selected.
Copy the manifest to search-trap.tsv using cp. Open only that copy in the text editor, and replace S01’s control label by untreated. Predict whether grep -F treated search-trap.tsv will select S01; run it and explain why literal text search is not a treatment-aware table operation. Save this as a demonstration of a limitation, not a corrected biological annotation.
Save the original treated matches to treated-audit.txt. Copy that extract to extract-backup.txt. Now run grep -F control samples.tsv > treated-audit.txt only on this disposable extract. Compare the files with less: the name treated-audit.txt no longer describes its contents. > replaces output; it does not check whether the filename makes scientific sense.
Restore the correctly named treated extract by rerunning the treated search. Write a note recording the misleading-name experiment and the corrected command. Never use samples.tsv itself as the output destination: shell redirection can truncate an input before the reader starts. Explain this hazard without experimenting on a raw input.







Hint: use known records to test the operation





In the unchanged fixture, wc -l samples.tsv gives 5 and the treated pipe gives 2. In the deliberately altered search-trap.tsv, the same substring search matches three lines, because untreated contains treated. A useful audit records both the command and the records selected. It does not silently rename those selected lines “three treated plants”.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Find a file discrepancy and report it
text:
Find a file discrepancy and report it
You are checking a received folder before analysis. The following discrepancies are created in a disposable copy so you can practise recovery; they are not claims that the supplied archive is faulty.

Copy the extracted lab-audit folder using the file manager to a separately named received-check folder. Confirm you are in that copy in both terminal and graphical views. Locate its measurements/S04.csv and rename it S04-renamed.csv. Keep its contents intact.
Starting from the copied manifest, check whether each listed relative file path exists by navigating and listing the relevant folder. Identify the one discrepancy. Explain why a manifest record can still exist while the named file cannot be opened.
Read the renamed measurement and identify S04 from its contents. Restore the original name using the evidence of the known deliberate rename. Recheck the manifest path, record the action, and distinguish a supported repair from guessing which similarly named file “probably belongs” to a sample.
Repeat the treated search on the restored copy. While inside received-check, save treated-received.txt (its path from the parent is received-check/treated-received.txt); use a pipe to count its records and a reader to inspect their IDs. Identify which command wrote a new file and which merely displayed information.
While still inside received-check, produce audit.txt (from the parent, received-check/audit.txt) with the original archive name, extraction location, header/record counts, search limitations, discrepancy, evidence, repair, and final check. Include the current computer, because the same path on a remote machine would describe different storage.
Close the measurement file, then locate it again using the manifest and your audit. Check its ID and length against the source archive. Explain in the audit why a line count alone could not detect the renamed file.

Check and retain: both audit notes, the preserved source manifest, search extracts, and the deliberately labelled trap file. S03’s length is 42.4 mm and S04’s is 39.8 mm. Restoring a filename does not alter either measurement.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Did grep change the manifest? Why does wc -l sometimes count a header?





grep reads the file; redirection saved its output separately. wc -l counts lines, not their meaning. The full manifest includes a header, while our saved matching lines do not. We must know the file’s structure to interpret the count.



Save today: treated-samples.txt, working/manifest-practice.tsv, and working/observations.txt in the extracted lab-data folder. Be able to show where the untouched archive and manifest are located.
Next: repeat the workflow and package your findings.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Why type commands?
text:
Why type commands?
The terminal gives us another way to ask the computer to work with files. It becomes useful when we repeat a task, inspect many text records, or work on a remote computer. The folders have not become a new kind of object: we are describing the same locations using words instead of clicks.
Today we will create a small shell workspace and move between its folders. Tomorrow it will hold files from a biological laboratory exercise.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Open the right terminal
text:
Open the right terminal
Follow the supported Windows/Mac setup page. Windows students use Ubuntu for these commands. Mac students use Terminal. If local installation is unavailable, ask the teacher for a supported environment.
On Windows, Ubuntu has a different home folder from Windows itself. For this week’s terminal exercises we deliberately use a separate folder in the Ubuntu home directory. Our native RStudio project will stay in the laptop Documents folder. We will practise transferring a file between these places explicitly.
A shell reads a command and starts the requested program. The terminal is the window through which we interact with the shell. You might see something like this:
anna@laptop:~$
This is a prompt. It means the shell is ready. Your prompt will differ and may end with % on a Mac. Type only the command after the prompt and press Enter.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Worked example: where am I?
text:
Worked example: where am I?
Run each line separately:
pwd
ls
pwd prints the current working directory. It might print /home/anna in Ubuntu or /Users/anna on a Mac. These are examples, not text to type. ls lists the names inside the current directory. Your list need not match anyone else’s.
Now create our workspace:
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing-shell/practice
cd introcomputing-shell
pwd
ls
cd means change directory; without a destination, it takes you home. mkdir means make directory. The option -p allows it to create the parent folder too and to accept folders that already exist. The final ls should include practice. An empty folder is still a real folder.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Check it in the file manager
text:
Check it in the file manager
In Ubuntu on Windows, run:
explorer.exe .
In Mac Terminal, run:
open .
The dot means the current directory. The graphical window should show the practice folder. Leave this window open for the next exercise. On a remote Linux system these laptop-specific commands are not the remote file-transfer method; follow the supplied remote instructions instead.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Make a map and follow it
text:
Make a map and follow it
From introcomputing-shell, run:
cd practice
mkdir seedlings
mkdir observations
ls
cd seedlings
pwd
cd ..
pwd
.. means the parent directory. The two pwd results should end in /practice/seedlings and /practice. Compare the file manager with this tree:
introcomputing-shell/
└── practice/
    ├── seedlings/
    └── observations/
Use the graphical window to open seedlings. Does this make the terminal move there too? Run pwd to check. Each window can have its own current location. Clicking in one does not automatically change the other.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Commands, arguments, and options
text:
Commands, arguments, and options
In cd seedlings, cd is the command and seedlings is its argument: the destination. In ls -l, -l is an option asking for a longer listing. You do not need to interpret every column yet; identify which column contains names.
Try these from practice:
ls -l
cd observations
ls
An empty listing from ls means there are no visible entries to list. It does not mean the command failed. Many commands report success by simply returning to the prompt.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Recover from an ordinary mistake
text:
Recover from an ordinary mistake
Return to practice with cd .., then try cd Observations. We created observations with a lowercase o. Ubuntu distinguishes uppercase and lowercase names. Many Macs do not distinguish them on their default disk, so this may work there. Always match the actual spelling so your work transfers between computers.
Now deliberately try:
cd no-such-folder
Read the message. The folder is missing; your computer has not broken. Run pwd and ls before trying again. Ask “where am I, and what is actually here?”






I’m lost. How can I return to the workspace?





Run cd ~/introcomputing-shell, then pwd. ~ is shorthand for your home directory. This route works even if you have navigated into several nested folders.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Small keyboard habits that save effort
text:
Small keyboard habits that save effort

Tab: type the first few letters of a folder, then Tab to complete a name when it is unambiguous. Try cd pra then Tab from the workspace.
Up arrow: recall a previous command. Read it before running it again.
Ctrl+C: interrupt a running command or clear a partly typed command. This is different from copying selected text. Ubuntu terminal windows commonly use Ctrl+Shift+C/V for copying and pasting; Mac uses Command+C/V.
Quotes: keep a name containing spaces together, for example mkdir "field notes". Without quotes those words can become separate arguments.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Predict, run, and recover
text:
Predict, run, and recover
Work in ~/introcomputing-shell, which is the shell workspace on the computer running this terminal. It is separate from the native RStudio project on Windows. A command sequence is easier to understand when you predict its effect on a drawn tree before running it. Save a plain-text command log with the command, your prediction, the observed result, and a correction if needed.

Draw the starting tree using the folders you actually have. Run pwd and ls to check it. Enter practice, create a child day03, and enter that child. At each step, predict the final part of pwd before asking for it.
Create two children in day03: readings and field notes. For the second, use mkdir "field notes". Quotes keep the two words as one argument. Inspect the names with ls, and practise tab completion to enter the spaced name. Record how many directories you created, not just how many words you typed.
Return to day03. Predict and run cd readings, then cd .., then pwd. Now try cd not-present. Read the error and run pwd again. Explain why a failed navigation did not create a destination or take you somewhere else.
Open a second terminal window and run pwd there. Navigate the first window to readings. Check both windows again. Each shell has its own current working directory; a command in one does not automatically move the other. Save both locations in the log and label their windows.
Use an absolute home-based route to return the first shell to the workspace: cd ~/introcomputing-shell. Reach day03 again with a relative route. Explain what extra knowledge a relative route assumes about your starting place. Test the same relative text from a different starting folder and describe the result without changing your real course project.
In the file manager, locate day03 through explorer.exe . on Ubuntu/Windows or open . on Mac after navigating there. Make a note graphically inside readings, refresh the terminal listing, and identify it. Editing a file through the graphical view does not make it a different kind of storage.







Hint: return to a known location





Run pwd to establish where you actually are, then return to ~/introcomputing-shell. Inspect ls before entering the next folder.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Write and test a route
text:
Write and test a route
Create a new subtree called route-challenge under your shell workspace. Save its tree and tested navigation routes in navigation-transfer.txt.

Inside route-challenge, create neighbouring inputs and results folders, and place a notes folder inside results. Draw the intended tree before creating it. Use only navigation, listing, and directory-creation commands already taught. A path to a new nested folder needs its parent to exist or the explained mkdir -p option.
Use the graphical bridge to save a small README.txt in route-challenge. State the purpose of each child and mark the data as a practice exercise. Locate it from the terminal without assuming that your browser Downloads happens to be the current directory.
Write three navigation routes: route-challenge to notes, notes to inputs, and inputs back to the workspace home. For each, state the starting folder. Include one route with .. and one with ~.
