title: Glossary: words we use in this course
text:
Word
Meaning here




File
A named, saved collection of information, such as text, measurements, or a picture


Folder / directory
A container organising files and other folders


File system
The way an operating system stores and organises files and directories


Path
An address locating a file or directory on a particular computer


Extension
A filename ending such as .csv, .R, .Rmd, or .html, indicating its intended format


Home directory
The starting personal folder for an account on a computer


Working directory
The folder relative paths currently start from


Operating system
Software managing the computer and the applications running on it


CPU
The processor that carries out instructions


RAM / memory
Working storage used by running programs; save work to persistent files


Process
A running instance of a program


Bit / byte
A bit is 0 or 1; a byte contains eight bits, with 256 possible patterns


Terminal
A window or interface through which you interact with a shell


Shell
A program interpreting commands such as cd and ls


Console
In this course, usually the R interface that reads R expressions


Local / remote
On your current laptop / on another computer reached over a network


SSH
A secure connection to a remote shell


Remote desktop
A graphical session on a remote computer


Archive
A package containing files and folders, for example a ZIP


CSV / TSV
Text tables whose fields are separated by commas / tabs


Object
A named value held in an R session


Function
A named operation applied to inputs, such as mean()


Argument
An input or setting given to a function or command


Package
A collection of R functions and related resources


Observation
A recorded measurement or set of measurements; not necessarily an independent replicate


Experimental unit
The independently allocated entity, such as a pot or culture flask


Technical replicate
A repeated measurement of the same underlying sample


Missing value
A measurement that is unavailable; represented by NA in R


Raw data
The original supplied measurements, preserved without overwriting


Theoretical mass
In the organic practice, the supplied maximum possible product mass for a run


Isolated mass
In the organic practice, the dry product collected, assumed pure for the simplified calculation


Percentage yield
100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass, using the same mass units


Percentage point
A difference on a percentage scale: 70% minus 60% is 10 percentage points


Derived data
Values calculated or cleaned from the originals with documented code


Render / Knit
Run a report’s code and combine results with its text to create a document


Reproducibility
Being able to regenerate a result from its stated inputs, code, and environment

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
text:
Start with the biological question and the independent experimental unit. Neither a large table nor a small p-value can repair a design with no independent replication.
An interval around the mean does not describe where 95% of individual plants will fall. Adding technical repeats of the same plant does not add independent plants to the sample size.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
section: The two comparisons taught here
text:
The two comparisons taught here
Independent groups: separate plants/pots allocated to control and treatment. Use a guided Welch two-sample t-test for the difference in mean growth. Define the direction before reporting it, such as treated minus control.
Paired observations: the same plant before and after a change. Compute after minus before within each plant, then analyse the differences. Correctly matching identifiers is essential; row order in two files is not evidence of matching pairs.
Both approaches need independent experimental units or pairs. For small samples, inspect unusual observations and strong skew. A test is conditional on its assumptions; you are not learning an automatic test-selection algorithm.
A p-value is the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Report the estimated difference, its units, confidence interval, sample sizes, and a biological interpretation. A small p-value does not establish a large or causal effect; a large one does not establish equality.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
section: A straight line
text:
A straight line
In lm(y ~ x, data = table), the intercept is fitted y at x = 0 and the slope is the fitted change in y for a one-unit increase in x. The slope’s units are y-units per x-unit. The residual is observed y minus fitted y.
For calibration, standards have known x values; invert the fitted line to obtain an unknown concentration from its signal, only within a supported range. This simple calculation provides a point estimate, without full uncertainty propagation. For an observational biological association, the slope does not establish what would happen if we intervened to change x.
See week 3 and week 4 for worked examples.

title: Quiz: Files and folders
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Which is a file: (i) Excel, (ii) seedlings.csv, or (iii) File Explorer?






Hint





A file stores named information; an application opens or changes it.









Answer





(ii). seedlings.csv stores measurements. Excel is a spreadsheet application; File Explorer is a file manager.




Q2. You close the application displaying a saved CSV. Has the saved file been deleted?






Hint





Distinguish the window displaying information from the file on storage.









Answer





No. Closing the application leaves the saved file in its folder. You can find it in the file manager and reopen it.




Q3. A practice copy of seedlings.csv is renamed seedlings.jpg. Has it become a photograph?






Hint





Does renaming rewrite the contents into another format?









Answer





No. The comma-separated table remains. The extension is now misleading. Open the practice copy as text to inspect its contents.




Q4. The first lines of a CSV are:
plant_id,treatment,initial_mm,final_mm
P01,control,25.7,44.3
How many plant records are shown? What was P01’s increase in length?






Hint





The first line names columns. Increase is final length minus initial length.









Answer





One plant record is shown; the header is not a plant. P01 increased by 44.3 - 25.7 = 18.6 mm.




Q5. You copy a file from data to output, then edit the copy. Which file changes? What route information would let you find it again?






Hint





A copy is another file. The application name alone is not a location.









Answer





The file under output changes; the original under data stays as supplied. Record the computer, folder route, and full filename of the saved copy.

title: Quiz: Paths and the working computer
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A project contains neighbouring data and reports folders. From the project root, data/seedlings.csv reaches the input. From inside reports, where does that same relative path point?






Hint





A relative path starts from the current folder.









Answer





It asks for data inside reports: reports/data/seedlings.csv relative to the project root. That is a different location. Return to the project root before following the original route.




Q2. Which remains after an ordinary application closes: (i) its running process, (ii) a deliberately saved text file, or (iii) every unsaved edit?






Hint





Storage and current application state have different jobs.









Answer





(ii). A saved file remains on storage. The process stops. Unsaved edits may be lost or recovered by a particular editor; inspect the saved file.




Q3. Would adding RAM automatically provide more space for saved microscope photographs?






Hint





Which component holds saved files between sessions?









Answer





No. RAM supports running work; persistent storage, such as an SSD, holds saved photographs.




Q4. You move the practice folder map-a into map-b. Does its note necessarily change? Will its old path still locate it?






Hint





Compare contents with location.









Answer





The note’s contents can stay identical while its location changes. Its old path no longer locates it; update the route to include map-b.




Q5. You see report.html in a remote desktop. Is that file automatically in your laptop’s Downloads folder? Is a ZIP beside the original a backup against losing the laptop?






Hint





Identify the computer and storage holding each copy.









Answer





No to both. Remote access displays another computer; file transfer is a separate action. A local ZIP is still lost with the laptop unless another copy is stored elsewhere.

title: Quiz: The terminal
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. You are in route-challenge/results/notes. The folder inputs is directly inside route-challenge. Which command reaches it?

cd ../inputs (ii) cd ../../inputs (iii) cd inputs







Hint





Draw the route back to the folder containing both results and inputs.









Answer





(ii). The first .. reaches results; the second reaches route-challenge. From there, enter inputs.




Q2. What differs between mkdir field notes and mkdir "field notes"?






Hint





How many destination arguments does the shell read in each command?









Answer





The first creates two directories, field and notes. The second creates one directory whose name contains a space: field notes.




Q3. A terminal is in practice. You run cd missing-folder, and the shell reports that the folder does not exist. What does pwd show afterwards?






Hint





Did the requested change of directory succeed?









Answer





The path to practice. A failed cd leaves the current working directory unchanged. Use ls to inspect the names that actually exist.




Q4. Two terminal windows are in the same directory. In the first, you run cd seedlings. Does the second window move too? Have any files moved?






Hint





Distinguish a shell’s current location from the stored folder tree.









Answer





Each shell has its own working directory, so the second stays where it was. cd changes a shell’s location; it moves no files or folders.




Q5. Which command creates a directory: pwd, ls, mkdir readings, or cd readings? What do the other three do?






Hint





Which commands inspect storage, and which change a location?









Answer





mkdir readings creates the directory. pwd prints the current directory; ls lists its entries; cd readings enters an existing directory.

title: Quiz: Inspecting an archive
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. What differs between unzip -l lab-data.zip and unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data?






Hint





The -l and -d options have different roles.









Answer





-l lists entries without extracting them. The second command extracts ordinary files into lab-data. Both leave the ZIP available.




Q2. A manifest has one header line and four sample lines, each ending with a newline. Two samples are labelled treated; the header lacks that word. What do these commands print?
wc -l samples.tsv
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l






Hint





The first counts all lines; the second counts only matching lines.









Answer





The counts are 5 and 2. Five lines represent four samples plus a header.




Q3. In a practice manifest, S01 is untreated, S03 and S04 are treated, and S02 is control. How many records match grep -F treated? Are they all treated samples?






Hint





Literal text matching also finds a search word inside a longer word.









Answer





Three records match: S01, S03, and S04. untreated contains treated, so a text match is not the same as selecting a treatment category.




Q4. What does grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt change if the destination already exists?






Hint





Consider both the input and the redirection destination.









Answer





It replaces treated-samples.txt with the matching lines. The distinct input samples.tsv stays unchanged. Redirection needs a separate destination because > can truncate a file before reading starts.




Q5. The manifest names measurements/S04.csv, but a practice copy contains S04-renamed.csv. What evidence would support restoring its name?






Hint





A similar filename alone does not prove sample identity.









Answer





In this exercise the rename was deliberate and known. Check the file’s recorded sample ID and 39.8 mm measurement against the source, restore S04.csv, and recheck the manifest path. An unexplained discrepancy would need source evidence.

title: Quiz: Packaging files and meeting R
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. You make report-v1.zip, then correct report/findings.txt. Will extracting v1 show the correction?






Hint





An archive stores a snapshot, not a live link to its source.









Answer





No. Create a new package after the correction, extract it to a new folder, and inspect the corrected sentence there.




Q2. Which check gives stronger evidence that a report package is usable: (i) giving the ZIP a clear name, or (ii) listing and extracting it, then reading the extracted files?






Hint





A name does not guarantee contents.









Answer





(ii). The check verifies the actual files and folder structure a recipient receives. A clear name is still useful.




Q3. Where should each instruction run: pwd, grep -F treated samples.tsv, and 44.3 - 25.7?






Hint





The shell and R are different interpreters.









Answer





Run pwd and grep in the terminal’s shell. Run the subtraction in the R Console, where it gives 18.6 mm for the supplied plant lengths.




Q4. The inventory has four sample rows plus a header; O02 and O03 contain ester, and no other line does. What should grep -F ester inventory.tsv | wc -l print? What has it selected?






Hint





The pipe counts the matching lines.









Answer





2. It selected text records containing ester; the supplied labels provide the chemical classification.




Q5. A scatter plot has initial length on x and final length on y, both in mm, with one point per plant. What do three points represent? Does the y-axis directly show growth?






Hint





Read what each axis measures before interpreting it.









Answer





Three points represent three plants. The y-axis shows final size. Growth would require subtracting initial length from final length for each plant.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
text:
Try each question before opening its answer. Use your file manager, terminal, and terminal reference to check actions as well as words.
Topic quizzes: 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 1. Find the saved work
text:
1. Find the saved work
You edited a note in an application, closed it, and cannot find it in the application’s recent-files list. What should you be able to identify, and why does the application name alone not tell you where the file is?






Answer and check





Identify the computer, folder, and filename where the note was saved. An application can open files from many locations. Navigate to the saved folder in the file manager and reopen the ordinary file. If the changes were not saved, the saved contents may differ from the previous screen.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 2. A relative path needs a starting place
text:
2. A relative path needs a starting place
From introcomputing-course, the path data/seedlings.csv works. From inside reports, why does the same path ask for a different location?






Answer and check





A relative path starts at the current folder. From reports it asks for reports/data/seedlings.csv, not the neighbouring data folder. Return to the project root, then locate data/seedlings.csv. The file did not move; your starting location changed. In a shell, use pwd to identify that starting place.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 3. Predict a pipe and a saved extract
text:
3. Predict a pipe and a saved extract
The supplied samples.tsv has a header plus four records: two control and two treated. The header does not contain treated. What does this print, and does the second command change the source manifest?
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt






Answer and check





The first command prints a line count of 2. grep sends matching lines through the pipe to wc. The second saves matches to treated-samples.txt; it does not change samples.tsv. > replaces any previous contents of the destination. This is literal text matching, not interpretation of treatment groups or chemical classes. It could also match untreated if that word occurred.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 4. Copy, move, and extract
text:
4. Copy, move, and extract
What remains after copying notes.txt to notes-copy.txt? How is moving the original different? Does opening a ZIP preview necessarily mean its files have been extracted into an ordinary project folder?






Answer and check





A copy leaves the original and makes another file. A move changes the original’s location or name. A ZIP preview is a view of an archive; use extraction to create the ordinary folder and files needed for the project. Locate the actual extracted .Rproj, rather than opening one inside an archive preview.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 5. Memory and storage
text:
5. Memory and storage
Would adding RAM automatically provide more room for saved photographs? Why can restarting R remove objects while leaving a saved CSV intact?






Answer and check





RAM supports running work; persistent storage holds saved files. They have different roles. An R object in session memory must be recreated after restart; the CSV remains on storage and can be imported again. Saving a script preserves the instructions, not an automatically running process.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 6. The same filename on two computers
text:
6. The same filename on two computers
You see report.html in a remote desktop. Is it automatically in your laptop’s Downloads folder? Would a ZIP stored beside the original be a separate backup against losing the laptop?






Answer and check





No to both. Remote access is not automatic file transfer, and identical names can refer to separate copies. Use the supported transfer route and name the destination. A ZIP on the same disk is a convenient sharing package; use supported separate storage for protection against losing that disk.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 7. A renamed extension
text:
7. A renamed extension
A practice copy of seedlings.csv is renamed name-test.txt. Did its plant measurements become a different format? What would you inspect?






Worked answer





The name changed; renaming did not convert the contents. Open the practice copy as plain text and inspect its comma-separated header and records. Use actual conversion software only when a task calls for conversion; no conversion is needed here. Keep the original CSV unchanged.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 8. Two terminal windows
text:
8. Two terminal windows
Shell A is inside day03/readings while Shell B is in the workspace root. You run cd .. in Shell A. What changes in Shell B?






Worked answer





Nothing automatically changes in Shell B. Each shell has its own current directory. Check pwd in both windows. The folders themselves did not move, and changing a shell location does not move an independent file-manager window.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 9. Quote the intended argument
text:
9. Quote the intended argument
You want one folder called field notes. Compare mkdir field notes with mkdir “field notes”. Which command expresses the intended single name?






Worked answer





The quoted command groups both words into one argument and creates one named folder. The unquoted command normally supplies two names and creates two folders. Practise only in the disposable workspace, then use ls and the graphical view to inspect what actually exists.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 10. A surprising grep count
text:
10. A surprising grep count
In a copy of the four-record manifest, S01 is labelled untreated; S03 and S04 are treated. How many records match grep -F treated, and does that count establish three treatment allocations?






Worked answer





There are three literal text matches because untreated contains treated. It does not establish three treated plants. Inspect the selected IDs and use the study description to understand labels. The unchanged source manifest still has two treated records.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 11. A manifest path fails
text:
11. A manifest path fails
The manifest lists measurements/S04.csv, but the copied folder contains S04-renamed.csv. Should you delete the record, change its measurement, or investigate identity?






Worked answer





Investigate. In the deliberate classroom rename, the file contents still identify S04 and 39.8 mm, and the known rename supports restoring its filename. In a real ambiguous case, obtain source evidence.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 12. The recipient has the old correction
text:
12. The recipient has the old correction
You edited ordinary report/findings.txt after creating report-v1.zip. You extract v1 and see the old sentence. What happened, and what is a useful verification?






Worked answer





The archive is a snapshot and did not update when the source changed. Create a newly named package, extract it into a fresh receiver location, and inspect the actual corrected sentence. Confirm both archive version and extracted folder before assuming editing failed.



Return to day 5 exercises for a complete file workflow, or continue to week 2.

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
A seedling was 20 mm long at the start of an experiment and 37 mm long at the end. How much did it grow? Save a calculation that reproduces the answer. The measurements are simulated teaching data.
Open the extracted introcomputing-course folder and double-click introcomputing.Rproj. R is the program that calculates. RStudio is the workspace we use to write instructions, run R, inspect results, and prepare reports. Its Console accepts R instructions. An R script is a saved text file containing instructions. Use the R Console for R expressions and the terminal from week 1 for shell commands such as ls.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Start with a calculation
text:
Start with a calculation
Type the following in the R Console, pressing Enter after each line. The Console already supplies the > prompt. The [1] in an answer labels the first printed element; it is not part of your measurement.

37 - 20
20 * 2
37 / 20

You should obtain 17, 40, and 1.85. The last value is a ratio, not a change in mm. The calculation can be correct while answering the wrong biological question.
Now choose File → New File → R Script, save it as day06.R in the project folder, and put this in the script:

# Measurements are lengths in millimetres.
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm

<- assigns the result on its right to a named object on its left. Read it as “store this value under this name”. A line beginning with # is a comment for people. R ignores the comment. To run a line from the editor, place the cursor on it and use Run. Saving a script does not run it; running a script does not save changes in the editor.
If RStudio is not ready, use the R and RStudio setup page. Keep the R reference sheet open while practising.
Object names are case-sensitive. growth_mm and Growth_mm are different names. An object in the Environment pane is in this R session’s memory. The script is a file on storage. Reopening the script does not recreate the object until you run the instructions.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: One name can hold several values
text:
One name can hold several values
c() combines values into a vector, an ordered collection. Functions have names followed by parentheses; the values inside are their arguments.

initial_mm <- c(20, 22, 19)
final_mm <- c(37, 40, 34)
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm
mean(growth_mm)
length(growth_mm)

The growth values are 17, 18, and 15 mm. R subtracts position by position here. mean() calculates their average, approximately 16.67 mm. length() counts values and gives 3. This only makes biological sense because both vectors list the same three plants in the same order. Matching observations matters.
Numbers, text, and logical values are different kinds of data:

plant_id <- c("P01", "P02", "P03")
growth_mm > 16

The comparison gives TRUE TRUE FALSE. Quotation marks identify text; "20" is text whereas 20 is a number. Plant IDs belong in text even if they contain numbers. To open help for a function, run ?mean in the Console and read its Description and Examples rather than every option.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Calculate growth and a ratio
text:
Calculate growth and a ratio

Keep the three-plant calculation in day06.R and explain the units in comments.
Add a fourth plant that grew from 21 to 39 mm. Extend both vectors, rerun the calculation, and check length(growth_mm).
Choose one ratio exercise: calculate each plant’s final/initial ratio in an object called length_ratio, explaining how it differs from growth in mm; or use the product-yield calculation below.
Change the first final length from 37 to 38 mm. Predict which growth value changes and check your prediction.
Save the script, restart R through Session → Restart R, and run its lines from the top. Everything it needs should be in the script.


Alternative ratio exercise: how much product was collected?
In a synthesis, starting materials are used to make a product. For this simulated example, the maximum possible product mass has already been calculated for you: 1.00 g. Call it theoretical_mass_g. The collected dry product has mass 0.62 g, called isolated_mass_g. Assume this collected material is pure product for this simplified calculation.
Percentage yield means the collected product as a percentage of the supplied maximum. Compute 100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass, using the same mass unit for both. Put this calculation in day06.R if you chose this alternative:

theoretical_mass_g <- 1.00
isolated_mass_g <- 0.62
yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
yield_percent

The answer is 62%. The gram units cancel in the ratio. Predict the result if collected mass changes to 0.70 g, then rerun; it should be 70%. Add a comment explaining why 0.62 g is a mass and 62% is a proportion relative to a maximum.






Hint: an object is not found





Check the spelling, including capitals, and run the line that creates the object. An editor line has no effect until it runs. If the Console shows +, an expression is unfinished: check quotes or parentheses, or press Esc to cancel it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Trace a calculation through its inputs
text:
Trace a calculation through its inputs
Create day06-extended.R at the project root. Keep all numerical inputs and comments in that file. Use the Console to inspect results, then recreate them from the saved script after a restart. Record predictions before running each changed calculation.

Begin with initial_mm <- 20, final_mm <- 37, and growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm. Print all three objects. Now change only final_mm to 39 and print growth_mm without rerunning the subtraction. Explain the stale value: assigning a number to one object does not make every previous calculation update automatically like a spreadsheet formula.
Rerun the subtraction, check the new answer, and add a comment identifying the dependency. Put the lines in their correct order and run the script from the top. A reliable source creates inputs before it uses them.
Recreate the three-plant vectors from the demonstration. Make a deliberately reordered copy of the final vector, c(34, 37, 40), and calculate apparent changes. Compare these with the correctly paired changes and explain the difference.
Return to the correctly ordered vectors. Print length(initial_mm) and length(final_mm) before subtracting. Extend both to four plants as in the earlier practical. Explain why equal lengths are necessary here but do not prove that the same plant occupies each position.
Convert the correctly calculated growth vector from millimetres to centimetres using division by ten. Store it under a new name ending _cm, print it, and compare its mean with the mean in mm.
Calculate the final/initial ratio for the corrected vectors, or the supplied product-yield ratio from the alternative task. Describe in comments which operation is subtraction and which is division, what quantity each produces, and why its units differ. Keep the input masses or lengths alongside the calculation so a reader can repeat it.







Hint: a name stores the current result, not a live recipe





With initial 20 and final 37, the assigned growth is 17. Updating final to 39 leaves that stored growth at 17 until you execute the subtraction again; it then becomes 19 mm. A script supplies an order of operations you can rerun. R may recycle a shorter vector; check both vector lengths and plant correspondence.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Calculate a solution concentration
text:
Calculate a solution concentration
A solution contains a substance in a solvent. A mole, abbreviated mol, is a unit of chemical amount. Molar mass tells us how many grams correspond to one mole. A concentration in mol/L is the amount per litre of final solution, not the amount per litre of solvent before adding the substance.

Use these supplied values: sodium chloride mass 0.2922 g, molar mass 58.44 g/mol, final volume 100 mL. Write them as named R objects with units in comments.
Convert final volume to litres by dividing by 1000. Calculate amount in mol as mass in g divided by molar mass in g/mol. Divide that amount by final volume in litres to obtain mol/L. Print the intermediate values so the unit conversions can be checked separately.
Multiply mol/L by 1000 to obtain mmol/L; one mmol is one-thousandth of a mol. Write the complete result and units in a comment. Predict the effect of doubling mass while keeping final volume fixed, then check with the script.
Instead restore the original mass and double final volume. Predict whether the concentration doubles or halves. Run the changed calculation from its inputs and explain how this differs from the previous experiment.
Repeat the original calculation for glucose using supplied mass 0.9008 g, molar mass 180.16 g/mol, and final volume 100 mL. Compare its mmol/L result with the sodium-chloride result. Different masses can correspond to the same amount concentration because the molar masses differ.
Save the source, restart R, and reproduce both original results. Add a short reports/calculation-check.txt stating the formula in words, the conversion factors, the meaning of final volume, and any error you corrected.

Check and retain: the original sodium-chloride and glucose examples each give 0.005 mol in 0.100 L: 0.050 mol/L = 50 mmol/L. Doubling only mass gives 100 mmol/L; doubling only volume gives 25 mmol/L. Keep these results in a saved script with inputs, not only a copied Console printout.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

What survives restarting R: an unsaved object or a saved script?
Why is mean(plant_id) not a useful operation?
What must be true for two vectors to be subtracted position by position?







Check your answers





The saved script survives; objects must be recreated. IDs name plants rather than measure quantities, so an average ID has no meaning. The vectors must refer to corresponding observations in the same order and have compatible lengths.



Keep: day06.R, with the four-plant example and comments about units. Next: import a whole table.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
We have lengths from 24 seedlings. Twelve independently potted plants were randomly assigned to a control group and twelve to a treatment group. Each plant was measured at the beginning and end of the same observation period. Can we bring the measurements into R without losing their meaning?
Open introcomputing.Rproj in the extracted course folder. Its data/ subfolder contains the supplied files and a README.md explaining them. A CSV is a text file in which commas separate columns. Its first line is a header naming those columns. The file is storage; importing creates an R object in memory.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Start from a known place
text:
Start from a known place
Create day07.R in the project root. Run:

getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")

getwd() reports R’s working directory. It should be your extracted project folder, not the data folder. The second line should return TRUE. The relative path data/seedlings.csv means “inside data, find seedlings.csv, starting here”. Your full home-folder path differs from a classmate’s; this relative path can stay the same when they open their own project.
If file.exists() returns FALSE, inspect the folder in the file manager. A common problem is opening the ZIP rather than an extracted project, or an extra folder layer. Avoid solving this by inserting your personal absolute path into every line of code. Open the correct project instead.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Import and inspect
text:
Import and inspect
The readr package provides a table importer. Packages add functions to R; installing a package puts it on disk, while library() loads it for this session. The software setup page explains installation. Loading is needed again after restarting R.

library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
dim(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
str(seedlings)

read_csv() returns a table, displayed as a tibble. head() shows its first rows, not the complete dataset. dim() gives 24 rows and 4 columns. names() returns column names. str() describes structure and types: plant_id and treatment are text; the two lengths are numeric. Suppressing the type message with show_col_types = FALSE does not remove the need to check types.
Read the first row aloud: plant P01 is in the control group; its initial length was 25.7 mm and its final length 44.3 mm. Each row represents one plant, each column one variable. Two lengths from the same row are measurements on the same plant, not two independent plants.

seedlings$initial_mm
length(seedlings$initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$initial_mm)

$ selects a named column from the table, giving a vector. The length is 24. A mean without a unit is incomplete: the average initial length is measured in mm. The numbers cannot tell you whether the file used mm or cm; the dictionary and measurement protocol provide that information.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Missing is different from zero
text:
Missing is different from zero
A missing measurement is represented by NA after import. NA means not available. It does not mean zero length, no growth, or a control treatment.

example_mm <- c(12, NA, 18)
mean(example_mm)
mean(example_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
is.na(example_mm)

The first mean is NA: R will not silently pretend all measurements are known. The second is 15 mm, calculated from two observed values. na.rm = TRUE requests omitting missing values for this calculation. A report must still explain how many observations were missing and why, if known.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Import seedlings.csv and save the import and inspection commands in day07.R.
Record in comments the row count, column count, column meanings, and units.
Inspect tail(seedlings) to see the last rows. Find P24 and its treatment.
Use sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm)) to count missing final measurements.
Import data/leaf-mass.csv into leaves, inspect it, and use its dictionary to explain what one row represents and what its columns mean.
Restart R and run your script from the top. The raw CSV files should remain exactly as supplied.







Hint: a function is not found





Run library(readr) before read_csv(). If loading fails because the package is not installed, use the setup instructions or ask for help. For column names, copy from names(seedlings); initial_mm and initial are different names.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Inspect an unfamiliar table systematically
text:
Inspect an unfamiliar table systematically
Create day07-inspection.R to investigate data/seedlings-transfer.csv. This simulated study has 18 independently potted seedlings, nine randomly assigned to control and nine to treated. Initial and final lengths are millimetres, measured seven days apart. Each row is one plant, not one independent measurement occasion.

Open the course project, print getwd(), and check the relative input path with file.exists(). Import into a new object called transfer; keep the original seedlings object separate so that outputs from the two studies cannot silently overwrite each other.
Use head(), tail(), dim(), names(), and str() on the imported table. Record what each command establishes and what it does not. For example, seeing six rows in head() does not mean the dataset has six observations.
Check length(transfer$plant_id) and length(unique(transfer$plant_id)). The latter counts distinct identifiers. Compare them and explain why different counts would prompt investigation. Repeated IDs can be legitimate in a repeated-measurement design, so the study description—not a universal “duplicates are bad” rule—sets the expectation.
Inspect unique(transfer$treatment) and table(transfer$treatment). Here table() counts the supplied labels. Check the expected group labels and nine records per group. Random assignment is stated in the study design; row order alone would not establish it.
Count missing initial and final lengths using sum(is.na(...)). Use range(transfer$initial_mm) and range(transfer$final_mm) to inspect minima and maxima. Range is a check on recorded values; it cannot determine the intended units or establish that every plausible number was measured correctly.
Make reports/transfer-import-audit.txt with the input path, dimensions, column types and roles, unique-ID count, group counts, missing-value counts, and units. State at least two things that required the data dictionary rather than a function call. Restart R and recreate the audit’s numerical checks.







Hint: use the object’s actual column names





A column request such as transfer$initial is different from transfer$initial_mm. Copy names from names(transfer) while learning. The intended table is 18 rows by four columns, with 18 distinct IDs and no missing initial/final readings. Matching these expectations helps identify the file but does not replace understanding its measurements.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Inspect quantities in different units
text:
Inspect quantities in different units
The supplied data/solutions.csv table contains six simulated calculation cases, not six independent treatment experiments. It lists solution IDs, a solute name, mass in grams, molar mass in grams per mole, and final total volume in millilitres. A mole is a unit of chemical amount; the supplied molar mass converts grams to moles. You will inspect the input today, then use these quantities in later calculation and report practice.

Import the table into solutions using a project-relative path. Before running str(), predict which columns should contain text and which should contain numbers. Compare the result with your prediction and explain why solution IDs and solute names are not measured quantities to average.
Check dimensions, unique solution identifiers, the two solute labels, and the absence or presence of missing values. Read Q01 aloud: 0.2922 g of sodium chloride, supplied molar mass 58.44 g/mol, final volume 100 mL. Identify the meaning and unit of every number before doing arithmetic.
Use range() on the numeric columns. Explain why the numbers for molar mass are not interchangeable with those for weighed mass, even though both types are numeric. A numeric storage type alone cannot authorise an operation.
Compare these two supplied vectors in a separate part of the script: c(10, NA, 20) and c(10, 0, 20). Calculate their means and, for the first, the available-value mean using na.rm = TRUE. Record available and missing counts. Explain why using zero for an unavailable measurement invents evidence.
Save reports/solutions-import-audit.txt describing the table, its units, and what you could calculate from the supplied inputs. Include the formula in words if helpful: amount = mass / molar mass; concentration = amount / final volume in litres.
Restart R and run the saved inspection script. Check which input generated each audit. If a table has 24 plants where its note promises 18, inspect the input filename and object name.

Check and retain: solutions.csv has six rows, five columns, six unique IDs, two supplied solute labels, and no missing inputs. The available-value mean of 10, NA, 20 is 15 from two observations; the mean of 10, 0, 20 is 10 from three. Your two audit notes should preserve that distinction.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding
Why is the header not a plant? Why does the file’s name not tell R the units? Why should the script work from a classmate’s project folder?






Check your answers





The header labels columns rather than containing an observation. Units are metadata supplied by people; R only sees column names and values. The script uses relative paths and the same documented folder structure rather than your username. There are no missing final lengths in the clean seedling dataset.



Keep: day07.R. Next: calculate growth and draw a figure.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Do plants that started longer also end longer? And how much did each plant grow? A new column and a labelled figure can answer these questions without editing cells by hand. Start a script called day08.R in your project root.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Create a derived measurement
text:
Create a derived measurement

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
head(seedlings)

mutate() returns a table with a new or changed column. We assign that returned table to seedlings. Within this function, R looks for final_mm and initial_mm in the supplied table. The original file on disk is unchanged. For P01, check 44.3 minus 25.7: the growth is 18.6 mm. A negative change would mean the recorded final length was smaller; it would deserve checking, not automatic deletion.
The new variable describes change, while final_mm describes size. These answer different questions. Always say which you are comparing.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Select observations and variables
text:
Select observations and variables

control_plants <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")
growth_table <- select(seedlings, plant_id, treatment, growth_mm)

filter() selects rows satisfying a condition. == asks whether values are equal; it does not assign values. Quotation marks mark the text label "control". select() chooses columns. Neither operation changes the original raw CSV. Inspect control_plants: it should have twelve rows. growth_table should have 24 rows and three columns.
Sometimes it is easier to read a sequence from left to right:

longer_control <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "control") |>
  filter(growth_mm > 15)

The base R pipe |> passes the result on its left as the first argument to the next function. Read this as “take seedlings, keep controls, then keep growth over 15 mm”. This is a convenience for joining steps, not a new biological operation. Run intermediate steps when diagnosing a problem.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Map columns to a figure
text:
Map columns to a figure

size_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = initial_mm, y = final_mm,
                                  colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Initial seedling length (mm)",
       y = "Final seedling length (mm)",
       colour = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal()
size_plot

ggplot() identifies the table. aes() maps columns to positions and colour. Each point is one plant. The + adds a layer or a display instruction to the figure. The plus at the end of a line tells R that the expression continues. Colour maps a group label; it does not mean the treatment is a numeric measurement.
Read the labels before interpreting the pattern. The horizontal axis is initial length, so this figure does not directly show growth. It also cannot by itself prove that starting longer causes a larger final length.

growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 8),
             alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot

This shows growth for each group. A small horizontal jitter separates points that would overlap; height = 0 leaves every measured vertical value unchanged. seed = 8 makes this display repeatable. No test is needed today: describe what you can see, including overlap and variation among plants.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Save something another application can read
text:
Save something another application can read



The worked figure shows individual seedling growth measurements by treatment; the groups overlap.



ggsave("output/seedling-growth.png", plot = growth_plot,
       width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 150)
write_csv(growth_table, "output/seedling-growth.csv")

The supplied project includes output/. These commands create files there; they may replace files with the same names. The plot object in memory and the PNG on disk are different things. Locate and open both saved outputs in the file manager.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Recreate both plots from the start of the script and calculate P02’s growth by hand to check the subtraction.
Save a table containing only treated plants’ IDs and growth measurements.
Choose one transfer task: make a plot of initial length against growth with axes labelled in mm, or adapt the same workflow to the organic-product table below.
Describe a visible pattern and identify a question the plot alone cannot settle.
Restart R and run the script. Confirm the saved files still open afterwards.


Alternative transfer task: a derived yield column
Our simulated table data/organic-recovery.csv records twelve separate runs of an organic synthesis, six assigned to each of two protocols, standard and modified. A run is one independently performed preparation. These labels identify the two procedures being compared.
Each row supplies a theoretical_mass_g: the maximum product mass from that run’s starting materials. isolated_mass_g is collected dry product, assumed pure for this simplified exercise. Both are grams. Calculate yield_percent = 100 × isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g. You are given the maximum for each run. The first run, Y01, has 1.00 g maximum and 0.62 g collected, so its yield is 62%.

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- mutate(organic,
                  yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
head(organic)

The runs started at different scales, so larger collected mass alone need not mean a greater yield. Inspect the supplied dictionary in data/README.md. Make a plot with protocol on x and percentage yield on y, using the familiar individual-point pattern. Label its y-axis “Isolated product yield (%)”. Save the derived table to output/organic-yields.csv and your plot to output/organic-yields.png. Keep its import and calculation in day08.R.






Hint: adapt the roles, not just the title





Use organic as the plot’s data, protocol for x, and yield_percent for y. Choose horizontal jitter with zero vertical jitter as above. Use write_csv() for the derived table and ggsave() for the figure. Expect 12 rows, no missing masses, and Y01 at 62%.









Hint: a plot or file is missing





Printing growth_plot shows the plot; assigning it alone may not. Check getwd() and dir.exists("output") if saving fails. If a column is not found, check names(seedlings) and run the earlier mutate() line.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Derive, select, plot, and verify
text:
Derive, select, plot, and verify
Start day08-transfer.R at the project root. The new seedlings-transfer.csv is an independent simulated seven-day study of eighteen plants, nine per group. Its variable definitions match the main seedling table, but its values and identifiers differ.

Import the new table into transfer, inspect it, and calculate growth_mm using mutate(). Check T01 by hand: 40.3 − 25.3 = 15.0 mm. Verify the row count before and after adding the column; a calculation should not itself remove plants.
Create a compact table of plant ID, treatment, and growth. Then create a separate table containing treated plants only. State in comments which step selected columns and which selected rows. Record the expected row counts before running each selection.
Make an initial-length versus final-length plot, then an initial-length versus growth plot. Keep the horizontal units in mm and label the actual vertical quantity on each. Explain why a conclusion about final size is not automatically a conclusion about how much a plant changed.
Make the individual-growth-by-group plot with horizontal jitter and zero vertical jitter. Change only the horizontal jitter width and compare the display. The measured growth values must not change. Explain that spreading points sideways helps visibility but does not create additional plants.
Save the derived full table, the selected treated table, and two useful plots under names starting transfer- in output/. Open each saved file graphically and confirm its contents. A plot object printed in R is not automatically an exported image; writing a CSV is not exporting a figure.
Write a caption stating the independent unit, outcome, units, and meaning of each point. Interpret the pattern and state a limitation. Compare the workflow with the main seedling example: which names changed, which operations stayed the same, and which conclusions depend on the new data?







Hint: check the result before polishing the plot





There should be 18 rows in the full derived table and nine in the treated subset. growth_mm has the same length as the input. Check the original columns remain available. Select treated rows with treatment == "treated", using the supplied label rather than the row order.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Calculate requested dilutions
text:
Calculate requested dilutions
A stock is a supplied solution of known concentration. Dilution uses some stock and solvent to reach a final total volume. Assume no solute reacts or is lost. The amount stays the same, so the stock volume required is target concentration × final total volume / stock concentration. Both concentrations are supplied in mmol/L; using mL for final volume gives mL for the required stock. These are numerical cases, not laboratory instructions.

Import data/dilutions.csv, inspect its four rows, and retain every original request. Use mutate() to add stock_volume_ml from the stated formula. Work D02 by hand before running the table calculation: stock 500 mmol/L, target 50 mmol/L, final total volume 50 mL.
Add a logical column possible_by_dilution using target_mmol_l <= stock_mmol_l. Explain that <= means “less than or equal”. A target more concentrated than the stock cannot be obtained by adding solvent alone. Retain and flag that row in the full output.
Inspect stock_volume_ml <= final_volume_ml as a second check for these positive supplied cases. Identify the request that fails and explain why a numerical result can be calculable while the intended procedure is impossible.
Save the complete flagged table as output/dilution-check.csv. Use filter(possible_by_dilution) to create a separate supported-results table. Plot final total volume against required stock volume for those supported cases, with both axes in mL. Explain how the supplied formula produces the plotted relationship.
Write reports/dilution-interpretation.txt with the requested outputs, impossible-case explanation, and a sentence distinguishing “bring to 50 mL total” from “add 50 mL solvent”. Preserve the denominator units in the source.
Restart R and regenerate tables and plot. Identify the impossible request from the saved flagged table without seeing your Console. Explain why its row still appears in the audit.

Check and retain: D01–D03 need 2.5, 5, and 10 mL of stock respectively. D04’s formula produces 100 mL stock for a 50 mL final request and must be flagged; its target is 200 mmol/L while its stock is only 100 mmol/L. The flagged row records a request that dilution cannot achieve.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Why keep the raw table?





A derived table lets someone trace the calculation back to the recorded lengths. P02 grew 8.0 mm. Selecting columns is not selecting plants; select() and filter() act on different parts of the table.



Keep: day08.R, your derived tables, and figures in output/. If you chose the organic transfer, its two organic-yields outputs replace the extra initial-length-versus-growth figure; retain the main seedling work. Next: put explanation and code in one report.

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Can someone read our explanation, inspect our calculation, and see the figure without copying results manually? An R Markdown report combines ordinary text with executable R code. Rendering turns that source document into a readable HTML report. An HTML report can be opened in a browser; the editable source ends in .Rmd and should be kept too.
These course webpages are built with Quarto. Your reports use R Markdown. You do not need to create a Quarto document or learn a second report system.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Open the supplied template
text:
Open the supplied template
Open the project and then report.Rmd from its root folder. First save an unchanged backup if you want one. Keep your working .Rmd at the project root so that data/seedlings.csv points to the supplied data. Moving it into reports/ would change the relative location of the data during an ordinary knit.
The template has a short header between --- lines, including a title and output: html_document. That header configures the document. Leave the output format unchanged for now. A heading in ordinary text starts with #, while a code comment starting with # lives inside a code chunk. Their location matters.
Here is a minimal complete report. The three-backtick fences in the box belong in your .Rmd file.
---
title: "Seedling growth"
output: html_document
---

## Question

How much did the seedlings grow during the observation period?

```{r import}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
```

There are `r nrow(seedlings)` plants in the dataset.

```{r mean-growth}
mean(seedlings$growth_mm)
```

Growth is final minus initial length, measured in millimetres.

The fences mark where an R chunk starts and ends. Chunk labels such as import are names for sections of code and must be unique within a report. The inline expression in the sentence inserts a calculated result into prose; R executes it during rendering. You can begin with ordinary prose and add inline calculations later.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Render, rather than assembling results by hand
text:
Render, rather than assembling results by hand
Save the source, then choose Knit. Rendering runs the chunks in document order and creates an HTML file. For an explicit equivalent command from the R Console, use the following command. Do not put it inside report.Rmd: a report must not try to render itself.

rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")

rmarkdown::render calls a function in the rmarkdown package without loading all of that package’s functions. Its output_dir puts the rendered result in reports/; the .Rmd stays at the project root. The Knit button may initially put its HTML next to the source instead. Both are HTML reports; locate the actual file rather than assuming it appeared in a particular folder.
A report must contain its imports and calculations. An object you created only in the Console may let a chunk run interactively, yet be absent during knitting. The saved source must be sufficient to rebuild the result from the saved data.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Add a figure and its meaning
text:
Add a figure and its meaning
In your report, load ggplot2 and reuse the growth plot from day 8. Give the figure a caption by starting its chunk with this line:
```{r growth-figure, fig.cap="Each point represents one independently potted seedling."}
# Put the plotting code here.
```

Replace the comment with the plotting code, keeping both chunk fences. Write a sentence below the figure explaining what the vertical axis measures. A caption identifies what a figure shows; the surrounding text explains why it matters. Code can be visible in this first report so that your method is easy to inspect.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Render the supplied template before changing it. Confirm the HTML opens.
Change its title, question, and author information; save and render again.
Put the import, growth calculation, and labelled plot in chunks in the right order. Remove repeated chunks that create the same object unnecessarily.
Add methods explaining what one row represents and how growth was calculated.
Deliberately misspell a column name, render, and read the error’s chunk name. Fix the spelling and render successfully. Practise recovery, not memorisation.
Restart R and render the document again using the command above.







Hint: rendering stops





Read the first useful error and its chunk label. Check that the document loads packages before using their functions, imports the data before calculating, and uses the exact filename and column names. Check every chunk has an opening and closing fence. Ask for help with the error text; never attach passwords.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Make and diagnose a small complete report
text:
Make and diagnose a small complete report
Save a root-level copy of the starter as report-workshop.Rmd. Make deliberate errors in this copy, record their messages and repairs, and restore a successful render after each.

Add a sentence describing the input file, simulated study, independent unit, and growth calculation. Read the report in source form and identify which parts are ordinary prose, chunk fences, R instructions, and header settings. A heading outside a chunk is not an R comment, even if both start with #.
Keep the import/preparation before the plot. Add an inline result displaying the number of input plants, using the pattern already shown in the lesson. Render with Knit, then find that number in the HTML and identify the code that produced it. Keep installation commands out of the report.
Give every chunk a unique descriptive label. In the disposable workshop copy, deliberately give two chunks the same label and attempt a render. Read the error, record it in reports/render-recovery.txt, then restore unique labels.
Deliberately misspell the CSV filename in the import, render, and record the first useful error. Check the project location and actual filename, then fix the spelling. Notice that an object left over in the Console does not make a wrong saved import path correct.
Move a plot chunk above the chunk creating its derived variable, render, and explain the dependency error. Restore the correct order and render successfully. Record which object must exist before the plotting instruction. When comparing errors, change one cause at a time.
Reopen the HTML in a browser after a successful render. Compare it with the .Rmd: which is the editable recipe, which is the reading copy, and where are the actual measurements? Close and reopen the project, restart R, and knit again without first running analysis commands manually in the Console.







Hint: record a small reproducible failure, not a screenshot alone





For each experiment write the changed line or chunk label, exact first useful error, diagnosis, repair, and successful check. A screenshot may support that record, but the saved source is needed to investigate code. Render using Knit or the Console.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Switch inputs without leaving misleading prose
text:
Switch inputs without leaving misleading prose
Create transfer-report.Rmd at the project root with Save As, leaving the workshop source intact. It will describe the eighteen-plant data/seedlings-transfer.csv study: independent pots, nine allocated to each group, lengths in mm measured seven days apart. This is another simulated study, not evidence about a real plant treatment. Use only skills already taught.

Replace the imported filename and use a consistent object name for that table. Include all library calls, import, and growth calculation in the report. Check dimensions, labels, and missing counts rather than relying on the template’s earlier 24-plant result.
Update the question, methods, caption, and any manually written sample-size text. Use an inline calculation for the total row count so the number is tied to the imported table. A report with a new figure but an old dataset description mixes two different studies.
Add the initial-versus-final plot and the individual-growth-by-group plot from your saved day 8 transfer script. Identify the vertical quantity in each caption. You may use the reference pattern rather than reconstructing every plotting option from memory. State what one point represents.
Describe what you observe, identify a question the plots cannot settle, and state a limitation.
Render from a fresh session, locate the produced HTML, and check that the caption, figures, inline count, input name, and prose all describe this same study. Search your source for the old filename and the number 24; investigate any remaining occurrence instead of assuming it is harmless.
Copy the source, introcomputing.Rproj, and required data inputs into a practice project folder, keeping relative locations. Include output and reports folders if your code writes there. Open that copy’s .Rproj and render from its root. Record any missing dependency in render-recovery.txt. This tests whether the project works from another location on your laptop.

Check and retain: the transfer report describes 18 plants, nine per group, with no missing initial/final lengths; T01 grew 15.0 mm. Keep both .Rmd sources, their HTML outputs, and the recovery log. The same workflow now has two deliberately separate input files and two narratives that must not be mixed accidentally.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Which files do you keep?





Keep the .Rmd source, its input data, and the generated HTML. HTML is convenient for reading; it does not replace the source needed to update the analysis. Changing a number in the prose by hand would break the link to its calculation.



Keep: your saved report.Rmd and a successfully rendered HTML report. Next: write your first complete short report.

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
What can we say about seedling growth from the measurements alone? Combine your import, calculation, plotting, and reporting skills in a reproducible report.
Open your course project and save a copy of report.Rmd as first-report.Rmd in the project root. Keeping both source files there preserves the familiar data/ paths. Your generated HTML can go into reports/.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: What a reader needs
text:
What a reader needs
A reader who was not in the room needs to know the question, what was measured, how you calculated the result, and what the figure shows. A list of function calls is not a methods explanation. “We calculated change in length as final minus initial length for each plant” explains the calculation in biological terms. The code makes the calculation repeatable.
The supplied experiment has 24 independently potted seedlings, twelve randomly assigned to each group. Initial and final measurements come from the same plant, seven days apart. The treatment label treated denotes a nutrient treatment; the nutrient formulation is unspecified. These are simulated measurements.
Start with the familiar analysis:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

Put these lines in a code chunk before any result that depends on them. Give the reader a few simple checks:

nrow(seedlings)
sum(is.na(seedlings$growth_mm))
range(seedlings$growth_mm)

The file has 24 plants and no missing growth values. The minimum and maximum are measurements, not plausible bounds for every seedling in nature. The range summarises this dataset; it is sensitive to unusual observations.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: A figure worth discussing
text:
A figure worth discussing
Recreate the plot of growth against treatment from day 8. Show every plant, label the growth axis in mm, and explain that each dot represents one independently potted plant. Include the caption and discuss the visible overlap between groups.
A useful opening could be: “Growth varied among individual plants in both groups.” Follow it with something specific you can see. Avoid declaring that a treatment “works” on the strength of a higher-looking cloud of points. We have not yet considered how much uncertainty surrounds a group comparison.
You can compute a simple mean for all plants using mean(seedlings$growth_mm). Make clear that this combines treatments and does not answer whether they differ. We will calculate and interpret group summaries during week 3.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Your practical: four short sections
text:
Your practical: four short sections
Create these sections in first-report.Rmd:

Question and data: state the question, the number of plants, the treatment allocation, and that these are simulated data. Explain the meaning of a row.
Methods: explain how the file was imported and how growth was derived. Include working code with relative paths. Say what the units are.
Results: include the labelled individual-plant figure and a small number of calculated facts that help answer the question. Use inline R for at least one result if you are comfortable; correct prose is more important than novelty.
Interpretation: describe the pattern, variation, and an important limitation.

Now restart R and run this in the R Console, not inside the report (a report must not try to render itself):

rmarkdown::render("first-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")

If it fails, work from the first error and add missing prerequisites to the report.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Transfer to a second table
text:
Transfer to a second table
Inspect data/leaf-mass.csv. It records one leaf from each of 18 independent plants, with area in square centimetres and dry mass in milligrams. Make an area-versus-mass scatter plot in a script called leaf-first-look.R. Use the actual column names from names(leaves). The two measurements have different units, so their difference would have no physical meaning. A larger mass and a larger area may be associated; one does not establish that one causes the other.






Hint: adapting the plot





Start with leaves <- read_csv("data/leaf-mass.csv", show_col_types = FALSE). Then map leaf_area_cm2 to x and dry_mass_mg to y. The same plotting structure can serve a different question when you deliberately change the table, columns, labels, and explanation.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Turn a draft into an evidence-based report
text:
Turn a draft into an evidence-based report
Revise your seedling report. Keep a log of the issue, correction, and result in reports/report-revision.txt.

Read your HTML without looking at the source. Mark where it tells you the biological question, independent unit, number of observations, group labels, measured units, and input filename. Add missing information to the source, not by editing HTML that will be replaced at the next render.
Select three claims from your interpretation. For each, identify the table, figure, or study-description sentence supporting it. Label the claim as a description of these observations, a design fact supplied by the dictionary, or an unsupported inference. Revise a claim that the present analysis cannot support.
Compare two figures made from the same plants: initial versus final length, and group versus growth. Choose the one most directly addressing your main question. Retain another figure only if it answers a stated useful question, rather than because the code produced it. Write an appropriate caption with the quantity, units, and observational unit.
Check the source from its first line. Are imports and packages present before use? Is growth calculated by subtraction? Are source inputs kept unchanged? Are output names informative? Remove obsolete scratch objects and duplicated chunks only after checking which later lines depend on them.
Read the HTML without the source. Locate the answer to the main question and a limitation. Does every treated plant outgrow every control plant? Replace vague wording such as “the graph shows a difference” with a description of the plotted observations.
Restart R and render again, using Knit or a Console render command. Check that the HTML’s figures and numbers reflect the saved revision. Save reports/report-revision.txt with the original issue, your correction, and evidence that the corrected report reruns. Keep the R Markdown source at the project root even if its HTML is written to reports/.







Hint: distinguish an observation from a universal conclusion





“The treated observations tend to be larger in this sample” is a descriptive statement you can examine on individual points. “The treatment always increases plant growth” extends far beyond these simulated observations. Before inference is taught, state the pattern, overlap, and limits of this small teaching study. The words should answer the actual plotted quantity, not a memorised template.

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Deliver a second, smaller laboratory brief
text:
Deliver a second, smaller laboratory brief
Choose one of the following familiar input contexts: seedlings-transfer.csv (another plant study) or solutions.csv (calculated solution concentrations). Produce one short report named laboratory-brief.Rmd at the project root.

Write a clear question and identify what one row represents. For seedlings, use the supplied independent-pot design and millimetre measurements seven days apart. For solutions, rows are six supplied numerical preparations, not independent treatment evidence. Define any chemistry term you use.
Import and inspect the selected table. Record dimensions, column types, identifiers, and missing counts in code or a small readable result. Explain the units from the dictionary rather than assuming R knows them automatically.
Calculate the quantity answering your question. For seedlings use final minus initial length. For solutions, amount in mol is mass in grams divided by supplied molar mass in g/mol; final volume in litres is mL/1000; mmol/L is 1000 * (mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol) / (final_volume_ml / 1000).
Make one labelled figure and a small derived table. For solutions, compare supplied mass and calculated concentration by solute, explaining why equal mmol/L need not mean equal weighed grams. For seedlings, show individual growth by group. No test or fitted line is required.
Explain your method, results, and a limitation specific to the chosen context. Distinguish concentrations calculated from a supplied formula from variation measured among plants.
Render in a fresh session, then locate the input and output using your report’s description. Save one derived CSV and figure using a laboratory-brief- filename prefix. Include the brief’s source and data in a tested practice package, and record its location in the revision log.

Check and retain: the plant route has 18 plants and T01 grew 15.0 mm. The solution route produces 50, 100, and 150 mmol/L for each solute. Keep one complete laboratory brief, your revised earlier report, and the audit/revision notes.

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Completion check
text:
Completion check
Open the HTML in a browser. Can you identify the question, units, meaning of a dot, and main limitation? Then restart R and check that the saved source renders.






Self-check





The .Rmd should contain the imports, derived column, and plot. The HTML should contain sentences that make sense without reading every code line. A personal path such as a username-specific Desktop location makes the report less portable.



Keep: first-report.Rmd, its HTML, and leaf-first-look.R if completed. Next: what happens when a laboratory table is imperfect?

title: Quiz: Check and repair data
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. The file is intended to have one row per plant. It has 25 rows but 24 unique plant IDs. What should you inspect before removing a row?






Hint





Compare every field in the repeated records and consult the source notes.









Answer





Inspect the repeated ID’s full records and the source notes. Here both P01 records are identical and the recorder confirms an import duplicate. In a time-series table, a repeated plant ID could be legitimate.




Q2. P21 has a final length of 4.38. Which evidence justifies changing it to 43.8 mm?

Other plants are larger.
The correction increases the group mean.
The original source record gives 43.8 mm.







Hint





A surprising value suggests a check; it does not specify the correct value.









Answer





(iii). The source record supports this correction. Size or a preferred result alone does not establish an error.




Q3. P06 started at 24.7 mm and its final measurement is missing. What growth would replacing the missing final value with zero produce? What should the cleaned table retain?






Hint





Growth is final minus initial. A missing value states that the measurement is unavailable.









Answer





It would invent \(0 - 24.7 = -24.7\) mm growth. Retain NA for final length and growth; there is no supported replacement.




Q4. After repair there are 12 plant records in each group, with one control growth unavailable. What are the available growth sample sizes?






Hint





Count observed values separately from enrolled plant records.









Answer





11 controls and 12 treated plants have observed growth. Both groups still contain 12 plant records. sum(!is.na(growth_mm)) counts available growths.




Q5. Which files allow you to reproduce and explain a repair?

Only the cleaned CSV.
Raw CSV, source notes, and repair script.
A screenshot of RStudio.







Hint





A reproducible repair needs both its input and the reasons for changing it.









Answer





(ii). The script regenerates derived data from the original, and the source notes explain the correction evidence.

title: Quiz: Mean, variance, and SD
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. For growth values 12, 14, and 16 mm, calculate the mean, sample variance, and sample SD, with units.






Hint
