The squared deviations from 14 are 4, 0, and 4. Sample variance divides their sum by \(n-1\).









Answer





Mean 14 mm; sample variance \((4+0+4)/2 = 4\) mm²; sample SD \(\sqrt{4}=2\) mm.




Q2. What will this return, and why?
mean(c(10, 10, 10, 100))
median(c(10, 10, 10, 100))






Hint





The mean uses every value; the median uses the ordered middle values.









Answer





The mean is 32.5 and median 10. The large value strongly affects the mean; neither result is an arithmetic error.




Q3. A vector has mean 14 mm and SD 2 mm. What happens when 10 mm is added to every value? What happens when the original values are divided by ten to express centimetres?






Hint





A common addition leaves deviations unchanged. Unit conversion rescales both measurements and their deviations.









Answer





Adding 10 mm gives mean 24 mm, SD 2 mm. Converting the original values gives mean 1.4 cm, SD 0.2 cm and variance 0.04 cm².




Q4. Two groups have the same mean but SDs of 1 and 6 mm. Which statement is supported?

The second group has greater observed spread.
Every second-group plant is larger.
The second group was measured incorrectly.







Hint





SD describes variation among observations, not its cause.









Answer





(i). The observations in the second group vary more around their mean. SD alone does not identify biological or measurement causes.




Q5. A synthesis run collects 0.62 g from a supplied maximum of 1.00 g. Percentage yield is 100 * collected / maximum. What is the yield? If another run yields 70%, how many percentage points higher is that?






Hint





Use the supplied ratio, then subtract the percentages.









Answer





62% yield; 70% is 8 percentage points higher. The difference is not an 8% relative increase.

title: Quiz: Group summaries and figures
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A table has 24 plants in two treatment groups. After group_by(treatment) |> summarise(mean_mm = mean(growth_mm)), how many rows should the summary have? What does one row mean?






Hint





A grouped summary produces one result per group.









Answer





Two rows, one per treatment. Each row describes a group; it is not an additional plant observation.




Q2. Which table supplies each layer in a plot showing individual dots and group-mean diamonds?






Hint





The individual layer and summary layer have different observational levels.









Answer





The plant-level table supplies individual dots. The grouped summary table supplies one mean diamond per treatment.




Q3. Why use horizontal jitter with height = 0 for a growth dot plot?






Hint





The vertical position encodes the measured growth.









Answer





Horizontal jitter separates overlapping dots without changing their measured growth heights. Vertical jitter would move the displayed measurements.




Q4. A histogram looks two-peaked with bins 2 mm wide and one-peaked with bins 6 mm wide. What can you conclude about the two peaks?






Hint





Small-sample histogram shape depends on how nearby values are grouped.









Answer





The apparent two-peak detail is sensitive to bin choice. Compare the individual points and describe broad features that remain stable rather than claiming two biological populations from this display alone.




Q5. A caption says “Bars show error.” What information is missing? If the figure has only individual dots and mean diamonds, what should its caption say?






Hint





Identify the plotted quantity, units, observation unit, and symbol meanings.









Answer





An error bar must specify its quantity, such as SD or a confidence interval. For this figure, state that dots are individual plants, diamonds are group means, and growth is measured in mm; include available sample sizes. There are no error bars to describe.

title: Quiz: Independent units and sampling
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. One plant is measured twelve times with a ruler. How many independently treated plants does this provide? What can the repeated readings help assess?






Hint





Separate the unit assigned to treatment from repeated measurement of it.









Answer





One plant. The repeats help assess measurement consistency; they do not create twelve independent plants.




Q2. Treatment is assigned to whole trays, with twelve plants in each tray. Which is the treatment unit?

A ruler reading.
Each plant independently.
A tray.







Hint





All plants in a tray receive the same allocation together.









Answer





(iii), a tray. Plants within it share the treatment unit and potentially the environment. More independently allocated trays are needed for independent tray-level replication.




Q3. The supplied simulation draws from one fixed source distribution. Will means of samples of sixteen usually spread more or less than means of samples of four? Does the source SD change?






Hint





Distinguish variation among observations from variation among estimated means.









Answer





The sixteen-draw means usually spread less. The stored source values and their SD stay unchanged.




Q4. What do the 400 values in means_16 represent?

400 newly measured plants.
Means of 400 simulated samples, each with sixteen draws.
Sixteen means from samples of 400 plants.







Hint





Read the outer repetition count and inner sample size separately.









Answer





(ii). replicate(400, mean(sample(..., size = 16, replace = TRUE))) calculates 400 means. The draws simulate sampling; they are not new measurements.




Q5. You increase simulation repetitions from 400 to 1000 while retaining sixteen draws per sample. Does this have the same effect as increasing plants per sample? What does set.seed() control?






Hint





One setting changes how well the simulated distribution is represented; the other changes what each estimate averages.









Answer





No. More repetitions give a more stable picture of the same sampling distribution; more independent draws per mean typically narrow it. set.seed() sets the random generator state so the simulated sequence can be reproduced.

title: Quiz: A descriptive report
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Which input gives 24 complete plant growth values: seedlings.csv or the repaired seedlings-messy.csv? What should a report state?






Hint





The repair exercise retains one unavailable final measurement.









Answer





seedlings.csv has 24 complete growth values. The repaired messy input has 24 plant records but 23 observed growths. State the input and report available sample sizes consistent with it.




Q2. A report says “Treated plants had a higher mean, so every treated plant outgrew every control.” What should you inspect, and how would you revise it?






Hint





A group mean summarises observations without ordering every pair of plants.









Answer





Inspect the individual-point plot for overlap. Report the larger observed mean with its units and sample sizes, while noting individual variation and overlap between groups.




Q3. What should the Methods and figure caption identify so a reader can understand the growth summary?






Hint





How were measurements obtained, and what does one point represent?









Answer





Identify the independent plant, treatment groups, initial/final readings seven days apart, growth = final − initial in mm, input file, relevant data checks, available n, and plotted symbol meanings. Label SD as individual spread.




Q4. Your HTML renders only while objects remain in the RStudio Environment. Which action tests and repairs this?

Save a screenshot.
Restart R and render, adding missing imports/calculations to the source.
Rename the HTML.







Hint





The source should create every object needed by later chunks.









Answer





(ii). A fresh-session render reveals hidden dependencies. Include loading, import, checks, derived variables, summaries, and plots in the saved workflow.




Q5. A report reads data from /home/sam/Downloads/plants.csv. Why might a copied project fail? Give a more portable layout.






Hint





A personal absolute path points outside the copied project.









Answer





That path may not exist elsewhere. Keep data inside the project, for example data/seedlings.csv, and use that relative path from the report at project root. Test the complete copy in a newly located folder.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
text:
Review questions from the week. See the statistics reference for definitions.
Topic quizzes:

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 1. Mean, variance, and SD
text:
1. Mean, variance, and SD
Three growth measurements are 12, 14, and 16 mm. What are the mean, sample variance, and sample SD? Show the units.






Worked answer





Mean = 14 mm. Deviations are −2, 0, and 2 mm; squared deviations sum to 8. Divide by n − 1 = 2 to obtain sample variance 4 mm². Its square root is sample SD 2 mm. SD describes spread among these measurements, not the uncertainty in their mean.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 2. A common shift and a unit conversion
text:
2. A common shift and a unit conversion
If every measurement above gains 10 mm, what happens to mean and SD? If the original lengths are converted from mm to cm, how do mean, SD, and variance change?






Answer and check





Adding 10 shifts the mean to 24 mm but leaves SD at 2 mm, since deviations from the mean are unchanged. Dividing lengths by ten gives mean 1.4 cm, SD 0.2 cm, and variance 0.04 cm². Variance scales by the square of the conversion factor.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 3. An unusual number is a question, not proof of an error
text:
3. An unusual number is a question, not proof of an error
The messy table contains final length 4.38 for P21. What permits correcting it to 43.8 mm? What should happen to the unavailable final measurement for P06?






Answer and check





The supplied source notes confirm a transcription/unit error and give 43.8 mm. The unusual value alone would not justify multiplying by ten. P06 remains missing because there is no supported replacement in this exercise. Preserve the raw file and record repairs in code; zero would invent a measurement.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 4. Rows versus available measurements
text:
4. Rows versus available measurements
After the confirmed identical duplicate is removed, the repaired table has 24 plants and one unavailable growth value in the control group. How many plant records and available growth measurements are there per group?






Answer and check





There are 12 control and 12 treated plant records, but 11 control and 12 treated available growth measurements. The complete clean seedling file used later is a separate teaching dataset with 12 available per group. State which file the analysis uses so its counts match the results.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 5. More readings or more independent units?
text:
5. More readings or more independent units?
One treated plant is measured twelve times. A second study independently assigns twelve plants to treatment. Are these equivalent sources of information about differences among plants?






Answer and check





No. Repeated readings of one plant may reveal measurement consistency but do not create twelve independently treated plants. The design determines the experimental unit. Likewise, reweighing one synthesis run does not create more independently prepared runs.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 6. Spread of observations versus spread of sample means
text:
6. Spread of observations versus spread of sample means
The supplied simulation draws means from samples of four or sixteen plants from the same fixed toy population. Why can the means of sixteen spread less without changing the population’s individual SD?






Answer and check





The source measurements stay the same. A mean averages independent sampling variation, so repeated means based on more observations typically vary less. The SD among repeated sample means describes sampling variability of an estimate; it is not SD among individual plants. A precise estimate can still be biased or based on an inappropriate design.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 7. A duplicate identifier needs a design check
text:
7. A duplicate identifier needs a design check
A file has two rows with the same plant ID. Is deleting one automatically justified? How does the answer differ between one row per plant and one row per time point?






Answer and reasoning





No. First establish the intended row meaning and compare the complete records. In the supplied messy exercise, an identical duplicate import is confirmed by source notes. In a repeated-time design, the same plant ID can legitimately recur. Different readings attached to one ID require investigation, not arbitrary deletion.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 8. What did the invented zero do?
text:
8. What did the invented zero do?
P06 initially measured24.7 mm and has no final reading. A student substitutes final length0. What growth does this calculate, and why is it different from retaining NA?






Answer and reasoning





It invents −24.7 mm growth. NA states that growth cannot be calculated from the available record; zero final length asserts a measured final size. Omitting an explicitly counted missing value in an available-case mean does not authorise making up a zero measurement.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 9. Same mean, different spread in a new source
text:
9. Same mean, different spread in a new source
The transfer study has a larger treated mean but a smaller treated SD. Is that inconsistent? What should the axis and summary table say?






Answer and reasoning





It is consistent: centre and individual spread describe different features. Use seven-day growth in mm, available n=9 per group, and the actual group summaries. Centre and spread need separate descriptions.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 10. Read the units after a transformation
text:
10. Read the units after a transformation
A vector has SD 2 mm and variance 4mm². What happens to SD and variance if every value is divided by 10 to express cm? What if10 mm is added to every value instead?






Answer and reasoning





Conversion gives SD 0.2 cm and variance 0.04cm². A common additive shift changes the mean but neither deviations nor SD/variance. The physical spread did not diminish merely because its unit changed.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 11. Two simulation settings
text:
11. Two simulation settings
One run draws 12 values for each mean and repeats that400 times. Another draws 12 values and repeats1000 times. Did the second acquire more independently measured plants or reduce the sample size of each mean?






Answer and reasoning





Neither. The source observations and 12 draws per sample stay fixed. More repetitions give a more stable picture of the simulated sampling distribution. Increasing the number of independent draws per estimated mean is a different change from collecting more simulation repetitions.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 12. Repair a descriptive conclusion
text:
12. Repair a descriptive conclusion
A report says: “The higher group mean proves every treated plant improved; the SD is the 95% uncertainty.” Repair the two errors without adding a test.






Answer and reasoning





A greater observed mean can coexist with overlapping individuals, so describe the group tendency and observations. SD describes individual spread, not a95% confidence interval. A descriptive report should state outcome, units, n, centre, spread and limits rather than inventing inferential or universal claims.



Return to the descriptive report, or continue to comparisons.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Does the treatment change how much a seedling grows? We already know how to describe the plants we measured. Today we distinguish a difference in our sample from evidence about a wider process. We begin with plants and pictures, then introduce the equal-means question.
Open introcomputing.Rproj. Use the clean, simulated data/seedlings.csv, not your data-repair exercise. Each row is one independently potted plant. Twelve plants were randomly assigned to each group and measured before and after the same growth period. The outcome is growth in millimetres. The treatment label describes an experimental condition; these teaching data do not establish a claim about any actual product or organism.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Start with the question and the independent unit
text:
Start with the question and the independent unit
Our comparison is mean growth in treated plants minus mean growth in control plants. State that direction now: a positive difference means greater growth in the treated group. Keep it the same in your code and report.
The independent experimental unit is a plant in its own pot. Measuring one plant three times with a ruler may improve the measurement; it does not create three independent plants. Similarly, the initial and final measurements belong to the same plant. We subtract them to obtain one growth value per plant, then compare growth between the two independent treatment groups.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- seedlings |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_growth_mm = mean(growth_mm),
            sd_growth_mm = sd(growth_mm), .groups = "drop")
group_summary

The control mean is about 15.28 mm; the treated mean is about 21.49 mm. Both groups contain 12 plants. Their observed difference is about 6.22 mm. A difference is a number with units, not merely a label such as “significant”.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Show the observations before summarising the evidence
text:
Show the observations before summarising the evidence

growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 16)) +
  labs(x = "Treatment group", y = "Growth over the study period (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot




Individual growth values in the supplied simulated dataset. The slight horizontal displacement separates overlapping dots.


The small horizontal displacement separates overlapping dots. It does not change their heights. You can see variation among individuals and overlap between the groups. Overlap does not automatically mean that the group means are equal; separated means do not mean that every treated plant grew more than every control plant. Compare both statements against the picture.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: A sample difference is not the whole story
text:
A sample difference is not the whole story
If we repeated the experiment with another set of plants, we would get another difference. Random variation can produce unequal sample means even when the underlying group means are equal. Tomorrow’s test asks whether the observed difference is difficult to reconcile with a particular equal-means model.
The null hypothesis for this exercise is that the population mean growth is the same under the two conditions. A two-sided alternative allows a difference in either direction. We choose a two-sided question before looking for the most favourable result.
A p-value describes how often a result at least as extreme as the one observed would arise under the null model and its assumptions. For the t-test, “extreme” refers to the test statistic, which compares the mean difference with its estimated sampling uncertainty. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it does not measure the biological importance of a difference.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Prepare a comparison report
text:
Prepare a comparison report
Save a copy of the root-level report.Rmd as comparison.Rmd, also at the project root so its data/ paths work. Keep your earlier reports. In this new file:

Write the biological question, outcome units, and independent experimental unit.
Add the import, growth calculation, group summary, and individual-point plot.
Calculate the treated-minus-control difference with the following explicit extraction. pull() takes one column out of a table as a vector.


treated <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "treated") |>
  pull(growth_mm)
control <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "control") |>
  pull(growth_mm)

observed_difference <- mean(treated) - mean(control)
observed_difference


Describe the sample difference and what remains uncertain about the wider population.
Save the figure with ggsave("output/day16-growth.png", growth_plot,    width = 6, height = 4) and render the report to HTML.







Hint: check a surprising sign





Read mean(treated) and mean(control) separately. The order in a subtraction matters. A negative result from mean(control) - mean(treated) would describe the reverse comparison, not a contradictory biological result.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

Can we conclude that every treated plant grew more? No; look at the dots.
Are 12 plants each measured twice 24 independent replicates per group? No; repeated measurements stay attached to their plant.
Does an observed mean difference alone tell us its sampling uncertainty? No; variability and sample size matter as well.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Check the comparison and its interpretation
text:
Check the comparison and its interpretation
Continue comparison.Rmd, retaining its imports and plant-level data.

Write the outcome, comparison direction, independent unit, allocation process, and units in an analysis plan. In this study the unit is an independently potted plant; twelve lengths from one shared treatment container would describe a different design. A table sorted by group is not itself evidence that allocation was random: use the study description.
Calculate initial length, final length, and growth summaries separately. Explain which quantity answers the growth question and which describes starting size. Keep their names and units visible.
Make two figures with common treatment labels: initial lengths by group, then growth by group. Show individual points. Compare what each can reveal about this particular small experiment. We are not adding an adjusted model; note any limitation that would require more design or modelling expertise.
Calculate treated minus control mean growth explicitly. Reverse the subtraction in a separate line and check that only the sign changes. Write a complete sentence for each direction without changing the biological observations. This is a test of interpretation, not two different datasets.
Locate the smallest treated growth and largest control growth. Use these observations to check the statement “the treated group grew more”. Revise it so that it distinguishes a difference in group means from a guarantee about every pair of individual plants. Show where overlap appears in the plot rather than treating overlap as a significance test.
Draft a results paragraph with n, group means, the directed difference, units, and individual spread. State what remains uncertain about the population mean difference.
Annotate each numerical statement with its source object or table. Save the figure and output/day16-plan.txt.







Hint: a group label is not a comparison direction





mean(treated) - mean(control) is treated minus control because of the argument order in that expression. Merely calling an object treatment_effect does not establish its sign. In the main dataset the difference is about 6.22 mm. The point plot also contains overlapping observations; neither fact replaces an account of independent units or uncertainty.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Compare growth in a second study
text:
Compare growth in a second study
Use data/seedlings-transfer.csv. The study has 18 new independent potted plants, nine per randomly assigned group, measured in mm seven days apart. The question is again mean growth.

Create transfer-comparison.Rmd at project root and state its question, input file, units, growth formula, and treated-minus-control direction. Import and check row count, unique IDs, missingness, and group labels.
Derive growth in code. Verify T01 by hand, then produce a group summary and plot of individual growth values. Keep the summary and raw-level table as different objects; two summary rows do not supply two new plants.
Calculate the two group means and directed difference. Save the descriptive summary to output/day16-transfer-summary.csv. Give sample sizes and units in the rendered output and in the figure caption.
Compare the observed difference with the first study’s difference. Explain how different samples and conditions could contribute to the difference between estimates.
Write a design challenge in your notes: suppose all treated plants shared one tray and all controls another. Identify which part of your current independence argument would fail and what independent replication is missing.
Write an interpretation ending with what you still need to know before judging the uncertainty or generality of the difference. Render from a fresh R session. Keep this report for day 17, when you will add an interval and test using the same stated direction rather than redesigning the question.

Additional outputs: the plan, initial/growth figure pair, descriptive results paragraph, and second study report.
Leave with: comparison.Rmd, its rendered HTML, and output/day16-growth.png.
Next: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Our sample shows about 6.22 mm more growth in the treated group. How uncertain is that estimated difference, and how does the experiment compare with an equal-means model? We will add a Welch two-sample t-test to yesterday’s report. We use this method for two independent groups and do not require their variances to be equal.
Open comparison.Rmd and run its import and preparation chunks to create seedlings, treated, and control. Keep that code in the report.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Check the design before calling a function
text:
Check the design before calling a function
Each value in treated is one plant’s growth; each value in control is another plant’s growth. The groups are independent, treatments were randomly assigned, and we have not selected plants according to whether their growth supports our expectations. Inspect yesterday’s plot for severe skew, questionable values, or one observation dominating a group. With small groups, these features can make the usual interval and test unreliable. Keep valid extreme observations and seek advice if the model looks unsuitable.
The test does not repair dependence, biased sampling, or measurement errors. We are using a small, deliberately simple dataset to learn an analysis workflow.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Run the comparison in the direction we stated
text:
Run the comparison in the direction we stated

comparison <- t.test(treated, control, var.equal = FALSE,
                     alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
comparison

The first vector is treated, the second control. The confidence interval therefore describes treated minus control. var.equal = FALSE explicitly selects Welch’s method. The other arguments make our two-sided question and interval level visible. You can inspect arguments with ?t.test; the R documentation also describes the returned result.
For these simulated data, key parts of the output are approximately:
Welch Two Sample t-test
p-value = 0.001517
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.701  9.732
sample estimates:
mean of x  mean of y
 21.4917    15.2750
Read the difference, interval, and p-value below; small printing differences are normal. The t statistic and degrees of freedom describe the test calculation.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Read the result in a useful order
text:
Read the result in a useful order
First state the estimated effect: treated plants grew on average 6.22 mm more than controls in our sample. Then state its 95% confidence interval: about 2.70 to 9.73 mm for the population mean difference, under the model assumptions.
The interval expresses uncertainty in a mean difference. It is not a range containing 95% of individual plants. A 95% confidence procedure would cover the true difference in about 95% of repeated experiments under its assumptions. This particular interval either covers that fixed difference or does not; we do not know which. Values near the interval’s centre fit the data better than more distant values, rather than all values in the interval being equally plausible.
Finally report the p-value, about 0.0015. An equal-means model would rarely produce a two-sided t statistic at least this extreme under the assumptions. This is evidence against equal population means in this model. It is not a 99.85% probability that the treatment works, and it does not tell us whether 6 mm matters biologically. That judgment needs the organism, duration, and purpose of the study.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Extend your report
text:
Extend your report
Add a Methods paragraph naming the two independent groups, growth calculation, direction of comparison, and Welch two-sample t-test. Keep the individual-point plot. Add the test chunk and a Results paragraph with the two means, sample sizes, estimated difference, interval, and p-value. A possible structure is:

In these simulated observations, mean growth was … in … and … in … . The estimated treated-minus-control difference was … mm (95% confidence interval … to … mm; Welch two-sample t-test, p = …). This suggests … under … .

Explain the biological size and limitations in the last sentence.
Extract numbers rather than retyping a long printout:

mean(treated) - mean(control)
comparison$conf.int
comparison$p.value

The $ selects a named component of the result. The interval’s two endpoints are the lower and upper limits in the direction we selected. If you later use a formula interface, check its group order carefully; the sign may reverse.






Hint: what if the interval includes zero?





Zero represents equal population means for this comparison. An interval spanning zero would show that the data do not resolve the direction at this confidence level. It would not establish equivalence or prove that there is no effect.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

Which has units of millimetres: the difference, the interval, or the p-value? The first two; a p-value has no measurement units.
Does group SD describe uncertainty in the difference? No; SD describes individual spread within a group.
If all these plants came from one shared pot per treatment, would the same analysis be justified? No; the independent-unit assumption would change.

Restart R and render the report.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Read and check the test output
text:
Read and check the test output
Keep the question and plant-level figure from day 16. Save these checks in day17-checks.R.

Predict the sign of the estimated difference from the group means before calling t.test(). Run it in the stated treated-minus-control order. Locate the mean estimates, confidence interval, p-value, and number of input observations. Explain which parts have units of mm and which do not.
Reverse the vector order in a second, clearly labelled calculation. Check the mean difference and interval endpoints. The two-sided p-value should be unchanged, while direction reverses. Write a sentence explaining why a negative sign here does not mean that the data changed.
Create a small output-reading table: quantity, value, units, and a plain language interpretation. Include both group means, their difference, the 95% interval, and the p-value. Keep SD among plants separate from the interval for the population mean difference.
Using the same observations, compare 90%, 95%, and 99% intervals by changing only conf.level. State which procedure gives the widest interval and why a higher coverage target produces a wider interval. Keep the stated 95% result as the main analysis.
Repair these statements in your own words: “There is a 0.15% probability that the treatment has no effect”; “95% of treated plants gained between 2.70 and 9.73 mm more”; “the test shows this difference matters in any biological setting.” Identify the conditioning, individual-versus-mean, and generalisation errors separately.
Discuss a supplied different study with a mean difference of 2 mm and a 95% interval from −1 to 5 mm. Explain whether equality has been established, whether positive differences remain compatible with the interval, and what information would help decide if such a difference would matter biologically.
Revise comparison.Rmd so the methods, figure, numerical results, and interpretation agree. Render after restarting, without creating the vectors manually in the Console first. Add a short note describing the checks you performed and retain their code.







Hint: separate an interval’s level from the data





Use t.test(treated, control, conf.level = 0.90) and compare its conf.int with the existing result and with conf.level = 0.99. Changing the level does not change the observed means. Reversing the two vectors reverses and negates interval endpoints, while a two-sided test asks the same equal-means question.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Add uncertainty to the second study
text:
Add uncertainty to the second study
Open transfer-comparison.Rmd from day 16. It uses data/seedlings-transfer.csv, with nine independent plants per group, their seven-day growth summaries, and an individual-point figure.

State the analysis direction before fitting: treated minus control mean seven-day growth, in mm. Extract the two numeric growth vectors by their supplied labels. Check their lengths and inspect observations before testing.
Run the guided Welch comparison with a 95% interval. Check the estimated difference by subtracting the means yourself. Read the interval endpoints in that same direction and verify that your prose agrees with the code.
Add a results paragraph containing the available n, two means, directed difference, interval, p-value, and a biological interpretation restricted to these simulated conditions.
Compare the width of this interval with the first study’s interval. List plausible contributing features, including sample size and observed spread. Consider both sample size and variability because both differ between studies.
Write a conclusion for a reader who does not know t-tests: what difference was estimated, how uncertain it is under the model, and what remains limited by design or context.
Render the HTML. Check that the comparison direction, units, and independent unit are clear from the report. Save the source, inputs, and output together.

Additional outputs: a test-output reading table, interval-level check, corrected interpretation statements, and the second study report.
Leave with: an updated comparison.Rmd and HTML that explain both the size and uncertainty of the estimated effect.
Next: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Ten plants had their leaf photosynthesis measured before and after changing the light conditions. Did their measurements tend to increase? Every plant appears twice, so this is a paired design. We compare changes within plants rather than pretending that the two sets of readings came from different plants.
The file data/paired.csv contains simulated measurements in micromoles of CO2 per square metre per second, written µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. A higher number means a greater rate of photosynthesis. Before and after were always measured in that order. That matters for our eventual interpretation.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Each row keeps a pair together
text:
Each row keeps a pair together

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

paired <- read_csv("data/paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
paired
anyDuplicated(paired$plant_id)

There should be ten rows and no duplicate identifiers; anyDuplicated() returns zero when it finds none. Each row contains one plant’s before and after values. The identifiers tell us which measurements belong together. If measurements came in two files, we would need to match them by identifier before subtracting. The fact that two files each contain ten rows would not be sufficient.
Never sort the before values and after values independently. That would change which values are paired and manufacture different biological changes. Sorting the complete table by plant identifier is safe because whole rows move together.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Make one change value per plant
text:
Make one change value per plant

paired <- paired |>
  mutate(change_umol_m2_s = after_umol_m2_s - before_umol_m2_s)

paired |>
  select(plant_id, before_umol_m2_s, after_umol_m2_s, change_umol_m2_s)

mean(paired$change_umol_m2_s)

Plant L01 changed from 5.87 to 6.95, an increase of 1.08 units. The mean of all ten changes is 1.983 units. Some plants start higher than others; analysing the within-plant changes recognises that each plant is its own reference.

change_plot <- ggplot(paired, aes(x = plant_id, y = change_umol_m2_s)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Plant identifier", y = "After − before (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)") +
  theme_minimal()
change_plot




Each point is one plant’s after-minus-before change; the dashed line marks no change.


The zero line means no change. This plot makes the paired comparison visible without requiring another data-reshaping tool. Inspect the changes, including the larger change for L02; a valid large change must not be removed merely because it is inconvenient.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: A paired t-test asks about the mean change
text:
A paired t-test asks about the mean change

paired_comparison <- t.test(paired$after_umol_m2_s,
                            paired$before_umol_m2_s,
                            paired = TRUE,
                            alternative = "two.sided")
paired_comparison

Here the first vector is after and the second before. The mean difference is therefore after minus before. The estimated mean change is about 1.98, with a 95% confidence interval from 1.25 to 2.71 units and p about 0.00017. The method describes uncertainty in the mean change, not the spread of individual changes. Its independent observations are the ten plants’ changes.
A paired t-test is also a one-sample t-test of the change values against zero. The following gives the same estimated change, interval, and p-value:

t.test(paired$change_umol_m2_s, mu = 0)

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: What this experiment can and cannot show
text:
What this experiment can and cannot show
The readings increased in this simulated dataset. But light condition and measurement order changed together. Time, acclimation, or equipment drift could also contribute. A small p-value does not untangle these possibilities. We can describe a before–after association and propose a better experiment, such as an appropriate control group and a design that addresses order effects.
This illustrates two different questions: are the observed changes consistent with a zero mean change, and what caused any change? A test addresses the first under assumptions; the experimental design determines what we can say about the second.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Write a paired report
text:
Write a paired report
Copy the root report template to paired-report.Rmd at the project root. Include:

The question, units, and ten independent plants measured twice.
An import and ID check, the change calculation, and the change plot.
The paired t-test and an interpretation in the stated after-minus-before direction.
An explanation distinguishing the confidence interval from individual spread.
A limitation about order and an idea for improving the design.

Save change_plot as output/day18-changes.png and render the HTML. All the measurements are complete here. In real paired data, do not remove missing before and after values independently, since that can misalign the remaining pairs. Keep rows together and account for any incomplete pairs explicitly.






Hint: check the direction with one plant





Before trusting the test output, subtract L01’s before value from its after value. It should be positive 1.08. The same order belongs in both the change calculation and the two vectors supplied to t.test().

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

How many independent units are present? Ten plants, not twenty readings.
Would pairing unrelated plants by their row position be meaningful? No.
Does a small p-value establish that light caused the change? No; the fixed measurement order remains a limitation.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Check the matching
text:
Check the matching
Continue paired-report.Rmd. A change is after minus before for the same identifier.

Inspect L01, L02, and L03. Calculate their changes by hand and compare with your derived column. Give units. Check that the two readings share an identifier, not merely a similar numeric size or neighbouring row position.
Make a plot joining before and after readings for each plant, using the pattern below. Retain your plot of within-plant changes as well. Explain what each display makes easier to see, including individual change and variation in starting levels.
Compare mean(after - before) with mean(after) - mean(before) for these complete matched rows. They agree, but that arithmetic equality does not justify forgetting the pairing. The uncertainty calculation also depends on the variation of the within-plant differences.
Create a separate demonstration object by sorting the before column and after column independently. Keep the valid paired object unchanged. Calculate changes and run the same paired function on this artificial matching. Compare its mean change, SD of changes, and interval with the valid result. Save both under unmistakably different names.
Explain the trap: the two marginal means and mean difference can remain unchanged while the paired variability changes greatly. A smaller p-value after sorting is not improved evidence; the identities were destroyed. Recover the original matching using the supplied rows and plant IDs.
Analyse the original change vector with the supplied equivalent one-sample calculation t.test(paired$change_umol_m2_s, mu = 0). Compare its estimate, interval, and p-value with the correctly paired call. This is a check of the same analysis, not an additional independent experiment or a search for a result.
Add a limitation paragraph naming the fixed before/after order and absence of an unchanged-light comparison. Explain why the observed change cannot isolate light from every possible time/order influence. A small p-value does not remove this design limitation.







Hint: connect each plant’s two readings





ggplot(paired) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 1, y = before_umol_m2_s,
                   yend = after_umol_m2_s), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = 0, y = before_umol_m2_s)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = 1, y = after_umol_m2_s)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), labels = c("Before", "After")) +
  labs(x = "Measurement", y = "Photosynthesis (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)") +
  theme_minimal()
Each segment uses one complete row, so its endpoints belong to the same plant.









Hint: preserve the valid object before the bad example





Use distinct names such as paired and wrong_sorted. Sorting rows while keeping all columns together preserves pairs; sorting two columns separately does not. The valid mean change is 1.983 in the stated rate units. The sorted-column demonstration has the same mean change but a different SD and interval, which exposes why means alone cannot validate paired analysis.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Interpret a small paired example
text:
Interpret a small paired example
A teaching example measures the same three independently sampled plants before and after changing light. The before rates are 5, 8, and 6; after rates are 7, 9, and 9, in micromoles CO2 per square metre per second. The plant IDs are D1, D2, D3 in that order for both vectors. These are illustrative supplied values, not a new measurement file or a randomised experiment. Three plants are very limited support for population inference.

Enter the supplied values in a three-row table using the familiar data.frame() pattern. Include IDs and both rate columns. Explain why this table has three independent pairs and not six independent plants.
Calculate the within-plant changes and check them by hand. Compute their mean and sample SD. Describe how much information would be lost by reporting only the mean and omitting the three observations.
Make a change plot with a zero reference line. Write a caption identifying the unit and the direction. Preserve the actual vertical values rather than adding vertical jitter to make the figure more attractive.
A guided paired calculation gives an approximate 95% interval of −0.48 to 4.48 for the mean change in these units. Interpret that supplied interval without claiming it contains 95% of individual plant changes or proves no effect. If you reproduce it in R, identify the very small n and the model assumptions rather than treating the function as a guarantee.
Write a design recommendation for a later real experiment: explain how more independent plants, a suitable comparison, and recording identities would address different limitations. Distinguish additional independent plants from repeated readings of the same plants.
Save paired-transfer.Rmd and render it after restarting. Include all values and code inside the source, a short interpretation, and a statement that the case is illustrative. Keep a note comparing it with the ten-plant source case without pooling the two unrelated examples.

Additional outputs: matching audit, valid-versus-sorted demonstration, change figures, revised main report, and the short supplied-case report.
Leave with: paired-report.Rmd, its HTML, and the change figure.
Next: Day 19 — A calibration line.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
A laboratory instrument gives an absorbance reading, but we want a concentration. We first measure solutions of known concentration, called standards. Can a straight line describe their readings well enough to estimate the concentration of an unknown sample?
This is a common quantitative laboratory workflow. The prepared standards in data/calibration.csv cover 0–10 mg/L. Absorbance is dimensionless. These are simulated data for a simple teaching example; no particular reagent or actual assay is implied. Each standard is one calibration point, not a plant or a replicate treatment group.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Put known concentration on the horizontal axis
text:
Put known concentration on the horizontal axis

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

standards <- read_csv("data/calibration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
calibration_plot <- ggplot(standards,
                          aes(x = concentration_mg_l, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Known concentration (mg/L)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()
calibration_plot

The readings increase approximately along a line. We describe that line as absorbance = intercept + slope × concentration. The intercept is the fitted reading at concentration zero. The slope is the fitted increase in absorbance for a one mg/L increase in concentration. A fitted line summarises the relation; it does not have to pass through every observation.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Fit the line in R
text:
Fit the line in R

calibration_fit <- lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l, data = standards)
coef(calibration_fit)

lm() fits a linear model. In its formula, ~ separates the response on the left from the explanatory variable on the right. data = standards says where to find the columns. coef() extracts the fitted intercept and slope. The R documentation for lm is a reference; we use only this simple straight-line case.
Your fitted coefficients should be approximately 0.03957 for the intercept and 0.06489 for the slope. Thus the line is approximately absorbance = 0.03957 + 0.06489 × concentration.

calibration_plot <- calibration_plot +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(calibration_fit)[1],
              slope = coef(calibration_fit)[2], colour = "steelblue")
calibration_plot

The [1] and [2] select the first and second coefficients. We retain the full-precision values for calculations; rounded values are useful for prose. The nonzero intercept may represent a background reading. Do not force the line through zero merely because concentration zero sounds like “nothing”.



Prepared standards and their fitted calibration line.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Check deviations from the line
text:
Check deviations from the line
A residual is an observed reading minus the line’s fitted reading. Positive means the point is above the line; negative means it is below. Residuals have absorbance units here.

standards <- standards |>
  mutate(fitted_absorbance = fitted(calibration_fit),
         residual = residuals(calibration_fit))
standards

residual_plot <- ggplot(standards,
                        aes(x = concentration_mg_l, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Known concentration (mg/L)", y = "Residual absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()
residual_plot




Deviations of standard readings from the fitted line, in absorbance units.


Look for curvature or a point that stands apart, not for all residuals to be positive or negative. These six small residuals show no obvious curved pattern. Six standards are still limited evidence: the picture does not guarantee that the relationship holds at arbitrary concentrations.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Estimate the unknowns within the calibration range
text:
Estimate the unknowns within the calibration range
Rearranging the line gives concentration = (absorbance − intercept) / slope. This is a point estimate; we are not calculating a full uncertainty interval for the unknown concentration.

unknowns <- read_csv("data/unknowns.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
intercept <- coef(calibration_fit)[1]
slope <- coef(calibration_fit)[2]

unknowns <- unknowns |>
  mutate(within_range = absorbance >= min(standards$absorbance) &
                        absorbance <= max(standards$absorbance),
         concentration_mg_l = if_else(
           within_range, (absorbance - intercept) / slope, NA_real_))
unknowns

The & requires both range conditions. if_else() assigns a numeric missing value, NA_real_, to unsupported estimates. U1 is about 4.17 mg/L and U2 about 7.40 mg/L. U3 exceeds the largest measured standard reading. Report it as outside the calibration range; do not present an extrapolated value as a valid result. A real laboratory might dilute the sample and measure it again using its assay protocol. Do not invent a dilution correction without such a measurement.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Transfer question: a newly measured dilution
text:
Transfer question: a newly measured dilution
Use this short calculation as a transfer check, rather than doing another complete calibration exercise. A dilution mixes some original solution with solvent to reach a larger final total volume. Assume that no measured substance is lost or reacts. Its concentration is reduced by the factor final total volume / original-sample volume.
A separate unknown was outside the instrument range. A new measurement is now provided: 1.00 mL of the original was diluted to a total of 10.00 mL, and the diluted reading was 0.520. This is not an instruction to add 10 mL of solvent, and it is not a new reading for U3. All data remain simulated.

Check that 0.520 is inside the measured standard-reading range.
Use the fitted line to calculate the diluted concentration in mg/L.
Multiply by 10.00 / 1.00 to estimate the original concentration.
State why this differs from extrapolating a line beyond its measured range.







Hint and numerical check





diluted_absorbance <- 0.520
dilution_factor <- 10.00 / 1.00
diluted_mg_l <- (diluted_absorbance - intercept) / slope
original_mg_l <- diluted_mg_l * dilution_factor
c(diluted_mg_l = diluted_mg_l, original_mg_l = original_mg_l)
Using unrounded coefficients, the estimates are about 7.40 mg/L diluted and 74.04 mg/L original. The diluted reading is within range; the original estimate follows from that new reading and a stated dilution factor. This does not make U3’s old out-of-range reading valid. Full measurement, dilution, and calibration uncertainty are still omitted from these point estimates.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Write a calibration report
text:
Write a calibration report
Create calibration-report.Rmd at the project root. Explain what a standard is, include the line and residual plots, describe the slope with units, and report the two supported concentration estimates. Explain why U3 needs another step. State that these simple inverse estimates omit full calibration uncertainty. Save the table with write_csv(unknowns, "output/day19-unknowns.csv") and both figures with ggsave(). Render after restarting R.






Hint: which way round is the model?





We prepared concentration and measured absorbance, so we fit absorbance as the response. We then rearrange that fitted line. Fitting concentration as a response is a different regression and is not the workflow used here.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

What does a positive residual mean? The observed reading is above the line.
Does a good fit from 0–10 mg/L justify a prediction at 100 mg/L? No.
Are concentration estimates exact? No; standards, measurement, and the fitted relationship all contribute uncertainty.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Check the calibration workflow
text:
Check the calibration workflow
Continue your calibration report. Keep raw standards, fitted results, and estimated unknowns distinct.

Make a small table identifying known concentration, measured signal, response variable, predictor, slope units, and intercept interpretation. Explain why the prepared concentration is on x even though the quantity ultimately wanted for an unknown is concentration.
For one standard, obtain the line’s fitted reading and subtract it from the observed reading by hand. Compare with residuals(calibration_fit). State its sign and what that sign means on the original plot. Residuals are measurement-scale discrepancies, not concentrations or p-values.
Calculate an in-range unknown with full fitted coefficients, then repeat using coefficients rounded to two decimal places. Compare the estimates and explain why rounded display values should not silently replace the calculation object. More displayed digits are not a claim of greater measurement precision either.
Check every unknown against the actual measured standard-reading range. Preserve its ID and original reading in the output table. Keep unsupported estimates missing with an explicit reason. A blank estimate should not conceal whether input was unavailable or available but outside range.
Revisit the separate new diluted measurement. Write original-sample volume, final total volume, factor, measured diluted reading, diluted estimate, and original estimate in one traceable table. Label which reading was actually measured within the tested range and identify this separate sample.
Draft a response to “The line fits well, so its estimate at any concentration must be reliable.” Identify what the residual check addresses and what it cannot establish beyond the standards. Include the uncertainty omitted by the simple inverse calculation and the fact that chemical specificity is not demonstrated merely by a straight line.
Save the range-checked table and a workflow explanation. Trace an output concentration to its measured reading, fitted coefficients, and any stated dilution. Revise ambiguous variable names and render again.







Hint: rounded coefficients are an intentional diagnostic





Use a separate temporary expression with round(intercept, 2) and round(slope, 2), keeping the fitted coefficient objects unchanged. The supported first unknown is about 4.17 mg/L with the full main calibration. The out-of-range reading is not repaired by giving its unsupported estimate more decimal places.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Calibrate a second instrument
text:
Calibrate a second instrument
data/calibration-transfer.csv supplies six standards from 0 to 5 mg/L and their absorbance readings. data/unknowns-transfer.csv supplies X1 and X2 readings. Absorbance is a dimensionless measure of light attenuation; known standards connect it empirically to concentration over the tested range.

Start transfer-calibration.Rmd at project root with its own loading, imports, design explanation, and units. Inspect the new column names and known range. Create separate objects for this instrument’s fitted coefficients.
Plot the six standards, fit absorbance as response to known concentration, and add the fitted line. Report the intercept and slope with meanings and units. Check which are empirical readings and which are model summaries.
Create and plot residuals against known concentration. Describe whether obvious curvature or an unusual reading is visible. There are only six standards; a tidy residual plot is limited evidence, not proof of a law.
Invert this new fitted line for the unknown readings only where the measured signal falls within the supplied standards’ range. Preserve both unknown IDs, signals, a supported-range flag, and estimated concentration or a documented missing estimate. Keep the original unknown file unchanged.
Check X1’s estimated concentration by inserting it back into the fitted forward equation. It should recover X1’s observed absorbance apart from numerical rounding. Explain why this algebra check does not independently validate the calibration or remove measurement uncertainty.
Write a short report recommending the next action for X2. If a new dilution is needed, specify the volumes and new reading that would have to be recorded. Render after restarting and save the source, two figures, and output table.

Additional outputs: audit table, precision/range notes, revised main report, and the independent transfer calibration report. Checkable anchors: the new slope is about 0.10009 per mg/L; X1 is supported and X2 is outside range.
Leave with: the calibration report, supported concentration table, and figures.
Next: Day 20 — A biological association.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Do larger leaves tend to have greater dry mass? We now fit a line to observations of different plants, rather than prepared calibration standards. The R function is familiar, but the biological interpretation changes. A relationship between two measurements does not by itself establish that changing one causes the other.
data/leaf-mass.csv contains simulated data from one sampled leaf on each of 18 independent plants. leaf_area_cm2 measures area and dry_mass_mg measures mass after drying. The study is observational: leaf area was not randomly assigned. Species, age, environment, and other features could influence both measurements. We begin with the simple question about association within the observed range.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Plot first, then fit
text:
Plot first, then fit

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

leaves <- read_csv("data/leaf-mass.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
leaf_plot <- ggplot(leaves, aes(x = leaf_area_cm2, y = dry_mass_mg)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Leaf area (cm²)", y = "Leaf dry mass (mg)") +
  theme_minimal()
leaf_plot

leaf_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = leaves)
coef(leaf_fit)

Read the formula aloud: explain dry mass using leaf area. The fitted intercept is about 9.48 mg and slope about 4.11 mg/cm². In these observations, a one cm² difference in leaf area is associated with a fitted mean difference of about 4.11 mg in dry mass. The line summarises a tendency, not a fixed ratio that every leaf obeys.

leaf_plot <- leaf_plot +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(leaf_fit)[1], slope = coef(leaf_fit)[2],
              colour = "steelblue")
leaf_plot
range(leaves$leaf_area_cm2)




One leaf from each of eighteen plants, with the fitted dry-mass relationship.


The observed areas range from 2.96 to 14.68 cm². An intercept is mathematically the fitted mass at zero area, outside the observed range. Its role here is to position the line over the measured areas; it is not a measurement of a zero-area leaf.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: A line leaves individual differences
text:
A line leaves individual differences

leaves <- leaves |>
  mutate(fitted_mass_mg = fitted(leaf_fit),
         residual_mg = residuals(leaf_fit))

leaf_residual_plot <- ggplot(leaves, aes(x = leaf_area_cm2, y = residual_mg)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Leaf area (cm²)", y = "Observed − fitted mass (mg)") +
  theme_minimal()
leaf_residual_plot




Individual dry-mass residuals around the leaf-area relationship.


Describe the residual pattern in ordinary language. Are points on both sides of zero? Is there obvious curvature? Does spread appear much greater at one end? These checks help identify limitations; they are not proof that every model assumption is satisfied. Independence still comes from how the plants were sampled, not from the residual plot.
Unusual points can influence the line, especially near the ends of the area range. We can explore that influence without deleting data from the main analysis:

without_a18 <- leaves |> filter(plant_id != "A18")
sensitivity_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = without_a18)
coef(leaf_fit)
coef(sensitivity_fit)

This is a demonstration, not a search for the slope we prefer. A18 has no known recording error and belongs in the main result. Compare the slopes and note whether omitting it changes the broad description.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Keep prediction within the evidence
text:
Keep prediction within the evidence
For an area of 8 cm², calculate the fitted mean mass using the line:

coef(leaf_fit)[1] + coef(leaf_fit)[2] * 8

The result is about 42.36 mg. It is a fitted mean, not a promise that the next leaf will have that mass. There is individual variation around the line and uncertainty in the line itself. An area of 80 cm² is far outside the measured range; extrapolating there would rely on an untested assumption that the same relationship continues.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Write an association report
text:
Write an association report
Create association-report.Rmd at the project root. Include the study design, point plot with fitted line, residual plot, slope interpretation with units, and observed range. Add a short sensitivity note explaining what the A18 exercise showed, while retaining all observations in the main model. Save the main figure as output/day20-leaf-line.png and render the report.
Answer these questions in the conclusion:

What association did we observe?
What does the fitted slope mean numerically and biologically?
What causal claim would this design fail to establish?

Then compare your reports from days 17 and 19. A two-group treatment question motivated a comparison of means; a concentration measurement motivated a calibration line; today’s two measured variables motivate an association. The biological question and design come before the choice of R function.






Hint: a precise slope sentence





Use “Within the observed area range, an additional 1 cm² of leaf area was associated with approximately … mg greater fitted mean dry mass.” Avoid “making the leaf larger causes …”, because this study did not manipulate area.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

Is the slope measured in mg, cm², or mg/cm²? mg/cm².
Does a strong relationship establish causation? No.
Would 18 leaves from one plant provide the same independent sample as 18 plants? No; leaves sharing a plant may be dependent.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Check units, predictions, and influence
text:
Check units, predictions, and influence
Continue the leaf report, retaining all observations in the main analysis.

Write a complete slope sentence before discussing a test: the fitted change in dry mass for a one-cm² increase in area in this observed sample. Include units. Explain why a slope of about 4.11 does not mean 4.11%, 4.11 cm², or a guaranteed increment for every individual leaf.
Read the minimum and maximum observed areas from the data. Choose a value inside that range, calculate fitted mass from intercept and slope, and mark it on a plot. Distinguish the fitted mean relationship from an exact prediction of an individual mass.
Select a measured leaf and calculate observed minus fitted mass manually. Compare with its residual. Identify whether it lies above or below the line. Inspect residuals for pattern without claiming that a small sample can validate every assumption through a picture.
Repeat the supplied sensitivity fit leaving A18 out in a separate object. Keep the full fit as primary and show both slopes and their difference. Explain why influence is a diagnostic question, not permission to exclude a valid observation because the preferred line looks tidier without it.
Convert the area column to mm² by multiplying cm² by 100. Fit the same relationship using the converted predictor and compare slopes and fitted values. The fitted masses should agree, while the slope’s numeric value and units change. Preserve both area columns for this demonstration.
Compare three claims: “larger leaves tended to have more dry mass”; “adding one cm² of area caused 4.11 mg extra mass”; “all leaves at this area have the same mass.” Retain the supported descriptive claim and explain the separate causal and individual-variation errors in the others.
Add a short recommendation for a future study to investigate a causal biological mechanism. State that this would require design and subject knowledge beyond a new lm() call. Save your sensitivity and unit checks with the source, then render the complete report afresh.







Hint: a unit change should not change fitted masses





Keep leaf_area_cm2 and create leaf_area_mm2 = 100 * leaf_area_cm2. The mg-per-mm² slope should be the mg-per-cm² slope divided by 100. The intercept and fitted masses are unchanged apart from numerical precision. A18 is retained in the main analysis; the separate fit only illustrates sensitivity.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Relate initial and final length
text:
Relate initial and final length
Use data/seedlings-transfer.csv, containing 18 independent plants, initial and final lengths in mm, and a supplied allocation label. Explore initial versus final length as an observational association. This is a different question from the mean treatment effect on growth. A line through the combined data does not adjust for allocation or establish causation.

In transfer-association.Rmd, state that final length is the response and initial length the predictor for this descriptive question. Import and check the data, retaining the allocation labels and the meaning of each row.
Draw a scatter plot coloured by allocation. Identify what the colour adds to a combined plot.
Fit the simple final-on-initial line using lm(). Report slope and intercept meanings with units. Explain why the intercept at zero initial length may be outside the meaningful observed range even though R calculates it.
Produce a residual plot and choose one observation to check observed minus fitted by hand. Calculate a fitted value at an initial length inside the measured range, while distinguishing that estimate from a measured plant.
Write two brief explanations: what the association describes in this sample, and why it cannot replace the independently allocated group comparison. Starting size, allocation, and other plant differences can contribute to the observed pattern. No causal intervention on initial size was performed.
Make a final comparison table describing three questions and outputs: independent mean growth comparison, paired before/after change, and a simple observational line. Give the experimental unit, outcome, units, appropriate supplied dataset, and one limitation for each. This is selection by question and design.

Additional outputs: the unit/sensitivity check, revised leaf report, transfer association report with figures, and the three-question comparison sheet. Keep both source and HTML and verify the input paths from a fresh session.
Leave with: a rendered association report and a clear explanation of how its question differs from a treatment comparison or instrument calibration.
Next: Day 21 — Work across local and remote computers.

title: Quiz: work on another computer
text:
Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. After connecting with SSH, which command shows your current folder on the remote computer?

hostname (ii) pwd (iii) exit (iv) getwd()







Hint





hostname names the machine. getwd() belongs in R.









Answer





(ii), pwd. It prints the working directory of that shell. hostname identifies the answering machine; exit ends the shell session.




Q2. A report rendered remotely, but your laptop’s Downloads folder is empty. Which step should come first?

Reinstall R. (ii) Render five more copies. (iii) Locate the remote output and check the transfer destination.







Hint





Rendering and transferring are separate actions.









Answer





(iii). Find the saved output on the remote computer, check whether it was transferred, and locate that destination on the laptop.




Q3. Two project copies both contain reports/receipt.txt. You edit and save the laptop copy. Must the remote copy change too? What should you inspect before sending it?






Hint





A shared filename does not establish shared storage.









Answer





No. Separately copied folders need a new transfer unless a configured sharing service updates them. Open the saved contents of the intended source and receiving copy; record their locations.




Q4. A received algae table has 24 rows and 23 available biomass measurements, matching the source. Does this establish that every recorded biomass is identical?






Hint





Two values can contain the same number of characters while differing numerically.









Answer





No. These are useful structural checks, but a changed value can leave both counts unchanged. Compare saved contents or named records using the supported method before making a stronger claim.




Q5. What happens to saved remote files when you run exit in an SSH shell? Does the same answer guarantee that a running R process continues?






Hint





A saved file and a running process are different things.









Answer





The shell connection ends; saved files remain subject to the service’s storage policy. Whether a running process continues depends on the service and how it was started.

title: Quiz: sequences and pixels
text:
Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Predict these results:
dna <- "ACGT"
length(dna)
nchar(dna)






Hint





Count stored strings separately from characters within a string.









Answer





length(dna) is 1; nchar(dna) is 4.




Q2. An invented sequence contains A11, C9, G9 and T11. Its first A is replaced by G in a new object. What are its length and GC fraction, defined as (G + C) / total letters?






Hint





Replacement changes a label without inserting or deleting a position.









Answer





The length stays 40. The new counts are A10, C9, G10 and T11, so GC fraction is 19 / 40 = 0.475. The original was 18 / 40 = 0.45.




Q3. A matrix contains 40 pixels at intensity 25 and 24 at intensity 210. What do these give?
sum(pixels > 210)
sum(pixels >= 210)
mean(pixels > 100)






Hint





> excludes equality; >= includes it. In a numeric calculation, TRUE counts as 1.









Answer





The results are 0, 24 and 24 / 64 = 0.375.




Q4. Add 30 to every intensity in that matrix. How many pixels are now above 220? Does the change establish that the pictured object became physically larger?






Hint





The two intensity levels become 55 and 240; the positions stay fixed.









Answer





24 pixels are above 220, compared with zero before the shift. This reflects brightness crossing a threshold. Physical area needs calibration and a justified definition of the object.




Q5. A plant image contains 64 pixels. Which statement is supported?

There are 64 independently treated plants.
There are 64 measured image positions.
The bright area must be one cell.







Hint





Ask what one matrix cell represents.









Answer





(ii). Pixels are image positions. They do not supply independent plant treatment allocation or establish a cell’s identity.

title: Quiz: a small biological study
text:
Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Twenty duckweed flasks were independently allocated to control or nutrient conditions, ten each. F17 in the nutrient group spilled before weighing. What is the experimental unit, and how many biomass measurements are available per group?






Hint





Fronds in one flask share a treatment allocation.









Answer





The flask is the independent unit. There are 10 control and 9 nutrient biomass measurements, 19 in total.




Q2. Which code preserves the documented unavailable measurement when selecting observations for a biomass plot?

Replace its biomass by zero.
Keep the original table and create available <- filter(duckweed, !is.na(biomass_mg)).
Delete every nutrient flask.







Hint





Keep the raw record and distinguish missing from measured zero.









Answer





(ii). The plotting object contains available measurements, while the original table retains F17 and its missing value. State the unavailable count in the caption.




Q3. You run t.test(nutrient$biomass_mg, control$biomass_mg). Which directed difference does its confidence interval describe?






Hint





For two supplied vectors, the comparison follows first minus second.









Answer





Nutrient mean minus control mean. A positive difference means the nutrient group has the larger mean biomass.




Q4. For a synthesis run, percentage yield is defined as 100 × collected mass / supplied maximum mass, with both masses in grams. A run collects 1.17 g from a supplied maximum of 1.50 g. Calculate its yield. Does this measure purity?






Hint





Divide matching mass units before multiplying by 100.









Answer





100 × 1.17 / 1.50 = 78%. This is yield under the supplied assumptions; it is not a purity measurement.




Q5. Protocol means are 68.67% and 77.00%. Express modified minus standard in the correct units. Is this the same as relative percentage change?






Hint





Subtracting percentages gives a difference on the percentage scale.









Answer





The difference is 8.33 percentage points. Relative change would divide that difference by the standard mean and multiply by 100, giving about 12.13%. These answer different questions.

title: Quiz: reproduce a saved analysis
text:
Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A report uses an object imported only in the R console. Which check is most likely to expose this dependency?

Change the plot colour.
Restart R and Knit from the saved source.
Rename the HTML.







Hint





Restarting clears interactive session objects.









Answer





(ii). The report should create its objects in its own chunks. Add the import before the analysis that uses it.




Q2. A share folder contains introcomputing.Rproj and duckweed-report.html. Is that enough to recalculate the analysis for new data? What is missing?






Hint





A project file sets context; HTML displays a result.









Answer





No. Include the .Rmd source, actual input CSV, dictionary, required output folder, and README naming packages and the file to render. The .Rproj does not contain the dataset.




Q3. In a disposable project copy, the input CSV is renamed but the report still requests its old path. In another copy, only the prose is changed to falsely say every duckweed flask had a measured outcome. Which fault should stop rendering?






Hint





Software can encounter an unavailable input without recognising a false scientific sentence.









Answer





The unchanged path to the renamed input should cause a file error. The false prose may render successfully, so counts and interpretation also need review.




Q4. A report renders correctly after extraction into a new folder. Which claim follows?

The source and supplied inputs regenerate the result in the tested environment.
The scientific interpretation is proved correct.
The ZIP protects against losing the only disk.







Hint





Reproduction, scientific validity and backup are separate checks.









Answer





(i). Successful reproduction is evidence about the tested source, inputs and environment. Design and interpretation still need review, and disk loss needs a separately stored backup.

title: Quiz: recover and check a complete workflow
text:
Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.
