Q1. A seedling’s initial length is 25.7 mm and final length is 44.3 mm. Repair this outcome calculation:
growth_mm = final_mm + initial_mm






Hint





Growth here means final length minus initial length.









Answer





growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm, giving 18.6 mm.




Q2. An estimated treatment-minus-control difference is 3 mm with a 95% confidence interval from −2 to 8 mm. Does this establish that the treatment has no effect?






Hint





The interval includes zero and values on both sides of it.









Answer





No. The estimate is positive, but the interval includes decreases and increases. Report the estimate and uncertainty rather than claiming equality.




Q3. The algae reference mean is 28.20 mg and supplement mean is 33.91818 mg. Omitting the largest reference value, A11, changes its mean to 26.97273 mg. Calculate both supplement-minus-reference differences. Which should be primary if A11 has no documented error?






Hint





Compare the unchanged supplement mean with each reference mean.









Answer





All available observations: about 5.72 mg. Omitting A11: about 6.95 mg. Keep the all-available result primary; label the other as a sensitivity check with a changed sample, not an established correction.




Q4. A summary shows 33.91818 mg; a rendered report shows 33.92 mg. Another report shows 34.32 mg. Which discrepancy is ordinary rounding, and what would you check for the other?






Hint





Round the first value to two decimal places.









Answer





33.92 mg is ordinary rounding. Investigate 34.32 mg by checking the saved input, available counts, group selection, exclusions, outcome calculation and which output file was opened.

title: Week 5 revision — reproduce and transfer
text:
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.
Topic quizzes: remote work · sequences and pixels · small study · reproduction · consolidation.

Q1. Name the location, not just the filename
Your report rendered remotely, but local Downloads is empty. What should you check? Does closing the SSH terminal necessarily delete saved remote output?






Hint





Rendering, transferring, and locating the received copy are separate actions.









Answer





Locate the output on the remote computer, then check whether it was transferred and to which destination. A remote desktop is not automatic synchronisation. Closing SSH ends a session, not saved files, subject to the service’s storage policy. Whether a running process continues depends on the service.




Q2. Count the represented thing
dna <- readLines("data/dna.txt") reads one invented 40-letter line. What are length(dna) and nchar(dna)? Why do they differ?






Hint





Count strings separately from characters within them.









Answer





length(dna) is 1 stored string; nchar(dna) is 40 characters in that string. Counting vector elements and counting characters answer different questions. The final newline in the file is not another DNA base.




Q3. Pixels are positions, not plants
The teaching image has 64 pixels, 24 above intensity 100. What fraction is bright? Does that make 64 independent biological replicates or identify one cell?






Hint





Divide bright positions by all positions; identify what those positions represent.









Answer





The fraction is 24/64 = 0.375. Pixels are related positions in one artificial image. Their count does not establish independent treatment replication or biological identity. Interpretation needs acquisition context, scale, and validation. The threshold count alone does not establish a cell’s area in mm².




Q4. Available duckweed measurements
Twenty independent flasks were started, ten per allocation. Nutrient flask F17 spilled before weighing. How many available biomass observations are there, and why is replacing the missing value by zero inappropriate?






Hint





Start with ten per group, then account for the documented spill.









Answer





There are 10 control and 9 nutrient observations, 19 in total. Zero would invent a known biomass; unavailable and absent biomass are different meanings. Retain the original row, report the loss, and make the comparison conditional on the observed data and missingness limitation.




Q5. A percentage difference needs its units
In the supplied alternative, percentage yield is 100 × collected mass / supplied maximum mass, with matching mass units. Protocol means are 68.67% and 77.00%. Is their difference an 8.33% relative increase? Does it establish greater purity?






Hint





Subtracting two percentages gives a difference in percentage points.









Answer





The modified-minus-standard difference is 8.33 percentage points. A relative percentage change would divide by the starting mean and multiply by 100; it is a different quantity. Greater yield alone does not establish greater purity, safety, sustainability, or general superiority. Product purity was an explicit simplifying assumption in this numerical exercise, not a measured finding.




Q6. Share a recipe, not only its output
A reader receives your HTML but cannot update the analysis for new data. What else should be in the shared project? Why test extraction in a new location?






Hint





HTML displays a result; source and inputs are needed to update it.









Answer





Include the .Rmd source, actual input CSV, dictionary, project file, required output folder if used, and a short README naming packages and the file to render. Testing a new location detects dependencies on personal absolute paths or missing files. The .Rproj does not contain the dataset. A fresh session detects hidden interactive objects. Include only the study files.




Q7. What does successful reproduction establish?
Your report renders successfully from the shared source and input. Does that prove the design and interpretation are correct, or provide a backup against losing your only disk?






Hint





Test reproduction, scientific validity, and backup separately.









Answer





It establishes that the supplied work regenerates the result in the tested environment. A flawed analysis can be reproducible. Scientific validity still needs the design, assumptions, checks, and reasoning. Backup is a separate action: keep a retrievable copy using supported separate storage.




Q8. Checks have limits
The received table has the same filename, byte size, row count, and column names as the source. Does this prove that every measurement matches? What would you check in a small transfer audit before making a stronger claim?






Hint





A changed value can leave a table’s dimensions unchanged.









Answer





No. A changed value can occupy the same number of characters, and tables can have identical dimensions but different contents. Inspect the intended saved input, verify named records and missing values, and compare the contents using the supported method. Record the actual source and destination locations. Check saved contents rather than an unsaved editor buffer.




Q9. One changed label, one unchanged length
The invented DNA string has A11, C9, G9, T11. Its first A is replaced by G in a new object. What are the changed A/G counts, total length, and GC fraction, defined here as (G + C) / all letters? Did the original file necessarily change?






Hint





Replacement changes a label, not the number of positions.









Answer





A10 and G10, still 40 letters, with GC fraction (10 + 9) / 40 = 0.475. The original fraction was 18 / 40 = 0.45. Changing a new R object does not write a file unless a save/write operation is performed. A count-based fraction does not establish what a DNA sequence does biologically.




Q10. A threshold can change its answer without moving an object
The toy image has 24 pixels at 210 and 40 at 25. Add 30 to every intensity in a new object. Compare counts above 220 before and after. What about counts above 100? Explain the difference between > 210 and >= 210 in the original.






Hint





The shifted intensity levels are 55 and 240. Read strict and inclusive comparisons separately.









Answer





Above 220 changes from zero to 24 because the bright pixels become 240. Above 100 stays at 24. Original > 210 excludes equality and selects zero, whereas >= 210 selects 24. Matrix positions did not change, so a threshold-count change alone cannot establish a larger organism or a change in physical object area.




Q11. A fresh dataset requires fresh counts
The algae table has 24 independent cultures, twelve per allocation. A19 in the supplement group spilled before weighing. Its available group means are 28.20 mg for reference and 33.91818 mg for supplement. Give available n and the observed supplement-minus-reference difference. Must supplement contain the largest single observation?






Hint





One supplement outcome is unavailable; subtract reference mean from supplement mean.









Answer





Available n is 12 reference and 11 supplement, 23 in total. The directed difference is 33.91818 - 28.20 ≈ 5.72 mg. A higher group mean does not require every value to be higher: reference culture A11 at 41.7 mg is the largest individual observation. Describe both the centre and observations.




Q12. A sensitivity check does not justify deletion
Omitting A11 lowers the algae reference mean to 26.97273 mg and increases the observed difference to about 6.95 mg. No source record identifies A11 as an error. Which result should be primary, and how should the other be labelled?






Hint





Ask whether the source record supports an exclusion.









Answer





Keep the all-available-measurements result primary: about 5.72 mg. The other is a diagnostic sensitivity calculation with an explicitly changed sample and no independent evidence for exclusion. Reweighing preferences or a more convenient p-value cannot justify removing a recorded observation. A19 remains a distinct missing measurement; omitting A11 does not repair that loss.




Q13. Rendering can miss the more serious fault
In a disposable report copy, an input is temporarily renamed. In another copy, the prose claims that every enrolled duckweed flask had a measured outcome. Which fault should stop rendering, and which may render successfully?






Hint





A missing input can stop execution; software can reproduce false prose.









Answer





The unchanged input path should fail when its required file is unavailable. Restore its exact name/path, rerun, and compare the result. The false prose can render successfully because software does not automatically validate the claim. It contradicts the documented missing F17 measurement. Check scientific meaning as well as execution; keep intentionally faulty copies out of the final package.




Q14. Is this a rounding difference or a different analysis?
One memo gives a mean of 33.91818 mg and the report displays 33.92 mg. Another report gives 34.32 mg. What should be investigated, and why should you check the input and calculation before changing display precision?






Hint





Round 33.91818 to two decimal places, then compare it with both displayed values.









Answer





33.92 is the first value rounded to two decimal places. 34.32 is not explained by that rounding. Check the saved input, available counts, group selection, outcome definition, and calculation, then confirm which rendered file was opened. Changing the number of displayed digits cannot repair a different input or an unrecorded exclusion. Retain full-precision values for subsequent calculations.



Return to day 25 consolidation and save your next-lab workflow with the reference pages.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: A project is a tree of locations
text:
A project is a tree of locations



A project parent folder contains data, output, and reports with their respective files.


data and reports are neighbours, not one inside the other.

Ask students to locate yesterday’s note first. Introduce parent folder and project root using the picture. Project root means the starting folder of this project, not the root of the entire computer. Have a student narrate the route from reports to data.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: An address can be absolute or relative
text:
An address can be absolute or relative
Example absolute path on Linux:
/home/anna/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
From the project root, the relative path is:
data/seedlings.csv
Your username and complete home path may differ.

Show Windows and Mac equivalents in the practical if needed. An absolute path supplies the full route from a drive or root. A relative path starts from the current folder. The illustrative username will differ from each student’s account; personal absolute paths are one reason analyses fail when moved.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: A relative path needs a starting point
text:
A relative path needs a starting point



The same relative path works from the project root but not from inside reports.


Current working directory: where relative paths start.

Physically move between the project root and reports in the graphical window. Say the route out loud. The file remains in data; changing the current folder changes the interpretation of a relative path. Tomorrow pwd will let a shell report this starting point.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Opening a CSV uses several computer parts
text:
Opening a CSV uses several computer parts



Saved data are read from storage into working memory and processed by the CPU.


The operating system manages files, memory, devices, and running programs.

Link each component to an action: storage retains the CSV, RAM holds working information, CPU carries out instructions. RStudio will later be an application and a process will be a running instance of it. More RAM does not automatically mean more persistent room for photographs. Avoid hardware shopping or binary arithmetic.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: An unsaved change and a saved file differ
text:
An unsaved change and a saved file differ
Try this only on a practice note:

Add a sentence, save, close, and reopen.
Add another sentence and discard the change when closing.
Inspect the actual file after reopening.

If the editor restores unsaved state, discuss what it has restored.

The exercise reveals the difference between storage and current application state. Autosave and recovery differ between editors. Ask the class where the saved note is and which sentence is actually stored there.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Home folders belong to particular environments
text:
Home folders belong to particular environments



Laptop storage, local Ubuntu storage on Windows, and a remote Linux home are distinct file locations.


An explicit transfer or configured sharing is needed to connect separate copies.

Windows students use native RStudio and a separate Ubuntu shell. Mac students do not need local Ubuntu, but remote storage remains separate for them too. A cloud copy may synchronise, but a remote desktop is not automatically a sync service. The course’s actual remote connection details are pending.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Which claim needs correcting?
text:
Which claim needs correcting?
“The note is in my editor, so I know where the file is.”
“I copied the ZIP beside the folder, so the laptop is backed up.”
“data/seedlings.csv means the same location from every folder.”

All need correction. The editor may be displaying an unsaved or recovered version; a same-disk ZIP does not protect against loss of that disk; relative paths need a starting folder. Ask for a concrete fix to each claim rather than vocabulary alone.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: A route starts somewhere
text:
A route starts somewhere



The route from reports to data first goes up to the project root.


From reports, data is a neighbour, not a child.

Trace the route graphically before naming relative paths. Students should draw a parent and two children. The exact personal absolute path differs across machines; the within-project relation is portable.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Try a move on a practice tree
text:
Try a move on a practice tree
Create map-a and map-b under practice.
Put a note in map-a, write its route, then move map-a into map-b.
Which written route needs revising?

Move only the disposable practice folder. Contents may remain identical while the address changes. Compare with copy: copying would leave the original route valid and create a second location. Ask students to predict before clicking.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Closing a process and saving a file differ
text:
Closing a process and saving a file differ



Closing a running process clears its working session while the saved note persists on storage.


Inspect the saved file to find out which changes survived.

Use the plain-text disposable experiment and acknowledge autosave/recovery. Some applications restore unsaved changes. RAM supports running information; storage retains deliberately saved information between sessions.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: A personal absolute path is a poor shared instruction
text:
A personal absolute path is a poor shared instruction
Illustrative laptop address:
/Users/anna/Documents/future-lab/data/seedlings-transfer.csv
Portable instruction from the agreed project root:
data/seedlings-transfer.csv

The second route still assumes an agreed root and an intact folder structure. It does not find data anywhere on the network. On a remote computer the same text refers to storage accessible there, not automatically to the laptop.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Installed program versus running instance
text:
Installed program versus running instance



One application saved on storage can be launched as running processes using memory and CPU.


More RAM and more saved-file capacity solve different problems.

Ask whether a closed editor remains installed. Yes, its saved program is still available to launch. A process is its current execution. Use these distinctions to explain everyday observation and recovery.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Plan the next laboratory folder
text:
Plan the next laboratory folder
A practical supplies measurements, photographs, and a protocol.
Where would you keep originals, notes, derived figures, and the report?
Write a README that another person can use.

The independent task creates a disposable future-lab project and text placeholders explicitly marked as such. Renaming text .jpg does not make a photograph. No particular folder scheme is scientifically mandatory; consistency and clear roles are what matter.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Connections do not all mean synchronisation
text:
Connections do not all mean synchronisation



Laptop, cloud service and remote Linux storage are distinct locations.


Draw only the copying or sync links you actually know are configured.

Cloud-managed folders can have local placeholders. A remote desktop is another interface, not automatic transfer. The course service details remain pending. Students can put a question mark on unknown links.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Test portability by moving the structure
text:
Test portability by moving the structure
Copy the complete practice project to a new location.
Find its README and data from the new root.
Explain which relative routes remain valid and which old absolute routes point elsewhere.

This is a test of organisation, not a separate backup against losing the laptop. Keep one clearly named working course project. The student output is two maps and an investigation note, tested by reopening the files along the documented routes.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Practise explaining the route
text:
Practise explaining the route
Open the exercises.
Save reports/day02-map.txt with:

A small project tree and the route to seedlings.csv.
One sentence distinguishing RAM from saved storage.
A note naming the computer holding your project.


The practical also creates practice/field-notes and figures for tomorrow’s navigation. Have students write directions, close their windows, and test the routes from the stated start. Keep backup discussions tied to the supported storage route when it is announced.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Four samples, one manifest
text:
Four samples, one manifest



The supplied manifest contains one header and four sample records linked to measurement filenames.


This small simulated shell dataset is separate from the 24-plant R dataset.

Read a manifest as a list of what is present. IDs connect metadata to measurements. The file paths locate measurements, while the README supplies their meaning and units. Distinguish four sample records from five text lines before discussing any command count.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: An archive is a package of files
text:
An archive is a package of files



Extracting lab-data.zip creates a folder of ordinary files while leaving the archive intact.


Copy the downloaded ZIP into the shell workspace deliberately.

On Windows the browser download is not automatically in Ubuntu. Open the shell workspace graphically and copy the file. On Mac use the same explicit location check. In a remote environment, use the provided transfer route; no login hostname is assumed here.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Inspect first; extract to a known destination
text:
Inspect first; extract to a known destination
unzip -l lab-data.zip
unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data
cd lab-data
less README.txt
-l lists; -d names the extraction destination. Press q to leave less.

The archive has four measurement files and supporting notes. If extraction asks to overwrite, inspect the existing destination and choose a fresh folder rather than automatically replacing work. These commands do not remove the original ZIP. Keep the command sequence tied to the current working directory.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Text search selects matching lines
text:
Text search selects matching lines



Literal grep search highlights the S03 and S04 records containing treated.


grep -F treated samples.tsv

-F requests literal text matching. The prepared file has control and treated labels; its header does not include treated. Explain that untreated would also contain treated, so grep does not understand treatment allocation or table columns. Inspect selected lines before interpreting them.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: A pipe connects the outputs and inputs
text:
A pipe connects the outputs and inputs



Four records enter a grep selection, two matching lines leave it, and wc counts two.


grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l

The pipe passes matching lines directly to the next program. wc -l counts newline-terminated lines, which represent records in this controlled file. No intermediate saved file is required. Ask students to predict 2 before running it, and compare with wc -l samples.tsv, which returns 5 including the header.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Redirection writes a separate output
text:
Redirection writes a separate output
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
less treated-samples.txt

The manifest is read; the extract is written.
> replaces existing contents at the destination.
Never use the input filename as this destination.


Students should explain which file changed. A text extract is not a full replacement manifest because it lacks the nonmatching header and control records. Show it in the file manager. Treat redirection as a concrete write action, not punctuation to memorise.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Work through one sample and one copy
text:
Work through one sample and one copy
head measurements/S03.csv
mkdir working
cp samples.tsv working/samples-copy.tsv
mv working/samples-copy.tsv working/manifest-practice.tsv
Which original files should still be present?

The original archive and manifest remain. Only the practice copy is renamed. The S03 measurement file has one observed length; find its units in README. cp and mv may replace a destination, so inspect the names before running. Ask students to identify S04’s path without copying the S03 line blindly.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: A substring does not understand a treatment
text:
A substring does not understand a treatment



Literal treated search selects untreated as well as the treated labels.


Test a search against known records before trusting its count.

The student makes search-trap.tsv from a copy, changes S01 to untreated, and preserves the real manifest. That trap gives three matches, not evidence for three treated biological samples. The baseline fixture remains two treated records.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Inspect selected IDs, not just a number
text:
Inspect selected IDs, not just a number
grep -F treated samples.tsv
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
A correct count is not proof that the right lines were selected.

Compare the same two commands on the trap copy. Explain -F literal matching. This is not a full table query language and should not replace structured data checks later in R.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: A line count depends on the file structure
text:
A line count depends on the file structure



Five newline-terminated lines represent one header and four sample records.


Headers name fields; they are not an additional sample.

Use the actual manifest with a final newline. wc -l counts newline characters, not an abstract number of biological observations. A CSV may contain quoted embedded newlines in general; this controlled TSV has one record per line, which makes the simple count valid here.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Follow a manifest path to a measurement
text:
Follow a manifest path to a measurement
Read S04’s listed path, then locate its file.
What if the record is present but the file has been renamed?
Investigate the file discrepancy using the manifest and source.

The independent exercise deliberately renames S04.csv only in a disposable received-check copy. The contents still identify S04 and length39.8mm. The manifest is an index of intended paths; it does not guarantee files currently occupy them.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: A filename can outlive its correct meaning
text:
A filename can outlive its correct meaning



Redirection replaces a treated-named extract with control records while retaining its filename.


Read the saved output after writing it.

Use the disposable treated-audit.txt experiment, retaining an extract-backup.txt. Show that > overwrites rather than appends. Never demonstrate input=output truncation on raw course data; explain the hazard without creating it.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Why input and output paths must differ
text:
Why input and output paths must differ
Unsafe pattern — do not run:
grep -F treated samples.tsv > samples.tsv
The shell may truncate the destination before grep reads its input.

Make the sequence explicit: the shell prepares output redirection, then starts the program. No deletion command is needed to lose data. A reproducible workflow preserves raw inputs and uses distinct informative output paths.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: A discrepancy needs evidence before repair
text:
A discrepancy needs evidence before repair



The manifest expects S04.csv while a renamed file retains the S04 measurement record.


Use the deliberately known rename as evidence to restore its path.

This does not establish a general rule to rename any nearby file to whatever is missing. Real ambiguous identities require source records or advice. Ask students to record the discrepancy, supporting evidence, repair, and verification in audit.txt.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Audit the recovered copy
text:
Audit the recovered copy
Keep:

Original source archive and manifest.
Search command and selected IDs.
The discrepancy and supported repair.
A checked output and explanation of the units.


The source archive still contains the original known fixture. The exercise ends with students locating the restored measurement from the manifest and explaining why line counts alone were insufficient. Record current computer and extraction location.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Save an inspection someone can explain
text:
Save an inspection someone can explain
Open the exercises.
Keep the selected records, a practice manifest, and working/observations.txt.
Explain 5 lines, 4 samples, and 2 treated records in your own words.

The practical also introduces the local/remote distinction via a teacher demonstration when access is ready. If service accounts are pending, complete the local file exercises and return to remote access when details are supplied.

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Ask which quantity you want
text:
Ask which quantity you want



The same plant is 20 mm initially and 37 mm finally; the increase is 17 mm.


Change is 37 - 20; the ratio 37 / 20 answers a different question.

Start from the simple biological question, not an overview of programming languages. All example plants are simulated. Growth has units of mm; a ratio of two lengths in the same units is dimensionless. Ask students to predict both before running R.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Assign a value to a name
text:
Assign a value to a name



An assigned object refers to a calculated value in memory, while the script stores instructions on disk.


Read <- as “store this under this name”.

The Environment pane shows current session objects; the editor shows saved instructions. Show that saving alone does not execute a line and executing alone does not save editor changes. An object does not remain available after an ordinary fresh session unless the instructions recreate it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Write and run a small script
text:
Write and run a small script
Save as day06.R in the course project root:
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm
R names are case-sensitive: growth_mm differs from Growth_mm.

Open the extracted .Rproj first. Run each line using the editor’s Run action. Explain the unit-bearing names and comments rather than requiring one preferred naming convention. The Console prompt is not typed. If an object is missing, check spelling and the line that should create it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Several values can share one object name
text:
Several values can share one object name



Three plant-specific pairs of initial and final measurements yield three matched growth values.


The order must refer to the same plants in both vectors.

Work through P02’s 40 minus 22 equals 18. The picture is positional arithmetic, not R automatically matching plant IDs. Later tables will preserve correspondence explicitly. Equal lengths alone do not establish matching plant identities.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Calculate, summarise, compare
text:
Calculate, summarise, compare
initial_mm <- c(20, 22, 19)
final_mm <- c(37, 40, 34)
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
mean(growth_mm)
length(growth_mm)
growth_mm > 16
Results: mean about 16.67 mm, length 3, comparison TRUE TRUE FALSE.

c combines values into a vector; mean and length are functions with parentheses. Greater-than gives logical values, not new measurements. Text needs quotation marks. Plant IDs are labels, so averaging them would not answer a useful question. Keep syntax explanations tied to these operations.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: A ratio can describe product yield too
text:
A ratio can describe product yield too



Collected mass 0.62 g fills 62 percent of the supplied maximum product mass of 1.00 g.


Percentage yield = 100 × collected dry mass / supplied maximum mass.

This is the optional substitute for the extra plant-ratio exercise. Define synthesis as making a product; supply the theoretical mass without reaction balancing. Assume collected product is pure only for this calculation. Both masses use grams. Changing collected mass to 0.70 g gives 70%.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Predict what survives a restart
text:
Predict what survives a restart
You have run the code but not saved the script. Then you restart R.

Which instructions are saved?
Which session objects must be recreated?
What should you run first after reopening?


The unsaved script changes may be lost or recoverable by the editor, but should not be relied upon. Save explicitly. In a fresh R session the objects need recreating from the beginning. Introduce error recovery as checking a dependency rather than running random lines until the error disappears. Esc cancels an unfinished expression marked by a plus prompt.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: An assignment is not a live spreadsheet link
text:
An assignment is not a live spreadsheet link



After final length changes, assigned growth stays stale until the subtraction reruns.


Name the input, stored result, and instruction that refreshes it.

Work through 20 to 37 mm giving 17 mm. Update final to 39, then print the old stored growth before rerunning the subtraction. The script records an order of computations; reopening it does not automatically execute it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Predict the stored result before rerunning
text:
Predict the stored result before rerunning
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
final_mm <- 39
growth_mm
Now rerun the subtraction and explain the difference.

The printed growth remains 17 until recalculation. Ask for the reason before showing 19. This is a concrete dependency exercise, not a request to write a function or build a spreadsheet application.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Equal vector length is not enough
text:
Equal vector length is not enough



Reordering one measurement vector destroys the intended within-plant correspondence.


R subtracts positions; it does not infer plant identities.

Correct vectors are initial 20, 22, 19 and final 37, 40, 34. A reordered final copy 34, 37, 40 yields 14, 15, 21: arithmetic on the wrong pairs. Equal lengths cannot certify matching identities.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Convert the values as well as their labels
text:
Convert the values as well as their labels
growth_mm <- c(17, 18, 15)
growth_cm <- growth_mm / 10
mean(growth_mm)
mean(growth_cm)
The means are about 16.67 mm and 1.667 cm.

A renamed object or axis label does not convert units. Preserve original values and assign converted values to a new name. Ratios cancel compatible length units; changes retain length units.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: A supplied solution rule can be traced through units
text:
A supplied solution rule can be traced through units



Mass divided by supplied molar mass yields amount; dividing by litres gives concentration.


A mole is a unit of chemical amount. Molar mass gives grams per mole.

Define molar mass as grams per mole. The supplied calculation is 0.2922 g / 58.44 g/mol = 0.005 mol; 100 mL = 0.100 L; amount divided by volume gives 0.050 mol/L, or 50 mmol/L. This is arithmetic, not laboratory preparation instructions.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Write every input into the source
text:
Write every input into the source
mass_g <- 0.2922
molar_mass_g_mol <- 58.44
final_volume_l <- 100 / 1000
concentration_mmol_l <- 1000 *
  (mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol) / final_volume_l

All numerical rules and constants are supplied. Keep intermediate quantities visible while learning so an incorrect conversion can be located. Avoid a single expression containing unexplained magic numbers.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Change one input and predict the response
text:
Change one input and predict the response



Original concentration is 50 mmol/L; doubling only mass gives 100, doubling only volume gives 25.


Different input changes answer different questions.

Restore original inputs between cases. Glucose mass 0.9008 g with supplied molar mass 180.16 g/mol in 100 mL also gives 50 mmol/L. Different weighed masses can produce the same amount concentration; no treatment effect has been inferred.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Diagnose a stale or missing object
text:
Diagnose a stale or missing object
Check in order:

Which saved script and session?
Were the input assignments run?
Were dependent calculations rerun?
Do names, units, and correspondences agree?


The outputs are day06-extended.R and a calculation-check note. Retain predictions even when wrong. A saved source that recreates the result after restart is stronger evidence than a successful result following unrecorded Console experiments.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Practise a complete, repeatable calculation
text:
Practise a complete, repeatable calculation
Open the exercises.

Add a fourth plant to both measurement vectors.
Change an input, predict the effect, and rerun.
Save day06.R; restart and run it from the top.


The worked mean uses three plants; the practical then extends to four. Keep the input values and comments in the saved source so the result can be reconstructed. Students doing the organic ratio choice still practise the matched-plant vector basics.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Growth is a derived measurement
text:
Growth is a derived measurement



A growth column is derived from each plant’s final and initial measurements, preserving the original inputs.


For P01: 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm.

The raw file records two lengths. Growth is their difference for the same plant, not a change to the source CSV. Distinguish final size from growth: a plant can start larger and still grow less. A negative change deserves checking, not automatic deletion.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Add the column in code
text:
Add the column in code
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings,
                     growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
Save the calculation in day08.R.

mutate returns a modified table that is assigned back to an object name. It finds the named columns in the supplied table. The packages must be loaded in this session. Ask students to inspect the new column and check P02’s growth, 8 mm, by hand.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Selecting rows is different from selecting columns
text:
Selecting rows is different from selecting columns



Highlighted treated rows are filtered, and then only ID and growth columns are selected.


filter() asks which observations? select() asks which variables?

Use control_plants <- filter(seedlings, treatment == “control”) and growth_table <- select(seedlings, plant_id, treatment, growth_mm) in the live demonstration. Explain that == compares while <- assigns. A pipe is a readable sequence of operations; it does not change their biological meaning.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Each plot answers a particular question
text:
Each plot answers a particular question



Actual simulated seedling data plotted with initial length on x and final length on y, coloured by allocation.


This shows final size against initial size, not growth against treatment.

Read the axes before discussing the pattern. Every point is a plant and colour is a group label. The plot is generated from the actual course CSV. It does not establish that starting larger causes a particular final size. The corresponding plotting code is in the practical.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Show growth for each plant
text:
Show growth for each plant



Individual seedling growth values overlap between the control and treated groups.


Horizontal jitter separates overlapping points; vertical values stay unchanged.

The practical’s position_jitter uses height = 0 and a seed for repeatable display. Ask the class what higher/lower means on this axis and whether the groups overlap. Describe the pattern and overlap; formal comparison and uncertainty come later.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Name the objects before exporting them
text:
Name the objects before exporting them
growth_table <- select(seedlings, plant_id, treatment, growth_mm)
growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(treatment, growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 8)) +
  labs(x = "Allocation", y = "Growth (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot
Assigning creates the object; printing displays it; exporting writes a file.

This supplies the objects needed by the following export slide. The complete sequence can run from the imports at the start of the deck. Separate selecting columns from mapping them to a figure; both retain the recorded raw input.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: A plot object and an image file differ
text:
A plot object and an image file differ
ggsave("output/seedling-growth.png",
       plot = growth_plot, width = 6, height = 4)
write_csv(growth_table, "output/seedling-growth.csv")
The output folder must exist. Locate the saved PNG and CSV in the file manager.

The preceding code creates growth_plot and growth_table before export. Naming a plot object does not save an image. An image does not contain the full source analysis. Both export operations can replace an existing destination, so use intentional names and keep raw inputs unchanged.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Transfer choice: percentage yield
text:
Transfer choice: percentage yield
For the optional organic-laboratory table, both masses are supplied in grams:
organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- mutate(organic, yield_percent =
                    100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
Compare percentages when starting scales differ; a larger mass alone is insufficient.

Define theoretical mass as the supplied maximum and isolated mass as dry collected product assumed pure for this numerical task. No reaction equation is required. Y01 is 62%. This choice substitutes for an extra plant-plot variation, not the main seedling workflow. Higher yield does not establish higher purity or general protocol superiority.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Rows and columns are separate decisions
text:
Rows and columns are separate decisions



Filtering retains observations while selecting retains variables.


Predict the row and column counts before running the selection.

Use the eighteen-plant transfer dataset. The full derived table has 18 rows; the treated subset has nine. Adding a growth column should not remove plants. Select using the supplied allocation label.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Derive from recorded values, preserve the input
text:
Derive from recorded values, preserve the input
transfer <- read_csv("data/seedlings-transfer.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
transfer <- transfer |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
T01:40.3−25.3=15.0mm.

Load the familiar packages and inspect names and types first. Derived values remain separate from the original CSV. Export the full derived table and selected subsets under informative filenames.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: The same plants can answer different plotted questions
text:
The same plants can answer different plotted questions



Initial versus final length and initial versus growth have different vertical quantities.


Read the axes before interpreting a pattern.

A final-size plot is not directly a growth plot. Both may be useful, but the scientific question determines the choice. An association plot alone does not establish causality.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Save, reopen, and interpret the derived result
text:
Save, reopen, and interpret the derived result
Export a CSV and two useful PNGs under a transfer-prefix.
Then open the saved files outside R and explain:

Which are values, and which are pictures?
What does one point represent?


Printing a plot object does not automatically save an image. write_csv exports a table, not a figure. Captions identify units and independent observations; the surrounding prose explains pattern and limitation.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: A calculated request can be impossible
text:
A calculated request can be impossible



The D04 calculated stock volume exceeds the final requested volume.


Retain and flag the impossible request.

Define stock as known concentration and dilution as adding solvent to a final total volume while conserving solute. D01–D03 need 2.5, 5 and 10 mL. D04 targets 200 from a stock of 100 mmol/L, so dilution alone cannot satisfy it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Add the supplied rule and a clear flag
text:
Add the supplied rule and a clear flag
dilutions <- read_csv("data/dilutions.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
dilutions <- dilutions |> mutate(
  stock_volume_ml = target_mmol_l * final_volume_ml / stock_mmol_l,
  possible_by_dilution = target_mmol_l <= stock_mmol_l)

Explain <= and logical columns. Both concentrations use mmol/L; final mL gives stock mL. Positive inputs are supplied. This numerical check needs neither a student-written conditional statement nor a new package.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Jitter changes visibility, not measurement
text:
Jitter changes visibility, not measurement



Horizontal jitter separates overlapping points while retaining every growth value.


Keep vertical jitter at zero for these plots.

Use actual transfer measurements. Different horizontal widths must not change measured y values or plant count. A prettier plot is not a reason to move measured values or hide observations.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Interpret calculated and observed relations differently
text:
Interpret calculated and observed relations differently
A dilution plot follows a supplied formula.
A plant scatter plot shows measured observations.
Which needs an explanation of the input rule, and which needs a description of observed variation?

These dilution cases illustrate supplied formulas rather than independent biological evidence. Save the complete flagged table, supported subset, plot and explanation of the impossible request.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Make a figure someone can read
text:
Make a figure someone can read
Open the exercises.

Use the intended table and columns.
Label axes with quantities and units.
Explain what one point represents and one limitation.
Save the source script, derived table, and figure.


Have students close and reopen the saved outputs, then rerun the script from a fresh session. A useful recovery question is whether a missing column was calculated earlier. Keep interpretation short and concrete; no new test or regression is needed in this lesson.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Describe what was independently measured
text:
Describe what was independently measured



A schematic shows separate control and treated pots; the actual study has twelve independent plants per group.


The simulated study measures 24 plants twice, seven days apart.

This briefing consolidates import, calculation, plotting, and reporting. Each plant has its own pot and a randomly allocated control/nutrient treatment. The nutrient formulation is unspecified. Two time measurements on the same plant are not two separate plants.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Explain the method in biological terms
text:
Explain the method in biological terms
“Growth was calculated as final minus initial length for each plant, in mm.”
That explains more than “we called mutate()”.
The report still needs the import and calculation code so someone can rerun it.

Distinguish a scientific methods explanation from a transcript of function names. The reader should understand the operation without speaking R. Students already have working code from previous days; their job is to place it in a self-contained report and explain it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: A readable figure shows the observations
text:
A readable figure shows the observations



Individual simulated growth measurements vary within both groups and overlap between allocations.


What is one dot? What does the vertical axis measure? Where is the overlap?

Expect one independently potted plant and change in length in mm. Ask for a concrete visible pattern and a limitation. Avoid p-values or an unsupported declaration that the treatment works. A mean across both groups would not answer whether groups differ; group summaries come next week.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Connect evidence to an interpretation
text:
Connect evidence to an interpretation



A biological growth question leads to observations and then a written pattern with a stated limitation.


Say what you observe and what the observations alone cannot settle.

Possible prose: growth varied among plants in both groups, and treated values tended to be higher but overlapped controls. The small simulated sample and lack of a quantified uncertainty comparison limit conclusions. Ask what evidence supports the student’s wording.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Keep the project portable
text:
Keep the project portable



A whole project can move to another folder while retaining the relative route from report source to its data subfolder.


data/seedlings.csv should not contain your personal username.

The .Rmd stays at the project root. Generated HTML can be next to it or in the documented reports/ output folder. A project file sets a working context; it does not embed the data. The diagram motivates testing the project from another folder.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Test it after restarting R
text:
Test it after restarting R
In the R Console, after saving first-report.Rmd:
rmarkdown::render("first-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")
If an object is missing, repair the source rather than hiding the gap in Console state.

Run this render command in the Console. Work from the first relevant error and its chunk. Check file paths, package loading, and the growth calculation before rewriting the whole report. A successful fresh-session render is evidence of reproducibility in this environment, not proof the interpretation is correct.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Descriptions need evidence
text:
Descriptions need evidence



Individual transfer-study growth values show overlap between the groups.


A difference in typical growth does not mean every treated plant outgrew every control.

Use the actual transfer data. Read three draft claims and identify a supporting figure, recorded value, or supplied design fact. Revise universal or causal claims that this descriptive exercise cannot establish.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Audit the report as a reader
text:
Audit the report as a reader
Can the HTML alone identify:

The question and independent unit?
The input and measurement units?
The calculation and plotted quantity?
A defensible conclusion and limitation?


Read without the source first to find communication gaps. Then locate the code and dictionary supporting each fact. Revise the R Markdown source, not only the generated HTML.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Connect the question to the recorded evidence
text:
Connect the question to the recorded evidence



A report traces a question through supplied data, analysis and a readable result.


Each section has a job in the reasoning.

Methods identify what was done; results describe what was observed; interpretation connects observations to the question within limits. Four clear short sections may communicate better than a long formal document.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Choose a figure because it answers a question
text:
Choose a figure because it answers a question
Compare final-size and growth plots.
Keep one as the main evidence. Retain another only if it answers a stated useful question.

More figures are not automatically better. This session expands revision and transfer rather than adding a statistical test. Have students identify which measured or derived quantity the vertical axis shows.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: The received project needs the same internal structure
text:
The received project needs the same internal structure



A complete report and data folder retain their relative relationship after copying.


Test from the received copy’s root in a fresh session.

A working original project is not proof that the received package reproduces it. Include the ordinary CSV and dictionary rather than a shortcut. Native Windows RStudio should use the extracted Windows project, not an unnoticed Ubuntu copy.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: A smaller brief tests transfer without new methods
text:
A smaller brief tests transfer without new methods
Choose the transfer seedlings or the supplied solutions table.
Import, check, calculate, plot, and write a short laboratory brief.
Save one selected brief, not both contexts.

For plants derive growth. For solutions, every formula and molar mass is given. The row roles differ: plants are experimental units, while solutions are numerical preparation cases. Distinguish a supplied formula relation from an observed biological effect.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Converting a label is not converting values
text:
Converting a label is not converting values



A value of 18.6 mm becomes 1.86 cm, not 18.6 cm.


Check the values, variable names and axis units together.

A unit-label error can leave R code running without warnings. Conversion needs a numerical change as well as a changed label. Encourage explicit comments and independent checks, not evaluation of appearance alone.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Leave a revision trail and a working brief
text:
Leave a revision trail and a working brief
Retain:

A revised earlier report and its source.
One laboratory-brief.Rmd and HTML.
Saved table/figure and a revision log.
A successfully tested practice package.


The solution checks are 50, 100 and 150 mmol/L for each solute. The transfer plant input has 18 records and T01 growth of 15.0 mm. These are practice products, not a grading rubric or an examination design.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Give the reader four short sections
text:
Give the reader four short sections
Open the exercises.

Question and data: design, measurements, independent unit.
Methods: import and growth calculation.
Results: a labelled figure and relevant calculated facts.
Interpretation: pattern, variation, and one limitation.


Save first-report.Rmd and its HTML. Open the HTML in a browser and identify the units and meaning of a point. The leaf-area/mass table provides practice transferring the import and scatter-plot workflow to different measurements.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: An average is not every plant
section: Same average; different observations
text:
Same average; different observations



Two toy growth groups have the same 14 millimetre mean but different standard deviations.


What does the mean leave out?

Give students a moment to read the axis before naming SD. Both sets have mean 14 mm; one contains 13,14,15 and the other 8,14,20. The second set has greater spread. We need to describe centre and variation, not choose one number to represent all plants.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Mean and median describe a centre
text:
Mean and median describe a centre
x <- c(10, 10, 10, 100)
mean(x)       # 32.5
median(x)     # 10
The mean uses every value. The median is the middle of the ordered values.

For an even number of observations, the median averages the two middle values. The large observation changes the mean strongly; it does not make either function wrong. Check unusual values against source information rather than deleting them to make summaries agree.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Measure deviations from the mean
text:
Measure deviations from the mean



Growth values 12,14,16 have deviations minus 2,0,plus 2 millimetres from their mean.


Adding the signed deviations gives zero, even with spread.

Work through the three numbers slowly. Subtraction uses the same units as the measurement. Positive and negative deviations cancel. Squaring is one way to avoid cancellation and leads to the sample variance used by R.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Variance has squared units; SD has the original units
text:
Variance has squared units; SD has the original units



A two millimetre deviation squared corresponds to four square millimetres.


For 12, 14, 16: variance = 4 mm², SD = 2 mm.

The sum of squared deviations is 4+0+4=8. Divide by n−1=2 for sample variance, giving 4 mm². The square root is 2 mm. Explain the denominator as a sample-variance convention that estimates population variance; no derivation is needed. SD is not an error bar for the mean.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Let R do the arithmetic, while you keep the meaning
text:
Let R do the arithmetic, while you keep the meaning
x <- c(12, 14, 16)
mean(x)
var(x)
sd(x)
A mean or SD needs its measurement unit in the report.

Ask students to predict 14,4,2 before running. Their task is not memorising function names: it is choosing the quantity that answers their question and labelling the output correctly. Neither SD nor variance means every observation lies within a specified range.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Our control plants vary around their mean
text:
Our control plants vary around their mean



Individual control growth values and their 15.275 millimetre mean are shown on one axis.


Mean ≈ 15.28 mm; sample SD ≈ 3.19 mm.

These are the complete clean seedling data, not yesterday’s deliberately incomplete export. State the switch explicitly:12 control plants now contribute. The mean is a summary, not an observed “average plant”. Biological and measurement variation may both contribute to spread.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Changing the origin is different from changing the unit
text:
Changing the origin is different from changing the unit



Adding a constant shifts the mean; converting millimetres to centimetres changes the numeric scale.


Predict what happens to SD before running R.

Adding 10 mm changes 13,14,15 into 23,24,25: mean shifts from 14 to 24, SD remains 1 mm. Dividing by 10 gives 1.3,1.4,1.5 cm: mean 1.4 cm and SD 0.1 cm. Variance divides by 100. This is a units check, not a new statistical method.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Transfer choice: a yield is a percentage
text:
Transfer choice: a yield is a percentage
A supplied maximum is 1.00 g; collected dry product is 0.62 g.
yield_percent = 100 × collected mass / supplied maximum mass

Yield = 62%; no reaction equation is needed.
SD of several yields is in percentage points.
A higher yield alone does not establish higher purity.


This is an alternative small task, not additional compulsory work. Theoretical maximum masses are supplied in organic-recovery.csv. Collected dry material is assumed pure for this simplified calculation. Across six standard runs mean yield is 68.67% and SD 4.32 percentage points. Distinguish a percentage scale from relative percentage change.

title: An average is not every plant
section: One changed observation can move several summaries
text:
One changed observation can move several summaries



Changing16 to26 mm alters the mean,median and spread differently.


Original: 12, 14, 16 mm. Changed: 12, 14, 26 mm.

The new mean is17.33 mm, median14 mm, variance 57.33 mm² and SD 7.57 mm. Ask for predictions before displaying numbers. This is sensitivity reasoning, not permission to remove a real large value.

title: An average is not every plant
section: A common shift changes centre, not deviations
text:
A common shift changes centre, not deviations



Every value shifts by 10 mm while the pattern of deviations stays unchanged.


Adding 10 mm shifts both the mean and each observation by 10 mm.

The shifted vector22,24,26 has mean 24 and SD 2. Show subtraction from each set mean. An SD change under a common shift would signal a calculation or comparison mistake.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Use units as an arithmetic check
text:
Use units as an arithmetic check



The same three measurements displayed in millimetres and centimetres have rescaled numerical summaries.


Unit conversion changes numbers; it does not change the measured plants.

Original variance 4 mm² becomes.04 cm²; SD 2 mm becomes.2 cm. Variance scales with the square of the conversion factor. The smaller numeric SD reflects a different unit, not less biological variation.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Calculate before rounding
text:
Calculate before rounding
x_mm <- c(12, 14, 26)
mean(x_mm)
median(x_mm)
var(x_mm)
sd(x_mm)
Keep full values for calculations; round the displayed table and prose.

R printing many digits is not proof of precise measurements. Students can show about 17.3 mm mean and 7.57 mm SD while retaining the calculation object. Confirm hand-worked deviations for the original simple vector first.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Another study separates mean and spread again
text:
Another study separates mean and spread again



The new treated group has a larger mean but a smaller observed SD than controls.


Larger mean does not require larger SD.

Transfer control mean 13.66 mm, SD 2.53 mm; treated mean 17.87 mm, SD 1.94 mm. Use actual values rather than the earlier study pattern, where treated spread was larger.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Recreate the calculation in a separate script
text:
Recreate the calculation in a separate script
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
transfer <- read_csv('data/seedlings-transfer.csv',
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
transfer_control <- filter(transfer, treatment == 'control')
sd(transfer_control$growth_mm)
T01 grew 15.0 mm; check that subtraction independently.

Load readr and dplyr as earlier. New data need their own import and growth column. Each group has 9 complete independent observations. Use separately named objects for the two studies.

title: An average is not every plant
section: The SD does not identify its own cause
text:
The SD does not identify its own cause
A group has a larger SD. Is that evidence of:

Greater biological diversity?
More measurement noise?
A less precise estimated mean?

SD describes the spread. Additional design and measurement information distinguish explanations.

Observed spread can have multiple sources. Uncertainty in a mean additionally depends on independent sample size and assumptions. A group SD alone does not evaluate all experimental technique.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Write a summary that survives a unit change
text:
Write a summary that survives a unit change
Include the quantity, units, n, centre, and individual spread.
If you convert to cm, revise the mean, SD, variance units, and axis together.
Which biological comparison should remain unchanged?

The ordering of group means and relative spread should remain consistent under a common positive conversion. A data table with correct numbers but wrong unit labels is still a misleading report.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Exercises: explain the number you calculate
text:
Exercises: explain the number you calculate
Choose one short transfer task and keep day12-variation.R.
What would stay the same if every measurement increased by 10 mm?
What changes when mm become cm?
Open exercises.

Keep the by-hand three-number example before the full dataset. Ask for an explanation of centre and spread. Students should retain the measurement unit and recognise that SD among plants is not uncertainty in a treatment difference.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: What received its own treatment allocation?
text:
What received its own treatment allocation?



Twelve separate pots illustrate individual plants as independently allocated units.


In our seedling study, the pot/plant is the experimental unit.

The picture illustrates separate pots, but physical separation alone is not proof of independence. The design description specifies independent allocation and handling. Ask students which entity could receive control while another receives treatment.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: More readings can still mean one plant
text:
More readings can still mean one plant



Six separate ruler readings all refer to the same plant P01.


Technical repeats help describe measurement variation.

Rereading the same plant may reveal consistency of the measurement process. It does not create new independently allocated plants or evidence about how different plants respond. The organic analogue is repeatedly weighing one collected product batch.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: A shared treatment can make the tray the unit
text:
A shared treatment can make the tray the unit



Plants grouped within two trays share one treatment per tray.


Count the independently assigned trays.

This is a schematic layout, not the actual course experiment. If treatment was assigned once to each tray, plants within that tray share its allocation and environment. Ask how many treatment assignments occurred, not how many measurements fill the spreadsheet.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: SD among plants and uncertainty in a mean differ
text:
SD among plants and uncertainty in a mean differ
Spread: how much individual plants vary.
Sampling uncertainty: how much our mean would vary across repeated samples.
A larger independent sample can stabilise its mean without making plants identical.

A group SD and a standard error answer different questions. Larger sample size does not make the underlying biological distribution narrower. Repeated dependent observations do not necessarily provide the information gain promised by more independent samples.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Each point in a sampling distribution is a mean
text:
Each point in a sampling distribution is a mean



Means of sixteen simulated draws cluster more tightly than means of four draws from the same toy distribution.


The source values stay fixed.

The supplied R demonstration uses the combined growth values as a fixed toy population and samples with replacement. It is not a new treatment experiment or a claim about nature. Each histogram entry summarises one simulated sample, not one freshly measured plant.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Read the horizontal axis before comparing spread
text:
Read the horizontal axis before comparing spread



Individual growth values,means of four draws,and means of sixteen draws are distinct distributions.


Individual values and estimated means are different objects.

This additional picture is regenerated from the course values using a fixed illustrative random generator; exact bins need not match the R demonstration. The concept is the narrower distribution of larger-sample means. Distinguish SD among means from SD among plants within a sample.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Run the supplied sampling demonstration
text:
Run the supplied sampling demonstration
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv('data/seedlings.csv', show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
population_mm <- seedlings$growth_mm
set.seed(14)
means_4 <- replicate(400,
  mean(sample(population_mm, size = 4, replace = TRUE)))
means_16 <- replicate(400,
  mean(sample(population_mm, size = 16, replace = TRUE)))
set.seed() makes the random demonstration repeatable.

The practical imports and defines population_mm before these lines. Explain sample as drawing values, replace=TRUE as allowing a source value again, and replicate as repeating the calculation. Students predict and interpret the result; functions and loops are not a new programming requirement.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: A stable estimate can still answer the wrong question
text:
A stable estimate can still answer the wrong question
If one unrepresentative tray is measured very precisely, have we learned the population mean accurately?
Which problem would another ruler reading fix?
Which problem needs another independently chosen unit?

Precision does not remove bias, dependence, or unrepresentative sampling. Another reading may help measurement consistency; another independently allocated or sampled unit addresses a different uncertainty. Avoid claiming that sample size alone guarantees a valid study.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: A new toy source makes the same point
text:
A new toy source makes the same point



Sample means from 12 draws vary less than means from 3 draws from the same fixed transfer source.


Both sampling processes reuse the same fixed recorded values.

This is a supplied simulation, not new biological measurement or a treatment comparison. The transfer source combines groups only to illustrate sampling. Keep the target fixed while changing sample size.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Number of repeats is not sample size
text:
Number of repeats is not sample size



Increasing simulation repeats smooths the display without changing the sample size of 12 draws.


More simulated estimates improve our picture of the sampling pattern.

Compare100 and 1000 repeats, each using12 draws. More repetitions do not create more measured plants or shrink the underlying distribution as increasing independent sample size does.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Follow the levels of information
text:
Follow the levels of information



Repeated simulated samples can contain the same source identifier multiple times.


Observed source → sampled draws → one mean → repeated estimates.

Replacement permits a value to appear twice. A stored source plant is not remeasured each time it is drawn by sample. Students should label each row in their simulation output as an estimate, not a new organism.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: A precise estimate can miss the question
text:
A precise estimate can miss the question



A shifted source produces a narrow distribution centred away from the original source mean.


Greater precision does not remove a common measurement offset.

This schematic uses a known5 mm shift for illustration. It does not diagnose bias in the course study. A narrow distribution can describe a biased or irrelevant process very precisely.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Adapt a supplied simulation without inventing a new method
text:
Adapt a supplied simulation without inventing a new method
transfer <- read_csv('data/seedlings-transfer.csv',
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
set.seed(14)
means_3 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(
  transfer$growth_mm, size = 3, replace = TRUE)))
Change size to 12 in a second object; preserve the first.

Load readr/dplyr before this supplied block. Students need to understand source, draw size, replacement, repetitions, and seed; they are not asked to author loops or a sampling algorithm.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Different repeat settings answer different questions
text:
Different repeat settings answer different questions
Change one setting at a time:

Seed: another reproducible random sequence.
Draw size: more values in each estimated mean.
Repetitions: more simulated means to inspect.

Which change alters the original recorded plants? None.

Avoid a recipe of trying seeds until a pretty plot appears. The saved source is unchanged, and the simulation is conditional on that source distribution.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Choose independent units before counting rows
text:
Choose independent units before counting rows
One plant measured twenty times and twenty independent plants are different designs.
What could technical repeats help assess? What needs additional independently sampled or assigned units?

Technical repeats can assess measurement repeatability under appropriate conditions. Questions about variation among plants or treatment allocations need independent biological units. This is why repeating balance readings of one synthesis does not create more independent runs.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: A defensible simulation explanation has boundaries
text:
A defensible simulation explanation has boundaries
State the fixed source, sampling rule, estimate, and comparison.
Then state what the demonstration does not establish about a natural population or treatment.

The required transfer note should distinguish source SD from SD among means, stable patterns from exact seed-dependent values, and a toy combined-treatment source from a real inferential design.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Exercises: draw the design and explain the mean
text:
Exercises: draw the design and explain the mean
Label independently treated units in three designs.
Run the supplied sampling demonstration and explain the axis.
Keep your diagrams and day14-sampling.R.
Open exercises.

Protect time for diagrams and discussion. The organic diagram can substitute for one plant example, not add another simulation. A useful explanation identifies what was repeated, what remained the same, and what increased the independent information.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Does nutrient allocation change seven-day growth?
text:
Does nutrient allocation change seven-day growth?



Twelve controls and twelve treated seedlings represent independent pot allocations.


Name the question, outcome, units, and independently allocated unit.

The course data are simulated. The study description supplies the random-allocation assumption; row order does not prove it. Growth is final minus initial length in millimetres. There are 12 plants per group, measured twice but contributing one growth value each.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Start with the observations
text:
Start with the observations



Individual plants show overlap and different group locations in growth.


A group mean does not describe every plant.

Ask students what a dot represents and whether any value obviously contradicts the documented measurement process. There is no known source error in this complete table. Keep valid measurements in the main analysis.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: State the direction before calculating
text:
State the direction before calculating



The treated mean exceeds the control mean by about 6.22 millimetres.


Treated minus control is our reported difference.

Control mean 15.275 mm, treated mean 21.49167 mm, difference 6.21667 mm. Reversing subtraction changes the sign without changing the observed experiment. A reader needs the direction and units to interpret an estimate.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: One change per independently treated plant
text:
One change per independently treated plant
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
treated <- seedlings |> filter(treatment == "treated") |> pull(growth_mm)
control <- seedlings |> filter(treatment == "control") |> pull(growth_mm)
mean(treated) - mean(control)
Keep this preparation in comparison.Rmd.

Load readr, dplyr, ggplot2 before these lines, as in the practical. pull extracts the numeric column. These objects are vectors here, not the full group tables. Tomorrow’s lecture and test use exactly these definitions and direction.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Paired observations require a real identity
text:
Paired observations require a real identity



Different plants form independent groups; the same plant measured twice forms a pair.


Two columns or two labels alone do not establish pairing.

Today compares separate plants. Later, the same plant measured before and after a light change will require within-plant matching. Pairing requires matching subject identity, not matching row positions.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Do we have plants or shared treatment units?
text:
Do we have plants or shared treatment units?



A tray-wide allocation creates shared treatment units even when many plants are measured.


The design determines whether the group comparison is justified.
