Revisit the replication concept before running inference. The shown tray layout is a counterexample, not the course study. One tray per treatment would not provide twelve independent treatment assignments per group. A function cannot repair that limitation.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Size of an effect and variability are separate questions
text:
Size of an effect and variability are separate questions
The sample difference is about 6.22 mm.
The group SDs describe how much plants vary within each group.
Tomorrow we estimate uncertainty in the population mean difference.

Within-group SD and a confidence interval for the difference describe different quantities. Variation among measurements is the starting information for uncertainty, but the quantities answer different questions. Avoid introducing an extra formula today.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: What might weaken the interpretation?
text:
What might weaken the interpretation?

Non-independent units or biased allocation.
Recording mistakes or a dominant questionable observation.
A small sample with severe skew.
An outcome that does not answer the biological question.


This list guides inspection, not a mechanical test-selection algorithm. For this introductory example the supplied design supports independent groups. If an actual practical looks unsuitable, seeking advice is a successful outcome; deleting genuine observations until a test works is not.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Starting size and growth answer different questions
text:
Starting size and growth answer different questions



Initial lengths and seven-day growth are displayed separately for the two groups.


Choose the outcome before choosing a summary or a test.

The study records two lengths per plant. Growth is final minus initial, not final size alone. Starting-size patterns can inform a limitation, but we are not adding an adjusted regression in this introductory course.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Write the analysis plan before the output exists
text:
Write the analysis plan before the output exists
State the outcome, direction, unit, allocation, and units.
For this study: mean seven-day growth; treated minus control; plant/pot; randomly assigned allocation; mm.

A group-sorted file does not establish random assignment. That information comes from the supplied design. Ask what would differ if all treated plants shared one tray and all controls another.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Direction is an arithmetic choice you must explain
text:
Direction is an arithmetic choice you must explain



The same two group means produce opposite signed differences when subtraction order is reversed.


Changing subtraction order does not change the observations.

Treated minus control is+6.2167 mm; control minus treated is−6.2167 mm. Neither direction is intrinsically wrong if labelled. A report that states one direction and calculates the other is wrong.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: A difference in means is not a claim about every plant
text:
A difference in means is not a claim about every plant



Individual control and treated growth values overlap even when group means differ.


Use individual points to check the word “every”.

The largest control growth exceeds some treated values. Rewrite the group statement to say greater mean growth in these observations, not that every treated plant outgrew every control. Overlap itself is not a significance test.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Describe the result without a threshold label
text:
Describe the result without a threshold label
Include n, group means, directed difference, units, and individual variation.
Then name the unanswered question: how uncertain is the estimated population difference?

Students should have a meaningful results paragraph before day17. Keep the experimental question and observed difference clear before introducing test output.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: An independent study gives another estimate
text:
An independent study gives another estimate



The transfer study has 18 plants and an observed treated-minus-control difference near 4.21 mm.


Another observed estimate is not automatically evidence that a mechanism changed.

The two simulated studies differ in actual values, group spread, and sample sizes. A smaller observed difference is not proof of no effect or failed treatment. Current descriptive work cannot resolve every comparison between studies.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Keep transfer inputs and outputs under new names
text:
Keep transfer inputs and outputs under new names
transfer <- read_csv('data/seedlings-transfer.csv',
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
transfer |> group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mm = mean(growth_mm),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm), .groups = 'drop')

Load readr and dplyr as in the main study. Confirm18 rows,9 per group, no missing values. Use transfer-comparison.Rmd rather than overwriting the main report; preserve the comparison direction.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Inspect a hypothetical design failure
text:
Inspect a hypothetical design failure
Suppose the label was assigned to one tray per group.
What remains observable? What independent treatment information is missing?
A different test cannot manufacture independently assigned trays.

The observed plant lengths still exist, but treating24 plants as24 independent treatment allocations would be misleading. Keep a design limitation separate from a data-entry error or computational bug.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Exercises: prepare before testing
text:
Exercises: prepare before testing
Create comparison.Rmd with design, growth calculation, observations, and the directed difference.
Explain why the two groups are independent.
Open exercises.

Ask students to read their difference aloud with units and direction. Tomorrow the report gains an interval and p-value; today’s work should already be scientifically intelligible without either.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Which two readings belong together?
text:
Which two readings belong together?



Plant IDs connect before and after observations even when their row order differs.


Pair by identity, not accidental row position.

The file paired.csv stores one plant per row with both readings, so matching is preserved. The diagram imagines two differently ordered lists to make the identity principle visible. The example teaches identity matching using the supplied single-table layout.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Read the within-plant paths
text:
Read the within-plant paths



Each of ten independent plants connects its before and after photosynthesis readings.


Ten plants, ten pairs; not twenty independent plants.

Photosynthesis rate is measured in micromoles CO2 per square metre per second. Each line links one plant’s non-destructive reading before and after increasing illumination. The prepared data show positive changes for every plant, but other datasets could have mixed directions.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Subtract within each plant first
text:
Subtract within each plant first



Three example plants show their after-minus-before change on the original measurement scale.


Positive change means the measured rate increased.

L01 changes 6.95−5.87=1.08; L02 changes 11.92−7.75=4.17; L03 changes 10.12−8.81=1.31. These examples show why pairing concerns each plant’s change, not merely comparing two unlabelled collections of readings.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: One paired comparison in R
text:
One paired comparison in R
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
paired_data <- read_csv("data/paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
paired_data <- paired_data |>
  mutate(change = after_umol_m2_s - before_umol_m2_s)
paired_comparison <- t.test(
  paired_data$after_umol_m2_s, paired_data$before_umol_m2_s,
  paired = TRUE)
After minus before is the direction of the result.

Load readr and dplyr first in the report. The paired argument tells t.test that each position in the first vector belongs with the corresponding position in the second. Keeping both readings in one ID-checked table prevents independent sorting. This is not a method for pairing arbitrary groups.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Changes differ among plants
text:
Changes differ among plants



The ten within-plant changes are plotted against plant identifiers.


Mean change ≈ 1.983 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.

The y-axis is the difference, not the after reading. Its zero line means no recorded within-plant change. L02 has a larger change than several others; this alone is not a recording error. The mean change and its uncertainty use 10 independent pairs.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Pairing changes the information used
text:
Pairing changes the information used
A paired comparison asks whether the mean within-plant change is zero.
A one-sample comparison of those changes gives the same result:
t.test(paired_data$change, mu = 0)
Keep before and after readings matched by plant ID.

This equivalence supports understanding, not a demand to learn another method. The subject-to-subject differences in starting level are accounted for through within-subject subtraction. Pairing must be justified by design, and the pairs still need to be independent of one another.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: The design has a limit the test cannot remove
text:
The design has a limit the test cannot remove



The study changes light condition while time passes between the before and after readings.


No unchanged-light group; the same order was used for every plant.

We observe a change after the procedure, but light, elapsed time and measurement order accompany one another. The paired t-test does not separate them. A small p-value does not isolate light as the cause.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Report change, uncertainty, and the ordering limit
text:
Report change, uncertainty, and the ordering limit
Mean after-minus-before change: 1.983 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.
95% CI: 1.255 to 2.711; paired two-sided p ≈ 0.000166.
These describe a change under the study conditions, not an isolated light effect.

The confidence interval concerns the population mean change, under the assumptions. It does not describe the range of most plants’ individual changes. Sensible precision and a direct order/time limitation matter more than copying every decimal from the console.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: The same marginal means do not validate a pairing
text:
The same marginal means do not validate a pairing



Valid pairings and independently sorted columns have identical mean change but different change variability.


Identity influences the uncertainty calculation, even when the mean agrees.

For the actual source, correct SD of change is about 1.018 rate units; independently sorted columns give about.505. The changed uncertainty is artificial. A smaller p-value after sorting is not improved evidence.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Look at which measurements the lines connect
text:
Look at which measurements the lines connect



Originalplant pairings and artificialrank matchings connect different before-and-after values.


Keep a plant identifier attached to both of its measurements.

Sorting whole rows preserves pairs; sorting columns separately destroys identity. A matching based on numerical rank is not a replacement for the recorded subject identifier.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: A deliberately wrong object exposes the trap
text:
A deliberately wrong object exposes the trap
wrong_sorted_change <- sort(paired_data$after_umol_m2_s) -
  sort(paired_data$before_umol_m2_s)
mean(paired_data$change)
mean(wrong_sorted_change)
sd(paired_data$change)
sd(wrong_sorted_change)
Never overwrite the valid paired object with this demonstration.

The first two means agree. The SDs differ. Ask why subtracting marginal means cannot check whether identities were preserved. Keep the source CSV untouched and label the wrong demonstration unambiguously.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: One analysis, two equivalent computations
text:
One analysis, two equivalent computations
Paired comparison of before and after: t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
One-sample comparison of correctly matched changes with zero: t.test(change, mu = 0)
These analyse the same within-unit differences.

The estimate,interval, and p-value agree when the exact same complete differences are supplied. They are not two independent pieces of evidence and should not be reported as separate confirming experiments.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Few pairs can leave substantial uncertainty
text:
Few pairs can leave substantial uncertainty



Threechanges of 2,1,and 3 have a mean of 2,but a95%mean-change interval spanning about−0.48 to 4.48.


Three plants are limited support for a population inference.

The three illustrative plants had before5,8,6 and after7,9,9 in the stated rate units. Mean change2,SD 1. The interval is provided to practise interpretation. The tiny sample provides limited support for model-based inference.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: A positive observed change does not prove a universal change
text:
A positive observed change does not prove a universal change
For the illustrative case:

Describe all three individual changes.
Interpret uncertainty in the population mean.
Name the small-sample and design limitations separately.


All supplied individual changes are positive, yet the model-based95% mean interval includes zero. This does not make the data erroneous or establish equality. Retain the stated analysis and explain its uncertainty.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Pairing does not remove an order effect
text:
Pairing does not remove an order effect



Both light and elapsed time change between the two readings in a fixed-order experiment.


Preserved identity and a valid causal comparison are different requirements.

The source study always measures before then after increased illumination, without an unchanged-light parallel group. The mean change is describable, but light cannot be isolated from every time/order influence.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Plan the next experiment by limitation
text:
Plan the next experiment by limitation
More independent plants → more independent pairs. Repeat readings of one plant → measurement repeatability. A suitable comparison/design → better separation of treatment from time.
These are different improvements.

Students create paired-transfer.Rmd from the supplied three-row example, including its values/code and a limitation. They should not pool this illustrative case with the unrelated ten-plant study or claim a new measured dataset.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Exercises: keep the pair visible
text:
Exercises: keep the pair visible
Make paired-report.Rmd with the design, matched changes, a figure, result, and limitation.
Could a reader identify what counted as one independent pair?
Open exercises.

Check the practical’s chosen source report filename and use its code from the top. Ask students to explain why two unrelated groups cannot become paired by putting them beside one another. No new biology or chemical prerequisite is needed.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Do larger leaves tend to have greater dry mass?
text:
Do larger leaves tend to have greater dry mass?



Leaves from different plants illustrate measured area and mass without any assigned treatment.


One leaf from each of 18 independent plants.

This is an observational dataset. We measured area and dry mass, not experimentally changed one while holding everything else fixed. One leaf per plant supplies the independent unit for this introductory example. The illustrated leaves are schematic; the plots use the actual course CSV.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Start by plotting the measured variables
text:
Start by plotting the measured variables



Leaf area and dry mass form a positive observed association with a fitted line.


Horizontal: area (cm²). Vertical: dry mass (mg).

Ask students to read the axes before describing the trend. These are not the calibration standards from yesterday, and neither variable was assigned experimentally. The line summarises the observed association; scatter around it matters.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Fit the same simple kind of model
text:
Fit the same simple kind of model
library(readr)
leaves <- read_csv("data/leaf-mass.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
leaf_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = leaves)
coef(leaf_fit)
Fitted mass ≈ 9.48 + 4.11 × area.

The input columns and units differ, but the lm syntax is the same as calibration. Intercept is about 9.476606 mg; slope about 4.110117 mg per cm². The intercept locates the line at area 0, outside the observed area range; it is not a measured mass of a zero-area leaf.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: The slope has units
text:
The slope has units



A one-square-centimetre step along the fitted line corresponds to about 4.11 milligrams in fitted mass.


Slope ≈ 4.11 mg per cm².

We say the fitted mass is 4.11 mg greater for a one cm² increase in area within this descriptive model. That does not establish what would happen under an intervention. The red step shows the line’s change, not a measured before/after change in a particular leaf.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Use the line inside the observed range
text:
Use the line inside the observed range
At area 8 cm²:
9.476606 + 4.110117 × 8 ≈ 42.36 mg
This is a fitted mean relationship, not the exact mass of every leaf that size.

Use the stored unrounded coefficients in actual calculations. The point prediction has uncertainty and individuals scatter around the line. Full regression inference is deferred. Here the point 8 cm² lies within the observed 2.96–14.68 cm² area range.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Residuals keep the scatter visible
text:
Residuals keep the scatter visible



Residuals show observed mass minus fitted mass across measured leaf areas.


Residuals are in milligrams, the outcome’s units.

A positive residual means heavier than fitted at that area. Look for structure or a dominating point while remembering that small samples provide limited diagnostics. The line need not explain every biological difference.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Investigate influence without deleting inconvenient data
text:
Investigate influence without deleting inconvenient data



The full fit is compared with a labelled sensitivity fit omitting A18.


A18 is not a known recording error.

The default result retains all 18 plants. A labelled sensitivity check can reveal whether a conclusion depends strongly on one point. Omitting A18 gives a slightly different slope, about 4.064927 mg per cm². This is an illustration of influence, not permission to choose whichever subset yields the preferred result.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: An extended line is not extended evidence
text:
An extended line is not extended evidence



The observed leaf-area range is separated from a dashed unsupported extension.


No measurements support the shaded region.

The dashed extension is deliberately drawn as a warning. A formula produces a number at 25 cm², but there are no such observations here and the relationship may change. Distinguish arithmetic from evidence. The same range principle applied to assay calibration.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Association does not establish an intervention effect
text:
Association does not establish an intervention effect
“Larger leaves tended to have greater dry mass in this sample.”
This does not prove that forcing area to increase would cause the fitted mass change.
Plant age, species, growing conditions, and other properties may vary together.

The named possible factors are examples of missing context, not measured covariates to add to a model. We are not introducing multiple regression or causal adjustment. The outcome is a restrained interpretation of an observational pattern.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: A slope changes numerically when its units change
text:
A slope changes numerically when its units change



Identical fitted leaf masses are shown with area in square centimetres and square millimetres.


The biological observations did not change.

One cm² equals100mm². Slope 4.1101 mg/cm² becomes.041101 mg/mm². The intercept and fitted masses stay the same apart from numerical precision. Preserve both area columns for the demonstration.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Check the unit conversion through fitted values
text:
Check the unit conversion through fitted values
library(dplyr)
leaves <- mutate(leaves, leaf_area_mm2 = 100 * leaf_area_cm2)
unit_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_mm2, data = leaves)
coef(unit_fit)
max(abs(fitted(leaf_fit) - fitted(unit_fit)))
The final difference should be essentially zero.

A tiny floating-point difference is normal. This is a consistency check,not another independent biological result. A smaller numeric slope in different units does not establish a weaker association.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: A residual is attached to a particular measured leaf
text:
A residual is attached to a particular measured leaf



One leaf observation and its fitted value are connected by its vertical residual.


Residual = observed mass − fitted mass, in mg.

Locate the same identifier in the table and plot. Positive residual means the observed leaf lies above the line. The fitted relationship describes mean tendency and leaves individual variation.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Influence is a question, not an exclusion rule
text:
Influence is a question, not an exclusion rule
Keep the full-data fit as primary. Fit without A18 in a separate object and compare.
Ask what changed and why; keep valid observations in the main fit.

The main slope is4.110117 mg/cm² and the fit without A18 is4.064927. The difference is small here,but sensitivity does not depend on getting a dramatic answer. Source evidence is needed for an actual correction or exclusion.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: A defined formula and an empirical relationship differ
text:
A defined formula and an empirical relationship differ



Calculated solution concentrations fall on a prescribed arithmetic relationship;measuredleaf values vary around an empiricalfit.


A perfect relationship created by a formula is not experimental validation.

The solution example supplies all masses,molar masses and volumes; its concentration calculation is arithmetic. The leaf line summarises measured associations. A line through formula-generated values illustrates the supplied arithmetic relationship.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: A new association retains its study context
text:
A new association retains its study context



Initial and final transferseedling lengths are plotted with allocationcolour and one descriptive combined line.


This asks about starting and final size, not the mean treatment effect on growth.

These are18 independent source plants,but the two lengths on each plant are related. Allocation and other differences may contribute to the combined pattern. The combined line is descriptive and does not adjust for allocation.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Fit the question you actually stated
text:
Fit the question you actually stated
transfer <- read_csv('data/seedlings-transfer.csv',
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
size_fit <- lm(final_mm ~ initial_mm, data = transfer)
coef(size_fit)
range(transfer$initial_mm)
Use an in-range initial length for a worked fitted-value calculation.

A predictor value of zero may be outside the useful biological range even though the model calculates an intercept. The report should include a residual plot and one checked observed-minus-fitted example.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Choose the analysis through the design and outcome
text:
Choose the analysis through the design and outcome



Independentgroups,paired measurements,and an observed scatter pattern lead to different familiaranalysisquestions.


Mean difference, within-unit change, and a slope answer different questions.

This is not an automatic menu based on a normality test or whichever function gives a small p-value. Name the independent unit,outcome,units,and limitation before applying the appropriate taught method.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Finish with a comparison sheet you can reuse
text:
Finish with a comparison sheet you can reuse
For each familiar question, record:

Independent units and what was measured.
Outcome, units, and the method/output.
A design or interpretation limitation.

Keep source, data, figure, and report together.

Students revise the leaf report and independently write transfer-association.Rmd. Their three-question sheet becomes a practical reference for future labs. Keep the comparison focused on question, design, and interpretation.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Exercises: explain the line, the residuals, and one limit
text:
Exercises: explain the line, the residuals, and one limit
Create association-report.Rmd with observations, fitted line, slope units, and residuals.
Keep the full-data result and label any sensitivity check.
Open exercises.

Check the exact source filename in the practical; use the root project convention. Ask students to choose one actual point and explain its residual sign. Their final report should distinguish descriptive association, supported range and a causal claim.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Different meanings, familiar representations
text:
Different meanings, familiar representations



DNA text, image pixels, and a plant observation illustrate three kinds of stored information.


Our task: identify what each stored value represents.

Use invented DNA and an artificial image to practise vectors, tables, logical comparisons, and interpretation.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: A file format gives bytes meaning
text:
A file format gives bytes meaning



Eight bits form a byte with 256 possible patterns.


Renaming photo.jpg to photo.csv does not convert the contents.

A bit has two possible values; eight bits yield 256 patterns. One format may use a byte for brightness; another uses encoded characters. The extension helps an application choose how to read it.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: One string is not forty vector elements
text:
One string is not forty vector elements
dna <- readLines("data/dna.txt")
length(dna)  # 1 stored string
nchar(dna)   # 40 characters in that string
length() and nchar() answer different questions.
bases <- strsplit(dna, split = "")[[1]]
length(bases)  # 40 separate letters

Run from the course project. The final newline is not another DNA base. strsplit returns a collection of results, and [[1]] selects the first. Supply this code rather than requiring list syntax as a new programming outcome.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Counts describe this invented sequence
text:
Counts describe this invented sequence



Counts from the supplied sequence: A11, C9, G9, T11.


table(bases) counts letters; it does not reveal a gene’s biological function.

Ask students to predict the result of replacing one A by a G. A falls by one, G increases by one, and the total remains forty. Preserve the source file and change an R object for this experiment. Meaning requires biological context.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: An image can be a rectangular numeric table
text:
An image can be a rectangular numeric table



The supplied 8 by 8 intensity table and the same values displayed as grayscale.


0 means black; 255 means white on this teaching scale.

The source image has only values 25 and 210. One byte could store each intensity, but the CSV uses text digits plus delimiters and a header. The 64 values need not occupy only 64 bytes in that representation. No physical scale is provided.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: A threshold is a stated comparison
text:
A threshold is a stated comparison



An intensity threshold of 100 selects 24 pixels; 220 selects none.


Changing a threshold changes the question we ask of the same values.

Both images come from the actual supplied matrix. Because this constructed image has only two levels, separating its centre is unusually easy. Noise, lighting, and overlapping real objects would complicate interpretation.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Reuse logical values to count
text:
Reuse logical values to count
pixels <- as.matrix(read.csv("data/pixels.csv"))
bright <- pixels > 100
sum(bright)   # 24
mean(bright)  # 0.375
TRUE contributes 1 and FALSE contributes 0.
The fraction is 24 / 64, not 24 independent organisms.

Here read.csv plus as.matrix supplies a simple numeric matrix. Normal biological tables still use read_csv. The calculation counts qualifying pixels; it has not identified cells or calibrated area in square millimetres.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: A pixel is not an experimental replicate
text:
A pixel is not an experimental replicate

An image position holds one brightness value.
Many positions can belong to one plant or one field of view.
A treatment assigned to one plant still has one treated plant.

What extra information would you need to interpret the bright object biologically?

Possible answers: acquisition context, physical scale, what was imaged, biological validation, and how treatment was assigned. Relate this to technical measurements and independent units from day 14, rather than introducing another test.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Prediction before code
text:
Prediction before code
Our only pixel values are 25 and 210.
What do these comparisons count?
sum(pixels > 50)
sum(pixels > 100)
sum(pixels > 220)

Ask before running: 24, 24, 0. A change in a threshold need not always change the count; it depends on which values occur. The threshold alone does not define a cell or specify physical area.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: The question determines what to count
text:
The question determines what to count
One string can contain 40 characters.
An 8-by-8 matrix contains 64 positions.
Neither size is automatically the number of independent organisms.

Ask students to name the represented thing before choosing length, nchar, dim, or a count of TRUE values. This is a transfer of familiar concepts rather than a survey of sequence or image software. Distinguish a file’s physical size in bytes from the number of meaningful values interpreted from that file.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Change one label; predict two counts
text:
Change one label; predict two counts



Replacing the first A with G changes A11/G9 to A10/G10 while keeping forty total letters.


The original object and file can remain unchanged.

The sequence begins with A. Predict the total and two counts before running the replacement. Make a changed R object while preserving the raw file. Counts are numerical descriptions of this invented string, not evidence about the function of a real DNA sequence.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Create a changed object explicitly
text:
Create a changed object explicitly
bases_changed <- bases
bases_changed[1] <- "G"
table(bases_changed)
table(bases)
[1] selects the first element. Inspect both objects after the change.

Inspect bases and bases_changed to distinguish the original and modified values. Ask which operation would save the changed string to a file.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: A fraction needs a stated numerator and denominator
text:
A fraction needs a stated numerator and denominator



GC fraction rises from 0.450 to 0.475 after the stated one-letter replacement.


GC fraction here = letters labelled G or C / all letters.

The original numerator is 18 and denominator 40; afterwards 19 and 40. This is a supplied definition with no molecular-biology prerequisite. In R, comparison with G or C uses a logical OR. It does not identify a gene, organism, or biological property beyond the count that has been defined.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Save a string, then verify the saved representation
text:
Save a string, then verify the saved representation
writeLines(paste(bases_changed, collapse = ""),
           "output/changed-dna.txt")
changed_from_disk <- readLines("output/changed-dna.txt")
nchar(changed_from_disk)
The new saved string still has 40 characters.

paste with collapse joins elements into one string without a separator. writeLines saves that text. Reading it back checks the saved file, not only the current object. The new filename protects the supplied raw sequence. These lines are given operations to understand and adapt, not a new programming API survey.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Same positions, different brightness
text:
Same positions, different brightness



Original grayscale intensities 25/210 become 55/240 after adding thirty, using the same display scale.


A changed threshold answer need not mean a larger biological object.

The plot scale is fixed at zero to 255 in both panels. This makes the brightness change interpretable. Every matrix position stayed the same; adding thirty changed the numerical values. For this controlled example no value exceeds 255. Real acquisition and biological interpretation require more context.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Show the response to the stated threshold
text:
Show the response to the stated threshold



Counts for the original image change from 64 to 24 to zero as a strict intensity threshold crosses the two stored levels.


A threshold is a comparison rule, not a discovered biological boundary.

For thresholds 0, 25, 100, 209, 210, 255 the counts are 64, 24, 24, 24, 0, 0. Only the values 25 and 210 occur, so the response is unusually simple. The plot shows a rule applied to known values; it is not a fitted model and does not validate a segmentation method for real microscopy.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Equality changes the selection
text:
Equality changes the selection
sum(pixels > 210)   # 0
sum(pixels >= 210)  # 24
sum(pixels > 220)   # 0
sum((pixels + 30) > 220)  # 24
Read the operator and the object before interpreting the number.

These are not inconsistent results. Strictly greater excludes equality; greater-or-equal includes it. Adding thirty changes the input while the threshold 220 stays fixed. These are the same logical distinctions used in row filtering, now applied to a rectangular collection of intensities.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Reorganising information differs from renaming a file
text:
Reorganising information differs from renaming a file



The text string ACGT is one line, while a CSV stores four position-and-base rows.


A new arrangement needs new delimiters and a header, not just a new suffix.

The practical asks students to create the tiny four-row CSV themselves and read it back. It is a format exercise, not sequence analysis. Merely renaming bases.txt to bases.csv cannot insert a table structure that was never present. Ask what one row represents in each version.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Explain the operation in a short report
text:
Explain the operation in a short report
Use two figures, the threshold table, and an interpretation.
Name the original object, controlled change, observed result, and limit.

The independent task is representation-report.Rmd, rendered from its own saved code. A reader should be able to distinguish pixel brightness from physical area and label counts from sequence function. The required short conclusions matter more than another elaborate plotting layer.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Exercises: explain the representation
text:
Exercises: explain the representation
Open exercises · Quiz.

Save representations.R, controlled copies, and the threshold table.
Render representation-report.Rmd with two figures and interpretation.
Explain the difference between one text string and a four-row CSV.
Keep original files intact and rerun from a fresh session.


Ask students to predict controlled changes, interpret the result, and test the saved report using the supplied operations.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Your screen may contain hidden prerequisites
text:
Your screen may contain hidden prerequisites



An interactive R object does not automatically become part of a saved report.


“It works on my screen” is a starting observation, not a reproduction check.

An imported object can remain in interactive memory while its import is missing from the report. Put the needed imports and calculations in the saved source.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Source and result have different jobs
text:
Source and result have different jobs



Input data and R Markdown source produce an HTML result.


HTML is readable. .Rmd plus inputs makes the analysis repeatable.

An HTML output does not by itself supply the original analysis recipe. Ask students which file they would edit when new measurements arrive and which they would send for someone simply to read.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Restart, then render from saved files
text:
Restart, then render from saved files

Save the source .Rmd.
Restart R.
Knit without manually recreating console objects first.
Read the first meaningful error and named chunk, if rendering stops.

Keep software installation separate from every report render.

The source should load its packages, import input files, and create all its objects. Restarting does not delete saved data files. If students use a Console render command, it belongs outside the report: a report must not render itself.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: A recipient needs the whole small project
text:
A recipient needs the whole small project



The share folder includes a project file, report source, data and dictionary, output, and README.


Use the selected study’s source and CSV; the .Rproj does not contain them.

For duckweed use duckweed-report.Rmd and data/duckweed.csv. For the organic alternative use organic-study.Rmd and data/organic-recovery.csv. Include the dictionary and required output directory. A shortcut to the author’s files is not a transferred dataset.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Copies do not update themselves
text:
Copies do not update themselves



Windows and Ubuntu hold separately copied folders; edits must be recopied before packaging.


Revised source → recopy → repackage → test the returned ZIP.

This is especially important for Windows students using Ubuntu shell tools but native RStudio. After making a ZIP in Ubuntu, copy it back to a normal Windows folder for extraction and the native application test. Check that it contains the revised source and relative input paths.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Test in a different location
text:
Test in a different location



A complete project is zipped and extracted into a fresh location before rendering.


Open its .Rproj, restart, and render the source without repairing it first.

A fresh folder on the same laptop checks portability within that software environment. Keeping the relative data/ path tests independence from the original project location.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Diagnose one dependency at a time
text:
Diagnose one dependency at a time







Symptom
First check




Object not found
Was it created inside the report, before use?


Function unavailable
Is its package loaded in setup?


Cannot open data
Which computer, project, and relative path?


Export directory missing
Include or explicitly create the destination.




Ask students to reproduce the exact failure before changing multiple things. The error identifies a question to investigate; it does not always identify the full cause. Credentials never belong in an error log or screenshot.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Review meaning as well as execution
text:
Review meaning as well as execution

What is the question and independent unit?
Are axes, counts, units, and comparison direction clear?
Does the prose agree with the actual results?
Are missing data and limitations explained?

The organic alternative uses descriptive means and SDs.

A successful render can reproduce a mistaken analysis. Ask the reader to locate evidence for the conclusions, not just confirm that an HTML file exists.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: A successful rerun is a bounded claim
text:
A successful rerun is a bounded claim
It establishes that the supplied source and inputs regenerate the result in the tested environment.
It does not establish:

Correct biological design or interpretation.
Compatibility with every future software version.
Protection against losing the only storage device.


Distinguish reproduction, scientific validity, and backup. Use sessionInfo when investigating software-version differences, without expecting beginners to interpret every field. A ZIP beside the original is not a separate backup.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Two checks, not one badge of correctness
text:
Two checks, not one badge of correctness



Execution success and supported interpretation are separate dimensions, with successful-but-misleading work possible.


A reproducible mistake is still a mistake.

Ask which check software can perform directly. It can report missing inputs or unavailable functions; it cannot automatically know that a scientific conclusion is warranted. The controlled exercise separates execution failures from false or unsupported prose in a document that renders successfully.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Investigate one controlled change at a time
text:
Investigate one controlled change at a time
Use a disposable copy:

Run the working reference version.
Change one known item and predict its effect.
Observe the error or inconsistency.
Restore, rerun, and compare the key result.


Preserve the original project. Students record the changed item, expected and actual consequence, repair, and confirming rerun. Changing several things at once makes diagnosis harder and can conceal which correction mattered. This is practical error recovery, not deliberate damage to raw measurements.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: A copied input with another name is unavailable to this path
text:
A copied input with another name is unavailable to this path



The report requests data/algae.csv while the received file has a different name.


Repair the copied filename or documented path; verify the rerun.

Use the current main report’s actual input in the exercise, not necessarily algae. Temporarily renaming it in a disposable project should cause a file error. Restore the exact name and confirm the original counts and main result. The absence of an error alone is not enough evidence of a correct repair.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Match the repair to the problem
text:
Match the repair to the problem
A missing file, a missing measurement, and an unknown R object are different.

Restore the required input file/path.
Preserve an unavailable measurement as NA.
Create an object through the saved import/calculation.


These problems need different actions. A copied input renamed for an experiment has not become a dataset of zeros. A missing observation does not justify removing all objects or installing packages. Ask the learner to classify the problem before choosing a repair.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Wrong prose can render successfully
text:
Wrong prose can render successfully



A false sentence in report source becomes the same false sentence in an HTML output despite a successful render.


Read the claims against the counts, plot, and assumptions.

In the controlled exercise, the false duckweed sentence says all enrolled samples had outcomes; the organic sentence says yield independently establishes purity. Both can render. Students must rewrite the claim and check they did not accidentally share an intentionally misleading diagnostic version.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Fresh memory and fresh location test different dependencies
text:
Fresh memory and fresh location test different dependencies



Restarting R checks hidden objects; moving a complete project checks paths and included files.


Use both tests when handing work to another person.

Restarting in the original folder may leave a personal file path accessible. Moving a project while retaining interactive objects may conceal a missing import. A fresh session in a new extracted folder tests both problems together, within the particular software environment being used.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: A source edit does not update an old HTML
text:
A source edit does not update an old HTML



A revised source file and old HTML remain inconsistent until the render is run again.


Locate and open the newly generated output after rerunning.

The file manager, editor, and browser may each display a different stage of work. Ask the learner to state which artifact they inspected. A browser tab with a familiar title is not a version check. Reopen the known output file rather than accumulating copies named final2 without tracing them.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Use the fresh culture memo for a small portable report
text:
Use the fresh culture memo for a small portable report
algae-brief.Rmd needs:

Its own imports and calculations.
Input and design, available counts, and one observation plot.
A short interpretation and missingness account.
A README for the recipient.


This transfers the already completed algae script and memo; it is not a new full project or statistical method. Save source in the project root so data/ paths remain consistent. Include actual inputs rather than shortcuts to the original project. The required available counts remain 12 and 11.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Compare numerical results with sensible precision
text:
Compare numerical results with sensible precision
33.91818 mg and 33.92 mg can be the same result at different precision.
33.91818 mg and 34.32 mg require investigation.
Check input, exclusions, outcome, and calculation before blaming rounding.

A comparison should include counts and definitions as well as printed digits. Rounding affects display, not the intended underlying calculation. Environment records such as sessionInfo can help diagnosis, but do not replace the source, input data, or an explanation of a changed exclusion rule.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Keep the failure investigation useful
text:
Keep the failure investigation useful
Record what changed, what you predicted, what happened, and what confirmed repair.
Share the corrected source, not an unresolved test case.

Keep a case log and give revised packages clear names. Revisit a diagnostic case after another exercise and follow the written procedure to expose any undocumented steps.

title: Reproduce the saved analysis
section: Exercises: keep a reproduction log
text:
Exercises: keep a reproduction log
Open exercises · Quiz.

Test the chosen main-study package and the brief algae-share package.
Record destination, first error, fix, and rerun outcome.
Retain source, input, HTML, and a supported backup copy.
Keep a controlled-failure log distinguishing execution from interpretation.

Use the study you chose yesterday.

Feedback should identify actions another person can reproduce. Keep this as formative practice, not a report-grading exercise. A fresh render is the endpoint.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: About this lecture
text:
About this lecture
Did a treatment make seedlings grow more? The measurements are in a file. Before we can analyse anything, we need that file on our own computer, and we need to be able to find it again.
Today you will:

download the course files and unpack them into a folder you choose;
find and open the seedling measurements;
save a note, close everything, and open the note again.

No programming today. Every later day starts from files you can find.

Keep the opening concrete. The biology question motivates the course; today’s job is getting the data onto the laptop and being sure where it is. Many students have only used files through “recent” lists or cloud apps, so finding a file by its folder is a real skill, not a formality.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: What goes wrong without these habits
text:
What goes wrong without these habits
Situations that are common in student lab work:







What happened
What it cost




The instrument export was “somewhere in Downloads” and was later cleaned away
The measurements had to be repeated


Values were corrected by typing over the original spreadsheet
Nobody could check what the instrument actually recorded


A report was rebuilt from results (2).csv, an older copy
The figure and the text disagreed


A table was sent as a screenshot
The receiver had to retype every number


report.docx was renamed report.pdf
The file no longer opened; nothing had been converted



Each row is fixed by one habit from today. None of them needs programming.

Ask the room whether any of these has happened to them, or to a group partner. These are ordinary, not careless-student stories: modern operating systems hide extensions, show “recent files” instead of folders, and autosave to places that are hard to find. The point of the slide is motivation: the cost of not knowing where a file is shows up as repeated lab work or as a report nobody can check. Come back to this table at the end; each row maps to one summary line.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Today’s data: one row per seedling
text:
Today’s data: one row per seedling


Our (simulated) study: 24 seedlings, each in its own pot. 12 treated, 12 control, assigned at random. Each plant was measured at the start and the end.
The file data/seedlings.csv stores this as a table:

The header names the fields: plant_id, treatment, initial_mm, final_mm.
Each record (row) describes one plant.
P01 grew from 25.7 mm to 44.3 mm — an increase of 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm, not 44.3 mm.

Units and meanings come from the data dictionary, not from the commas.




The header labels fields while a record describes one plant.




Introduce the dataset we will use for weeks: a randomised treatment/control comparison of seedling growth. Read P01’s row aloud field by field and give the units from the dictionary. Work the subtraction: 44.3 minus 25.7 is 18.6 mm. Stress that the computer cannot infer the study design, the units, or which column is the outcome from the comma characters; that knowledge lives in the dictionary and in your notes. A control is a comparison group that shows what might have happened without treatment.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: From download to a folder you can find again
text:
From download to a folder you can find again



Download the course ZIP with the browser.
Show it in the file manager (File Explorer or Finder) — note the folder, usually Downloads.
Extract the whole archive, then move the extracted folder to Documents.
Open files from the extracted folder, not from a preview inside the ZIP.
Find data/seedlings.csv by opening folders, not via “recent files”.

A download that you cannot locate afterwards is not yet usable data.




The project contains data, output, and reports folders; seedlings.csv is inside data.




Demonstrate on the supported operating system and pause after locating Downloads so everyone has caught up. Windows Extract All and Mac double-click can create an extra parent folder; check what is directly inside the folder you will work in: data, output, reports, report.Rmd, introcomputing.Rproj. “Recent files” is convenient but hides the location, and location is exactly what tomorrow’s lesson on paths depends on. If someone has a cloud-managed Documents folder, check the files are really on the laptop.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Keep the raw data untouched
text:
Keep the raw data untouched



The original file is your evidence: it is what the instrument or the notebook recorded.
Copy data/seedlings.csv to output/seedlings-practice.csv and edit only the copy.
Two locations, two names: you always know which file is the source.
If an analysis goes wrong, you can start again from the original. If the original is changed, you cannot.





Copying the raw CSV into output creates a separate practice file while retaining the original.




Demonstrate the copy in the file manager. The scientific reason matters more than the computing one: a reviewer, supervisor, or you in six months must be able to see what was actually measured. Corrections are made later in a traceable way (week 3 covers this), never by typing over the source. Our supplied data are simulated, but practise the habit as if they were your own thesis data.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Saved means: close everything, then reopen
text:
Saved means: close everything, then reopen



Write a sentence in a plain-text editor.
Save as day01-notes.txt inside reports/.
Close the editor and the file manager.
Navigate back through the folders and reopen it.

Editors may autosave or restore drafts. The only reliable test is the saved file: you can state its folder and full name, and it opens from there.




An edited note is saved to disk and then reopened from its folder.




Use a plain-text editor, not a word processor. If the editor appends .txt automatically, check the final name rather than producing a doubled extension. Some editors restore unsaved text when reopened, which can make students think something is saved when it is not; ask what is in the actual file. Have each student say out loud the computer, folder, and full name of their note.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Worked example: receiving a new table
text:
Worked example: receiving a new table
A second class sends seedlings-transfer.csv (18 plants). Before using it, write a short receipt note:







Question
Answer for this file




Where is the original, and where is my copy?
data/seedlings-transfer.csv; copy in output/


What does one row record?
One plant: ID, treatment, initial and final length


Units?
mm (from the dictionary)


A check of one record
T01: 25.3 → 40.3 mm, change 15.0 mm


How do I find it again?
Folder path and full filename, written in the note



The same five questions apply to any file you receive from an instrument, a lab partner, or a supervisor.

This is the independent transfer task in miniature: new data, same habits. T18 is a treated plant, 21.6 to 43.0 mm. The receipt is deliberately not about R; it is about knowing what you have and where it is. In later courses, replace “second class” with “the plate reader” or “my supervisor’s spreadsheet” and the questions are unchanged.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Summary
text:
Summary

A file is saved in a folder. Programs only open and show it.
The full filename includes its ending, such as .csv.
Keep the original data unchanged; work on a copy.
Saved means you can close everything and open it again from its folder.

Next (Day 2): writing down where a file is, as a path.
Now: open the Day 1 exercises. Leave with reports/day01-notes.txt and output/seedlings-practice.csv, and be able to find both after closing every window.

The exercises give the detailed click sequence and hints. A student who cannot yet find their files again needs help before Day 2, because paths build directly on this.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: About this lecture
text:
About this lecture
On Day 16 the treated seedlings grew 6.22 mm more on average than the controls. But a second experiment with 24 new seedlings would give a different number. How much should we trust 6.22 mm? Almost every results section you will read or write answers this with three numbers: an estimate, a 95% confidence interval, and a p-value.

The estimate is the observed treated-minus-control difference in means, with units and a direction.
The confidence interval is a range of population differences compatible with the data, under the model.
The p-value asks how surprising the data would be if the true means were equal.
Welch’s test (t.test in R) produces all three for two independent groups, without assuming equal spread.

This is a reading and writing day: we do not derive the t formula. We learn to run the test, read every number, and write a result sentence that is correct.

Motivate from the reader’s side: students will meet “mean difference 6.2 mm (95% CI 2.7 to 9.7; p = 0.002)” in every paper and every lab report they mark or write. The aim today is that they can produce that sentence from R and explain each part, including what it does not mean. Continuity: Day 16 set up the comparison and the direction; today adds uncertainty. Day 18 changes the design to paired measurements.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: The problem: groups overlap
text:
The problem: groups overlap



Treated mean 21.49 mm, control mean 15.28 mm, 12 plants each.
Difference: 6.22 mm (treated − control).
But the dots overlap: several control plants grew more than several treated plants.
Plants vary. A different random set of 24 would give a different difference.

Question: is 6.22 mm a stable feature of the treatment, or could chance variation between plants produce a gap like this?




The two seedling groups overlap despite a higher treated mean.




Use the figure saved in comparison.Rmd on Day 16. Point at an individual control plant above the treated mean. The inferential question concerns the population mean difference under the study’s conditions, not whether every treated plant beats every control. This is the motivation for the whole day: a difference observed in one sample is a starting point, not a conclusion.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Check the design before any test
text:
Check the design before any test
Welch’s test fits this study because:

Independent units: each plant is its own unit, randomly allocated to a group.
One value per plant: growth = final − initial, computed once.
Unequal spread is allowed: treated SD 4.87 mm vs control SD 3.19 mm is fine for Welch.

A test cannot repair the design:

Repeated readings of the same plant are not extra plants (Day 14).
Before/after on the same plant needs a paired analysis (Day 18).
In very small samples, look at the dots for strong skew or a single dominating value; keep genuine unusual values and ask for advice if the simple model looks unsuitable.


State the assumptions in biological terms, not as a ritual. Welch’s version does not assume equal population variances, which is why it is the default in R. It does assume independence, and nothing in the output will warn you if that is violated. Random allocation is what lets us interpret a difference as a treatment effect within these conditions.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Reading the output
text:
Reading the output









R prints
Value
Units
Meaning




mean of x, mean of y
21.49, 15.28
mm
Group means (treated, control)


difference of means
6.22
mm
The estimate, treated − control


95 percent confidence interval
2.70 to 9.73
mm
Uncertainty in the mean difference


t
3.70
none
Estimate divided by its standard error


df
19.0
none
Welch’s approximate degrees of freedom


p-value
0.0015
none
See the next slides




Sample sizes are not printed: get them from your data (12 and 12).
The interval and estimate carry mm; t, df and p have no unit.


Ask students to annotate their own printout with exactly these four columns: quantity, value, units, meaning. The difference of means is not printed directly; it is the subtraction of the two printed means. Do not spend time on the t formula; the important skill is knowing which number answers which question and which carry units.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: The estimate and its confidence interval
text:
The estimate and its confidence interval

The estimate 6.22 mm and 95 percent confidence interval 2.70–9.73 mm are shown against zero difference.
Estimate 6.22 mm; 95% CI 2.70 to 9.73 mm.
Zero marks “no difference between population means”. This interval lies entirely above zero.
The interval is about the mean difference, not about individual plants: it does not contain 95% of plants.


Units and sign matter. Read the interval as: population mean differences from about 2.7 to 9.7 mm are compatible with these data under the model. Values near zero are not well supported; neither are differences of 15 mm. Students often read every interval as a spread of individuals; the next two slides separate those ideas.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: What “95%” refers to
text:
What “95%” refers to



Imagine repeating the whole experiment many times, each time computing a new interval.
The true difference is fixed. The intervals move from study to study.
A 95% procedure covers the truth in about 95% of repeats — under its assumptions.
We do not know whether our one interval is one of the hits.





Illustrative repeated studies produce intervals around separate estimates; the true difference is fixed.




This is a conceptual illustration, not additional seedling experiments. Some intervals miss the fixed truth; that is part of what 95% means. The probability statement is about the procedure, not about this particular interval. Avoid “there is a 95% probability the true value is in this interval” — under this frequentist framework the truth is fixed and either inside or not.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: What the p-value conditions on
text:
What the p-value conditions on


Definition: if the two population means were equal (and the assumptions held), how often would a statistic be at least this extreme, in either direction?

Here p ≈ 0.0015: rarely.
The shaded tails lie beyond the observed |t| = 3.70.

It is not:

the probability that the null hypothesis is true;
the probability that the treatment works;
a measure of how large the effect is.





The Welch equal-means reference distribution shades both tails beyond the observed statistic magnitude.




The reference curve uses the actual Welch statistic and approximate degrees of freedom. It is not a distribution of possible treatment effects. The key phrase is “if the means were equal”: the p-value is computed under that model. Two-sided means both tails count. A large biological effect and a tiny one can both give small p-values with enough data, which is why the estimate and interval must be reported too.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Direction is a choice; reversing it flips the interval
text:
Direction is a choice; reversing it flips the interval


reverse <- t.test(control, treated)
comparison$conf.int   #  2.70   9.73
reverse$conf.int      # -9.73  -2.70
comparison$p.value    #  0.0015
reverse$p.value       #  0.0015

Same data, opposite sign: control − treated.
The two-sided p-value is unchanged.
Keep the direction you stated in advance as the reported result; save the check in a separate object.





The same comparison in opposite directions produces reflected confidence intervals.




This is not a new experiment, only the same contrast described in the other direction. The function’s argument order determines the sign, not an object name such as treatment_effect. Using a separate object keeps the primary result intact in the report.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: What makes an interval wider or narrower?
text:
What makes an interval wider or narrower?





The 90%, 95%, and 99% intervals use identical observations but different widths.


Confidence level: 90% → 3.31 to 9.12; 99% → 1.41 to 11.02 mm. More coverage requires a wider interval. Keep 95% as the stated analysis.




Main and transfer study intervals differ in estimate and width while also having different spreads and sample sizes.


Data: width depends on sample size and spread together. The transfer study (9 per group) has a narrower interval than the main study (12 per group) because its plants vary less.


Changing conf.level does not change the observed means; it changes how wide the procedure must be to achieve its long-run coverage. On the right, do not teach “bigger n always gives a narrower interval” when spread also differs: transfer SDs are about 1.9 and 2.5 mm against 4.9 and 3.2 mm in the main study.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: When the interval includes zero
text:
When the interval includes zero

An illustrative 2 mm difference has a 95% interval from −1 to 5 mm, covering zero and both directions.
Illustrative small study: estimate 2 mm, 95% CI −1 to 5 mm.
Both a small harmful and a moderate helpful effect remain compatible with the data.
Including zero is not proof of no effect. “Not significant” means inconclusive here, not equal.


These are illustrative numbers, not output from the course data. Ask students what positive and negative differences remain inside the range. A common error in student reports is writing “the treatment had no effect” from p > 0.05; the honest statement is that this study could not determine the direction.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Write a result, not a threshold label
text:
Write a result, not a threshold label
Good: “Treated seedlings grew on average 6.22 mm more than controls (95% CI 2.70 to 9.73 mm; Welch two-sided test, p ≈ 0.0015; 12 plants per group).”
Then one sentence on biological size and one on design limits.







Misreading
Better




“The null hypothesis has probability 0.0015.”
Under equal means and the assumptions, a statistic this extreme is rare.


“The result is significant.” (alone)
Give estimate, units, interval and p.


“p is small, so the effect is large.”
Size comes from the estimate and interval, not from p.


“p > 0.05, so there is no difference.”
The data are inconclusive about direction.




Random allocation supports a causal comparison within these study conditions, but p alone never establishes causality or generalisation beyond them. Encourage a sentence on biological relevance: is 6 mm over a week a lot for a seedling of about 20 mm? Precision of wording is part of the analysis, not editing afterwards.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Worked example: a second class’s study
text:
Worked example: a second class’s study
transfer <- read_csv("data/seedlings-transfer.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
new_treated <- transfer |> filter(treatment == "treated") |> pull(growth_mm)
new_control <- transfer |> filter(treatment == "control") |> pull(growth_mm)
transfer_test <- t.test(new_treated, new_control)
transfer_test



Quantity
Value




Plants per group
9 and 9


Estimate (treated − control)
4.21 mm


95% CI
1.95 to 6.47 mm


Welch p-value
0.0012



“Treated seedlings grew 4.21 mm more on average (95% CI 1.95–6.47 mm; Welch, p ≈ 0.0012; 9 per group).”

Use transfer from its own saved import and growth calculation in transfer-comparison.Rmd, not leftover console objects. Have students write the result sentence before showing the last line. Point out the estimate is smaller than the main study’s, yet the interval is narrower: less plant-to-plant variation.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Summary
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Estimate
Treated − control difference of means, in mm; direction set by argument order


Welch’s test
Two independent groups; spreads may differ; t.test(x, y)


Design first
Independence and one value per unit; a test cannot repair design


95% CI
Range of mean differences compatible with the data; procedure covers the truth in ~95% of repeats


CI vs SD
CI is uncertainty in the mean difference, not spread of plants


p-value
How extreme the data would be if means were equal — not P(null), not effect size


CI includes 0
Inconclusive about direction, not proof of equality


Reporting
Estimate + units + CI + test + p + n, then size and limits in words



Next (Day 18, paired observations): when each plant is measured twice, the two readings are not independent, and the analysis must keep each pair together.
Now: open the Day 17 exercises. Add the method, estimate, interval, sample sizes and p-value to comparison.Rmd, keep the individual-point plot, restart R, and render.

Recite the result sentence once more as the model answer. The exercises extend comparison.Rmd and transfer-comparison.Rmd; the rendered HTML should be understandable without R’s printout. Students should check direction and units in the rendered output, not only in the console.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: The data: one row per seedling
text:
The data: one row per seedling



The header labels fields while a record describes one plant.



24 seedlings: 12 treated, 12 controls. Each was measured at the start and at the end (mm).
P01 grew from 25.7 mm to 44.3 mm, so it grew 18.6 mm.


These are simulated teaching data. Read P01’s row aloud: plant ID, group, initial length, final length. The units come from the data dictionary in the data folder; the file itself only contains commas and numbers.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Download and unpack the course files
text:
Download and unpack the course files



Download the course ZIP.
Show it in File Explorer (Windows) or Finder (Mac).
Extract the whole ZIP.
Move the extracted folder to Documents.
Open data, then seedlings.csv.

Open files from the extracted folder, not from inside the ZIP.




The project contains data, output, and reports folders; seedlings.csv is inside data.




Demonstrate on the supported system and wait until everyone has found the Downloads folder. Windows “Extract All” and a Mac double-click can create an extra folder level; check that data, output and reports are directly inside the folder you will work in. Find the file by opening folders, not through “recent files”.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Keep the original; work on a copy
text:
Keep the original; work on a copy



Copying the raw CSV into output creates a separate practice file while retaining the original.


Copy data/seedlings.csv to output/seedlings-practice.csv. Change only the copy.

The original is what was measured. If something goes wrong in the copy, start again from the original. Demonstrate the copy in the file manager.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Two similar folders? Pick one
text:
Two similar folders? Pick one



One original can lead to several extracted project folders with similar names.


Downloading or extracting twice gives similar folders. Choose one to work in, and do not delete the other until you know what is in it.

Show a “course-files (1)” example. The working folder is the one with data, output, reports and the .Rproj file directly inside. Students should ask before deleting anything.

title: Find, save, and reopen
section: Check yourself
text:
Check yourself

You close the editor. Is the saved note gone?
You change seedlings-practice.csv. Did data/seedlings.csv change?
You rename a .csv to .txt. Did the numbers change?
You know a file’s name. Do you know which folder it is in?


Answers: 1 no; 2 no, it is a separate copy; 3 no, renaming does not convert; 4 not necessarily, several folders can contain files with the same name. Ask students to check 1 and 2 on their own computers rather than just answering.
